...the mast supports them as they swell with the wind: but once the mast is broken, they fall. So it is with the elevated and proud person; as long as such pride supports them, they swell with importance. But once that pride is silenced, they become base. **CRUEL BEAST.** Avarice is called a "cruel beast" because it is alienated from all humanity, harming both itself and its neighbor; and it is truly cruel for this very reason. <note>This commentary, likely by Cristoforo Landino, uses the metaphor of a ship's sail to describe how pride inflates a person before their inevitable fall.</note>

->CANTO SEVEN. 50<-

[Left Column]

Thus we descended into the fourth hollow, <term>laccha</term> <note>original: "laccha"; a Tuscan term for a pit, ditch, or the cavity of a hillside.</note> taking in more of the sorrowful bank that sacks up all the evil of the universe. Ah, Justice of God! Who heaps up so many new labors and pains as those I saw? And why does our guilt so waste us away? Like the wave there above Charybdis, <note>A famous whirlpool in the Strait of Messina from Greek mythology, paired with the monster Scylla.</note> which breaks against the wave it encounters, so must the people here perform their "round dance." Here I saw more people than elsewhere, both on one side and the other, with great howls, rolling weights by the force of their chests. They struck against each other, and then right there, each turned back, rolling his weight in reverse, crying out: "Why do you hoard?" and "Why do you squander?" <note>These two cries represent the two extremes of financial sin: Avarice (hoarding) and Prodigality (wasteful spending). The sinners are forced to crash into each other eternally.</note> Thus they ran through the dark circle from every side...

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the Aristotelian "Golden Mean" applied to the sins of Avarice (greed) and Prodigality (wastefulness), likely from a commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto VII.</meta>

# INFERNO.

...because everyone leaves it <note>Referring to the "middle way" or virtuous mean</note> and they arrive at the opposite point where the excesses lie. But one goes to the right and the other to the left; for the prodigal departs from the middle way by giving more than generosity <note>original: "liberalita," the Aristotelian virtue of the proper use of wealth</note> requires and reaches the extreme, which is excess. The miser departs by not giving what is appropriate and reaches the other extreme, which is deficiency. Therefore, it is in the middle ground alone that virtue consists. 

Thus Horace says: *There is a measure in things, there are certain fixed limits, beyond or short of which virtue cannot find its place.* <note>original: "Est modus in rebus sunt certi denique fines: Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere virtus." (Horace, Satires 1.1.106–107)</note> From this middle point, the miser and the prodigal depart, and they travel toward different extremes by different paths. 

The poet <note>Dante Alighieri</note> imagines that these souls push heavy stones with their chests. In the chest resides the heart, and within it are the worries and thoughts which, for the miser, are constantly burdensome. His heart is never at rest. Instead, he is continually rolling some ponderous stone—that is, he revolves some laborious thought in his mind. 

Hence Horace says: *You see what you believe to be the greatest evils are small...* <note>original: "Vides quae maxima credis esse mala exiguum"</note>

<summary>This passage explains the symbolic punishment of the greedy and the wasteful in Hell, using Horace's poetry to illustrate the Greek philosophical concept that virtue is the middle point between two extremes.</summary>
<keywords>Dante, Inferno, Avarice, Prodigality, Horace, Golden Mean, Aristotelian ethics, symbolism of the stone</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Fourth Circle of Hell, where the Prodigal and the Avaricious are punished. Landino is explaining the symbolic significance of their movements and why Dante specifically targets the clergy in this passage.</meta>

->### CANTO SEVEN. 51<-

...said **liberality**. But they sinned either in "too much"—from which they became **prodigals**—or in "too little," and were **avaricious**. And this is clearly demonstrated by their voices when they come to the two points of the circle where they meet, and where they say: *Why do you hold?* and *Why do you squander?* And he said they **bark**, <note>original: "abbaia"</note> comparing them to dogs because they bite one another with words. Or perhaps he says "bark" as if to say they speak in vain, because any reproof given there is worth nothing, as Hell is no place for penitence. Similarly, in "moral hell," there is no redemption once a habit has been contracted into vice. **WHERE Contrary guilt**—that is, prodigality and avarice, which are opposing vices—**PARTED THEM**, meaning it separates them, because each of the groups returns backward through its half-circle until it reaches the other point. 

Then he responds to Dante’s question and affirms that all those he sees with the **tonsure** <note>The shaved patch on top of a cleric's head, symbolizing their status.</note> were clerics. He shames the priests in this place for two reasons: first, because they are more entangled in these two vices than all other men—witnessed even without examples from past centuries by the laments of our own Petrarch: *The greedy Babylon,* etc., <note>Petrarch, *Canzoniere* 137. Landino refers to Petrarch's "Babylonian Sonnets" criticizing the Papal court at Avignon.</note> and elsewhere: *May flame from heaven rain upon your tresses.* 

Who has not seen in our own times men—or rather, monsters of men—without letters and without morals, not even fit to be committed the care of a village chapel in the countryside? Yet fortune has elevated them to great dignity. In those positions, they have practiced every extreme of avarice to accumulate infinite treasure through **simony** <note>The illegal buying or selling of church offices or roles.</note> and various types of theft; and afterward, they show the height of prodigality by consuming it in every kind of shameful luxury. In this, <term>Sardanapalus</term> <note>An ancient Assyrian king legendary for his decadent luxury.</note> and <term>Heliogabalus</term> <note>A Roman emperor notorious for his eccentricities and excess.</note> could be considered most continent in comparison to them. 

This is very distressing to any well-ordered mind within the Christian name. Nevertheless, it hurts even more those prelates who are adorned with every kind of learning—a most lucid mirror to all others in life and conduct, most prudent in every action, and most wise in contemplation. Because there is such infamy in their Order, it seems impossible that some part of it does not overflow onto them, however undeservedly. For this reason, as much as a most just indignation drives me against those most luxurious misers, I am equally moved by compassion toward these most innocent ones. But the reverence I bear for such a college makes me silent about what is known to the whole world. 

Therefore, this is the first reason that moved Dante to shame the priests. The second is that the vice is more shameful in them than in the laity, since the **Apostolic** (that is, priestly) Church is founded upon chastity and poverty. Thus Petrarch said: *Once you were not nurtured on feathers in the shade, but naked to the wind and barefoot among the thorns; now you live so that the stench reaches God.* <note>Petrarch, *Canzoniere* 138, describing the early Church's poverty versus contemporary corruption.</note> Furthermore, they are those who have the government of the Christian Republic. For this reason, they are called **clerics**, that is, "the chosen" or "the selected" and "magnates," because <term>cleros</term> <note>Greek term meaning "lot" or "inheritance."</note> signifies "strength," <note>Landino provides an unconventional etymology here; usually, "clergy" refers to being God's portion.</note> and we are called **laity**, that is, "the commoners," because <term>laos</term> signifies "the people." 

They ought, therefore, as administrators, to give the best example of faith. Especially since the shaving of their hair signifies nothing other than having cut away every superfluity and pruned every greed. The circle of hair below the shaved part represents a **crown**, to denote that they are our kings, and it is their office to rule us and direct us onto the good path. The third reason is that there is no cause that should make them greedy to accumulate treasure, as they have neither wives nor children to support. **IN WHOM** (that is, in those) **Avarice uses its excess.** It is as if he says: although every avarice exceeds moderation, either by pulling to itself or by not giving, nevertheless, in prelates, it uses its "super-excess"—that is, it possesses as much excess as can possibly exist within it. **AND I, MASTER...** Dante marvels that among so many prelates he does not recognize a single one. To which Virgil responds:

<meta>This page continues a commentary on Dante Alighieri’s Inferno, specifically Canto VII, where the souls of the Avaricious (the greedy) and the Prodigal (the spendthrifts) are punished. The previous page likely discussed the middle ground of virtue—liberality—and its opposing vices.</meta>

->INFERNO.<-

...parsimony <note>original: "parsimonia"; here used in the sense of a measured, virtuous frugality</note>: which are virtues. Therefore, these two vices have taken the **fair world**—that is, the beautiful world—from these people.

It is as if to say it has taken the happy life away from them: because men would certainly live in the highest happiness if greed and prodigality did not deprive them of all peace and tranquility. For both the prodigal and the miser are always anxious, and eager to seize things: the latter to keep for himself, the former to squander on others. Or, truly, it has taken the **fair world** from them: meaning heaven and the eternal life, in which there is the highest beauty and delight. 

Some explain <term>giving ill and keeping ill</term> <note>These are specific references to Dante's text: "Mal dare e mal tener," describing the sins of the spendthrift and the miser</note> the fair world: that is, worldly goods, which by their nature are beautiful. It "has taken them": that is, it has taken these people away from themselves. For greed and prodigality rob a man of his own self. Therefore, "It has taken them" from themselves and placed them in this <term>scuffle</term> <note>original: "zuffa"; refers to the eternal jousting match where the two groups of sinners crash heavy weights against each other</note>. For just as a sold slave no longer belongs to himself, but to the master who has bought him, so when a man is made a servant to greed, he is no longer in <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, likely continuing with "possession of himself"</note>

<summary>This passage provides a philosophical commentary on Dante's Inferno, explaining how the vices of greed and wasteful spending rob individuals of both earthly peace and the "fair world" of heaven. It uses the metaphor of slavery to describe how person is lost to their own desires.</summary>

--- Page 6 ---
71 ->INFERNO.<- ->CANTO VII<-

This was truly understood by Cicero the Platonist <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator. Landino calls him a "Platonist" because he often synthesized Platonic and Stoic philosophy</note>; the meaning of his *Stoic Paradoxes* <note>original: "paradoxe"</note> is that nothing can be called "mine," "yours," or "another’s" if it can be stolen, pilfered, or lost in any way. The city of Priene had fallen into the hands of enemies under the condition that its citizens were allowed to leave with as much of their property as they could carry. Bias—one of the Seven Sages of Greece and a citizen of that city—was leaving empty-handed. When asked why he carried nothing, he replied that he was indeed carrying everything that was his. A true word, and fitting for such a wise man, because he knew that by carrying the virtues of his soul, he was carrying everything he truly owned. 

Perhaps I have strayed too far from the topic. But I have recounted all this so we may understand that although we have called it "Fortune," and though all fleeting and transitory goods are placed within her recklessness and fury, the soul nevertheless remains free. Without her help and despite her, the soul can become happy—not only in the next life, but in this one. 

But returning to the text: Dante says, "Tell me, Virgil: what is this Fortune who has worldy goods 'within her claws' <note>original: "TRA BRANCHE"</note>?" That is, who has temporal goods in her power—temporal goods, according to the principle: "My kingdom is not of this world" <note>original: "Regnu meu no e de hoc mudo" (John 18:36)</note>.

**AND HE**—meaning Virgil—said to me: **"LISTEN TO ME"**—that is, understand—**"O FOOLISH CREATURES."** We call a food "foolish" <note>In Italian, *sciocca* can mean both "foolish" and "unsalted/tasteless"</note> when it lacks salt. And because we often take "salt" to mean "prudence," we call an imprudent person "foolish." **"HOW GREAT IS THE IGNORANCE THAT HARMS YOU"**—meaning your intellects. And he rightly says "harms," because while the intellect becomes perfect through science and knowledge, it conversely becomes imperfect and "harmed" through ignorance. This ignorance makes us believe that Fortune is placed in the soul just as it is in the body, and that she is a master rather than a servant. 

**"SWALLOW MY JUDGMENT"** <note>Dante uses the word "imbocche," meaning to take into the mouth</note>—that is, receive it. He uses a metaphor of a dog when it takes its prey into its mouth. **"HE WHOSE WISDOM TRANSCENDS EVERYTHING"**—meaning God, whose wisdom advances and surpasses all others and pours itself into everything—**"MADE THE HEAVENS."** As the Psalmist says: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their power" <note>original: "Verbo dei coeli firmati sunt & spiritu oris eius omnis uirtus eor" (Psalm 33:6)</note>. Similarly, He created all other things, but here Dante names the heavens because he intends to show that every turn of fortune is born from their motion. 

**"AND HE GAVE THEM THOSE WHO GUIDE THEM"**—because according to Aristotle, God assigned to each heaven an "Intelligence" <note>In medieval cosmology, these are angelic beings or movers</note> that would move it. This is an opinion the author also follows in a song of his, the beginning of which is: "You who, by understanding, move the third heaven." 

**"SO THAT EVERY PART"** of their power **"SHINES UPON EVERY PART"** of the world fit to receive it. **"SHINES"**—by pouring itself out. But we shall speak more conveniently of this splendor and light in the *Paradiso*, explaining how it exists in God, in the angels, in reason, in the spirit, and in the body. And if you first delight in understanding it all, read in the second book of the *Epistles* of our Marsilio Ficino <note>Ficino (1433–1499) was the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a contemporary of Landino</note>—the most learned of all the Platonists of our age—and you will be satisfied. 

**"DISTRIBUTING EQUALLY"**—because God the giver pours Himself out equally into all creatures, but they receive more or less according to their capacity. **"SIMILARLY FOR WORLDLY SPLENDORS"**—that is, for riches, dignities, and honors—**"HE ORDAINED A GENERAL MINISTER"**—because Divine Providence, which has disposed these worldly goods temporally by means of Fate and Fortune...

<summary>Landino interprets Virgil’s explanation of Fortune, using the story of Bias of Priene to show that virtue is the only true possession, and explaining that God moves the world through celestial intelligences and the "minister" of Fortune.</summary>
<keywords>Fortune, Bias of Priene, Cicero, Marsilio Ficino, Divine Providence, Celestial Intelligences, Stoic Paradoxes, cosmology, virtue</keywords>

->SEVENTH CANTO. 53<-

...poison that kills us. **YOUR wisdom has no power against her**: this carries nearly the same meaning as the verse stating: *Against the defense of human understanding*. <note>This refers to Dante’s *Inferno*, VII.81: "oltre la difension d’i senni umani" (beyond the defense of human wisdom).</note> **IT HAS NO** contrast: meaning it cannot resist, because she <note>Fortune</note> foresees her strikes. Indeed, there have been many who, whether through prophecy or some other form of divination, have foreseen their own downfall, and yet they could not resist it. 

For example, Astyages <note>The last king of the Median Empire (r. 585–550 BCE)</note>, King of the Medes, saw in a dream that a vine grew from his daughter’s womb, and its branches shaded all of Asia. The diviners <term>soothsayers|individuals who interpret dreams and omens to predict the future</term> interpreted this to mean that a son would be born to her who would seize his kingdom. Thus, even though Astyages took many precautions against this—first marrying his daughter in Persia to a man of very low station, and then ordering that the newborn son be abandoned in the forest to wild beasts—nevertheless, Fortune willed that the child, who was Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Empire</note>...

<summary>This page discusses the irresistible nature of Fortune, illustrating how human wisdom and precautions cannot prevent destiny, using the classical example of King Astyages and the rise of Cyrus the Great.</summary>

->**INFERNO.**<-

**When I moved, staying too long is forbidden** <note>original Italian: "quãdo mi moſſi el troppo ſtar ſiuieta"; a quote from Inferno VII, 98</note>—not Anger: and Sloth. <note>The commentator clarifies that the "staying too long" refers to the time spent observing the previous sins before moving toward the wrathful.</note> Here Virgil admonishes Dante to
hurry himself, showing that the night—in which alone they could
be in Hell—had already passed more than halfway. Therefore, as
so much of the path remained to be traveled, and since
more than half the time was already spent, it was necessary to hasten.
NOW let us descend: as if he were to say "we have stayed long enough"; and it
almost intends to imply that Dante was slower in departing than
was fitting. This allegorically demonstrates
that it is a difficult thing for sensuality <term>sensuality: in Renaissance philosophy, the "lower" part of the human soul governed by physical appetites and worldly attachments</term> to leave behind riches and
the goods of Fortune: those who care for and value these things too much
can never rise to true contemplation. For which reason the Truth <note>A common title for Christ or the Gospel in medieval texts</note> said in the Gospel:
**No man can serve two masters, God and Mammon** <note>original Latin: "Nemo poteſt duobus dominis ſeruire deo & mamone"</note>: that is, God and money: because he who is greedy for the treasures of earthly things cannot
elevate his mind to divine things: And [this explains] the difficulty that is placed upon the rich man in entering heaven.

# CANTO SEVENTH 54

...divisible: <note>original: "fibile," the conclusion of the word "indivisibile" (indivisible) from the preceding page.</note> Nevertheless, because it has various powers and various forces, we say it divides itself into such powers and forces: and one we say to be the **vegetative** <note>The most basic level of the soul in Aristotelian philosophy, responsible for life-sustaining functions like nutrition and growth.</note>. Another the **sensitive** <note>The faculty of the soul shared by humans and animals that governs perception, movement, and basic emotion.</note>. Another the **rational** <note>The highest faculty of the soul, unique to humans, which governs reason, logic, and the intellect.</note>. And the sensitive faculty has its senses, which are partly exterior <note>The five physical senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.</note> and partly interior. From the senses proceeds judgment. Because, for instance, when the eye sees that a thing is yellow, the <term>common sense</term> <note>In medieval psychology, the internal faculty that unifies different sensory inputs into a single coherent object.</note> judging it to be sweet causes the <term>cogitative faculty</term> <note>The mental power that compares and evaluates specific sensory perceptions to determine if they are useful or harmful.</note> to conclude that it is good. Therefore, these faculties determine which thing is good and which is the contrary. 

After the senses, there is another power in the soul: which, once the judgment of the senses is understood, rises up to desire that which is already judged to be good, or to flee that which is judged to be evil. This power is called **appetite**: and that which it desires is the <term>concupiscible</term> <note>From the Latin "concupiscibilis"; the aspect of our nature that seeks out pleasure and things that sustain life.</note>. That which it flees is the <term>irascible</term> <note>From the Latin "irascibilis"; the aspect of our nature that resists difficulty or fights against things perceived as harmful.</note>. And just as through the concupiscible we desire that which...

<summary>This page explains the Scholastic breakdown of the soul's faculties, detailing how sensory perception is transformed into judgment and how that judgment triggers the "appetite" to either seek pleasure or avoid harm.</summary>

...by way of <note>original: *per mō* (per modum), a Latin philosophical shorthand for "in the manner of"</note> the nature of their punishment.

<margin>Aristotle's Ethics</margin>
The text describes the "reason why" <note>original: *Ilperche*, transcribed from *Ilpche* with a stroke abbreviation</note> these souls are submerged. Drawing on classical philosophy, it explains that they are **sullen** or **bitter**—those who kept their anger bottled up inside.

As if <note>original: *quasi*</note> their internal rage has become their external environment, they remain in an equal <note>original: *equali*</note> or constant state of misery. This hidden anger "swallows" <note>original: *inghiottisce*</note> the soul from within, just as the marsh now consumes their bodies.

The scene ends as the travelers move along the edge of the swamp:

->Thus we circled the filthy pool<-
->a great arc between the dry bank and the center,<-
->with eyes turned toward those who swallow the mud.<-
->We came to the foot of a tower at last.<- <note>original: *al dazeſſo* (da sezzo), an archaic Italian phrase meaning "at the end" or "finally."</note>

# CANTO EIGHT 95
## EIGHTH CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

[Woodcut initial I]
**I say, continuing, that long**
**before**
**we reached the foot of the high**
**tower,**

**because of two small flames we saw placed there,**

[Woodcut illustration: Dante and Virgil are ferried by Phlegyas across the Styx towards the flaming towers of the city of Dis. In the water, souls are seen suffering.]

**A**lthough the canto changes, it nevertheless still continues in the fifth circle, where the wrathful and the slothful <note>Original: "accidiosi." In the context of the Styx, these are often described as the "sullen" who are submerged beneath the mud because they were gloomy in the light of the sun.</note> are punished. And it shows how, by a signal made from the tower, Phlegyas <note>In Greek mythology, Phlegyas set fire to Apollo’s temple in a rage; Dante casts him as the ferryman of the wrathful across the Styx.</note> came and took them into his boat; and while sailing, they found Filippo Argenti <note>A wealthy Florentine politician known for his hair-trigger temper and for having his horse shod with silver (hence "Argenti"). He was a personal and political enemy of Dante.</note> in the marsh; and finally they arrived at the city of Dis <note>The inner city of Hell, containing the circles of those who sinned through malice rather than just loss of self-control.</note>. I SAY: "Continuing, that long before." We can simply understand that the author, wishing to connect the beginning of this chapter with the end of the preceding one, uses these words.

# INFERNO

I asked what this says and what responds
that other fire, and who are they who made that signal?
And he to me: "Over the filthy waves
already you can discern what awaits,
unless the smoke of the marsh hides it from you."
No bowstring ever shot an arrow from itself
that sped away through the air so swiftly:
as I saw a tiny little boat
coming through the water toward us in that moment
under the guidance of a single pilot:
who shouted, "Now you are caught, wicked soul!"

<note>Dante sees two signal fires on a tower, answered by another far off. This marks the transition to the city of Dis.</note>

For [this part], interpret it in the same way. **THIS** which says: that is, the fire of this tower which intends to signify something. **AND THAT OTHER**: that is, the signal in the other tower that responds. And if you consider this triplet with diligence, you will judge it worthy to be numbered among the most elegant for its marvelous brevity: with which it expresses many things with supreme clarity and no small ornament. And Virgil responds to Dante: "You can already discern over the **filthy waves**" — that is, dark and black — "what awaits." For Virgil already saw the boat in motion. **UNLESS THE SMOKE OF THE MARSH HIDES IT FROM YOU**: This demonstrates that marshy and swampy places are always filled with thick vapors, and these create a mist which impedes the sight.

But allegorically, Virgil — that is, <term>Superior Reason</term><note>In Renaissance philosophy, "Superior Reason" refers to the part of the soul capable of perceiving divine or abstract truths, while "Inferior Reason" deals with worldly matters and emotions.</note> illuminated by doctrine — suddenly discerns the truth. But he doubts that Dante — that is, <term>Inferior Reason</term> — might be impeded by the smoke. For in this [lower part of the soul] is born anger; and because anger is a boiling of the blood, it raises certain thick vapors to the brain, and these impede the senses so that they cannot discern the truth. 

Afterward, he demonstrates the speed of the ship by comparison to a bolt shot from a crossbow. Therefore, no crossbow string ever shot an arrow from itself, which **FAST** — that is, straight and clean — sped away through the air; and he says "fast" because an arrow that is crooked or too thick is not as swift as one that is straight and clean. **AS I SAW A TINY LITTLE BOAT**. By the boat, he represents the movement of the <term>irascible appetite</term><note>The "irascible appetite" is a scholastic term for the part of the soul where anger and the drive to overcome obstacles reside.</note>, and shows it to be under the guidance of one alone. This is to demonstrate that this is the irascible appetite when it is disobedient to reason, and therefore it is a vice. For that which is obedient to reason is not a vice. Thus, [reason] is not at the helm of this ship. And he wrote **Galeoto** <note>The pilot Phlegyas.</note> with one "T" and not with two, although it should be written with two: but this is granted to the poet so that the rhyme corresponds to *voto* <note>original: "voto" (vow)</note> and *aloto*. <note>Dante's original rhyme words in Canto VIII are 'voto', 'nuoto' (swim), and 'galeoto'. The commentator is noting the poetic license taken with spelling to maintain the rhyme scheme.</note>

->CANTO EIGHT. 56<-

...that is from pride <term>Superbia; the root of all sins in medieval theology</term>: because envy wishes for the neighbor's harm so that they do not become equal to us. Anger <term>Ira</term> is born from the love of the neighbor's harm through the desire for vengeance. Therefore, these four vices are similar, because they are deservedly punished together. And certainly, as soon as pride is born in us, envy also awakens: because, desiring a vain name and power, we begin to have envy for others so that they do not match us. And because of this, we lose our gentleness <note>original: "mansuetudine"; the virtue of being mild-tempered or meek</note>, and in its place succeeds anger, which saddens us and leads us into sloth <term>Accidia; a state of spiritual apathy or "dryness" often linked to deep sadness</term>. For which reason we can conclude without error that these four vices are punished in this marsh <note>The marsh of the Styx, where Dante encounters the wrathful and the slothful</note>. And the two towers serve both the ascent and elevation of anger, and the haughtiness of pride, which is twofold: because we become proud of our intrinsic goods <note>Internal qualities like intelligence or talent</note>, attributing everything to our own wisdom and our learning, as well as extrinsic goods <note>External things like wealth or status</note>

<gloss>He said "he wanders": that is, he toils in vain.</gloss> Because the Florentine <note>Dante</note> says he goes wandering about when he makes no progress in his efforts. And to show that it is no wonder they are so bold as to set themselves to defend what they cannot defend, he says it is their <gloss>ancient custom</gloss> to do this. Wherefore the Psalmist said: <note>original: "Tollite portas principes uestras & introibit rex glorie."</note> "Lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of Glory shall enter." This signifies that all laws and sentences given against the disobedience of the first man were broken. **WHICH still remains without bolts:** because from the passion of Christ until now, it can no longer retain the souls of the baptized righteous. **ABOVE IT you saw the dead writing.** He responds to that. "These words of dark color I saw written at the top of a gate." **AND ALREADY on this side of it he descends the slope.** He says that already the Angel sent by God to open the gate has entered the first gate and descends the slope. Every steep place has a "climb" and a "fall": but it is called a "climb" [*erta*] to one who ascends it, and a "slope" [*china*] to one who descends it. Therefore he used "climb" for the "slope" since the Angel was descending, just as Virgil puts the end for the beginning: <note>original: "Oceani fine iuxta:solemque cadentem."</note> "Near the limit of the Ocean and the setting sun." Or truly he said "climb" in relation to himself, who being already below, it seemed a climb to him. **PASSING through the circles without an escort:** because divine power has no need of a guide. **SO THAT by him:** <gloss>that is, through your means</gloss> **the gate of the land shall be opened:** <gloss>that is, of the city.</gloss> And we will explain this allegory better in the following chapter.

[Woodcut illustration: The massive stone and iron walls of the City of Dis are shown. Dante and Virgil stand before the closed gate, while above on the towers, the Furies appear. A celestial figure, the Messenger, is seen approaching across the Stygian marsh to force entry, while the demons atop the walls shrink back.]

**IN** this ninth chapter, he describes Virgil’s counsel regarding the entry into the city; and the infernal monsters that are there; and by whose help they entered; and finally shows with what punishments the heretics are tormented. The subject matter is almost new, and here are horrible sins which deserve no compassion, because they do not arise from the impulses of the flesh—such as disordered love, gluttony, or anger—but from wicked malice and a perverse soul. And although in all vices frequent acts create a habit, nevertheless in the previous ones there was more **incontinence** than **intemperance** <note>Technical Aristotelian terms: 'Incontinence' is doing wrong through passion despite knowing better; 'Intemperance' is choosing evil through a settled, corrupt character.</note>. But in these, one sees a most perverse obstinacy. And because for those who make a habit of these it is almost impossible to withdraw themselves, he therefore places them inside the city girded with iron walls to denote that it is impregnable, as we said above.

But to return to the text: the meaning of the first tercet is that Dante was frightened, and because of this grew pale due to the change he had seen in Virgil's face. And perceiving this, Virgil suppressed his indignation and his perturbation, and cleared his face, returning it to its natural color so that Dante might also lay down his fear. And certainly, every time the rational part of a man becomes dismayed at not being able to achieve something, his **sensuality** <note>In this context, 'sensuality' refers to the physical emotions and bodily reactions.</note> becomes very frightened. And it secretly admonishes that whoever is placed in government and rule over others should often show good courage in small things, so as not to dismay those who are under his governance. Which Virgil attributes to Aeneas when he says: <note>original: "Spem uultu simulat premit altu corde dolore"</note> "He feigns hope in his face, while deep in his heart he suppresses his grief."

And the text is ordered thus: **That color which cowardice**—that is, fear—**painted** outwardly. Understand: on the face. For paleness in the face is nothing but a lack of blood, which through fear flees to the heart and leaves the veins of the face empty. **SEEING my leader turn back.** As if to say, without victory and driven back; for we say an army is "turned back" when, overcome by enemies, it turns its back. **MORE QUICKLY restrained his own new [color] within.** The pale color was "new" in Dante, because fear had made him turn pale. Similarly, the flushed color was "new" in Virgil, for he had been flushed in the face. For since anger is the boiling of blood around the heart, as it boils it runs through all the veins, but appears most in the face, because here there are many subcutaneous veins—that is, so close to the skin that they manifest everything. But...

# INFERNO

Virgil, seeing Dante's <note>The original transcription "Dathe" is a common typographical variant for Dante.</note> fear arise from the change in his own face, pretended to immediately suppress that color. Therefore, that color—which was in me because of fear born from what I saw—more quickly repressed his "new" color, meaning Virgil's. For Virgil removed from his face the new color—that is, the unnatural color—which had newly appeared because of his indignation <term>indignation: Virgil's righteous anger or frustration at the demons' resistance</term> upon seeing that Dante was afraid because of it. And this was said to indicate that the wise man can anticipate and cast off from himself the disturbances of the soul <note>original: "pturbatiõi delaio," likely *perturbationi dell'animo*</note>.

**H**E STOOD ATTENTIVE. It happens that when we wait for someone in a dark place, because the eye is of no use and unable to discern anything, we use our hearing; so that by a clatter or any other noise, we might notice when they arrive. Virgil did the same thing: but allegorically it is understood that when the intellect cannot see the truth by itself, being occupied by the shadows of ignorance, it attentively awaits divine inspiration and help. **AS A MAN** who listens—once the anger ceases—**FOR THE EYE** could not lead him <note>These lines refer to Dante's description of Virgil listening for the arrival of the Heavenly Messenger who will open the gates of Dis.</note>.

It further provides an allegorical reading of "listening in the dark" as the human intellect waiting for divine inspiration when blinded by ignorance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto IX of Dante's Inferno, specifically addressing Virgil’s reassurance to Dante and the arrival at the gates of the City of Dis.</meta>

->CANTO NINTO 06<-

He makes you feel secure about the path alone; and if one were to ask what motive moved Dante: that in wanting to imitate Virgil, he might be contradicting him. He responds that it is not as contradictory as it appears. Virgil speaks when he shows that the Sibyl does not want to lead Aeneas inside this city. **It is not lawful for any pure soul to tread the threshold of the wicked** <note>original: "Nulli fas casto sceleratum insistere limen"</note>. Nor does he mean anything else by saying that it is not permitted for any good person to stop there; except that no one can be good who stays there: that is, who makes a habit of vice. But rather, it was better for the Sibyl to describe the vices to him and keep him outside—that is, to give him knowledge of them without him making a habit of them. And Dante feigns that although Virgil leads him there, he nevertheless does not stay there. This signifies the same thing: namely, entering into the knowledge of vice, but not making a habit of it. And this is more in accordance with the Christian religion, which believes that everyone enters this city: that is, everyone sins in some way. Whence David said, **Every man is a liar** <note>original: "Omnis homo mendax"</note>. And elsewhere: **Seven times a day the righteous man falls** <note>original: "Septies in die cadit iustus"</note>. But they do not—or rather, should not—make a habit of it. **IN THIS** bottom of the wretched shell: in this low part of Hell, which he has described in the shape of a vessel, which begins at the top with a wider circle and narrows the lower it goes. **FROM THE** first level. From the first circle where Limbo is, and where he placed the souls of virtuous men who were without faith, who have this as their punishment: that is, a place of penalty. **CIONCHA**: that is, "lopped off" or "shortened" <term>cionca: a term meaning mutilated or cut short</term>, as he said above: that without hope we live in desire. *Cioncho* is a Lombard word and means lopped and diminished, and so he takes it here. But in Florentine, *cionchare* means to drink immoderately. **I MADE** this question: that is, this inquiry. Because *querere* in Latin means to search and to ask. **IT WAS THAT**. And that Virgil responded, saying: **SELDOM it happens**. It rarely intervenes. "To encounter" means to intervene or to happen upon. **THAT ANY** of us: that is, of us souls, **MAKES** the journey by which I go. He says that although it rarely happens, it does happen sometimes. And allegorically, he shows that few are those who descend into the meditation of vices in order to purge themselves of them. **TRUE IT IS that another time**. He shows that he had been there shortly after his death, conjured by Erichtho. And Dante feigns that Virgil feigns this to comfort him, as we have said. Erichtho was, according to Lucan <margin>Q.</margin> <note>This "Q" likely refers to "Questio" or a specific citation mark in the original manuscript regarding Lucan.</note>, a female sorceress in Thessaly, who at the request of Pompey (son of Pompey the Great) drew a soul from Hell back into its body and made it say what end the civil war between Caesar and Pompey would have. Dante therefore feigns that Virgil holds this of himself for his comfort. And besides this, it fits an ancient opinion that Zoroaster, the inventor of this art <note>The "art" here refers to magic or necromancy</note>, practiced it to have knowledge of the immortality of the soul and its nature and power. And we will speak of the magical arts below when that sin is treated. But as for the present text, it is to be doubted how Dante posits that the soul of Virgil was conjured and constrained, since our religion forbids it; for theologians do not want the magical art to have this power. For this reason, Aurelius Augustine writes that the pythoness <note>The Witch of Endor</note> described in the first book of Kings, who spoke in the person of the prophet Samuel, was not Samuel, but a demon who feigned being Samuel. But the response is that these are not the words of Dante or his own opinion, but those of Virgil, who speaks according to the opinions of the pagan poets, as we see in Homer, Lucan, and others. Furthermore, happening upon the subject, Dante notes in this place the **fourth descent** into Hell established by the ancients. For as we said above, one descends into Hell in the first way when the soul, departing from the body in mortal sin, goes into eternal damnation. In the second way, when still in the body, one descends into the habit of vice. In the third, when still in the body, one descends into the contemplation of vices to purge oneself of them. And according to these first three ways, he always writes through this entire first canticle. He touches upon the fourth in this place—not because he approves of it, but so that he does not omit any. **BUT SHORTLY my flesh was naked of me**: the flesh was naked, that is, deprived of me, Virgil. And he says "of me" most excellently, because although man consists of soul and body, nevertheless, because man is defined by reason and intellect, truly the soul is what is "man," and the body is like a garment to the soul. **INSIDE THAT wall**: which you see is made of iron, to draw out a soul which was in the lowest circle, in which Judas is punished, and from him it is called *Judecca*. **THAT IS** the lowest place. If Hell descends to the center of the earth, and this circle is the lowest, it follows that it is at the center. And because every center is the furthest part from the circumference, it is therefore furthest from the heavens **WHICH ALL** revolve. The heaven which, in revolving, contains everything within itself. **WELL I KNOW the way**. He perceived that Dante feared he did not know the way because he had not been there, and therefore he concludes that he knows it. And perhaps Dante feigns that Virgil feigned having been there to show that, morally, wise men often say what is not true, not to deceive, but to comfort and encourage perseverance in good works for those who are seized by some terror.

*This marsh which breathes out the great stench*
*surrounds the sorrowful city all around,*
*where we cannot enter now without anger.*
*And he said more, but I do not have it in mind*
*because my eye had drawn me entirely*
*toward the high tower with the glowing summit,*
*where in a moment there stood up swiftly*
*three infernal furies stained with blood,*
*who had feminine limbs and gestures,*
*and were girt with the greenest hydras.*

He shows that this Stygian marsh "breathes"—that is, has the breath of—a great stench, because from it rise vapors and mists of foul odor, which is natural to any swamp. But also allegorically, from the sadness of the heart many stenches are born: that is, many vices. **SURROUNDS** all around the city of Dis. **SORROWFUL** because of the various and unbearable torments that are there. And certainly, vices leave behind nothing but repentance and pain. Whence Petrarch excellently said: *Repentance and pain follow behind the shoulders.* **WHERE WE CANNOT**: where we will not be able to **ENTER without anger**: because the adversaries oppose them. Let no one wonder that he shows anger in the place where anger is punished; for here the poet wants to show that there can be anger which is not only not a vice, but is a virtue: because it is a just indignation.

->**INFERNO.**<-

...is truly expressed in Homer through Hercules, and in Virgil through Aeneas. And similarly, the <term>moral good</term> <note>original: "bene honesto," referring to virtue or goods pursued for their own sake rather than for utility or pleasure</note> is represented, provided that the doctrine is certain; but when it is uncertain, as among the <term>Academics</term> <note>Members of the Platonic Academy who, in their later "Skeptical" phase, argued that certain knowledge was impossible</note>, such a descent is symbolized by Amphiaraus. The <term>pleasurable good</term> is represented by Orpheus, and the <term>useful good</term> by Theseus and Pirithous. And in this, he takes Theseus to represent the soul and Pirithous to represent the body; and just as these were the closest of friends, so the soul and the body are joined in the greatest friendship. And he demonstrates <term>reason</term> through Theseus and <term>sensuality</term> through Pirithous—matters certainly worthy of his doctrine and genius.

But because these explanations are lengthy <note>original: "prolisse"</note> and not very pertinent to this section, I will omit them. Let it suffice to say that the demons complain of not having punished Theseus, who dared while still living—that is, through speculation and study—to descend to Hell for the knowledge of the "useful" good. [The narrator] has taken the same daring approach. For if they have not restrained him who descended to Hell for the knowledge of the useful, a thing altogether...

->CANTO NINE. 62<-

It beats down branches, shatters them, and carries them away;
dusty in front, it moves on proudly,
and makes the wild beasts and the shepherds flee.

He came over the praise of the Styx. <note>original: "lode di styge." The commentator notes that the light received from God in this part was for the knowledge of infernal things.</note> **A CRASH** of a sound. That is, such a sound as is usually found in a crash: and we specifically call a "crash" a great sound which proceeds from the ruin and breaking of things: because to "fracture" means to break. **FULL OF TERROR** accords with the theologians; who say that every vision that proceeds from God terrifies at the beginning and reassures at the end. We can also understand that when, through the arrival of divine grace, we enter into the knowledge of the greatest vices: and we recognize what a cruel plague and what a grave danger they are to our soul. From such knowledge, there is born terror and no small consternation of mind: but rather a mind full of horror. **FOR WHICH** both shores tremble: that is, one and the other bank of the marsh. The interpreter from Imola <note>Referencing Benvenuto da Imola, a famous 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> interprets this figure who comes to open the gate as Mercury, the god of eloquence: and he cleverly fits the text to this allegory. But anyone who diligently looks at Dante’s purpose easily knows that it cannot be anything other than the **divine grace** already mentioned above. **NOT OTHERWISE** formed than a wind. He excellently compares the angel, who is incorporeal, to the wind, which is such a thin body that it remains invisible. And beyond this, it demonstrates with what speed divine grace descends to a well-disposed will. **WHICH STRIKES.** Which strikes, that is, hits. **IMPITUOUS** through diverse heats: which takes its impetus from the heats diverse from it, that is, placed against it. Winds are generated from hot and dry vapors: and elevated from the earth up to the region where the clouds exist. And there, struck back by the higher heats, they are pushed sideways: and they strike the air: and the struck part strikes the other: and that one the next, hand to hand: because wind is nothing other than struck air, and the more the heats are adverse, the more the wind is impetuous. There are also certain more impetuous species in a form that can be called almost like lightning, such as the <term>Ecnephia</term> <note>A Greek term for a storm-wind breaking from a cloud.</note>, the <term>Typhon</term>, the <term>Whirlwind</term>, and the <term>Prester</term> <note>A fiery whirlwind or waterspout.</note>. The nature and distinction of these, because it is lengthy, I leave behind.

He released my eyes and said: "Now direct the
nerve of your sight across that ancient foam, 
to where that smoke is most harsh."
As frogs before their enemy 
the snake, all vanish through the water 
until each one huddles on the ground,
I saw more than a thousand destroyed souls 
fleeing thus before one who at a pass 
was crossing the Styx with dry feet.

He has described the impetus of the angel’s arrival. Now he relates how Virgil—who previously, so that Dante would not see Medusa, had closed his eyes—now on the contrary opens them for him: so that he may see the angel. For it is the duty of our intellect to rule the appetite in such a way that it has its eyes closed to every perturbation: and thus open to every divine inspiration. Sensuality is very far from divinity, but the intellect is in that middle ground: and in many things, it rules the senses by itself. And in those things in which it is not sufficient to rule them by itself, it at least disposes the senses to receive that which will rule them by divine grace. **HE RELEASED MY EYES.** Removing his hands and mine for the reason already stated above. **AND SAID DIRECT THE NERVE** of the face: as if waking the visual power, putting "nerve" for the "power." For the bodily forces consist in the nerves: or rather, he said "nerve" because the visual power consists in the cross of the optic nerves which come from the brain to the eyes. **ACROSS THAT ANCIENT FOAM.** If he moved the waters, it was necessary that foam should be born from it. And he says "ancient": not because that foam was old, having been born from a new movement, but ancient: that is, from the ancient marsh. Some say "ancient foam" means white: because all foam is white, just as the Latins say <note>original: "canas pruinas"</note> "hoary frosts," meaning white, because the hair of an old man is white. So Dante said "ancient foam" as if to say "hoary foam": that is, white. But it fits well that he calls the Styx an "ancient marsh": because sadness is ancient in the human generation: since the first man Adam, as soon as he had fallen into sin, fell into sadness and sorrow. The angel did not come flying over the marsh: but came *through* the marsh: although he walked it without wetting his feet. This denotes that such grace was an aid to the knowledge of vices and not of virtues. **WHERE THAT SMOKE IS MOST HARSH**: most vehement and most obscure. For such grace comes not through luminous places: because the intellect sees those by itself: but through the obscure ones which the intellect does not see without it. Or rather, he makes him come through an obscure place: because such grace comes hiddenly, nor is it recognized along the way. **LIKE THE FROGS.** An excellent comparison from frogs, marsh animals, to the souls placed in the mire. And it is a fitting thing to say that the damned souls flee the grace of God: because all those who have made a habit of vice and take pleasure in it make themselves most inept at receiving divine grace: because <note>original: "In animam malevolam non introibit spiritus sapientiae."</note> "Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul" <note>A quote from the Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note>. Therefore, to make oneself unable to receive the grace of God is to flee it. Furthermore, just as the saved are confirmed in an optimal will: so the damned can no longer not be obstinate in sinning. **SNAKE.** A serpent. And it is a figure called <term>onomatopoeia</term>: that is, the fiction of a name: because "biscia" <note>The Italian word for grass snake.</note> is a name created in imitation of that noise the serpent makes when it goes whipping and slithering with velocity. **THEY VANISH.** To vanish <note>original: "dileguare"</note> means to disappear, a word drawn from the Latin <note>original: "deliquesco"</note> which means to melt: because he who vanishes suddenly leaves the eye’s sight, like snow when it melts. **HUDDLES.** <note>original: "sabbica"</note> To accumulate. A "bicca" is a heap in the likeness of what the Latins call a <term>meta</term> <note>A cone or pyramid shape.</note>: which is a round form and, rising little by little, becomes pointed. And in this form, the farmer accumulates sheaves of grain. Whence to "abbissare" is to accumulate. **DESTROYED.** Damned. Because the soul deprived of its "good" can be called undone. **FLEEING BEFORE THE PASS** at the place where the passage was. **WITH DRY FEET.** Because the grace of God, and he who contemplates with it, cannot be wetted in the marsh of...

And he organizes the text thus: I saw more than a thousand souls fleeing before one who crossed the Styx <note>The marshy river of the fifth circle of Hell, where the wrathful and sullen are punished.</note> with dry feet, just as frogs scatter through the water before their enemy, the snake, until they all huddle on the ground.

waving his left hand frequently before him,

CANTO NINTH 63

easy to open it. But if I am not mistaken, it is to be understood in this place that the poet—having proposed to himself to imitate Virgil and the other ancient poets where Christian theology does not forbid it—feigns here the angel sent by God. This is consistent with our religion, but to adorn the passage with poetic fiction, he gives him the wand of Mercury <note>The caduceus, a staff carried by the Roman messenger god Mercury, which had the power to put people to sleep or wake them.</note>. And in this way, he does not simply present him as Mercury—as the commentator from Imola <note>referring to Benvenuto da Imola, one of the earliest and most famous commentators on Dante’s Divine Comedy.</note> suggests—because that would seem like idolatry; nor does he depart entirely from poetic fiction, giving him the wand as if he were Mercury. But here the wand signifies the power which resides in the grace of God for governing and instructing the human soul. Such grace carries the wand, that is, the scepter, to signify that no one can resist His command, and that every diabolical force and fraud yields to it. And that grace opens the door for us to the knowledge of internal things.

# INFERNO.

Within we entered without any struggle;
and I, who had a desire to observe
the condition that such a fortress encloses,
once I was inside, I cast my eyes around:
and I see on every hand a vast plain
full of sorrow and of cruel torment.
Just as at Arles where the Rhone slows <note>original: "Arli oue rhodano ſtagna." Arles is a city in southern France famous for the Alyscamps, a vast Roman necropolis.</note>,

so they did here on every side,

that no craft requires iron to be hotter <note>A reference to the intense heat needed in blacksmithing; the tombs are hotter than any metal in a forge.</note>.
X All their lids were suspended:
* and from them issued such hard laments

<keywords>City of Dis, Heretics, Arles, Pola, Sarcophagi, Virgil, Sixth Circle of Hell</keywords>

--- Page 29 ---
CANTO NINE. 64

to look at what condition—that is, what state and fortune that place had. **AND I TURN MY EYES AROUND.** I circle with my eyes. **AND I SEE a great plain.** A large flatland; and by the great space of the place, it shows a vast **Y** <margin>Y</margin> multitude of sinners. **ARLES** is a city in Provence located at the mouth of the Rhone, not further from Avignon than three leagues. In Latin, it is called *Arelate* <note>original: "Arelate"</note>. And concerning the abundance of sepulchers that are around it, they tell this story: Charlemagne fought in this place with a great number of pagans and achieved a most bloody victory, for many Christians were killed there. And Charlemagne, desiring to recognize the bodies of his own from those of the enemies in order to bury them, found a great abundance of tombs the following morning; and all the Christians had **Z** <margin>Z</margin> their names written on their foreheads. For this reason, they were buried in such tombs. But it is more likely to be believed that ancient custom created such sepulchers. **POLA** is a city at the head of Istria, near the gulf in the Adriatic Sea called Carnaro <note>The Gulf of Kvarner</note>. This is about forty miles wide and is very dangerous because of the South wind, which in that region is likewise called Carnaro. **WHICH CLOSES ITALY**, because here Italy ends, and the shores of the Carnaro are the borders of Italy. Nor do I find a history that narrates the origin of such burials. I believe that through long custom, they have multiplied. **THAT REQUIRES NO MORE IRON** in any art. The sepulchers were so heated that no craftsman ever heats iron more when he wishes to forge something or give it a new shape. Because in this place, heresy is punished. We shall note that <term>heresy</term> <note>The commentator explains the etymology of "heresy" from the Greek *hairesis*, meaning choice.</note> is a Greek word and means "election" or "choice." This is because the heretic departs from common opinion or faith and chooses for himself what he wishes to believe. We shall say, therefore, that heresy is the election of one's own opinion against the determination of the Apostolic Church. And briefly, we shall say that a heretic is anyone who holds an opinion different from the true religion. This cannot happen without supreme arrogance, because he attributes too much to his own wit who deviates from the common opinion of many most learned men. It is, therefore, one of the daughters of pride. There are some who, in this sin, interpret the Furies, placing Alecto for "evil thought," Tisiphone for "evil publication" of such thought, and Megaera for "evil operation," and Medusa for when one openly approves of his own falsehood. But such an allegory does not seem to me preferable to the one I placed above; nevertheless, let each person approve the one they judge fits better. **A** <margin>A</margin> <term>Heresiarchs</term> <note>original: "Herefiarche" — meaning the leaders or founders of a heretical movement.</note>, that is, the leaders of heresies, were many. But taking the beginning from where Gratian <note>A 12th-century canon lawyer</note> takes it, we shall say the first was Simon Magus, whom Peter cursed in the Acts of the Apostles because he tried to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit with money. From him, those who sell or buy sacred things are called <term>Simoniacs</term>. Their heresy is that the creature was not made by God, but by a certain supreme power. The Menandrians take their name from Menander the Magician, a disciple of Simon; they say the world was not made by God but by angels. The Basilidians from Basilides, who did not want Jesus Christ to have suffered. The Nicolaites from Nicholas the Deacon, who along with Stephen was appointed by Peter the Apostle; he left his wife to her own judgment to join with whomever she pleased, and he instituted the changing of marriage. The Gnostics want to be so called for their "excellence of knowledge" <note>Greek: *gnosis*</note>. These people say the soul is of the nature of God, and that God is both good and a captive. The Carpocratians from Carpocrates, who said Christ was only a man and born of a male and a female. The Cerinthians from Cerinthus; these observe circumcision and say that for a thousand years after the resurrection, they will live in the pleasures of the flesh. Hence, in Greek they were called <term>Chiliasts</term> <note>original: "ciliaste" — those who believe in a literal 1,000-year reign</note> and in Latin <term>Millenarians</term> <note>original: "maciliste," likely a transcription error for "miliaste" or "millenarii"</note>. The Nazarenes confess Christ and yet live according to the law of the Old Testament. The Ophites are named after the serpent, which in Greek is called *ophis* <note>original: "ophis"</note>. They worship the serpent and say that he introduced the knowledge of virtue. The Valentinians believe that Christ took nothing of a body from Mary, but entered into her as if through a channel or a small pipe. The Apellians—from whom they are named—held that an angel was the God of the Law of Israel, and they affirm him to be of fire; they said Christ was not God in truth but had appeared as a man in imagination <note>A reference to Docetism, the belief that Christ's body was an illusion.</note>. The Archontics hold that the universe created by God is the work of the Archangels.

## CANTO TEN 65

of the truth. And because of various and many doctrines, those of great authority can never rest. Dante asks, therefore, who are those buried in the chests: that is, the sepulchers: whom he understands to be there because he hears their sighs. These sighs arise from the utmost anguish of the soul. And certainly, anyone who does not acquiesce to common opinion while searching with their mind for what seems more true, their foolish intellect is always in anxiety and anguish. **AND HE TO ME** <note>Dante is referring to Virgil's response.</note> said, listen. Here, in these sepulchers, are the **HERESIARCHS**: that is, the leaders <term>heresiarch: from the Greek 'hairesis' (choice/sect) and 'archon' (leader)</term> of heretical sects, of whom we have briefly spoken above. **AND THEY ARE VERY FULL**, that is, replenished. **THE TOMBS.** The graves. **MORE THAN YOU BELIEVE.** This is to note that among men, there are more heretics than one might believe. Therefore, in order not to always use the same word—which causes boredom for the reader—he uses this variation, which brings with it ornament and delight, saying now "sepulcher," now "chest," now "tomb," now "vault." **LIKE** Here, with like in the sepulchers: as if to say Manicheans with Manicheans, and Priscillianists with Priscillianists, and so on with the others. **AND THEN TO HIS** right he turned. Here he notes that Virgil turned to the right hand. And then he shows that a little after some journeying, he turned to the left. This denotes that the journey began to the right because they went to gain knowledge of sin, and not to be defiled by it, but to purge themselves of it, which is a virtuous action. Then he turned to the left, to note that although the operation is virtuous, nonetheless the matter and the subject is vice. Therefore, he wisely takes the leftward journey from the right hand. **MARTYRS.** <note>original: "Martyres i lingua greca son testimonii"</note> Martyrs in the Greek language are "witnesses." But because those who have preferred to suffer pain and death rather than deny the Christian religion have been the best witnesses that it is true, they have been called martyrs: that is, witnesses of our true faith. This is the proper meaning of the word. But because they gave such testimony with heavy torments and bitter deaths, for this reason we often take "martyrdom" to mean pain and torment, and so it is here. Thus Petrarch said: "Brief help for such long martyrdoms." **AND THE OTHER BATTLEMENTS.** <note>original: "spaldi"</note> This word is not very common nor known to many. Therefore, some say *spaldi* signifies the walls. Others say that *spaldo* in the Romagnola dialect signifies what we call the space, and the Latins call the *pavimentum* <note>original: "pauimento" (pavement or floor)</note>.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, specifically the opening of Canto X where Dante and Virgil enter the circle of the Heretics.</meta>

# INFERNO

**O Virgil, you who are of supreme virtue.** **WHO TURNS ME:** who revolves me as it pleases you. **THROUGH the impious Circles.** That is, through the circles of the impious, or where the impious and pitiless sinners are. Because there can be no greater impiety than not having a good opinion of God. Some texts have **WIDE** <note>original: "AMPI"</note>, meaning broad, to denote the abundance of sinners. **SPEAK TO ME** And satisfy me: that is, speak to me in a way that satisfies my desires and my will. This is the order of the text. But let us remember that, as has been said at other times, the epithets the author gives to Virgil are always suited to the place where he puts them. Therefore, here he calls him "supreme virtue" because Virgil—that is, the intellect—has five virtues: **intelligence** regarding principles; **science** regarding the things that follow from principles; **wisdom**, which, while embracing the two already mentioned, is nonetheless neither of them, but a third virtue beyond the two; **prudence**, which is the right guide in particular actions and civil life; and **art**, which is technical knowledge. Of these five, the most excellent is wisdom, because it is the knowledge of things not only human but divine. Therefore, he could not lead him safely among the heretical falsehoods except with wisdom, which has true knowledge of divinity as far as the capacity of the human mind allows. And not without reason did he say: "Turn me as it pleases you," because although in all forms of knowledge it is necessary that lower reason and the senses allow themselves to be turned and guided by the intellect, it is especially necessary in this. And he makes an excellent preface to this brief speech because he first gains goodwill by calling him "supreme virtue." And by those same words, he demonstrates that what he asks of him is easy, since he possesses supreme virtue. Therefore, he can do it. Then he shows that he *ought* to do it because equity requires that we satisfy the will of one who gives himself entirely to our judgment. **THE PEOPLE HAVE** Up to this point, he has shown both that Virgil *can* and that he *ought* to answer him. Now he poses the question for which he wants an answer: which is whether he can see those who lie in the tombs. He believes this can easily be done, both because the tombs are open and because no guard is seen there to forbid looking at them. The reason why they are open we shall explain shortly. There is no guard because the Holy Church does not keep heretical opinions hidden, nor does it forbid that they be read and understood. Rather, it refutes them with effective reasons. And then it wishes that the foolishness of the heretics and the wisdom of the sacred theologians be known to everyone, so that when what they say is understood to be false and disproven with true reasons, they may be mocked and scorned rather than imitated and appreciated. And certainly, just as a pit in the road should not be hidden but manifested so that no one falls into it through imprudence, so false opinions must come to light along with their true refutations, so that no one falls into similar error through ignorance.

And he to me: "They shall all be locked up
   when from Jehoshaphat <note>The Valley of Jehoshaphat, traditionally the site of the Last Judgment.</note> they return here
   with the bodies they have left up there.
They have their cemetery on this side
   with Epicurus and all his followers
   who make the soul die with the body.
Therefore, regarding the question you ask me,
   you shall soon be satisfied here inside,
   and also regarding the desire you keep hidden from me."
And I: "Good leader, I do not keep my heart
   hidden from you except to speak little,
   and you have disposed me to this not just now."

The first speech is that of a good teacher, who often not only answers what the disciple asks but also adds of his own accord all the other things he judges useful for him to know. Dante asked if the people in the tombs could be seen, since they were open. And Virgil not only answers that they can be seen, but even says they will be locked after the universal and final judgment, which will occur at the end of the world. At that time, all human generation, having taken back their own bodies, will gather in the valley called Jehoshaphat near Jerusalem, where Jesus Christ will descend to judge the good to eternal glory and the wicked to eternal pains. Jehoshaphat signifies "He judges" or "Judgment of the Lord." Then, these summoned souls will return to their own bodies, and after the judgment, they will return with them to these tombs, and then they will be locked. They remain open now because the bodies are not there, and this is the reason regarding the essential Hell. But regarding the allegorical sense, we can understand

that as long as human generation lasts, they remain open to receive the heretics who arise from time to time. It is as if he says there are and always will be heretics. But once the world ends, they will cease because human generation will fail. Or rather, we shall understand with more subtlety: that beneath the universal judgment, he demonstrates the particular judgment, and means that the heretic, as soon as he is in such error, has his reason buried. But the tomb is not locked until his particular judgment (death), because he can still return to the true faith. They remain open, therefore, because divine grace can, before judgment—that is, death—draw them out of the darkness and lead them back to the light. This is why heretics should not be killed, but imprisoned, admonished, and led back as much as possible. **For who [thinks] the wandering should be killed? Rather, they should be led back to the cause.** <note>original: "Quis enim errabunda occidi non debet: Sed ad causam reduci"</note> This is also shown in the Book of Kings, when Absalom, son of David, went in to his father's concubines; where by the concubines they understand the heretics. **THEIR CEMETERY.** He orders it thus: all the followers of the philosopher Epicurus, together with him, have their cemetery on this side. And he rightly said "cemetery," since there are tombs there. For "cemetery" is where Christians bury the bodies of dead men; it is a Greek word <note>from *koimeterion*</note> and means "place of lying down," because here the dead bodies lie; named from *cime*, that is, "I lie." **WHO MAKE THE SOUL DIE WITH THE BODY.** A most wicked opinion and the ultimate ruin of the future life. But no one of sound mind believes this. But they, as the Psalmist says: **They have placed their hope in a lie, and have hoped in the works of a lie.** <note>original: "Posuerunt mendacium spem suam: & mendacium opi sperauerunt."</note> and Solomon: **They have erred in the paths of their own cultivation, and gather fruitless things in their hands.** <note>original: "Semitas propriae culturae erraverunt. & colligunt i manibus infructuosa."</note> Epicurus the philosopher said the soul dies together with the body. Various are the opinions on the soul according to different philosophers: for many believed it to be a body; many believed it to be something corporeal...

<summary>In this passage, Virgil explains the fate of Epicurean heretics who deny the immortality of the soul, noting that their tombs will be sealed only after the Last Judgment at Jehoshaphat. The commentary by Landino discusses the intellectual virtues of Virgil and argues against the execution of heretics, suggesting they should instead be reclaimed through reason.</summary>

87. ->**INFERNO.**<-

**Therefore you can understand that all** <gloss>that which has bad light.</gloss> There are two types of imperfect
**our knowledge will be dead from that** sight. For some have clear sight but not much: and
**point when the gate of the future shall** these see better from close up. Others have much sight:
**be closed** <note>Farinata explains that after the Last Judgment, when time ends and there is no more "future," the damned will lose all knowledge, as they cannot perceive the present.</note> but it is dark: whereby they see better from a distance: because as the <term>visual rays</term> <note>The original text uses "erazi uiſiui" (raggi visivi). Ancient and medieval optics often relied on "extramission theory," the idea that the eye sends out rays to "touch" objects.</note> go out, in the process they become clearer and become bright and fit for seeing. But [the author] explains why those who have <term>visual spirits</term> <note>original: "ſpiriti uiſiui"; these were thought to be subtle vapors that carried sensory information through the nerves.</note> that are too bright—if they proceed too far through the <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: "diaphano"; refers to the transparent medium, like air or glass, through which sight travels.</note>—the illumination exceeds them in light: and therefore they do not see. Therefore Farinata says: We are like those who have bad light, that is, they have dark visual spirits: which do not see unless [the rays] proceed across a long distance.

<summary>Farinata degli Uberti explains the mechanics of the damned's vision, comparing it to an optical condition where one sees distant objects clearly but is blind to things nearby. He notes that this limited knowledge will vanish entirely after the Last Judgment when the future ceases to exist.</summary>

**CANTO ELEVEN 69**

...and finally he greatly afflicted the Roman court: and greatly weakened the Guelphs of Tuscany, supporters of the Church: and sent against the Florentines with fifteen hundred cavalry one of his sons born of a princess of Antioch: and for this reason he called him Frederick of Antioch. <note>Frederick of Antioch (c. 1223–1256) was an illegitimate son of Emperor Frederick II and served as his father's vicar in Tuscany.</note> The princess of Antioch did not want to join with Frederick, hearing that he had a wife: wherefore he caused two ships to come with black sails: and in those were ambassadors who falsely said that the wife was dead: and with this fraud he deceived the princess: Finally he died in Puglia. Because he had heard from the astrologers that "Florence" [Firenze] would be fatal to him: and there he was to die, he never wanted to pass through our lands. And finally he fell ill in Puglia. And was led to a place in Puglia called Firenzuola. <note>Firenzuola translates to "Little Florence." The legend suggests Frederick II tried to avoid the city of Florence his whole life due to a prophecy, only to die in a town with a similar name.</note> Because of which, understanding the name later, he judged himself dead: and so he died excommunicated. And there are those who say that Manfred, his natural son and Prince of Taranto, smothered him with a pillow to occupy his treasures. He was a man of a military nature and great spirit, much feared: both by Christians and by Saracens. And if he had not been irritated by the fraud of the Pope, perhaps he would not have been so cruel toward the Church: which he treated in a way that he can deservedly be placed among the heretics.

### THE CARDINAL
All writers agree: and especially those close to the times of Dante: that he refers here to Cardinal Ottaviano degli Ubaldini: who certainly was a man of great governance and unconquered spirit: but of a life and customs more tyrannical than priestly: and so favorable to the Ghibellines: that he did not care to act against the pontifical authority in aid of them. By whom then, not being helped in certain of his needs: he said that if a soul exists: he had lost it for the Ghibellines. <note>This famous quote attributed to Cardinal Ottaviano indicates his Epicurean skepticism regarding the afterlife, which is why Dante places him among the Heretics.</note> These words showed him to be an Epicurean: So great was his prudence and authority that he disposed of the Roman court in his own way. And once he held it in the mountains of Mugello in the lands of the Ubaldini: and against the will of the Pope he always favored the Ghibellines. His favor created the first Archbishop of the Visconti of Milan. And brought them to the dominion of that city. Nor was he called anything other than "The Cardinal": and every time it was said "The Cardinal says" or "does," it was understood to be him.
