| Then he hid himself, and I toward the ancient<br>poet turned my steps, reflecting<br>on that speech which seemed hostile to me.<br>And he moved, and then while going<br>he said to me: "Why are you so bewildered?"<br>and I satisfied him as to his question.<br>"Let your mind preserve what you have heard<br>against yourself," that sage commanded me,<br>"and now attend here," and he pointed his finger.<br>"When you shall be before the sweet ray<br>of her whose beautiful eye sees everything,<br>from her you shall know the journey of your life."<br>Then he turned his foot to the left hand;<br>we left the wall and went toward the middle<br>by a path that strikes a valley<br>which even up there made its stench felt. | Farinata finished his words: and returned below. And Dante turned back to Virgil, reflecting on that speech which Farinata had made concerning his exile: which seemed to him hostile and harsh. And Virgil asked him why he was so bewildered in his thoughts: and understanding that it was because of the adverse fortune which Farinata had predicted to him, he gives him an excellent precept. Which is that he should preserve in memory what he has heard. And then he should wish to understand from Beatrice the whole process of his life. This denotes that when evil is announced to us, we must not wish to afflict ourselves with excessive fear nor make judgment with sensuality as to how unhappy and miserable that thing might be. Because that judgment of the senses is bad: because it wants all the adversities that come to the goods of the body or of fortune to be great and intolerable: and that because of them men become miserable. Which is very false. Therefore reserve this judgment for Beatrice, and she will show you that only he is in misery who is divided and separated from God by the vice committed by him, even though he were in every abundance and plenty of riches and status. And on the contrary, he is most happy who by virtue is joined with God. This sentiment is not only Stoic: but Christian: that nothing is evil except vice: which alone takes away from us the blessed life. And because vice cannot be given to us except by ourselves: therefore John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquence.</note> wrote the paradox: by which he proves that no one can be offended: except by himself. |

Because only vice and sin can harm: and vice and sin do not come except from our own will and choice. Nor can any power force us to this if we do not wish it. **AND NOW ATTEND** and here he pointed his finger. He pointed his finger to make him attentive: and to demonstrate with that gesture that what he had to say was a notable thing. Because we point the finger when, speaking of anything, we wish to testify that it is true: and of some importance. Or truly he wishes to demonstrate: that it was not enough that he should attend to the precepts of Beatrice: but it was necessary that he put those into practice. And by the finger and by the hands, action is signified. Wherefore the Psalmist said: <note>original: "Et leuaui manus meas ad mãdata tua que dilexi"</note> "And I lifted my hands to your commandments which I loved." Which signifies nothing else—raising the hand to the commandments of God—than putting them into operation. **WHEN YOU SHALL BE BEFORE THE SWEET RAY.** Because sacred theology contains in itself the truth: with which it illuminates the minds of all: And her eye sees every thing: because she sees the truth. Therefore in Hell one knows the loss that is made of temporal things. But the remedy against the pain that those bring with them is not shown to us except by Beatrice: and she teaches us the journey of our life: and what is the supreme good: and what are the vain goods. **TO THE LEFT HAND** to depart from the wall and enter through the middle. Which he declares saying: **WE LEFT** the wall and went toward the middle. **BY A PATH** by a way: and it is a French word <term>sentier (path)</term>: which **STRIKES** [fiede] hits: that is, it directs itself to a valley where one descends into the seventh circle. **WHICH EVEN UP THERE**: which valley stank so strongly: that even to the end of that path. **MADE SPRING FORTH**: almost to reverberate. **ITS STENCH** [lezo]: that is, its smell. Strictly *lezo* is a vehement odor that displeases: which does not arise from a corrupt body like *fetore* [fetidness] and *puzo* [stench] that...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of "lezzo" (stench) before transitioning into the text and detailed explanation of Canto XI of the Inferno.</meta>

...something rotten and decayed. But it is natural for such a thing: and it proceeds from the sweat and evaporation that a body casts off, even if it is not corrupted. Thus, a living buck or goat does not stink <note>original: "pute"</note>, but it has a rank smell <note>original: "lezisce"</note>. But it stinks when, being dead, it begins to rot. Nor is this rankness only in the sense of smell, but also in taste. Thus we say that meat that is turning <note>original: "busolina"</note> has a rank smell, and when tasting certain herbs we say they taste rank. And it is properly either in taste or in smell what Pliny in his *Natural History* and other Latin writers call *virus* <note>original: "uirus"; here meaning a slimy liquid or potent stench, though as the text notes, it can also mean poison</note>. Although this same word sometimes signifies poison. And he specifically said "rankness" <note>original: "lezo"</note> because such a stench is natural to this place, as we will demonstrate more clearly a little further on.

## CANTO ELEVENTH OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

**Upon the edge of a high**
**bank**
**formed by great broken stones**
**in a circle**
**we came above a more cruel throng.** <note>The word "stipa" suggests a packed crowd or a storage of souls.</note>
**And here, because of the horrible excess**
**of the stench that the deep abyss throws out,**
**we drew back behind a lid**
**of a large tomb, where I saw an inscription**
**that said: "I guard Pope Anastasius,**
**whom Photinus drew from the straight path."**

->[Illustration: Dante and Virgil stand before a raised tomb in a rocky landscape. The tomb is inscribed with the words: PAPA ANASTASIO IO GVARDO (I guard Pope Anastasius).]<-

In this eleventh canto, he describes the descent into the seventh circle. But so that we may have full knowledge of what follows, the author places the punishments of the violent and the fraudulent in the seventh, eighth, and ninth circles. And because both of these sins proceed from malice, there is no doubt that their end is injury. Injury is done by violence either to one's neighbor, to oneself, or to God. To one's neighbor, injury is done either to their person—such as beating, wounding, or killing them—or to their possessions—such as arson, theft, and robbery. To oneself, injury is similarly done by killing oneself or squandering one's own goods. In the third place, injury is done to God by blaspheming Him, denying Him, or acting against His things: that is, against nature. Therefore, this seventh circle is distinguished into three smaller circles or rounds. In the first and uppermost, those who have used violence against their neighbor are punished. In the second, against themselves. In the third, against God, against nature, and against art <note>By "art," the author refers to industry or human labor, the "grandchild" of God</note>. Afterward, we will follow to the eighth and ninth circles, where fraud is punished. This is committed either against those who do not trust the person <note>Simple fraud</note>, and these are punished in the eighth circle; or against those who do trust them <note>Treachery</note>. For the latter, the ninth circle is established because it is more grave, since it breaks two bonds of love: the natural and universal bond, and the accidental and particular bond <note>Meaning the specific bond of trust between individuals</note>. **VPON THE EXtremity of a high bank.** He shows by this into what a precipice such sinners fall: because they ruin themselves from the excellence of man to a bestial depth. No animal is higher than man because no animal is rational except man; if this reason is converted to vice, no animal is more pernicious. **GREAT STONES.** Because the ground would not support them. And by the hardness of the stones, understand the firm and immutable habit of these vices, and the great weight of these sinners: that is, how much they are burdened by conscience. **WITH GREATER throng.** <note>original: "stipa"</note> That is, a hedge that surrounds sinners worthy of a more enclosed prison. Or "stipa," meaning "stowage," because *stipare* in Latin signifies to surround and to pack in: and we shall call it a "stowage" when there is a great filling-up of cruelty, as we will understand better below. He places the stench here to represent the abomination of these sins and the supreme infamy which such sinners incur. For if, as Augustine says: "Good fame is a good odor" <note>original: "Fama bona est odor bonus"</note>, it follows that infamy is a heavy stench. **I SAW a writing that said: I guard Pope Anastasius.** Photinus, a cleric of Thessaly, together with Acacius, were heretics and held that the Holy Spirit did not proceed from the Father, and that the Father was greater than the Son. And they persuaded Pope Anastasius to this heresy. This man was a Roman and sat as Pope in the time of the Emperor Theodoric. Making an open profession of such heresy and being reproved by many prelates, he fell into such obstinacy that he wished to maintain it in public consistory. But it happened that while disputing, he was compelled by the necessity of his belly to go and "lay down the weight," where at once all his entrails came out, and so he perished. And not without reason does the author place the inscription on this tomb: because it denotes that heresy in a Supreme Pontiff must be known to all; for the more excellent the sinner, the more notorious the sin. Whence Juvenal, as [it is said]... <note>Dante likely confuses Pope Anastasius II with the Emperor Anastasius I, or relies on medieval chronicles that conflated the two regarding the Photinian heresy.</note>

<margin>in faith of</margin>
<margin><unclear>the heretic</unclear></margin>

...appropriately demonstrates: and we have clearly declared a little above. **TO GOD**, to oneself, to one's neighbor: These are the three persons against whom violence can be committed. And to each of these three it can be done in two ways: that is, either to the person or to their things. And note that when he proposes these three persons, he follows the natural order. Because for everyone, in the first degree, one must place God first; then oneself; and in the last, the neighbor. But afterwards, when he distinguishes these sins, he leaves this order and follows the order of the three rings of the seventh circle. Because in the first ring dwell the less grave sinners, he speaks first of those who have used violence against their neighbor, who have a less grave sin; and he lists many types of injuries which are done to the neighbor: To the person, death and beatings. To goods, ruins, fires, and "takings"—that is, robberies. **THROUGH DIVERSE** bands. As if to say, murderers in one group, destroyers in another, and so the others in the others: although all are in the first ring.

A man can have a violent hand against himself
and against his goods: and therefore in the second

Whoever deprives himself of your world,
gambles away and dissipates his wealth,
and weeps there where he should be joyful.

[Commentary to the right of the first block]
The second species is of those who use force against themselves by killing themselves, or against their goods by dissipating them. **OF YOUR** world, <note>original: "del vostro mondo"</note> that is, of this life. **Without profit** he repents. Because repenting in Hell is of no value. And morally, although he who has formed a habit repents, it can only be changed with difficulty. Nor is it to be understood that he repents with true penitence because, as we have shown elsewhere, just as the saved are confirmed in grace and in perfect will, so the damned are in perpetual obstinacy. But he says "he repents" because he grieves that he formed such a habit in vice from the beginning.

Sodom and Gomorrah were two cities in Syrian Palestine which, because of the wicked vice against nature, God affirmed to Abraham after his circumcision that he would destroy. And he sent two angels to Sodom in the form of boys, who stayed in the house of Lot, an innocent man who invited them. And before they went to sleep, the crowd of Sodomites came to attack the house to seize the angels and violate them. Lot begged them to cease from such fury and offered them his two beautiful daughters who were still virgins. But they, persevering in their most evil purpose, were struck by the angels and immediately went blind. Lot and his wife and two daughters were led by the angels into Segor <note>The biblical city of Zoar.</note> so that they might be saved. And God rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah and burned the city and the surrounding region with all inhabitants, animals, and plants. **Sodom** signifies in the Hebrew language: "flame," "sterile," and "blindness"; or "silent pasture." **Gomorrah** signifies "blindness," "sedition," and "a fearing people." <note>These are medieval etymologies rather than modern linguistic ones.</note> Solinus writes that in this region the earth, which is black and almost ash, demonstrates the past fire. And he adds that the fruits which are generated there, when they appear ripe on the outside, are soot inside, and when slightly pressed, they dissolve into ash. A certain divine miracle, so that through all ages there remains eternal testimony of divine judgment and severe punishment for a vice so bestial—or rather, above bestial, because no animal except man commits it. **Cahors** is a city in Provence for many centuries filled with usurers.

--- Page 44 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Canto XI of the *Inferno*, where Virgil explains the structural logic of Hell to Dante. On the previous page, Virgil began clarifying why some sinners are punished inside the City of Dis and others outside.</meta>

# **INFERNO.**

[Main text block 1]
If you consider well this judgment,
and recall to mind who those are
who undergo their penance outside the city:
You will see clearly why they are separated
from these wicked ones, and why divine justice
smites them with less anger.

[Commentary to the right of main text block 1]
**Division:** This is the distinction which, if Dante—representing lower reason combined with sensuality—had seen, he would not have fallen into this doubt. Therefore, Virgil, in answering him, aptly rebukes him for falling into such error, saying: **WHY does your wit so rave?** <note>original: "delira"</note> That is, why does it leave the straight path? In Latin, the word *lira* means "furrow." From this, they say a plowman "raves" <term>delira; from the Latin 'de-lira', meaning to go out of the furrow</term> when he wanders from the straightness of the furrow. By a certain metaphorical extension, we say an old man "raves" when he becomes childish; likewise, anyone who leaves the straight path of reason is said to rave. **FROM THAT which it is accustomed.** It might seem Dante praises himself too much by having Virgil say that he does not usually depart from the straight path when judging vices and moral virtues. However, Dante attributes this to himself not for self-praise, but to show that his character—representing reason exercised in practical matters—is not accustomed to erring in moral virtues. **OR where else does your mind look?** We err in two ways: either when our intellect is insufficient to find the truth, or when, even if sufficient, it is so occupied with many other things that it does not attend to the matter at hand. **DO YOU NOT remember?** Do you not recall **THOSE words** which **TREATS PERFECTLY:** <note>original: "pertracta"</note> that is, thoroughly discusses. **YOUR ETHICS:** the book of *Ethics*—the moral philosophy of Aristotle. Virgil does not call it "yours" because you wrote it, but because it is a text you are very familiar with and understand well. **THE THREE dispositions** that heaven does not want because they are vicious; and "heaven"—meaning the Divine Majesty—rejects all things that are full of vice.

[Marginal note: <margin>N</margin>]

[Long commentary block]
To better understand this, we must recall that Aristotle, in the seventh book of his *Ethics*, establishes three types of dispositions that must be avoided in life and character. He states that a good choice cannot exist without true reason and a right appetite. Therefore, when one of these is missing, such a choice must be avoided. 

If the perversion proceeds from the appetite, yet reason remains straight, **incontinence** is born. This happens when reason judges correctly, but the disturbed appetite pulls it in the opposite direction. An example is Medea in the works of Ovid, who judged correctly that it was a supreme wickedness to betray her father and abandon her homeland; yet her appetite to be with Jason pulled her against her reason. Hence she said: *I see the better things and approve of them, but I follow the worse.* <note>original: "Video meliora proboque. Deteriora sequor."</note> 

However, if sometimes the corrupted and perverse appetite rises so strongly against reason that it becomes its absolute master, reason itself becomes corrupted. Then, reason follows the appetite, judging whatever the appetite proposes to be "good," and thus makes a captive choice. This is called a "bad judgment," and such a disposition is **malice**. In the first case (incontinence), only the appetite sinned while reason judged correctly but was pulled by force. In the second case (malice), both sin, and they agree that what is evil is good. An example is Dido, of whom the poet Virgil says: *No longer does Dido meditate a secret love: she calls it marriage.* <note>original: "Nec iam furtivum dido meditatur amorem: Coniugiumque vocat."</note>

But sometimes the perversion of appetite and reason is so great that they not only agree to sin, but they nearly forget what it is to be human. They overstep every limit of the human species and take on the habits and nature of a beast; this disposition is called **bestiality**. 

Against these three vicious dispositions are excellent remedies. To **incontinence**, "continence" is opposed. To **malice**, "moral virtue." To **bestiality**, "heroic virtue"—which is more than human. Heroes, according to the ancients, are more than men and less than gods, such as Hercules, Theseus, and the like. To understand how a man acquires heroic virtue, we must know that the human soul is in the middle between angels and brute animals, as it shares intellect with the former and senses with the latter. Just as the sensitive part can become so depraved that a man becomes like a beast—called bestiality, exceeding human malice—so, conversely, the intellectual part can be so strengthened and perfected that it rises above the common mode of human perfection to a likeness of the angels. This the ancients called **heroic virtue**, through which they believed men were converted into gods, like Hercules. Just as this virtue is rare among men, so is bestiality—its opposite—rare. It arises from bestial customs, such as living without law or learning, like the cannibals <note>original: "antropophagi"</note>, the "strigoni" <term>witches or folklore monsters</term>, and the Cyclopes. Aristotle mentions wild men living in forests near the Black Sea who eat human flesh. Jerome, in his work against Jovinian, says there are certain barbarians who eat the buttocks of infants and the breasts of women. 

We conclude, therefore, that **incontinence** is bad, **malice** is worse, and **bestiality** is the worst. Therefore, the first is punished outside the city, while the latter two are punished inside the City of Dis.

how nature takes its course

[Commentary, right column and middle block]

And in many other places: that nature takes its course and its process from the divine intellect, because God is the primary cause of all causes; and from his art: that is, from his work and his will. For just as God understands, so he wills; and as he wills, so he acts. **YOUR Physics**: that is, the *Physics* in which you take much delight. **NOT many pages in**: Because it is not far from the beginning of the book. **THAT our art follows that as much as it can**: <note>original Latin: "Ars imitatur naturam quo ad potest"</note> Art imitates nature as far as it is able, just as **The Student**: that is, the pupil follows the master. **ALMOST a grandchild**: by a certain similarity. For if nature proceeds from God as from its principle, it is his daughter; and if then our art proceeds from nature, being its daughter, it is the grandchild of God; because God has implanted art in the minds of men by means of nature. Aristotle says: God is the eternal and best living being, from whom heaven and nature depend; which nature is imitated by our art as much as possible. Therefore, since art depends on nature, it is like its daughter, and consequently a grandchild to God. Thus, he who offends nature offends God immediately. And he who offends art offends God through the medium of offended nature. But the usurer offends nature: because it is not natural that money should give birth to money or undergo its own corruption <note>In Aristotelian thought, "corruption" is the process of one thing ending so another can begin.</note>. Nature intends that the corruption of one thing be the generation of another. Likewise, he offends God: because he does not exercise art according to what God commanded the first man when he said: <note>original Latin: "In sudore uultus tui uesceris pane tuo"</note> "By the sweat of your brow you shall eat your bread." Likewise, it is not "artistic" <note>In the sense of human industry or craft.</note> that money should give birth to money, as the usurer wants, who places "use" in a thing where no use can be given. For if I lend you a garment or a horse, these things are consumed through use, but not money. And other arts and trades are subject to the accidents of fortune, but not the usurer. **IF YOU call to mind Genesis**: that is, the sentence written in Genesis, where it treats the creation of the world and the first man and the order of life, which began where it is written: <note>original Latin: "Oportuit ab initio seculi humanum genus sumere uitam, & excedere unum alium per naturam & artes"</note> "It was necessary from the beginning of the age for the human race to take up life and to surpass one another through nature and the arts." **In the beginning**: that is, as it appears in its beginning. **FITTING for people to take their life**: that is, the mode and order of living. **AND to advance** one another in wealth and temporal goods: and this is lawful either through one’s industry and exercise, or through possessions, or through livestock, which things naturally yield fruit. **AND because the usurer takes another way**: other than that of nature, not keeping money in livestock; and other than that of art, because he does not work and does not labor. **He despises in itself**: that is, as much as is in him, nature and its follower, which is art. He acts against nature because inanimate things cannot multiply as animate ones do. Usury is prohibited in the Old Testament. Whence in Leviticus: <note>original Latin: "Pecuniam tuam non dabis fratri tuo ad usuram: & frugum superabundantiam non exiges"</note> "You shall not give your money to your brother for usury, nor shall you exact an overabundance of fruits." And the Psalmist: <note>original Latin: "Quis habitabit in tabernaculo tuo? Qui pecuniam non dederit ad usuram"</note> "Who shall dwell in your tabernacle? He who has not given his money for usury." And in the New Testament, Luke writes in the text: <note>original Latin: "Date mutuum nihil inde sperantes"</note> "Give a loan, hoping for nothing in return."

[Commentary, lower right and bottom block]

Just as Virgil had been the reason for their staying still, so now he is the reason for continuing. And certainly, every power of the soul ought to submit to the intellect and follow according to its judgment. Virgil says, then: it pleases me to follow the journey, because the **Fishes** are already at our horizon. This shows that the day is already approaching. We showed above that Dante feigns having had this vision on Good Friday before daybreak. And therefore he said the sun was in Aries; because from the month of March until the 11th of April it is in that sign. And he intends to have spent that whole day struggling with the beasts and reasoning with Virgil. Afterward, he shows that on Friday night he descended into Hell, when he said: "The day was departing and the air was growing dark." Now he adds that a great part of that night had already passed in this search of Hell, and it was almost two hours before day. For if the sun rose in our hemisphere with Aries, and the Fishes precede Aries, and each of these rises with sixteen degrees—that is, with one hour and one-fifteenth of an hour—it follows that two hours of the night remained, during which they had to search all of Hell. And therefore he admonishes Dante that no time is to be lost. And this place is similar to that in Virgil: <note>original Latin: "Hac uice sermonum roseis aurora quadrigis..." A quote from the Aeneid, Book VI, where the Sibyl warns Aeneas that time is passing while they talk.</note> "During this exchange of talk, Aurora in her rosy chariot had already crossed the midpoint of her ethereal course... but his companion the Sibyl briefly warned him: 'Night is coming on, Aeneas, and we spend the hours in weeping.'" **THAT the fishes flicker**: He had respect for the nature of the fish which flickers; that is, it runs through the water with great ease. And the meaning is they were already beginning to rise at our horizon. **UPON the horizon**: the horizon was that circle which divides one hemisphere from the other, which is called the horizon: that is, the ender and terminator, which terminates our sight; because of the whole sky, which is round and spherical, we see only half. Therefore that last part which we see all around the sky where our sight ends, because the earth prevents us from seeing more...

# INFERNO

below the aforementioned horizon. And because the heavens make a full revolution in twenty-four hours, it is necessary that some sign of the zodiac always rises at our horizon. At that time, Pisces was rising; these, as I have said, last for one hour, and the fifteenth part of that hour remains entirely outside the horizon; and after those, Aries rises with the sun, the birth of which brings the day. Therefore, as much of the night remained as it took for the entire sign of Pisces to emerge, along with all those degrees of Aries that preceded the degree where the sun is located. Pisces is the final sign of the zodiac and is the house of Jupiter <note>In traditional astrology, Jupiter is the planetary ruler of Pisces.</note> and of this triplicity. But in *Purgatorio* we shall speak of this more accurately. **The Wagon lies entirely over Caurus.** <note>The "Wagon" refers to the constellation Ursa Major (the Big Dipper); "Caurus" is the Latin name for the Northwest wind, indicating the constellation's position in the sky.</note> This is the second sign the poet uses to show that day is approaching. For if Pisces was rising at that time, it followed that Leo—the sign opposite to them—must be going down. So that this may be better understood: the Wagon consists of seven stars which revolve around the North Star. The first four stand two by two and form the wagon, and then three come in a line—though the last one curves somewhat—and they form the pole. This last star is always pointed toward Leo. Therefore, when Leo is about to set, the pole is pointed toward the west, and the four that make up the wagon have already turned between the west and the north, from whence the Caurus wind blows. Thus, he rightly said: "and the Wagon lies entirely over Caurus."

[Woodcut illustration depicting the Minotaur—half-man, half-bull—gnashing his teeth. Dante and Virgil stand nearby, while Centaurs patrol a river of blood below.]

**I**n this twelfth canto, the poet describes the descent from the sixth circle into the seventh; he divides it as we have said above and places there the punishments for the violent: first against their neighbors, then against themselves, and lastly against God. He places the monstrous Centaurs as guards of the place, and especially the Minotaur of Crete. He shows that this descent was a precipice of broken and ruined boulders, and so harsh that it is like the landslide of Mount Marco <note>Specifically the "Slavini di Marco," a massive prehistoric landslide near Rovereto, south of Trento.</note> between Treviso and Trento. And on the edge of the ruin where the descent begins, the Minotaur was stretched out. Mount Marco, having had its roots heavily eroded by the river—either by this or by earthquakes—collapsed in great part into the Adige river, in such a way that it moved aside for a good distance; and because of this ruin, the rock—that is, the stones and the bank of the mountain—is so shattered from the summit to the plain that it would provide some path, though it would not be very easy. **FOR ONE WHO WAS ABOVE:** that is, for whoever was at the top. **SUCH WAS THE DESCENT OF THAT RAVINE:** from that ruin. The Florentines call a deep ditch a "burato," almost like an "abyss." **AND ON THE EDGE:** on the summit. **OF THE BROKEN GAP:** <gloss>the descent</gloss>, from the verb *labor* <note>original: "labor"; Latin for "to slip" or "to slide."</note>. **LAY OUTSTRETCHED:** almost as if lying down. **THE INFAMY OF CRETE:** that is, the Minotaur; having been born on the island of Crete (today called Candia), he was the infamy of said island, being not a man but a monstrous thing. **WHICH INFAMY:** that is, the monster. **WAS CONCEIVED:** that is, the Minotaur was conceived. **IN THE FALSE COW:** So that this may be more clearly understood, we will briefly narrate the fable. Because Venus was discovered in the adultery she committed with Mars by the Sun, and was accused to her husband Vulcan, she became such an enemy to him that, unable to take revenge on him, she took revenge on his daughters. Therefore, Pasiphae, wife of King Minos of Crete and daughter of the Sun, was so inordinately incited to lust by Venus that she was driven to love a bull from her husband's herds. Some say that Minos, desiring to have a suitable animal for a sacrifice he wished to make to his father Jupiter, was sent a very beautiful and handsome bull by Jupiter. But Minos, moved by greed and a desire for such a beautiful animal, sent it to join his own herds and sacrificed a less beautiful bull to Jupiter. Therefore, the angered Jupiter induced Pasiphae to love that bull. But whichever bull it was, they add that Pasiphae asked Daedalus to show her how she could join with the beloved bull. And Daedalus made a wooden image of a cow and enclosed her within it; and thus she joined with the bull, which believed her to be a cow. From this union was born the Minotaur, a horrid monster, who was half man and half bull...

->CANTO TWELVE. 79<-

"Evil was your will, always so quick for that." <note>The commentator is interpreting the nature of the violent impulse mentioned in the poem.</note> Violence is force used to the harm and evil of others; and it is born from greed, which has its origin in pride. **IN a curved ARCH**: because it went in a circuit, according to the site he describes. **AT THE FOOT of the bank**: between the roots of the mountain.

**AND THAT ditch. CENTAURS** armed were running in a line: that is, all in a row as if following the track of one another. "Track" <term>traccia: a footprint or mark left by a passing person or animal</term> signifies a footprint and mark. Hence "to track" means to follow footsteps. The poets say that the Centaurs <margin>Q</margin> <note>The letter 'Q' in the margin likely stands for 'Quaestio' (Question) or 'Quod,' marking a point of inquiry or a notable citation.</note> were monstrous men in Thessaly; they were half horse and half man, the sons of Ixion. He was the son of Phlegyas of Thessaly. And he was the first among the Greeks who attempted to occupy a tyranny by force: for this reason, the poets feign that he wanted to unite with Juno, wife of Jove. And Jove, mocking him, made an image of mist similar to Juno; and Ixion united with that, believing it was the true Juno: and from such a union, the Centaurs were born.

By Ixion, we understand all men greedy for kingdoms or powers, who attempt to acquire principalities or lordships beyond their strength. And because Juno is the goddess of kingdoms <note>In Roman mythology, Juno (Hera) presided over the public sphere and the wealth of nations.</note>, they feign that he wished to unite with her: but she mocks and deceives him by showing him such an image as we have said. For there is no one who can unite with Juno as he desires: that is, to acquire as much lordship as he proposes in his mind, which in the life of a tyrant is insatiable. For having acquired what he first desired—and in which he believed he would find rest—there is born in him a desire for something greater; and he never arrives at that quiet life he proposes for himself. He would reach it quickly if he put a brake on greed and remained content with his present state, as the wise Cineas aptly demonstrated to the infuriated Pyrrhus. <note>Cineas was a diplomat who famously asked King Pyrrhus what he would do after conquering each nation, eventually showing that the "rest" Pyrrhus sought was already available to him if he simply stopped fighting.</note> This makes men...

# INFERNO.

"Even if he tires out the others, one by one,

**AND HE DOES NOT** seem to care for the fire, because through pride he wishes to show that he will not allow himself to be conquered. **AND HE LIES**, not humble or with repentance for the error committed, **BUT** scornful and twisted. This signifies the obstinacy of his spirit and his perversity—a mind that is not upright and a depraved opinion. **SO THAT** the rain <note>The rain of fire falling upon the blasphemers in this circle of Hell</note> does not seem to ripen him. We call the spirit of one who remains stubborn and resistant against that which he ought to obey "unripe" <term>acerbo: literally sour or green fruit; used here to describe a soul hardened against God</term>. And by contrast, we say a person is "mature" <note>original: *maturo*</note> who finally, after many lashes <note>original: *flagelli*; refers to divine punishments</note>, recognizes his faults, surrenders, and humbles himself. This comparison is drawn from fruit, which, while they are unripe, are stubborn and harsh to the taste.

--- Page 65 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on the properties of elemental fire and atmospheric vapors, specifically focusing on the different colors of flames and the formation of thunderbolts.</meta>

...somewhat ignited, and red like the color of wine. The first type is generated from vapor that is not very dry; and the moisture gives it a red color, like the flame found in green wood. In this case, because the moisture holds the matter together and prevents it from scattering, it ignites more easily. 

The white flame comes from dry vapor, like the flame found in dry wood; for this reason, it does not scatter and does not ignite anything except very flammable <term>incendibili</term> <note>things that are highly susceptible to catching fire</note> objects. The red flame, because it is made of very dense and earthy vapor, does ignite things. 

But the thunderbolt <term>saetta</term> <note>literally "arrow," used historically to describe a bolt of lightning</note> falls in four ways. The first is when the red, inflamed vapor falls from a green and deep cloud; and this generates a stone <note>the author refers to the ancient and medieval belief in "thunderstones" or ceraunia, physical stones thought to be forged in the air and cast down by lightning</note>. This happens because the vaporous mixture of the earthy vapor ignites, and upon touching the green cloud—which is already turning into water—it hardens just as flour becomes dough when mixed with water. Because the intense heat of the fire does not allow the moisture of the cloud to extinguish it, it instead hardens through the vehemence of the heat; and it becomes...

<summary>This passage explains the physical properties of colored flames based on their moisture content and describes the medieval scientific theory of how lightning strikes create physical stones in the atmosphere.</summary>
<keywords>meteorology, Aristotelian physics, thunderstones, types of fire, atmospheric vapors, lightning, medieval science</keywords>

->**INFERNO**<-

...because they think of nothing else but earthly things. And these most vile thoughts want to be more powerful than God. Therefore they place mountains upon mountains: <note>A reference to the Giants of Greek mythology who piled Mount Pelion on top of Mount Ossa to reach the heavens and challenge the gods.</note> that is, they accumulate thoughts and undertakings that are bloated and proud. But the celestial bolt: which is divine wrath, casts them to the ground. But returning to the fable, this battle was in Thessaly. And according to some poets, it was in that stretch of countryside where Pozzuoli and Cuma are, which is called Phlegra according to Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer; Phlegra was the legendary site of the battle between the Gods and the Giants.</note>. Nevertheless, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist.</note> in his geography places Phlegra not far from the mountains mentioned above; which seems more likely.

**u** Virgil spoke to the proud speech of Capaneus. HE SPOKE with force: that is, with sharpness and with vehemence: and with a great cry he rebuked him: in such a way that Dante affirms he had not yet heard him speak so bitterly. This signifies that the intellect is not disturbed more by any other vice than by this impiety. IN THIS, that your pride is not extinguished, you are more punished. It is a very true sentiment that no punishment is greater for the proud than the rage and the anger they feel at being defeated and suppressed, which grows all the more as they are trampled. AND NO other punishment. That is, fury and punishment that anyone might use against you. WOULD NOT BE complete pain. That is, sufficient and enough punishment. THEN HE TURNED to me with better lips. With better lips: that is, with better words: which are formed in the mouth by the tongue, the teeth, and the lips. And this is the way of the wise person, because he rebukes vice with grave sharpness. But in admonishing and in teaching the man eager for knowledge, he uses human and loving words. SAYING That was...

**Then my leader spoke with such force**
**that I had not heard him so loud before:**
**"O Capaneus, in that your pride is not quenched,**
**you are punished all the more;**
**no other pain except your own rage**
**would be a punishment complete for your fury."**
**Then he turned to me with a kinder face,**
**saying: "That was one of the seven kings**
**who besieged Thebes; he held, and seems to hold,**
**God in disdain, and seems to prize Him little;**
**but, as I told him, his own insults**
**are ornaments well-suited to his breast."**

**T** One of the seven kings who "sat": that is, who besieged Thebes. Laius, king of the Thebans, had a son named Oedipus: who according to the oracles was to kill his father: therefore he gave him to servants to kill him. They, out of pity, spared his life: and having pierced his feet with a cord <note>The name "Oedipus" literally means "swollen foot" in Greek, referring to this injury.</note> they left him in the forest. Found by shepherds, he was given to Polybus, king of Corinth: and by him he was raised as his own. Later, having reached full age, he heard from the oracle of Apollo that in Phocis of Boeotia he would find his true father. He went therefore to Phocis and killed his father without knowing him. There was at that time in Thebes a monster called the Sphinx: which proposed riddles: that is, obscure sayings, with this condition: that whoever did not know how to solve them should be killed: and whoever solved them should have as a wife Jocasta, queen of Thebes, then a widow because of the death of Laius. Oedipus solves the riddle: which was this: "What animal is it that first goes on four feet: then on two, and finally on three?" And Oedipus said this was man: who as a small child goes on all fours. Then he goes on two feet: and finally in old age he goes with three feet: because he supports himself with a staff. Because he knew how to solve the riddle, he deserved to be given the queen as a wife: who was Jocasta: and he took her not knowing she was his mother. And by her he had two sons, Eteocles and Polynices. And finally, recognizing his father and mother, and the wickedness he had committed, he blinded himself and lived in darkness. And after his death, discord arose between the sons: because each wanted to rule. And finally they agreed to rule in turn, each for his year. And it falling first to Eteocles: Polynices, leaving the fatherland to his brother for that year, arrived in Argos: and from Adrastus, king of Argos, he was given the king's daughter as a wife. And the year having finished: and Eteocles not wanting to observe the pacts: Adrastus together with six other kings went against Thebes. The kings were Adrastus, Polynices, Tydeus, Hippomedon, Amphiaraus, Parthenopaeus, and Capaneus. This man was a despiser of all religion: and affirmed that there was no God: and that fear was what had induced men to believe there was a God. He trusted much in his own strength: because he was very large and robust. And in the battle given at Thebes, by force he climbed the walls: and crying out...

### CANTO XIV. 84

...the Greek poets, describing various ages under the figure of various metals <note>This refers to the classical "Ages of Man" (Gold, Silver, Bronze, and Iron) described by poets like Hesiod and Ovid.</note>: he introduces a third meaning which fits his purpose. He therefore places a great statue of an old man on Mount Ida <note>Mount Ida is a mountain on the island of Crete, chosen by Dante as the center point of the world's history.</note>: and this statue turns its back to **Damietta**: which is a noble city in Egypt located on the Nile; and its face turns toward **Rome**. By this he means Time, which began together with the world and with the world will end. Time is nothing other than the movement which is the measure of the motion of the heavens and the stars. Therefore, before the creation of the world there was no time, but only eternity: into which time then entered. He imagines this statue as old and large: because among things that have had a beginning and will have an end, almost nothing is older than time; and time is a grand thing among mortal matters. But he does not simply present such a statue to represent Time; because along with that, he intends to express the human race <note>original: "generatione humana"</note>: which is placed within this flux and course of time; and its various states. For which reason this old man shall be Time. He shall be the...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIV, focusing on the allegorical "Old Man of Crete" statue and the origins of the four rivers of Hell.</meta>

# INFERNO.

...of the statue being made of baked earth <note>terracotta</note>, which signifies the fragility of human things and how weak the foundation is of empires and other goods subject to fortune and death. He said the **right foot** was used because the power of empires—denoted by the right foot—consists entirely of earthly things void of all virtue, both moral and intellectual. There are few princes who approve of the sentence of Plato, who affirms that republics cannot be happy unless they are administered by wise men. Instead, all their trust is in the strength of the body and in riches, which are earthly things. The statue was broken in every part except for the gold <note>representing the Golden Age of innocence</note>. This rupture signifies vice, which has broken integrity and innocence, thus staining every age except for the state of innocence, which was without vice. From this rupture are born the tears which create the infernal rivers—that is, human miseries—which generate the punishments that afflict us. For just as virtue makes a man blessed, happy, joyful, and glad, so vice makes us miserable, sad, and full of mourning. These tears pierce the grotto that separates this part where men live from Hell. It is certainly true that from our vices is born that sorrow which opens the path leading us to unhappiness. The poet, therefore, wished to place the origin of the infernal rivers in that place where there is tyrannical pride, from which all other vices are born that lead us to Hell. These tears form the four rivers.

First is **Acheron**, which signifies the "deprivation of joy" <note>from the Greek 'acharis', meaning without grace or joy</note>, because sin generates repentance in us and deprives us of happiness. From Acheron is born **Styx**, which means "sadness," because sadness follows the deprivation of joy. And then follows **Phlegethon**, which means "burning" <note>ardor</note>, because whoever is established in sorrow always feels a fire boiling in their mind through various cares. Whence Virgil says: *And he fluctuates with a shifting tide of angers* <note>original: "Varioque irarum fluctuat aestu"</note>. From Phlegethon the water descends down to the bottom of Hell and forms the stagnant **Cocytus**. Thus, from the deprivation of joy, from sorrow, and from the burning of cares, Cocytus is generated—that is, "weeping"—which signifies a confirmed or hardened grief. Therefore, he wishes for it to be stagnant in the lowest part of Hell, because perpetual mourning places us in the depths of the abyss and holds us there in eternal misery.

**[Commentary - Right Column and surrounding]**

Regarding this river: which is the Montone. It is to be noted that **Vesulo** <note>Modern Mount Monviso.</note> is a mountain in the Alps above Monferrato, which separates Provence from Italy. From this point the **Apennines** begin; although some say the Apennines commence at Monaco on the Genoese Riviera, and come along coasting toward **Pietrapana**, leaving to the left Monferrato, Tuscany, and Vercelli, and to the right **Lunigiana** and part of the Riviera. Proceeding from there, it leaves Bologna, Romagna, and the Marches to the left. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the transition between the eighth and ninth circles of Hell, specifically focusing on the appearance of the monster Geryon, who represents Fraud.</meta>

->**INFERNO**<-

...wonderful to every steady heart:
Just as he returns who goes down
sometimes to loosen the anchor that catches
on a reef or something else hidden in the sea,
Who stretches his upper body and draws in his legs.

That which by its nature seems incredible, the poet shows he knows what we have said: but that he is constrained by necessity to say it; for if he did not do so in this place, the work would remain imperfect. He says it, then: and to give it credibility, he affirms it with an oath by those things which are dearest to him, and he swears in this sentiment: "So may these notes—that is, the words of this <term>Comedy (the title Dante gave his poem, implying a work that begins in tragedy but ends in joy)</term> which I write—be full of long-lasting grace, as surely as I saw this beast coming." This is a powerful oath, because there is nothing a writer desires so much as that his written work should find favor. And Dante desires this especially, not for vainglory, but because in writing things necessary for the salvation of man, he desires to be read so that his laborious vigils might produce the best fruit for many. **THAT I SAW** through that thick and dark air a figure come swimming upward. Many have been deceived, believing that because he says "come swimming," the place must be full of water. They do not realize that he is imitating Virgil, who makes a reciprocal metaphor between the sea and the air. Whence he said *the sail-flying sea* <note>original: "mare velivolum," meaning a sea navigated by sails</note>, which is to say, that through which one flies with sails. And flying is only for the air, and so from the air to the sea. Whence, regarding Mercury, he said *the rowing of wings* <note>original: "remigio alarum"</note>, although oars belong only to the sea. Similarly, Dante said "come swimming," even though swimming is proper to water. And certainly, it is a marvelous fiction and entirely worthy of the divinity of such a genius. He wishes to describe <term>Fraud (the sin of using trickery or deceit to harm others)</term> and says, "I saw a figure." But he did not yet see what kind of figure it was, which denotes that fraud is seen, but at first is not recognized. The Trojans saw <note>Sinon was a Greek spy who pretended to have deserted his army; his lies convinced the Trojans to bring the Wooden Horse into their city.</note> Sinon and heard his words, but they did not know for what purpose he had come. Furthermore, he saw it through the "thick and dark air," which not only denotes that in Hell—that is, in the habit of vice—there is darkness (meaning ignorance), but he wishes to show that fraud is always shadowed and darkened so that it cannot be discerned. It "came swimming through the air" to signify that it does not stand on solid or firm ground (that is, in the truth). Instead, it swims, because the fraudulent person always varies and changes things; when you think he is in one place, he is in another. It "came upward" because fraud comes into the light from a hidden place at some point. And it is "wonderful to every steady heart" because no one is of such a composed mind that they do not fear fraud. For the force that is done to us openly gives some space for foresight and defense, whereby the high-minded man takes confidence; but fraud strikes us before we can foresee it, which is why a generous man cannot exercise or show any of his strength to resist it, and for this reason, he fears such assaults greatly. Understand, then, why Dante saw it through the dark and thick air; why it came swimming; why it came from below to above; why it was terrifying even to steady men; and finally, he shows that in coming up, it acted like one who has gone to the bottom of the water to grasp an anchor caught on a reef or something else covered by water, who, in returning up, stretches his upper parts (that is, the neck and arms) and his lower parts (which are the legs) he draws in (that is, he crouches). And truly, the fraudulent person always stretches his upper parts, because he begins with something true and wants that to be manifest; then at the end, he attaches the falsehood, and this he "bunches up" and wraps around so that it stays hidden and is not understood.

**CANTO XVII OF THE FIRST <term>CANTICA (one of the three major divisions of the Divine Comedy)</term> OF DANTE.**

<meta>This page continues the transition from the seventh to the eighth circle of Hell. Having encountered Geryon, the embodiment of Fraud, Dante and Virgil prepare to descend. This page focuses on the description of the usurers and the symbolic nature of Geryon's appearance.</meta>

->INFERNO.<-

[Main Text]
So that most evil beast stayed
upon the edge that locks the sand in stone.
In the void, all its tail was twitching,
twisting upward its venomous fork,
which, like a scorpion’s, armed the point.

[Commentary Block 1]
**The beaver** <note>original: "castore." The commentator confuses the beaver's habits with medieval bestiary myths.</note>, so called because it castrates itself <note>A common medieval folk etymology held that beavers bit off their own testicles to escape hunters seeking them for medicinal "castoreum."</note>. It has a terrible bite; it cuts trees with its teeth no differently than a man with iron. If it bites a man, it does not let go until it feels it has crushed the bone of the limb it bites. It is similar to the otter, and like it, inhabits both land and water. But it has back feet like a goose, with which it is very nimble at swimming. Its tail is wide and scaly like a fish, and it always keeps it in the water; this tail alone is considered precious food, while the other limbs are of a foul stench. It builds ingenious houses on rivers with several stories, so that even as the water rises and falls, it can keep its tail in the river and the rest of its body dry. It feeds on fish and the bark of trees. Those who have more strength make slaves of the weaker ones, forcing them to go upside down through the river, and between their back legs and bellies they load them with wood for the construction of their houses, pulling them by the tail to the chosen spot. **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> writes that it is false that they castrate themselves, because they have their testicles attached to the spine or the backbone in a way that they cannot be removed without death. **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist.</note> affirms the same. Useful hats are made from their skins. **AMONG the gluttonous Germans** <note>original: "tedeschi lurchi." "Lurchi" was a derogatory term for heavy drinkers or gluttons.</note>; that is, among those of great appetite; he says this because the Danube, where beavers are found, flows through these people. **TO WAGE its war against the fish** on which it feeds. **UPON the edge that locks the sand in stone.** This was the bank of the river made of stone, which held back the sand so it would not be eroded by the river. They appeared clearly out of the water and were upon the stone. Because the beginnings of fraud, as I said, start from things that are true and solid; but then the rest twitches, because they are things covered and vain; and they twist the fork upward because finally the venom appears.

[Main Text]
The leader said: "Now we must bend
our path a little, as far as that
wicked beast that couches there."
Therefore we descended to the right breast <note>meaning the right side</note>,
and took ten steps upon the edge
to fully avoid the sand and the flames:
And when we had come to it,
a little further along the sand I saw
people sitting near the empty place <note>the abyss</note>.
There the master, so that you may carry
full experience of this place,
said to me: "Go, and see their condition <term>mena: behavior and movement</term>."
Let your talk there be brief;
while you return, I will speak with this one,
that it may grant us its strong shoulders.

[Commentary Block 2]
**Virgil shows** that it was necessary to go all the way to the beast, because to have full knowledge of the fraudulent, it was necessary to consider their cunning. **NOW we must bend our path.** He says this because until now they had always turned to the left, except for sometimes to cross over as they do now; we have already shown above why he creates this fiction. **THEREFORE we descended to the right breast:** To denote that the consideration of cunning was for the purpose of guarding against it, and not to use it. **AND TEN steps we made upon the edge:** Understand this as being on the rim of the seventh circle. By "ten steps," he means the ten species of cunning <note>A reference to the ten "Malebolge" or evil ditches of the eighth circle, which Dante is about to enter.</note> which he will treat successively in the eighth circle. Afterward, Virgil sends Dante to know the people who are there, and he remains to reason with the beast. This signifies that for the knowledge of particular things, **lower reason** <note>human observation</note> is enough; but to consider the whole nature of universal cunning, one needs Virgil—that is, **higher reason** and the intellect which persuades the beast to place them on its strong shoulders and carry them into the eighth circle. For our intellect cannot reach the knowledge of the punishments in that circle unless it knows the types of cunning and can distinguish the places according to their species. **PEOPLE sitting nearby:** One and the same punishment—namely, flames falling from heaven—punishes both the sodomites and the usurers, because each of these does violence to nature. But the sodomites walk and the usurers sit, to show that usury is a greater sin, because it does violence not only to nature but also to art <note>In Dante's philosophy, "art" refers to human industry and labor, which usury bypasses by making money from money.</note>. **THERE THE MASTER:** We have already explained this place above. **THEIR condition** <note>original: "mena"</note>: their bearing, actions, and movements; for *menare* means to move. Hence we say "he moves [mena] his head." **LET your talk be brief.** Because once we have known the nature of usury, we must immediately depart from such consideration. **WHILE you return I will speak:** It has already been stated that only higher reason understands the universal.

[Main Text]
So again, along the furthest head
of that seventh circle, all alone
I went to where the sorrowful people sat.
Through their eyes their grief was bursting out;
with their hands they scurried here and there,
now against the vapor, now the hot soil.
Not otherwise do dogs in summer,
now with snout, now with paw, when bitten...

[Commentary Block 3]
**He shows** how he went alone to the usurers. And he shows how they sit and do not walk, and we have stated the reason above. He makes a comparison: just as dogs continuously defend themselves from the bites of worms that bother them, so these people defend themselves with their hands, now from the flames raining down, now from the hot soil—that is, from the hot earth. And because we have arrived at such a sin, we will speak briefly of **usury**. Usury is the sale of the "use" of things that have no use <note>Meaning things that cannot be separated from their use</note>, or of those things that are consumed solely by use. And it should be noted that certain things have "use" and certain things do not. Those things have "use" which are useful to human life either by necessity or for well-being, such as bread, wine, and clothing.

<summary>Dante approaches the edge of the seventh circle to observe the usurers while Virgil negotiates with Geryon. The commentary identifies Geryon with the beaver and explains usury as a sin against nature and industry.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of usury from Canto XVII of Dante's Inferno, transitioning from the theoretical sin to the specific punishment of usurers in the Seventh Circle.</meta>

->CANTO XVII. 92<-

...from fleas, from flies, or from gadflies. They do not have use of those things without which we can live comfortably, such as gems; and they do not have multiplication, because gold does not make more gold, nor do gems make more gems <note>This is the classic Aristotelian argument that money is "barren" and should not be able to "breed" interest</note>. Furthermore, of the things that have use, some are consumed in that very use, such as bread and wine. Others are consumed over time, such as houses and clothing and the like. Therefore, he who takes a price for loaned money sins, because it has no use <note>Meaning it has no use-value independent of its exchange-value</note>. Similarly, he who takes a price for loaned bread or wine commits usury because it is consumed in its use; but in lending a house, which is consumed by time and by use, one does not commit usury by taking a price for it, because it worsens in use, and it is necessary that from time to time it be repaired. But of usury we spoke in the eleventh chapter.

**As soon as I directed my eyes toward their faces,**
**on which the painful fire falls,**
**I recognized none of them; but I noticed**
**that from the neck of each hung a pouch**
**which had a certain color and a certain emblem,**
**and there it seems the eye feeds itself.**
**And as I came among them, looking around,**
**I saw upon a yellow purse something blue,**
**which had the face and bearing of a lion.**
**Then, as the path of my gaze proceeded,**
**I saw another, red as blood,**
**displaying a goose whiter than butter.**

<margin>d</margin> This shows that these people were so scorched by the fire that they could not be recognized. This is intended allegorically, meaning that this vice of usury makes men infamous and strips them of every good name and reputation; and among generous souls and prudent men, they are held in no value, and men do not deign to know them. And certainly, although ambition is a great vice, it nevertheless has some generosity of spirit. Lust has some species of benevolence. But avarice is a sordid, vile, and ignoble thing. For this reason, he feigns that he knew them only by the pouches <note>The pouches are money-bags decorated with family coats of arms</note> which they had at their necks. This shows that such men are not known for any virtue of their own, but only for the pile of coins illicitly gathered; and on these pouches were painted the arms of these people, because their dignity consists in nothing else. By the blue lion on the yellow field, he shows that man to be of the house of Gianfigliazzi <note>A prominent Florentine family of Guelph usurers</note>. THEN, as the path of my gaze proceeded: This is like a passing over, because the eye proceeds continuously from thing to thing, just as a chariot proceeds on its journey. And by the white goose on the red field, he means the Ubriachi family; which was once very honored in our republic.

**And one who had his little white sack**
**marked with a blue and pregnant sow,**
**said to me: "What are you doing in this pit?**
**Now go away; and because you are still alive,**
**know that my neighbor Vitaliano**
**shall sit here at my left side.**

**With these Florentines, I am a Paduan,**
**and many times they thunder in my ears,**
**shouting: 'Let the sovereign knight come,**
**who will bring the pouch with the three goats!'**
**Then he twisted his face and stuck out**
**his tongue, like an ox licking its nose.**

<margin>f</margin> Following this, he places Messer Rinaldo degli Scrovegni, a Paduan knight. This family had on a white field a blue and pregnant sow. And in short, he shows that the usurer has no fame of his own, but only that of his money and his family. THUNDER in my ears: because they shout. LET the sovereign knight COME: spoken with irony, as he is vile and a miser; and he refers to Messer Giovanni Buiamonte, whose arms carry three goats <note>original: "tre becchi," referring to the Buiamonte family of Florence</note>.

**And I, fearing that staying longer might anger**
**him who had warned me to stay only briefly,**
**turned back from those weary souls.**
**I found my guide, who had already climbed**
**upon the rump of the fierce animal,**
**and he said to me: "Now be strong and daring.**
**Henceforth we descend by such stairs as these;**
**mount in front, for I wish to be in the middle,**
**so that the tail cannot do you harm."**

<margin>n</margin> One can never go safely through Hell—and from there exit through Purgatory all the way to Heaven—if Dante does not obey Virgil in all his precepts. Therefore, because he had been warned to be brief, he returns immediately; and he finds Virgil already climbed upon the beast. Because to pass through these circles of the fraudulent, it is necessary that Dante—that is, the lower reason or sensuality—knows the particulars; and Virgil—that is, the superior reason—knows this craftiness in its general nature, and climbs upon it; that is, he submits it to himself, and wants Dante to ride it as well. That is, that the appetite should also dominate and submit it to itself. I FOUND my guide, who had already climbed upon the rump: While Dante considers craftiness in this or that particular man, Virgil knows it in its abstract genus, separate from every particular. And having known it, he rides it as we have said; and he was on the rump, that is, he was at the final species of craftiness. AND he said to me: "Now then." Mount up: because it is necessary that sensuality be exhorted by reason so that it does not let itself be corrupted by vice. And Virgil places himself between the tail of the beast and Dante, so that the tail does not offend him. For when sensuality has recognized craftiness, it might perhaps slip into following it; and in this way, its end would be harmful if reason did not interpose itself.

M ii <note>Printer's signature mark</note>

| As one who approaches the shivering | <note>n</note> It is not to be wondered at that Dante was terrified seeing where he had to climb; for although **sensuality** <note>The physical desires or instincts</note> obeys **reason**, nevertheless, until a firm habit of **fortitude** is established, the appetite is bound to be dismayed in great undertakings. He says, therefore, that hearing the words of Virgil, he trembled, thinking he had to climb upon that beast: just as he trembles who approaches the shivering, that is, the "shudder" <note>original: *capricio*</note> of the quartan fever. **The Shadow.** <note>original: *El Rezo*</note> The shade. **BUT HIS THREATS MADE ME ASHAMED.** Virgil did not actually threaten him; but we understand that every command has implicit threats within it: because when someone held by you in the highest reverence commands you, it seems that such commands are threats. **WHICH IN THE PRESENCE OF A GOOD LORD MAKES A SERVANT STRONG.** When the servant knows he has a good—that is, a just and discreet—lord, and feels himself threatened by him, he takes heart: because he knows the lord would not command things he could not do, nor things that would not be useful to him. **I WISHED TO SAY.** Thus I wished to say: that is, "make sure you embrace me." They feign this because he was king of three islands, namely the two Balearics, which are Majorca and Minorca, and Ibiza <note>original: "maiolica & minolica & debuſo"</note>; and that Hercules, fighting him, killed him in three stages, killing one body each time. # CANTO XVII 93

...[the sun's] chariot, which the poets imagine to be guided by four horses. These are: **Pyroeis**, **Eous**, **Aethon**, and **Phlegon**. <note>These Greek names symbolize the sun's progression: 'The Fiery One,' 'The Belonging to the Dawn,' 'The Burning One,' and 'The Blazing One.'</note> Phaethon was already in the middle of the sky when the horses, no longer fearing their driver as they ought, abandoned the **fourth heaven** <note>In the Ptolemaic system used by Dante, the Sun resides in the fourth celestial sphere, preceded by the Moon, Mercury, and Venus.</note> in which the sun revolves. They descended not only below the third heaven of Venus and the second of Mercury, but even below the moon, which is in the first heaven. The Earth felt the excessive proximity of the sun, and everything began to burn. Because of this, moved to compassion, **Jove** <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods in Roman mythology.</note> struck Phaethon with celestial lightning and cast him into the **Po** <note>The river Po in Northern Italy, associated with the mythical river Eridanus into which Phaethon fell.</note>; and there he died, serving as an example to all men, which warns them not to undertake enterprises beyond their own strength.

**Icarus** was the son of **Daedalus**, whose entire history would be too long to narrate here. However, being unable to escape from Crete by any other means—and because he was a man of the highest industry and skill in many things—he fashioned wings for himself and for his son: that [one]...

**INFERNO**

**CANTO XVIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.**

Place there is in Hell called <term>Malebolge</term> <note>original: "malebogle"; literally "Evil Pouches" or "Evil Ditches," referring to the ten concentric trenches of the eighth circle.</note>
all of stone and of an iron-gray color,
like the circular wall that surrounds it.

**X** Right in the center of the malignant field
there yawns a pit, remarkably wide and deep,
of which I will describe the structure in its proper place.

That space that remains is therefore circular,
between the pit and the foot of the high, hard bank,
and its floor is divided into ten valleys.

**i** In this eighteenth canto, the author begins to treat the eighth circle, where fraud against those who have no special bond of trust is punished <note>Dante distinguishes between "simple fraud" (theft, flattery, etc.) and "treachery," which is fraud against those with whom one has a specific bond like family or country.</note>. For in the preceding canto, he described cunning in general in the figure of <term>Geryon</term> <note>A mythological monster representing fraud, possessing the face of a "just man" but the body of a serpent and a stinging tail.</note>, by whom they were transported from the circle of the violent to that of the fraudulent, and there Geryon set them down. This signifies that after the contemplation of fraud in general, they began to consider its specific types and details. And because there are ten types of fraud, this circle is likewise divided into ten ditches. However, in the present canto, only the first is treated and the description of the second begins.

[Left Column]

In this place, shaken off from Geryon’s
back, we found ourselves. The poet
kept to the left, and I moved behind him.
At the right hand I saw new miseries,
new torments, and new scourgers,
with which the first ditch <note>The first "bolgia" or circular trench of the ten that make up the eighth circle.</note> was filled.

Just as the Romans, because of the great crowd

So that on one side all have their faces
toward the castle <note>Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome.</note> and go toward Saint Peter’s,

On this side and that, up along the dark rock,
I saw horned demons with great whips,
who beat them cruelly from behind.
Ah, how they made them lift their legs <gloss>original: lerze</gloss>

awaited the second or the third.

While I was going, my eyes upon one
were met; and I immediately said:
"I am not hungry for the sight of this one;" <note>An idiomatic way of saying "I have seen this person before."</note>
Therefore, to recognize him I fixed my eyes;
and my sweet leader stopped with me,
and consented that I go back a little.
And that scourged one thought to hide himself
by lowering his face, but it availed him little,
for I said: "You, who cast your eyes to the ground,
If the features you carry are not false,
you are Venedico Caccianimico..."

[Right Column and Bottom Section]

**Geryon**, shaking his back, unloaded us in the place mentioned above. This denotes that after the consideration of fraud in general, they began to consider the particulars, as we said a little while ago. And the poet kept to the left for the reason we have already alleged above, and Dante kept behind him. **AT THE Right hand.** Because, in circling the place from the left hand, the place where the sinners were remained to the right. **NEW TORments:** because he had not yet found souls who were whipped, nor demon scourgers of said souls.

At the bottom were naked sinners who were being beaten. And it shows that this ditch was divided into two parts. For on the side toward Dante, the sinners came to meet them. The others who were in the other part went along with us, but with longer strides than ours. Therefore, this ditch was divided like the bridge at Sant'Angelo in the **YEAR of the Jubilee**; which, divided lengthwise, on one side receives those who go toward Castel Sant'Angelo and toward Saint Peter’s. On the other side, those who come from Saint Peter’s. **YEAR of the Jubilee.** Jubilee in the Hebrew language signifies "a year of remission and liberation." <note>The Hebrew term "Yovel" (ram's horn) marks the 50th year when debts were forgiven and slaves freed.</note> For the Hebrews, having finished the seventh seven-year cycle, which is the fiftieth year, liberated all servants, and remitted and canceled all debts; and they called such a year the Jubilee. In imitation of this, the Christian Church later ordained that every fiftieth year the Supreme Pontiff should liberate [people] from their sins, granting a plenary indulgence to all those who, confessed and contrite, visited the Roman churches. And because in this year there is an infinite gathering of men in the city of Rome, and a great crowd forms on the bridge at Sant'Angelo from those who go to or come from Saint Peter’s in the Vatican, Pope Boniface [VIII] instituted in the year 1300 that the bridge should be divided by its length, and one part should serve those going to Saint Peter’s, and the other those returning. So, then, is this path of the *Malebolge* <note>The "Evil Ditches" of the eighth circle.</note> divided: and through one part go those who have corrupted women either with words or with money to supply them to others; and through the other, those who in the same way have corrupted them to have them for themselves. These people, then, are never allowed to rest, but have demons behind them who beat and drive them with whips. For just as they did not let the women live in their peace, but with the "whips" of flatteries or rewards pushed them to their will, so now the demons drive them. And we can rightly understand by the demons the **remorses of conscience** which always afflict one who is stained by such a vice.

**ON THIS SIDE AND THAT:** that is, both where those who are going are, and where those who are coming are. **UP ALONG the dark rock.** Black and ugly. I saw demons who, running behind them, beat them cruelly in a way that made them run quickly; and always at the first lash they would leap away. **LIFT their legs.** <gloss>lerze</gloss> The legs. Here it should be noted that he shows the punishment of seducers. And "seduction" is to induce someone by deceit to do what they should not. And although seduction is of many types, nevertheless here he treats the seduction that induces the vice of the flesh. And this is committed in two ways: either by seducing a woman in a way that she consents to someone else, or truly to himself. And because the vice of lust is the least grave sin among mortal sins, he therefore places seduction in this vice as less grave than in the others.

**HERE** he introduces having found **Messer Venedico de’ Caccianimici** from Bologna; and not without reason does he suggest that he tried to hide himself. For such a vice is so abominable not only among the good but even among the wicked, that no one is so impudent or so shameless that they are not ashamed to be noted for such infamy. There are many vices which, although they should be fled, nevertheless have in them some shadow of virility. But this one is noted as the most vile even of the most vile. Messer Venedico de’ Caccianimici of Bologna was the middleman <note>A pimp or procurer.</note> through whom the Marquis Obizzo da Este, Lord of Ferrara, had his sister, who was called Ghisolabella. **AND NOT only I here weep as a Bolognese.** This denotes that many Bolognese are filthy with such vice, saying that there are not as many tongues [as there are sinners of this type]. **TAUGHT:** that is, prepared. **TO SAY sipa.** <note>A dialectal term from Bologna meaning "yes."</note> Between the Savena and the Reno [rivers]. There are not as many tongues [spoken] in Bologna...

...such length, nor shall we leave them entirely behind; so <margin>Z</margin> that the reader does not remain entirely ignorant of these matters. There were in Thessaly <note>A region in northern Greece.</note> two brothers: Pelias, king of that region, and Aeson. From Aeson was born Jason, who, because he was very beautiful of body, robust, and of a great and excellent spirit, desired to do something worthy of memory. At this, his uncle [Pelias] encouraged him, not so much to favor his glory, but because he feared—having no male children of his own—that Jason and his father might plot a fraud to take the kingdom from him. He hoped that by setting Jason to arduous tasks full of danger, he might easily perish. Therefore, he urged him to undertake the capture of the Golden Fleece of the ram of Phrixus, which was in Colchis, a city of the Pontus <note>The Black Sea region.</note>. 

But so that we may briefly mention the Golden Fleece: <margin>A</margin> From Athamas and Nephele were born Phrixus and Helle; these were later driven out by their father through the treachery of their stepmother, Ino. Juno commanded them to climb upon the back of their ram, which their father had given them, and with it cross the sea. But during this passage, Helle, a fearful girl, fell into the sea; and from her, that sea is since called the Hellespont <note>The "Sea of Helle," modern-day Dardanelles.</note>. Phrixus reached Colchis where Aeëtes reigned, and he consecrated the skin of the ram to Mars. This is what Jason wanted, and for this, he built the ship on Mount Pelion, which was called *Argo* after the craftsman who composed it, or else for its speed, because *Argos* in Greek means "swift" <note>original: "argos in greco fignifica ueloce"</note>. 

With him went the principal men of Greece, among whom were: Hercules, Telamon, Orpheus, Castor, and Pollux. And first they arrived <margin>B</margin> at Lemnos, which was an island without males. This was because, having gone against Thrace, the men had performed sacrifices to all the gods except Venus. Venus wished to take her revenge, and for this, she ignited those women with such fury that by common counsel they first killed those few men who had remained on the island. Later, when the others returned in victory, the women waited for the night; and as they fell asleep, each woman killed her husband, except for Hypsipyle—or more correctly, *Hisypyle*. Moved by compassion for her father Thoas, the king, she secretly sent him away from the island, pretending with honorable funeral rites that she had already killed him. In Lemnos, the Argonauts stayed for one year, mingling with the women. And Jason, to have Hypsipyle (who was then queen), promised to take her as his wife and to return there; but he left her pregnant with two sons, Thoas and Euneus. He never returned to her thereafter. He reached Colchis, but he could not have the Golden Fleece unless he first killed the great serpent that...

and she beats herself with her palms:
