->**and it forms the shape of a cross: AND IT MAKES OF THAT BANK a shoulder**<- to another circle: that is, to the second. Having described the path that led them above the second pouch, he describes what kind of torment is contained within it. He shows, therefore, that this pouch is full of human excrement: and in it the souls are submerged: who in such a form *moan* <term>nicchiano; a term meaning to lament or complain with a low, querulous voice</term>. **HE PUFFS:** <term>sbuffa; to blow in such a way that the breath comes out with force and hidden anger</term>. Because when an angry person grieves and at the same time insults and threatens with arrogant words, we say that he "puffs." **THE BANKS were crusted with a mold.** This happens in damp and enclosed places where the vapors rising from such moisture, unable to escape, remain attached to the walls and create mold. So in this place the breath—that is, the exhalation rising from the bottom—rose up so thick that it stuck to the banks: and created such a crust that it fought a battle with the nose and the eyes: it offended the nose by its foul smell, and the eyes by its ugliness. And the bottom was so deep that one could not see well without climbing onto the back of the rock, which was like the arch of a bridge. From there, one could look straight down. In such a vile and filthy place are punished the flatterers: who in the Florentine language are called *moinieri* <note>original: "moinieri," from "moine," meaning affected caresses or fawning gestures</note>. Flattery is nothing other than speech containing false praise for the sake of pleasing and gaining the favor of the person being praised. Such a vice proceeds only from a vile and servile soul, in which there is no trace of freedom. Truly they can be called the dregs of men, because nothing remains in them but corruption. And just as in the body of an animal the dregs are nothing but the corrupted part—which nature separates from incorruptible nourishment during the first digestion in the stomach and sends down to the lower bowels—so from the incorruptible truth which nourishes the soul and maintains moral life, flattery is separated as something corrupted and harmful to human life. Deservedly, then, it can be said that the flatterer is submerged in dregs, and eats and spews it. Because the flatterer being full of lies, he is nothing but corruption: he feeds on nothing else, and feeds others on nothing else. This man shows friendship and benevolence, yet is the worst enemy. Nothing more pernicious is found by anyone established in dignity and lordship than flattery: which, to please him, persuades him that what is evil is good and just; from here proceed many errors that are often the cause of the ruin of princes and great men. Because believing the false praise, they not only do not correct their evil, but are confirmed in their foolishness; because being in prosperous fortune, they repute themselves almost as gods. And there is nothing so great that they do not believe about themselves. Regarding this, Juvenal said: <note>original: "Nihil est quod credere de se non possit cum laudatur diis æqua potestas"</note> *There is nothing a man cannot believe about himself when he is praised as having power equal to the gods.* And rightly Diogenes the Cynic, when asked which beast bites most fiercely, replied: "Among wild animals, the slanderer; and among domestic ones, the flatterer," because with his false praise he leads you to ruin. And he added that composed words, used not to reveal the truth but to please, are a honeyed noose. And Plato shows that the difference between a true friend and a flatterer is the same as that between a doctor and a cook. For the doctor, in giving food, does not seek to please the taste but to promote health; the cook attends only to pleasing the taste, regardless of whether it is healthy or harmful. So the true friend only respects telling the truth to his friend to preserve him in virtue and lead him to it. But the flatterer does not care if others err; it is enough for him to say what pleases in order to achieve his own convenience. Therefore, Cicero in his book *On Duties* warns us: <note>original: "Atque etiam in secundissimis rebus..."</note> *And even in the most prosperous circumstances, the advice of friends should be used most, and greater authority should be attributed to them than before. Finally, in these times we must take care not to open our ears to hangers-on, nor allow ourselves to be flattered, in which it is easy to be deceived. For we think ourselves such that we are rightly praised; from which innumerable sins are born when men, inflated by opinions, are shamefully mocked and wallow in the greatest errors.* We can also say that the poet puts them in such punishment to punish their superfluous delicacies, excessive luxuries, and splendid meals, which they sought with their flatteries and fawning while they were alive: because most excellently one contrary is punished with another contrary.

And while I searched down there with my eyes
I saw one with a head so fouled with dung,
that it wasn't clear if he were layman or cleric.
He cried out to me: "Why are you so greedy
to look at me more than the other filthy ones?"
And I to him: "Because, if I remember well,
I have seen you before with dry hair;
and you are Alessio Interminei of Lucca:
therefore I eye you more than all the others."
And he then, beating his pate:

->**M**<-esser **Alexo interminegli**, a knight of Lucca and a very great flatterer, is placed in this spot. **LAYMAN or cleric.** These two words are Greek. Here it should be noted that Christians are divided into two kinds: that is, priests and seculars. The priests are the apostolic church: and are the part chosen to rule the seculars and instruct them in the best precepts and honest life: for which reason they are called *clerici*: that is, the chosen: but through corruption of the word we say *cherici* <note>cleric/priest</note>. The seculars are the catholic church: that is, the universal: and in spiritual life they have to obey the priests. And therefore they are called *laici* <note>laymen</note>, almost as if to say "of the people" <note>from the Greek 'laos'</note>. This concludes that doctrine should be in the priests: for which reason great infamy is in those who are entirely unlearned.

He identifies Alessio Interminei of Lucca among the damned and discusses the moral and social corruption inherent in flattery.</summary>

[Top right column]
**Thais** is a prostitute from the works of Terence <note>A Roman playwright</note>: to whom Thraso, a soldier, gave a young maidservant—or you might say a slave girl—and later asking Gnatho (the middleman through whom he had sent the maid) if the gift had been pleasing to Thais, and if she returned great thanks to him. Gnatho, in order to flatter him, answered, "Not great, but greatest." Thus the actual flatterer was Gnatho; but the poet Dante places Thais here because it was by her will that he used such flattery. And because every prostitute, as they do not love the man but his money, is always full of endearments and flatteries. And because there are two kinds of flatterers: those of some name and dignity, although they stain it with such a vile vice; and others who are entirely low, and intent on the lowest gain. Therefore he placed Alessio for the first type, and Thais for the second. **DISHEVELED WENCH**: the punishment of the lustful woman once adorned with beautiful hair, who is now disheveled; and the punishment of the stubborn pride she showed toward her lovers has made her a slave to torment. The long filth of feces punishes the overly exquisite perfumes she sought in life. And that she now crouches and now stands has its allegory, but it is better to leave wrapped in its own obscurity that which cannot be decently explained. <margin>D</margin>

[Bottom commentary block]
This is the nineteenth canto, in which it is shown that in the third ditch the Simoniacs are punished. **Simony** is the sale or purchase of sacred and spiritual things for money, or for things equivalent to money. Therefore, whoever sells or buys the sacraments of the Church, or any spiritual dignity, or benefices, or other similar things—for which the true price is not gold nor silver, but sanctity of life and of morals, and virtue, and learning—is a Simoniac. This name comes from **Simon Magus**, who was the first who attempted this wickedness in the New Testament. In order that this may be more clearly understood, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that after the death of the first martyr Stephen, Philip preached the word of God <note>original: "verbum dei"</note> in Samaria and converted many through the incredible miracles he performed. There WAS at the same time in that city Simon, a philosopher and mage, <margin>F</margin> who, by the things he did with his magical arts, was in high authority and reputation. He, along with the others, believed Philip and was baptized. But the Holy Spirit was not yet in those baptized in Samaria; but when Peter and John arrived, they prayed for the baptized; and after the prayer, they placed their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it appearing to Simon a great thing that through the laying on of hands the Holy Spirit should come, he offered money to the apostles, so that they might give him such power: that by placing his hand upon a baptized person they would receive the Holy Spirit. To whom Peter replied: "May your money perish with you. And certainly, because you thought that the gift of God could be obtained for money, you have no part or lot in this matter. AND your heart is not right in the sight of God. KEEP your money, and pray to God if it be possible that this thought may depart from your heart; for I see you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity." FROM this **SIMON**, therefore, those who trade for a price sacred things are called Simoniacs in the New Testament. JUST AS in the Old Testament they were named after **Gehazi**, the servant of Elisha the prophet. Elisha the prophet cured from leprosy Naaman, the prince of the army of the King of Syria, by the power of God. HE WOULD NOT receive any reward from him, although he had brought many treasures. But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, having already departed, followed after Naaman and reached him, and claimed <note>original: "fixe" - likely "disse" (said)</note> that two of the sons of the prophets had come to him from Mount Ephraim, and he asked for them a talent of silver and two changes of clothes. Naaman gave him the clothes and two talents. Elisha knew... <margin>E</margin>

# **INFERNO**

## [Canto XIX]

Elisha <note>The biblical prophet Elisha, who famously punished his servant Gehazi for his greed (2 Kings 5).</note> revealed the fraud and greed of his servant. And he predicted to him that the leprosy of Naaman would cling to him and would remain within his lineage. And immediately he became white with leprosy. These men [the Simonists], therefore, act against the Gospel of Matthew, who writes in the tenth chapter: "What you have received freely from God, give freely" <note>original Latin: *Quod gratis donate deo accipitur gratis detur*; a reference to Matthew 10:8: "Freely you have received; freely give."</note>. Christ therefore commands through Matthew that the spiritual things which they receive without price from God, they should likewise give to those who deserve them without price.

O Simon <note>Simon Magus, a practitioner of magic in the New Testament (Acts 8) who attempted to buy the power to confer the Holy Spirit, giving his name to the sin of "simony."</note>, the first author and prince within the Christian church of such wickedness; and so he is the first in this <term>bolgia<note>A "ditch" or "pouch." Dante's Eighth Circle of Hell is divided into ten of these trenches, each containing a different type of fraudulent sinner.</note></term> to receive a fitting punishment. **MAGICIAN**: that is, an enchanter. In the Persian language, "magus" signifies a "wise man." For this reason, those who were called "philosophers" among the Greeks are called "magi" by the Persians. And of this species of philosophers were those three who came to adore Jesus with offerings of gold, incense, and myrrh. But because Zoroaster, one... <note>The text cuts off here, likely preparing to discuss Zoroaster as a historical figure associated with the origins of magic.</note>

| "Who is he, Master, who is so vexed, | Dante asks who it is who is vexed more than the others; and Virgil says he does not know, but promises to carry him down to him. This signifies, as we have said several times, that <term>science</term> <note>Meaning "systematic knowledge" or "theory" in the medieval sense.</note> does not provide knowledge of specific individuals, but it leads you to them. For example: science does not show that Boniface is a Simoniac. But by demonstrating the universal truth—that whoever sells sacred and divine things for money is a Simoniac—it leads the senses and lower reason to recognize that Boniface, who sells sacred and divine things for money, is a Simoniac. Therefore, Virgil carries Dante to the bottom where the soul was: that is, the higher intellect carries the lower reason to the knowledge of that vice in general, in which Dante then sees Boniface; that is, he recognizes the specific case. **Twitching more than his companions:** that is, the others who are placed in the same sort of punishment. **Redder flame:** The redder the flame, the greater the vitality and force it demonstrates. **Sucks:** <note>original: "SUCCIA"</note> correctly stated. Because heat draws moisture to itself. Therefore, it sucks it. **Which lies deeper:** which is more profound. **Of himself and his wrongs:** that is, of his errors and vices. For just as every virtue has rectitude, so every vice is "wrong" or "twisted." **So much does it seem beautiful to me:** <note>original: "TANTO me bello"</note> that is, it seems so good to me as it pleases you. He means that according to how much or how little it pleases you, it seems more or less "beautiful" to me—that is, desirable. Here the author shows that the lower reason and the senses submit entirely to the higher reason. When this happens, there is never discord in the soul, but it always has right and true judgment. To understand this better, let us imagine two people: in one, the senses are entirely in accord with reason. In the other, they are in discord. We will see that in the latter, there will be two different judgments. Reason will judge that one should value divine things more than money. But the senses will judge that money should be preferred to divine things. In the former, the senses are so obedient to reason that they always approve its judgment. Therefore, only that thing is beautiful and good to Dante (the senses) which pleases Virgil (the intellect). **You, Lord.** Because the superior reason must command and the senses obey. It never departs from his will when it is well-disposed. Furthermore, because reason has true knowledge when the senses are joined to it, it understands not only what is said, but also what is thought, even if one remains silent. **So much is beautiful:** that is, lovable and desirable, because love, according to Plato, is nothing other than the desire for beautiful things. **You are my lord and you know that I do not depart from your will.** He explains the same point more clearly. **And you know what is left unsaid.** For reason can comprehend the thoughts of the soul. This was also signified above when he said: *Ah, how cautious men must be against those who do not see just the surface, but look into the thoughts with their wisdom.* **Upon the fourth bank:** which is between the ground and the fourth ditch. And the master did not put him down until he arrived at the pit: because knowledge does not leave us until we reach the particulars. **Shank** <note>original: "ZANCHA"</note> signifies leg. |

He <note>Referring to Jason, a figure from the biblical Book of Maccabees who bought the office of High Priest</note> obtained the abandonment of ancient sacrifices and the Mosaic laws; he instituted the cult of the Gentiles, wrestling schools, and gymnasiums where he made the young men exercise lasciviously. <note>Dante is addressing Pope Nicholas III, who is buried upside down in a hole for the sin of simony.</note>

A carnal church corrupted by <term>simony</term><note>The sin of selling or purchasing spiritual offices or roles, named after Simon Magus.</note> and by lust. # INFERNO.

**D** Of a new punishment I must now make verses,
and give matter to the twentieth canto
of the first song <note>original: "canzon"; here referring to the *Inferno* as the first part of the *Divine Comedy*</note> that I submerged.
I was already fully prepared
to look into the uncovered depths
which were bathed in anguished weeping.

The poet continues in his description of the trenches <note>original: "bolgie"; the ten circular ravines of the eighth circle of Hell</note> and establishes that in the fourth, the diviners of every kind are punished. It was certainly a very ancient opinion, confirmed by the consensus of all nations, that among men there is a certain presumption and science of future things, which the Latins call "divination" and the Greeks call *Mantice* <note>original: "Mátice"; prophecy or the mantic arts</note>. This is either natural or artificial. Natural divination contains within itself divine frenzy and dreams. Since many, moved by divine frenzy, as among the pagans—

[Woodcut illustration depicting a group of people in a rocky landscape, walking in a circle with their heads turned 180 degrees to face backwards. Various figures are shown in different states of distress. Small numbers and letters like 'D', '1-80', '880', '100', 'b', and '<<<80' are integrated into the image.]

—utilized oracles, and among the Hebrews, the prophets predicted future things. Dreams are of three types. Since sometimes one dreams of what is to be, but it needs interpretation—like the man who dreamed of pressing grapes into a cup, and Joseph interpreted that he would become the king's cupbearer <note>A biblical reference to Joseph interpreting dreams in Pharaoh's prison</note> and serve him at the table with the cup. Sometimes one dreams of seeing the thing in the same way it will happen; this is called a vision. Sometimes there appears in the dream someone who relates things exactly as they will be, and this they call an oracle. But often they are combined, as in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, where Aeneas saw Hector in a very sad and mournful form and heard the words in which he comforted him and told him to flee. 

**P** Artificial divination includes within it Haruspicy <note>original: "Aurispicina"; divination by inspecting entrails</note>, Augury, Astrology, and Lots. Haruspicy includes the divination taken from the shape, position, and color of the internal organs of the animal which was sacrificed—as on the morning of the day Julius Caesar was killed, the heart of the ox he sacrificed was not seen. Augury is divination made either from the feeding or the chirping of birds. For the augurs sometimes offered food to chickens which they kept enclosed for this purpose, and according to how they fed, they interpreted the outcome of the matter. Sometimes they watched the sky, the flight, and the song of birds, and according to their kind they judged. For the raven gives one omen, the crow another, the woodpecker another, and others differently. And it is one thing for them to sing and fly in one way, and another in another. And it is one thing if they appear on the right, and another on the left. Nor is it only birds; other animals also give good and bad omens, such as wolves, foxes, dogs, and serpents, and the like. Nor are monsters and portents very different from these, which occur against nature. Whence in the army of Xerxes, because a mare gave birth to a hare, the augurs announced the timid flight of that army. 

Astrology predicts future things according to the various courses of the stars in which there are conjunctions, oppositions, sextiles, trines, quadratures, and other aspects. And of this they say Geomancy <note>divination by patterns in the earth or soil</note> is a species, which we will treat in the *Purgatorio*. And Lots, found according to the ancients in the city of Praeneste, today called Palestrina. And Pyromancy, done with fire. Necromancy, with dead bodies to which the soul is recalled. Hydromancy, done with water. Chiromancy, which is considered in the lines of the hand. All these things would require their own discourse if we wanted to explain them in their order. But time is not enough for one who sets himself such a long and diverse subject. 

**OF A NEW** punishment: almost unusual and unheard of, and greater than the others; it makes the listener attentive by promising unusual and significant things. **AND GIVE** matter to the twentieth canto: that is, to the twentieth chapter. **OF THE** first song: that is, of the first canticle. There are three canticles: *Inferno*, *Purgatorio*, and *Paradiso*. And the *Inferno* contains thirty-four cantos, and the other two contain thirty-three cantos each. Thus, in all there are one hundred cantos divided into three canticles. **WHICH** I submerged: that is, which I plunged into the center of the earth. He does not submerge the canticle, but describes the submerged Hell in it. Some texts have "Of the first songs and of the submerged": that is, of the damned who are submerged in the center of the earth. And it follows that he was already prepared to see the bottom of the earth uncovered, which he could see from the bridge where he was. **WHICH** was bathed in the tears of those who are punished there.

And I saw people through the circular valley
coming silent and weeping at the pace
that litanies <note>religious processions involving prayer and chanting</note> make in this world.
As my sight sank lower into them,
it appeared wonderfully to be twisted.

He establishes their punishment to be this: that they have their faces turned backward. And to want to see where they are going, they must walk backward. This is a very fitting punishment <note>a "contrapasso," where the punishment mirrors the sin</note>, that the contrary is punished with its contrary. And he who wanted to see too far forward should now see only what is behind. And he who was so bold as to want to see the future—which God has denied to man as something not useful—nor is it likely that God, being able to give us true knowledge...

# THE COMMENTARY of Cristoforo Landino of Florence on the Comedy of Dante Alighieri, the Florentine Poet.

**A**LTHOUGH there is no category of learned writers, my most illustrious lords <note>Landino is likely addressing the Signoria, the governing body of Florence, to whom this work was dedicated.</note>, to whom the human race does not owe the greatest, innumerable, and immortal gratitude. This is especially true considering that they have contributed all their industry, discipline, most watchful study, and laborious nighttime toil <term>lucubrations<note>original: "lucubratio". This refers to scholarly work produced by staying up late by candlelight, signifying intense dedication.</note></term> to the common good. They do this so that they might live not only for themselves and their contemporaries, but also bring significant benefit to all people who will exist in the various ages and succeeding years to come. 

Nevertheless, after having often reviewed in my mind the nearly infinite number of those who left a memory of themselves in either the Greek or Latin languages, I find no one who is fit to be compared or equated to this poet <note>Referring to Dante Alighieri.</note>. He, certainly through the depth and variety of his learning, as well as the elegance, richness, and sublimity of his style, is able to reveal great things to us, both for our lives and for...

Therefore, forty thousand <note>The text likely refers to gold florins or ducats, the standard currency of trade</note> make one <term>load</term> <note>original: *soma*, a unit of weight based on what a single pack animal could carry</note> of four hundred pounds. This wealth was, for the most part, gathered from the taxes contributed by private citizens. 

And certainly, just as we see bees from a single hive spread themselves across the entire region and bring back honey from every side, so does this people spread throughout the whole world; with great industry, they accumulate wealth and bring it home. For this reason, Italy has no city that—after Rome—is better known or more famous. In every land, she is honored with three titles: that she is most famous, most beautiful, and that she abounds with the most subtle intellects.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Inferno, the first part of Dante's Divine Comedy. It includes the famous opening verses followed by the extensive commentary of Cristoforo Landino, a prominent Renaissance scholar whose 1481 edition helped cement Dante’s status as a "divine" poet.</meta>

->**CANTO ONE. ii**<-

->**CANTO ONE OF THE FIRST canticle or rather comedy of the divine Florentine Poet Dante Alighieri. Chapter I.**<-

[Large woodcut initial **N** containing a figure of a man writing at a desk]
**IN the middle of**
**the journey of**
**our life**
**I found myself**
**within a dark**
**woods**
**For the direct**
**way was lost**
Ah, how hard a thing it is to say what it was like,
this wild woods, harsh and difficult,
which in thought renews the fear!
So bitter was it that death is little more;
but to treat of the good that I found there,
I will tell of the other things I perceived.
I cannot well repeat how I entered there,
so full of sleep was I at that point
that I abandoned the true way.
But after I had reached the foot of a hill,
there where that valley ended
which had pierced my heart with fear,
I looked up and saw its shoulders
clothed already in the rays of the planet <note>In the Ptolemaic astronomy of Dante's time, the Sun was considered a planet that moved around the Earth.</note>
that leads others straight along every path.
Then the fear was somewhat quieted
that had endured in the lake of my heart
through the night I passed with such anguish. <note>original: "pieta". In this context, it refers to intense suffering or fear rather than modern "pity".</note>

[Woodcut illustration: A landscape with trees and rocks. Dante is seen in the foreground, and Virgil stands before him. Three beasts—a leopard, a lion, and a she-wolf—block the path.]

<margin>h</margin> We have narrated not only the life of the poet and the title of the book and what it means to be a poet, but also how ancient and antique, how noble and varied, and how useful and joyful such a doctrine <note>The "doctrine" refers to the art of poetry itself.</note> is. We have shown how effective it is in moving human minds and how much it delights every noble spirit. Nor did we think it right to remain silent about how excellent the genius of our poet was in such divine discipline. In this, if I have been briefer than perhaps was appropriate, let the reader consider that the numerous and almost infinite abundance of things which must be treated forces me—not wishing the volume to grow beyond measure—to compress and involve rather than explain and extend many things, especially those which, even if I were silent, would not leave the exposition of the text obscure. We shall come, then, to the work itself. But because I believe there is no reader of such low wit or poor judgment that, having understood the depth and variety of the learning and the excellence and divinity of the genius of our Tuscan and Florentine poet, they would not be persuaded that this beginning of the first canto must, by its sublimity and grandeur, be equal to the stupendous learning of the things that follow. Therefore, with all industry, we will investigate what allegorical sense this "middle of the journey" brings with it, and what "the woods" might be. Regarding this, I see no small difference among the interpreters and expositors of this canticle. For some say that the middle of human life is sleep; they are moved, I believe, by the sentiment of Aristotle <note>original: "aristotile"</note> saying in his *Ethics* <note>original: "ethica"</note> that there is no difference between the happy and the miserable during the half of their life, because the nights, which are half of our time, bring us sleep; and from that, it arises that we can feel neither good nor evil. Because of this, these interpreters want the poet to use "the middle of life" to mean the night, and "the night" for sleep, to note that this poem is nothing other than a vision that appeared to him while sleeping, through which he gained knowledge of the things described in these three comedies. They say, therefore, that he imitates John the Evangelist, who, while sleeping upon the breast of Christ the Redeemer, had a vision of celestial things; or alternatively, he sets the scene at night to show that he began his poem at night, a time when the soul, withdrawing into itself and being absolved and liberated from every care, understands better. But although such a sentiment fits the poet, nevertheless the words do not demonstrate it except with such obscure ambiguity that it does not seem worthy of the elegance of such a poet. First, because it does not follow that even if nights occupy as much space in the revolutions of time as days, I should mean "I wrote in the middle of my age" by saying "I wrote at night"; for nights occur in the beginning and the end of human life just as in the middle, and similarly for the day. Therefore, by the same logic, one could make such an interpretation for the day as for the night. Others say that by "the middle of the journey" he means that he gave a beginning to his poem in the middle of his age. But <margin>A</margin> there is not one single opinion regarding the limit of our age, because different writers feel differently. <margin>B</margin>

Below the verse, Cristoforo Landino begins his scholarly commentary, debating whether "the middle of the journey" refers to literal sleep, a spiritual vision, or the poet's chronological age.</summary>

->**INFERNO.**<-

Aristotle, in his *Politics* <note>original: "de republica"</note>, seems to approve the opinion of certain poets who divide human life by the <term>septenary number</term> <note>the number seven, which was historically considered to have mystical and biological significance</note>, attributing the first seven years to infancy. The second seven to childhood. The third, reaching twenty-one, to adolescence. Afterward, they place two septenaries <note>two periods of seven years</note> for youth, arriving at thirty-five; and Aristotle maintains in the same work that this age is the perfect time to celebrate marriages. After youth follows the <term>virile age</term> <note>the age of mature manhood</note> which, through two more septenaries, reaches the forty-ninth year. In this time, because men possess perfect judgment and have not yet lost their physical strength, that great philosopher judges that man is most fit for the government of the republic. And finally, he places the rest of life in three septenaries. He intends the limit to be seventy years, almost as if foreseeing his own death, which occurred in the seventieth year of his life. He was moved to this conclusion especially because the number seven is not only made of seven, but is also multiplied by ten, a perfect number. This same opinion is held by the Psalmist <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms</note> saying: "Our years shall be considered as a spider’s web. The days of our years are seventy years. If, however, by reason of strength, they be eighty years: and their further span is but labor and sorrow" <note>original: "Anni nostri sicut aranea meditabuntur. dies annorum nostrorum in ipsis septuaginta anni. Si autem in potentatibus octuaginta anni: & amplius eorum labor & dolor"</note>. Pythagoras of Samos set the end of life at the eightieth year; and likewise, he died at that time. Solon of Athens also set eighty years. The astrologers, who refer everything to the course of the stars, grant ninety-five years. They claim the Moon contributes four; Mercury ten; Venus eight; the Sun nineteen; Mars fifteen; Jupiter twelve. Afterward, in the remainder of the <term>decrepit age</term> <note>extreme old age</note>, Saturn reigns; and in this stage there is coldness, fatigue, distress, and heaviness of body and mind. Because of this, few reach it. There were some who, as Servius <note>a 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> reports in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*, said there were three kinds of limits to our life: of nature, of fate, and of chance. They want Nature to extend to the fourth course of Saturn; because he completes his revolution in thirty years, this would be one hundred and twenty years. Fate fills three courses of Saturn; therefore, death comes in the ninetieth year. But if the benevolence of some happy star breaks the malice of Saturn, a man can reach the aforementioned fourth course. Hence Josephus <note>the Jewish historian</note> in his *Antiquities* writes that God, after Noah’s flood, shortened the years of human life—which before the flood had passed nine hundred in some cases—and decreed that the final limit should be one hundred and twenty. And for this reason, certain interpreters of Statius <note>a Roman poet</note> claim that when he writes of King Adrastus: "The King Adrastus ruled his people there, passing into old age, tranquilly at the middle limit of life" <note>original: "Rex ibi tranquille medio de limite uite. In senium uergens populos Adrastus habebat"</note>, he means he was in his sixtieth year, which is the middle of one hundred and twenty. Nevertheless, because the common opinion of men follows Aristotle and David, they understand the middle of life to be thirty-five years. But although such an exposition is not at all discordant with the truth, it seems that for so lofty a poem, another beginning is required. So that we may better express this, we will briefly repeat some matters from further back, which will clearly reveal the mind of the author to us, so that it will be easy to interpret this beginning. It is likely, then, that Dante proposes for himself the same goal that Homer among the Greeks and Virgil among the Latins had proposed. And just as they—one through Ulysses, the other through Aeneas—demonstrate how, by coming to the knowledge of vices and, having known them, purging oneself of them, one finally arrives at the contemplation of divine things; so Dante, under this fiction of the pilgrimage he feigns to have made with Virgil, demonstrates that same thing in your person. Man is composed of soul and body. The soul is divine, simple, immortal, and incorruptible. And because it is produced by God in His image and likeness, it is divine and full of light, and is capable through contemplation of reaching the knowledge of divine things and enjoying God, in which consists our supreme good, as we shall treat more fully in another place. The body, on the contrary, being composed of the matter of the four elements, is by its nature corruptible, dark, and full of shadows. The soul, therefore, is submerged in this dark prison and loses almost all its celestial vigor; and through the shadows of the body, it remains almost deprived of all light of reason. 
<margin>B</margin> And it can be said that the soul is buried under the corporeal mass. Hence the divine Plato wisely posits two species of death. One he calls "death of the animal," a thing known to all, which occurs when the soul is separated from the body. The other is "death of the soul," and this is when the soul, as we have already said, is submerged by the weight and darkness of the body and loses so much vigor that none of its excellent powers can operate. Because of this, we see that man—not only in the first years of infancy and childhood, but for a great part of adolescence and youth—lives only according to the senses. And because he knows nothing else, he does not believe himself to be anything else; he considers nothing good except those things that delight the bodily senses. Nor does he consider anything evil except that which saddens them. Like a drunkard or one oppressed by deep sleep, he neither knows himself, nor understands for what purpose he was produced, nor knows his own ignorance or misery, until—having reached a mature age—partly through the experience of many things, partly through learned doctrine and precepts received from those wiser than himself, reason begins to awaken. Then, finally, he realizes he is in a dark wood; that is, his soul is oppressed by ignorance and vice through the contagion of the body. This, then, is the meaning of the text: **I FOUND MYSELF IN A DARK WOOD.** This signifies: I perceived that my soul was submerged in the body, through the contagion and darkness of which it had lost the straight and true path. **MIDWAY THROUGH THE JOURNEY OF OUR LIFE.** That is, in the middle of the course of human life, at which time discretion begins to awaken in man, which until that point had been almost extinguished. And being awakened, he realizes his error and takes the path of salvation, unless he allows himself to be so conquered by sensuality that he does not proceed forward, but rather returns backward into the darkness of the wood. From which misery David prays to the Lord to keep him, saying: "O Lord, do not call me back in the midst of my days." Nor is it necessary to interpret the "middle" as an exact point, but rather that which is equidistant from the extremes.

It further interprets the "Dark Wood" as an allegory for the soul being trapped in the "death" of bodily senses and ignorance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on Canto I of Dante's Inferno, specifically focusing on the meeting between Dante and Virgil and the philosophical necessity of the journey through the three realms.</meta>

-># INFERNO.<-

The soul is not purged of every vice first, as we have shown above; nor can it be purged of vices if it does not first recognize them. From this it follows that Dante could not arrive at heaven—that is, at the knowledge of celestial things—if he did not first go through Hell and through Purgatory. This means he first had to recognize the vices, and then, having recognized them, purge himself of them. And because our human frailty makes it either impossible or very difficult to make this journey without a leader and guide, the poet shows himself taking Virgil as his guide. 

First, because he [Dante] truly and most subtly imitated him in this work of his. Next, in an allegorical sense, he takes Virgil to represent **moral philosophy** and all the **teachings of the pagans** <note>The "Gentiles" or non-Christians.</note>. In this regard, such teaching is sufficient to achieve the first two parts: that is, recognizing vice, and having recognized it, purging oneself of it. But it is not sufficient to give us true knowledge of divine things, which cannot be drawn from any other source except from that of the **sacred theology of the Christians**. Therefore, he establishes that Virgil guides him only through Hell and Purgatory, because for Paradise, as we shall see in its proper place, he will have need of a more learned guide <note>Referring to Beatrice, who represents Divine Revelation/Theology.</note>. 

But so that in the progress of the poem this name does not lead us into any error or difficulty in understanding the allegorical sense, let it be known here at the beginning that "Virgil" will be used not in one single sense, but in various ways. Sometimes he will signify nothing other than the poet himself. At other times, he will signify **human reason** simply, and Dante will represent **sensuality** <note>The lower, physical impulses.</note>. At other times, we shall interpret him as the **intellect** enlightened by many and various teachings. At yet other times, we shall express through him **superior reason**, and then Dante will signify not sensuality alone, but also **inferior reason**.

Returning then to the text, it follows: *While I was rushing down to a low place* <note>original: "Mentre ch'io rovinava in basso loco"</note>—that is, while the she-wolf <note>Representing avarice or worldly desire.</note> was preventing me from ascending to contemplation and was making me fall back into the lowly desires of earthly things. Whereupon, despairing of being able to overcome such a cruel beast by myself, Virgil appeared before me. 

And in this part, he demonstrates what usually happens to circumspect men: who, seeing for themselves that they cannot reach where they desire, search for someone who might be a more useful guide. Thus, as Dante searched his mind, Virgil offered himself, *who through long silence seemed hoarse* <note>original: "fioco". This is a famous Dantean crux: Virgil's voice is "faint" or "hoarse."</note>. Because, signifying by Virgil the teaching and the rational part of man, he was not undeservedly "hoarse" through long silence; for a long time passes in a man where sensuality is awake before reason is. And sensuality governs and commands the man, and with its bestial government rules him, and reason—as if asleep—remains silent. Nor does it wake or speak before one is "midway through the journey." And then it speaks hoarsely because, despite reason beginning to stir, it is nonetheless still submerged in sensuality and cannot speak clearly from the start. Therefore, in the early years, reason is totally silent; then it begins to speak, but speaks hoarsely because it is still confused and does not discern well; finally, it speaks clearly. 

We can also say that Virgil seemed hoarse through long silence because, until Dante's time, the Latin language had been poorly understood for many centuries and was almost in silence, and especially Virgil. Dante was the first who investigated the other meanings of Virgil. Because it would be very tedious to report these here, I expressed and declared them as much as my talent allowed in the third and fourth books of our *Camaldolese Disputations* <note>Landino refers to his own famous philosophical work, the "Disputationes Camaldulenses" (c. 1472).</note>, which volume Andrea Cabini, our disciple, translated into the Florentine language. 

*When I saw him in the great desert* <note>original: "QUAndo vidi colui nel gran deserto"</note>. He sees Virgil in the desert, but does not yet know who he is. That is: he sees reason beginning to appear, though faintly, in the uncultivated forest of the infinite impulses of sensuality; but he does not recognize it. Yet, because he already understands his misery, he asks it for help. There is a time in which we are in ignorance and do not realize it; then comes a time when we begin to realize it, but not very clearly because reason is still confused; yet we still seek a remedy. For reason urges us, having recognized our ill, to seek help against it. 

*Have mercy on me* <note>original: "MISerere di me"</note>, I cried to him: because when sensuality sees itself perishing, it asks help from reason. *I cried* because, being hunted by the she-wolf and seeing himself in manifest danger, he wanted to show that he had need of immediate and undelayed help. And by this, he admonishes us that when we perceive ourselves to be persecuted by vices, we should not delay in asking for help; because by delaying, such a habit can be formed that we are later too late. The rest of the following verses are simple history and do not require allegory. He asks if he is a "shade" or a "certain man," certainly because in desert places shades or phantasms often appear. And allegorically, often in the "desert"—that is, in the sensitive part of the soul—there appear not "men" (that is, true reasons), but "shades" (that is, vain and false reasons), which show a thing to be good which is not. But he who goes wandering through the "forest" (that is, who is still entangled in vices) asks help from the shade as if from a "certain man" (that is, he allows himself to be persuaded by false reason as if by true reason, whereby he remains deceived).

Virgil therefore responds that he is not a man, but was one. For neither the soul alone nor the body alone is called "man," but these two joined together according to the **Aristotelians** <term>Aristotelians: followers of Aristotle's philosophy who defined man as a "rational mortal animal," a composite of body and soul.</term>. Whence man is defined: to be a **rational mortal animal**. "Animal" signifies an animated body. Therefore, there is no "animal" where there is not soul and body together. Nor is man "mortal" except from the part of the body, because the soul is immortal. Nevertheless, the **Platonists** <term>Platonists: followers of Plato who emphasized the soul as the true essence of the person.</term>, when they say "man," mean only the soul; and they want the body to be like a vessel where the soul is contained. But of this, we shall dispute more extensively in a more convenient place. Furthermore, we can say that here too is allegory, and Virgil says: "I was a man, and at present I am not such..."

->He answered me: "No, not a man; a man I was once,<-
->and my parents were Lombards,<-
->and Mantuans by fatherland, both of them.<-
->I was born under Julius, though it was late,<-
->and I lived at Rome under the good Augustus<-
->in the time of the false and lying gods.<-
->I was a poet, and I sang of that just<-

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto I of Dante Alighieri’s Inferno, specifically focusing on the philosophical and allegorical interpretations of the soul and the character of Virgil.</meta>

**INFERNO.**

...well: or to flee that which is or seems evil. For this reason, the divine Plato, wishing to express the essence and the powers of our soul, said it was like a chariot whose yoke was winged and was pulled by two horses, one white, beautiful, and well-formed, and one black, ugly, and deformed; and upon the chariot he places the charioteer—that is, the ruler of the horses. The chariot, then, is the essence of the soul. The horses that pull it are the appetite: and by the white he means the <term>rational appetite</term> <note>The desire for things that align with reason and virtue.</note>; by the black, the irrational. This was not unknown to the divine genius of Petrarch, who, wishing to show how the appetite in himself was disobedient to reason, describes it in the likeness of the black horse, saying:

*My foolish desire is so led astray*
*In following her who is turned in flight,*
*And, light and loose from the snares of Love,*
*Flies before my slow running;*
*For the more I urge myself to follow her*
*Through the safe road, the less it listens to me.*
*Nor does it avail me to spur it or turn it,*
*For Love by its nature makes it restive.*
*But once it gathers the bit to itself by force,*
*I remain under its lordship,*
*For against my will it carries me to death.*
<note>original: "Sì traviato el folle mio disio..." from Petrarch’s Canzoniere, Song 6. The "her" refers to Laura, or more broadly, a distracting earthly desire.</note>

The Platonic poet demonstrates, therefore, that the black horse carries us to death because the irrational appetite leads to vice, which is the death of the soul. The chariot is thus our soul; the horses are the appetite; and the charioteer or ruler is the mind and the reason which rules and governs the soul. The reader should therefore commit this division to memory, not only for the explanation of this text, but because it will be necessary many times in the progression of the work. 

But to return to the subject: Dante, who desires to leave the forest and climb the mountain but cannot because he is hindered by the beasts already mentioned, signifies the rational appetite obedient to "lower reason": that is, to the <term>active life</term> <note>The life of worldly action, social duty, and politics, as opposed to pure meditation.</note>. The active life cannot by itself come to the blessedness which consists in the doctrine and knowledge of celestial things, because the active life contains within it the "beasts"—that is, various disturbances of the soul. Since man is disquieted by these, he cannot have a soul as tranquil as is necessary for one who wishes to be fit and suitable for <term>contemplation</term> <note>The "contemplative life" focused on spiritual and philosophical truth.</note>. 

This was wonderfully expressed by Him who performs the truth—rather, who is Truth itself—in the Gospel of Matthew <note>original: "evangelio di Matheo". Landino actually refers to the story of Martha and Mary, which is found in Luke 10:38–42, not Matthew.</note>: in which, putting Mary for the contemplative life and Martha for the active life, He says Martha is full of cares and anxieties and takes up disturbances in many things, while Mary has chosen the best part, which never abandons the soul. This is because the active life and civil operations—signified by Martha—last only as long as we live in this present mortal life. But the contemplation of divine things is never taken from us and follows us into the other life, which is eternal. 

Dante, therefore, desires but cannot climb the mountain. Thus Virgil—who signifies "higher reason" and knowledge and the contemplative life—looking upon Dante's good will, is moved to compassion. Sent by the Graces (of whom we will speak below), Virgil promises him his help. But it should be noted that Virgil signifies only the "doctrine of the gentiles" <note>The philosophy and wisdom of the pre-Christian Greeks and Romans.</note>, through which we can know vices and, having known them, purge ourselves of them. However, this is not enough without Christian theology to give us that knowledge of celestial things where our blessedness consists. For this reason, Virgil will be able to guide him through Hell and Purgatory—that is, to show him the nature of vice and how one can be purged of it—but he will not be able to lead him to Paradise. Let this be said briefly for the exposition of this passage. 

Now returning to the text, it follows: *WHEREFORE I for your sake think and discern.* "Wherefore"—that is, for which cause—is the conclusion of all the words already said. "Think" and "discern" are different acts; for we "think" when, searching for the best in a thing, we go about examining and weighing all the parts to understand which of all of them is the one to be most accounted for. Then, having examined them all, we "discern"—that is, we choose the best one and elect it. 

Here it should be noted that every path a man takes must be prudently considered. And <term>Prudence</term>, according to Plato and Aristotle, is a certain reason with which we administer all things rightly in the active and civil life. To this, Aristotle attributes in the sixth book of the *Ethics*: good consultation, skill, sagacity, and judgment. Two things exist, as the same Aristotle posits in his book on the Republic <note>Likely referring to the *Politics*.</note>, in which consists all praise of right operation and government: one, that the end which we propose for ourselves be true and right; the second, that we find the things which lead us to the end already proposed. 

Therefore, for Prudence—the end of which is to dispose all human operations rightly and with the best method and order—several things are necessary: first, all the virtues that lead us to the end and those that work toward the end. And first is "consultation." This is nothing other than a diligent inquiry into those things that lead us to the end. Counsel has three offices: first, it investigates if any way can be found that leads us to the end; then, if such ways are found, it asks what they are; and having found one or more, in the third place, it seeks in what way we can use them. All of this is within deliberation and consultation. After this follows "judgment." The office of judgment, once we have found the aforementioned ways, is to dispute and weigh which of those is most suitable, or most honest, or most useful. Once this judgment is given, "election" follows, which is nothing other than taking that which we have already judged to be best. 

The philosophers define "election" as "consulted appetite" and desire for those things that lead us to the end. Counsel is made right and directed by good consultation and skill. To "consult well" is nothing other than to lead conveniently to a good end through honest ways and means. And "skill" is a prompt and alert investigation of the aforementioned ways and means. Judgment becomes perfect through "sagacity," which is right and most prompt judgment, and also through "sentence"; they define "sentence" as the judgment of goodness and equity. 

Virgil, therefore, wishing to persuade Dante to follow him, wants to show that he had taken such a path with optimal prudence. When he said, "I THINK," he placed the counsel investigated with good consultation and skill. And when he said, "I DISCERN," he placed the judgment aided by sagacity and election. For this reason, Dante must consent to the path taken with all the parts of prudence. But let the reader understand that our order and purpose is that every time, through the interpretation of the text, it happens that we have to explain any point of philoso—

# INFERNO.

...the evil of ignorance and of vice. **AND WORSE**, that is, the damnation which follows from not recognizing how much evil is within vice. He who does not know how pestiferous vice is does not flee from it; from this follows grave detriment: and from this is born another even graver, because by not fleeing it, it becomes a habit which kills the soul. **SO THAT I MAY SEE the gate of Saint Peter.** By this, understand the entrance to Purgatory. This is because Peter—that is, the Supreme Pontiff—and all the priests who have authority from him, by absolving the soul from guilt, make it capable of being able to go to purge itself; and not being absolved, it would be damned to Hell. ## SECOND CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE.

**L**o, the day was departing, and the darkened air
was taking the animals that are on earth
from their labors; and I, alone,
prepared myself to sustain the war
both of the journey and of the pity,
which memory, that does not err, shall retrace.

->[Woodcut illustration showing Dante and Virgil in a landscape, with Beatrice appearing in the sky within a radiant circle. Labels: "BEATRICE", "Virgil", "Dante".]<-

We can say that the preceding chapter was almost a "proposition" <note>A formal statement or summary of the themes to follow</note> of the whole work: through which the author not only demonstrates with brief words what he has to say throughout the entire work, but also the reason why he maintains such an order. The appetite awoke, searching for its good; and illuminated by reason, it fled the forest and climbed the mountain where it saw the sun. But its way was blocked by the beasts, by which the climbing was forbidden to him. This signifies that having recognized—though not very distinctly—that the supreme good consisted in enjoying God, he sought the knowledge of that in the "civil life" <term>civil life</term> <note>original: "uita ciuile"; the active life of a citizen and moral virtue in society</note> where lower reason reigns. This reason is often deceived by the senses. And there, where the civil virtues are not perfect, the perturbations of the soul have great power. These souls, seeking pleasure, honor, and utility, do not follow true joy nor even true utility (which can never be separated from honesty), nor true honor (which is nothing other than true and sincere praise for its own sake). Even if it is not sought, honor follows virtue as the shadow follows the body, and it is the reward of virtue itself; it should not and cannot be given except to the good. But in place of these three, they follow the pleasure of the body, the possession of fleeting and earthly goods (which is avarice), and finally the vain glory of the world (which is ambition). Therefore, the human mind cannot, with lower reason alone and in the life...

<meta>This page provides a philosophical and allegorical commentary on the opening lines of Canto II of Dante’s Inferno. Although the heading reads "Canto I," the text focuses on the transition to evening and the beginning of the poet's journey with Virgil, which takes place at the start of the second Canto.</meta>

# CANTO ONE. <margin>zi</margin>
<note>While the heading says Canto I, the commentary actually describes the beginning of Canto II: "The day was departing..."</note>

He describes the time. He shows the author descending into hell during the night. He feigns this truthfully because one goes into hell by night—that is, through the shadows of ignorance—because every sin comes from ignorance <margin>V</margin> when disordered appetite extinguishes the light of reason within us. This is why some ancient philosophers said it was easy to go to hell: because one went there with eyes closed. And Virgil said: *They went darkling through the lonely night amid the shadows.* <note>original: "Ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbras." A quote from the Aeneid, Book VI.</note> Or truly, by "night," he wishes to show the nightly vigils which are necessary for anyone who wishes to make progress in the **contemplation** of great things. The mind is much more sharpened in nightly studies because it is free from all the noise and tumult of the day. He shows, then, that at that hour in which the night comes and spreads shadows throughout our hemisphere, all animals give themselves over to sleep and rest, while he alone prepared himself to endure the "war." This passage is drawn from the fourth book of Virgil, where he depicts Dido keeping watch due to pain and distress at the hour when all animals rest.

**AND THE brown AIR:** <note>Referring to the line "Lo giorno se n'andava, e l'aer bruno..."</note> The air is a <term>diaphanous</term> <note>A technical term for a substance that is clear or allows light to pass through, like glass or air.</note> body—that is, penetrable and transparent—but by its nature, it is dark if it is not illuminated by the sun or another light. Therefore, when the sun descends to the other hemisphere, the shadow of the earth spreads through ours and creates night. For night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth. **TOOK AWAY** the animals that are on earth from their labors; because the night, being useless for performing any work due to its shadows, invites animals to sleep, which is a great recreation for the body. Allegorically, he shows that he alone—that is, the man devoted to <term>speculation</term> <note>In this historical context, "speculation" refers to deep philosophical or theological study and meditation.</note>—is "alone" because it is necessary for him to live in solitude, separated from every crowd, frequency, and tumult that might impede thought. He consumes the night in speculation, while other men and animals who seek the comforts of the body consume it in sleeping. Therefore, "I alone," meaning I placed in solitude. Or truly, "I alone" demonstrates that the contemplative are alone and very few. Thus Petrarch wrote: *“Poor and naked you go, Philosophy,” says the crowd intent on base gain. “Few companions will you have on your path.”* <note>original: "Pouera & nuda uai philoſophia. Dice la turba al uil guadagno atteſa Puochi cõpagni harai per la tua uia."</note> And certainly, because man, considered as this composite of soul and body, always seeks company, <margin>X</margin> one does not find those who live alone unless they are someone whose imagination is corrupted by a melancholic humor and has become almost like a beast, or someone who, through highness of intellect, despising human things, transcends through speculation to divine things. Hence Aristotle rightly said in his *Politics*: that he who leaves the sociable and civil life has become either a beast or more than a man.

**PREPARED to sustain the war.** Both of the journey and of the pity. The literal sense is that traveling through dark places was fatiguing, and the pains of the damned moved him to pity. But allegorically, he shows that one cannot go into "hell"—that is, have a true knowledge of vices—without war and combat, because in this, the soul often fights with itself. This happens because the sensory part is dragged into the contemplation and recoils from such labor, while the mind and the intellect seek to understand, because "the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." Furthermore, it is a war because the appetite judges a thing one way, and reason judges it another. For example: in defrauding a family of their owed nourishment, the appetite of the greedy man falsely judges this to be a virtue called "thrift," while reason truly judges it to be a vice called "avarice." He was, therefore, prepared to endure this war. Also, the "war of pity": because we cannot know vices without also knowing that they proceed from the infirmity and imbecility of human nature, which proceeds from the corporeal mass that weighs down the soul. And this properly moves any wise man who enters such speculation to compassion. Whence: *God saw our framing and had mercy on us.* <note>original: "uidit deus figmẽtũ noſtrũ & miſertus eſt noſtri." Likely a reference to Psalm 103.</note> And for this same reason, Heraclitus of Ephesus, seeing the continuous infinite errors in human life, wept constantly, moved to compassion by the misery of it.

**WHICH:** that is, which journey and which pity my **mind** will retrace—as if it will describe it and commit it to letters. For it was not the hand of the poet, which is merely an instrument, but the mind, in which he holds such knowledge, that wrote it. **The mind that does not err WILL RETRACE:** He captures attention and goodwill. For we become well-disposed and listen attentively to that writer who promises to write true things without error. And he most excellently said "the mind that does not err." Because the inferior reason, which administers practical and civil life through prudence, consists of particulars where one can err. But the "mind"—that is, the intellect and the superior reason—because it exercises itself in universals, of which there is true science, cannot err. But so that we may better understand what "mind" is: <margin>T</margin> I say that although our soul is one, simple, uncorrupted, and indivisible, it nevertheless has various and diverse names according to various powers and virtues. Therefore, insofar as it gives life to the body, it is called **soul** (*anima*). Insofar as it feels, **sense**. Insofar as it has wisdom, it is called **spirit** (*animo*). Insofar as it understands, they call it **mind** (*mente*). Furthermore, when it discerns, it is called **reason**; when it remembers, **memory**. The rational and intellectual light with which we make any discourse and understand is called "mind" by philosophers. This is formed in the image and likeness of God, for it is formed by Him without the interposition of any other nature. It is called "mind" because it is a very eminent—that is, excellent—part of the soul. In short, the mind is the eye of our soul. The gaze of this mind is reason, and its seeing is the intellect. It is, therefore, necessary for every rational soul to have this, its eye.

It also defines the various faculties of the soul, identifying the "mind" as the highest, divine-like element of human understanding.</summary>

**CANTO TWO 23**

And certainly this poet, besides his learning, was also remarkable in the adornment of his words. Because, having to make mention of Aeneas and Paul twice, he used artful variety which relieves the listener’s ears of boredom. Therefore, in the first instance, he did not use their proper names, but used a rhetorical device called <term>circumlocution</term> <note>A roundabout way of speaking, using many words where fewer would do.</note>: which is when that which can be said by a proper name is said through several common ones, such as when we want to say "Hercules," we say "the unconquered grandson of Alcaeus." And for this reason, he said "the father of Silvius" <note>Referring to Aeneas.</note> and the "chosen vessel" <note>original: "vas delectione"; referring to Saint Paul, based on Acts 9:15.</note>. This brings ornament with it. Now, in this second place, by using their proper names, he says: "I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul." These two names bring with them gravity and authority. **FOR IF I abandon myself to coming.** He correctly concludes that it is not cowardice of spirit but a reasonable fear that moves him to doubt that his coming might be "folly," that is, foolish; and certainly it would be a foolish thing to undertake something that was not destined to succeed: because it is the judgment of all wise men that it is better not to begin than to have to abandon the undertaking later. **IF YOU ARE WISE and understand me, for I do not speak.** According to Hesiod, the Greek <note>original: "Heliodo greco"</note>, there are three generations of men: Of the best are those who, through their own wisdom, know what is good and the straight path, and follow it; and these are very rare. The second generation is of those who, recognizing that they do not know by themselves, willingly follow the counsel of those who do know, and obey them. These men, though they are not perfect, nonetheless deserve no small commendation; because it is no small wisdom to know one's own deficiency and seek a remedy for it: for **virtue is the flight from vice, and the first step to wisdom is to have been free from folly** <note>original: "virtus e vitiu fuger & sapiẽtia prĩa stultitia caruisse"; a quote from the Roman poet Horace, Epistles I.1.41-42.</note>. The third generation is of those who neither know by themselves nor want the counsel of others: and these are not useful in any part. Therefore, the poet places himself in the second generation; and in this place he does several things. For first, he demonstrates morally that we ought to ask for counsel from those wiser than ourselves in great undertakings. He also demonstrates the method of asking for counsel. For when we wish to be advised in any matter, we should first examine it ourselves with all diligence; and we should propose all the doubts that occur to us together with the thing in which we seek advice. And finally, through allegory, he demonstrates that "lower reason" <note>In medieval philosophy, the part of the mind dealing with earthly, practical matters.</note> in universal things ought to submit itself to "higher reason" <note>The part of the mind dealing with divine or eternal truths.</note>. And it follows:

| Et quale è quel che disvuol ciò che volle | And like one who un-wills what he willed |

| et per nuovo pensier cangia proposta | and by new thought changes his intent |
| si che dal cominciar tutto si tolle | so that he withdraws entirely from the beginning |

| sì che pensando consumai l’impresa | so that by thinking I consumed the enterprise |

**INFERNO.**

O courteous Mantuan soul,
whose fame still endures in the world
and shall endure as long as the world lasts;
my friend, and not the friend of fortune,
is hindered on the deserted slope
so much in his path that he has turned back in fear.
And I fear he may already be so strayed
that I have risen too late to his rescue,
judging by what I have heard of him in heaven.
Now move, and with your ornate speech
and with whatever is needed for his escape,
help him so that I may be consoled.
I am Beatrice who causes you to go;
I come from the place where I desire to return;
love moved me, which makes me speak.
When I shall be before my Lord,
I will often praise you to Him.
She then fell silent, and then I began:

<margin>q</margin> This is the oration that Beatrice makes to Virgil to persuade him to move immediately to Dante’s aid. And if we wish to understand the oratory and poetic art within it, we would say it belongs to the <term>deliberative genre</term> <note>A style of rhetoric used to persuade or dissuade someone regarding a future action.</note>. And first, in the beginning, she performs a <term>captatio benevolentiae</term> <note>Latin: "winning of goodwill." A rhetorical technique to make the audience well-disposed toward the speaker.</note> through Virgil’s person, praising him for his generosity, and she observes the oratorical precepts. For we must always praise the virtue in the person from whom we wish to obtain something—the very virtue we want them to use toward us. Therefore, since Beatrice needed Virgil to be generous in offering help to Dante, she said: *Courteous soul*, meaning generous. Then she follows with praises, demonstrating the long-lasting nature of his fame, which has not only lasted so many centuries but will also endure "as long as the world lasts," meaning for a very long time. After the introduction, she places the narrative in which she shows she is asking for a just thing; for it is just to ask for the escape of one who is a true friend. And it is not through malice but through frailty that he falls into ruin. And so that the rescue may be swift, she shows that since he has already turned toward ruin, the help will be of no use if it is not prompt. She also shows that it will be easy for him because of his eloquence and learning. And so that he understands she deserves to be heard, she says she is Beatrice, that she comes from heaven, and that she is moved by love; and finally, she promises him a reward. And this suffices to demonstrate the craftsmanship of this oration. Now follows the exposition of the text:

O COURTEOUS SOUL. She rightly says "soul" because he was without a body. COURTEOUS: which she had understood because he had offered himself when he said: "So that I requested it before the command." And certainly, Virgil—that is, the intellect—is not a body but is incorporeal; and his help had to be of things not corporeal, but spiritual. And the intellect is "courteous" because it is that which gives us every excellent teaching. She adds afterwards that Virgil's fame is to last as long as the world: because the fame of human learning is not meant to be eternal like the knowledge of celestial things.

*My friend, and not the friend of fortune.* True friendship is that of one who loves the friend and not his good fortune; for there are many who, like swallows, come in the summer and flee in the winter. So they, while the "summer" of prosperity lasts for a friend, are always around him. But when "winter" comes—that is, some adversity—they immediately leave him, just as Polymnestor left Priam. Therefore, Beatrice rightly says that Dante is her friend, and not a friend of her good fortune; for many love Beatrice—that is, the doctrine of divine things—not for herself or to possess her, but to acquire worldly fame, reputation, riches, and dignity. These things are the "goods of fortune." Therefore, they do not love her, but her good fortune. Many become great theologians not to amend their errors with that doctrine which reveals the Supreme Good and directs us toward it, but to obtain honors and dignity, and to become bishops, archbishops, and cardinals. Hence, these cannot be called virtuous because they do not seek virtue for the sake of wanting it or living according to it, but to become famous, powerful, or rich. Wherefore Juvenal said: <note>original Latin: "Quis enim uirtute amplectitur ipsa p̄mia si tollas."</note> *For who embraces virtue itself if you take away the rewards?*

<margin>D</margin> And concluding according to the distinction of the holy doctors: Some desire to know solely for the sake of knowing, and this is curiosity. Some desire it to be known as wise—that is, to be famous and respected—and this is vanity. Others seek it for gain, and this is avarice. Others seek it to build up themselves and also others, and this is true charity. And these are the friends of Beatrice and not of the fortune and happiness that proceeds from her. Of the first three, Solomon writes in the *Book of Wisdom*: <note>original Latin: "Vani sunt oēs homines i quibus non est scientia dei."</note> *Vain are all men in whom there is no knowledge of God.* And in *Ecclesiastes*: <note>original Latin: "In multa sciētia est multa indignatio."</note> *In much knowledge is much sorrow.* Of the last ones, he similarly speaks in *Wisdom*, saying: <note>original Latin: "Dedit illi sciētiā factorū: & honestauit illū i laboribus."</note> *He gave him knowledge of holy things and prospered him in his labors.* Therefore, Beatrice shows that Dante is among those who love and seek doctrine according to these last ones. Or, we can say "my friend and not of fortune" because Dante was a friend of divine doctrine, but fortune was always adverse to him, as we see in his life. This most often happens to the learned. Wherefore Aristotle says in the book *On Good Fortune*: where there is much virtue, there is little fortune. Nevertheless, the first interpretation fits better in this place.

HE IS HINDERED by the beasts already mentioned on the slope of virtues. DESERTED: abandoned because, as we have said, few follow them. WHO TURNED BACK because of frailty; for which the man who errs is worthy of greater compassion. AND I FEAR that he may already be so "strayed" that I have risen too late to help. Understand in the Tuscan dialect that a thing is called *smarrita* <note>strayed or misplaced</note> when, although it is not found, it must eventually be recovered. And *perduta* <note>lost</note> is that which is not found, nor will it ever be found.

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, he who turns away from the true path that leads to salvation goes by the way of vices that lead to perdition. Our sinning is in three degrees. First, the wicked thought is born, and the vice is directed. Secondly, one stops in the captive thought and frequently performs vicious actions. In the third, through frequent operations, one has become so established in sin that the frequent acts have formed a habit. Wherefore the prophet says in the first Psalm: *Blessed...*

The commentator distinguishes between those who seek knowledge for vanity or profit and those who seek it out of true charity, placing Dante in the latter category.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto II, specifically discussing Beatrice's concern for Dante's soul. The commentator (likely Cristoforo Landino) uses Psalm 1 to illustrate the progression of sin from thought to habit.</meta>

->CANTO TWO 25<-

**Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of pestilence.** <note>original Latin: "uir qui non habit [abiit] in consilium impiorum: & in uia peccatorum non ſtetit & in cathedra peſtilentiæ non ſedit." This is the opening of Psalm 1, used by the commentator to categorize the degrees of moral failure.</note> Which is to say: Blessed is the man who does not go along with the counsel of the ungodly—that is, he who does not take bad advice in his actions. Next: **and did not stand in the way of sinners**, which signifies one’s acts and deeds. **He did not sit in the chair of pestilence**, <note>original Latin: "in cathedra peſtilentiæ non ſedete"</note> that is, he did not turn vice into a **habit**. <term>habit (habitus): In medieval philosophy, this refers to a settled disposition where a behavior becomes part of one's nature, making it very difficult to change.</term> There is, therefore, first the **vicious intention**; next, the **act** and the **deed**; and finally, the **habit**. In the first two stages, a man is not truly lost because he can still return to the true path. However, he is "astray" <note>The commentator is linking the Psalm to Dante’s famous opening line about being "astray" in a dark wood.</note> because, until he returns, he cannot find his true self. In the third stage, he is lost because, as **Aristotle** says: "He who has made a habit of vice finds it impossible, or very difficult, to leave it behind." And for this reason Beatrice says: *and I fear he may already be so far astray*; that is, she fears he may have committed such frequent acts of sin that he is already close to making it a habit. If that were the case, help would come too late. **BY WHAT I have heard of him in heaven.** Those who
