[Right Column]
We have shown above that as soon as human reason, with its free will, turns to seek the way out of the forest of ignorance—from which all vices proceed—God is moved to compassion for our weakness. Because He sees that we lack the power rather than the will, He inspires the graces which we have mentioned above. And first is a grace which, because it comes through simple divine liberality, is called <term>prevenient</term> <note>Grace that "comes before" human action to stir the soul toward God.</note>. Hence the prophet Jeremiah says: *Turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the Lord my God.* <note>original: "Conuerte me & conuertar quia tu deus meus"</note> And it is called "freely given" <note>original: "gratis data"</note>. This directs the will of man toward the good purpose already chosen by free will. And after this comes the second, called <term>illuminating grace</term>, through which our good will (born from reason and free will and confirmed by the first grace) is illuminated and made capable of undertaking the truth and showing him the way. This way is to know God and oneself through the means of true theology, toward which whoever directs themselves acquires [knowledge]. Hence the Psalmist says: *Thou hast made known to me thy ways.* <note>original: "Notas mihi fecisti uias tuas."</note> And elsewhere: *For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell.* <note>original: "Quoniam non relinques animā meā i inferno."</note> And elsewhere: *For thou hast delivered my soul from death, and my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of the living.* <note>original: "Quoniā eripuisti animā meā d morte: & pedes meos a lapsu ut placeā corā deo i lumine uiuētiū."</note> The third grace is called <term>cooperating</term>, that is, "working together," because it cooperates or works in unison with man. Likewise, it is called <term>consummating</term>, that is, "perfecting," because it leads to the required end. Dante, therefore, places this "gentle lady" for the first, Lucia for the second, and Beatrice for theology together with the third grace. Although we have set out these graces at length above, nevertheless, because it is not easy for every man to understand, it was not burdensome for me to repeat them briefly. GENTLE Lady. <note>original: "DONNA Gentile."</note> "Gentile" in Tuscan

[Bottom Section]
signifies "noble," derived from the Latin, because *gens* stands for "family"; therefore, "gentile" is like saying a man of family. But because the Hebrews called all those who were not of the people of God "gentiles," and therefore Christians call all pagans "gentiles," this name "gentile" has different meanings. Inasmuch as theologians, following the custom of the Hebrews, say "gentiles" for pagans; and the Latins say "gentiles" for those who are of the same race, that is, family, whom we call "kinsmen"; and the Tuscans say "gentile," meaning noble. And it is in this [latter] sense that the poet uses it.

# HELL.

--- Page 159 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, specifically focusing on the famous inscription found at the entrance to Hell in Canto III. The commentator explains the rhetorical structure of the inscription and provides a philosophical definition of what constitutes a "city."</meta>

->CANTO TERTIO. 29<-

[The memory of the] night stimulates us, as does the fear of civil punishments, infamy, and the wrath of God. And note that the poet adorns this beginning with two rhetorical "colors" <term>colors: a medieval term for figures of speech or rhetorical ornaments</term> using repetition and exposition. They call it repetition <margin>I</margin> whenever multiple clauses begin with the same expression or word: as here, where the three verses are three clauses. And understand that a clause is a part of speech which, as a part, is complete; for example, saying: "Through me one goes into the city of suffering." We see that this is a complete part of speech. There are, therefore, three clauses in three verses, and each begins with this phrase: "Through me." This, then, is repetition. Exposition occurs <margin>K</margin> when, although the words in several clauses are different, the meaning remains nearly the same. For instance, although the words vary—"Through me one goes into the city of suffering," "Through me one goes into eternal pain," and "Through me one goes among the lost people"—the sentiment is essentially the same. Furthermore, he builds an argument, for he arranges these three verses in such a way that what follows always adds something more. The first mentions "suffering," the second "eternal pain," and the third "perdition" <note>original: "perditione"</note>, which makes the suffering greatest of all. It is, therefore, suffering, then eternal suffering, and finally the greatest suffering. The poet could not have used more horrendous words to frighten men away from vice. He also makes no mention of the gate being opened; it follows, then, that it stands always open. This denotes that at any time, at any age, and in any state, a man can fall into vice. But to return from those vices to virtue is difficult. <note>original: "Facilis descensus averni. Noctes atque dies patet atri ianua ditis. Sed revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras Hoc opus hic labor est."</note> "The descent into the underworld is easy; the gate of dark Dis stands open night and day. But to retrace one's steps and escape to the upper air—this is the task, this is the toil." <note>This is a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, emphasizing how easy it is to fall into sin compared to the difficulty of returning to a state of grace.</note>

**IN THE CITY.** He used this name "city" as the common people do, who call any large gathering of men a city, regardless of how they live. But the learned call a city only a multitude of men gathered in harmony to live well and rightly. Hence, Cicero demonstrates that Rome was not truly a city during the time the wicked ruled and the good were in exile. However, it seems that Aurelius Augustine <note>Saint Augustine, author of 'The City of God'</note> wishes to call every class and congregation a "city." Therefore, he establishes two of them: one according to the flesh, and the other according to the spirit. The one according to the flesh is the city of the wicked, and he calls it **Babylon**, which signifies "confusion," because in vice there is always confusion. It began with Cain, who out of envy killed his brother Abel; thus he committed the first homicide and was a fratricide. The other city, which is according to the spirit, is that of the good; it began with Abel and is called **Jerusalem**. That city of Babylon casts its inhabitants down into Hell and makes them citizens of that place—which is why it can be called a city in this sense. That of Jerusalem makes them ascend to Heaven, where the celestial Jerusalem is inhabited by the blessed, whom the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> calls <note>original: "cives sanctorum et domestici dei"</note> "fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household." And just as these are two different cities, so from them arise two species of different loves: for the celestial city loves God so much that it holds itself as nothing.

<summary>This page provides a rhetorical and theological analysis of the Gate of Hell's inscription, explaining its use of repetition to inspire dread. It also contrasts the "City of Man" (Babylon/Vice) with the "City of God" (Jerusalem/Virtue) based on the writings of Cicero and St. Augustine.</summary>
<keywords>Repetition, Exposition, City of God, Babylon, Jerusalem, St. Augustine, Virgil, Aeneid, Cain and Abel, Rhetoric</keywords>

->INFERNO<-

...voluntary. Because from the beginning it was in his power to draw or not to draw the arrow. **OF A DARK COLOR.** <note>Referring to Inferno III, 10: "These words of a dark color I saw written..."</note> A fitting color for Hell: which, being underground, must necessarily be dark. And Hell is dark because where the rays of the sun do not reach, there must be darkness. The sun signifies knowledge <term>scientia (from the Latin for knowledge or systematic learning)</term> and truth; while these are within a person, the darkness of ignorance—from which every vice proceeds—cannot exist. There is, therefore, obscurity and darkness in Hell to denote that every vice is born when the light of reason is extinguished in the soul: wherefore the soul remains in the darkness; and he who walks in the darkness stumbles <note>original: "percuote," meaning to strike against an obstacle or fall</note>. Wherefore it is a wholesome precept of the Lord that we should walk while we have the light <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:35: "Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you."</note>. Truly, the words written about Hell were of a dark color to denote that just as one discerns with difficulty in the dark, so it has been difficult to understand Hell: seeing as Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253), an early Christian scholar whose views on the temporary nature of Hell were later deemed heretical</note>—so great a man, of such learning, and of such excellent life—and some others, greatly erring there, believed...

It concludes by noting the historical difficulty in understanding the nature of Hell, citing the controversial views of the Church Father Origen.</summary>

<meta>This page appears to be from a commentary on Dante’s Inferno (likely by Cristoforo Landino). It transitions from a discussion of the "coldness" of those in Hell to a Neoplatonic explanation of Love as the engine of human action.</meta>

**HELL.**

As Terence said: "Truly, here men are cold." <note>original: "fe Teretio. Nimirum hic homines frigent." A reference to the Roman playwright Terence, suggesting that without the "warmth" of love or purpose, humans become spiritually frozen.</note> Furthermore, they are cold because they are without love, which alone makes men ardent in action. Hence poets call love a flame. From this comes that saying: "A soft flame eats the marrow," <note>original: "Est mollis flamma medullas," from Virgil’s Aeneid, describing Dido’s love for Aeneas.</note> and "Unhappy Dido burns." <note>original: "Vritur infelix Dido."</note> Love is, therefore, the beginning of action; thus the first order of the first hierarchy of angels is that of the <term>Seraphim</term> <note>The highest rank of angels in medieval Christian theology, their name is derived from the Hebrew word for "burning ones," representing their intense love for God.</note>, whose name signifies heat and love. But we will speak of this more extensively and starting from a higher perspective in the places that will more require it. 

Let it suffice for now that love is the principle of our actions. But because—as Plato writes in the *Symposium*—there are two kinds of love, there are also two Venuses: one celestial and the other earthly. The celestial one draws us to the love of heavenly things, from which are born in our souls the virtues, actions, and contemplations according to them. The earthly one inflames us with the love of earthly and fleeting things, from which all vices are born in us, as well as ignorance of God and of ourselves. Therefore, in summary, we shall say there are three types of men: first, those not in love, who perform neither good nor evil. And second, those in love...

<summary>This page explores the philosophical definition of Love as the source of all human movement and heat, contrasting the "cold" souls in Hell with the "burning" Seraphim. It introduces the Neoplatonic concept of the two Venuses to distinguish between virtuous heavenly love and vice-ridden earthly desire.</summary>
<keywords>Love, Neoplatonism, Plato’s Symposium, Seraphim, Venus, Virtue and Vice, Terence, Virgil, Dante’s Inferno, Cristoforo Landino</keywords>

# CANTO THREE. 31

And their blind life is so low,
that they are envious of every other fate.
The world allows no memory of them to endure;
mercy and justice disdain them:
let us not speak of them, but look and pass on.

# INFERNO.

...not speaking: because they either do not speak, or do not yet have their speech fully ready. **THE GOOD MASTER:** A teacher is good who not only teaches when he is asked, but even invites the disciple to ask. **GO <note>original: "ANDI"</note>:** "Go" is a Roman word, not Florentine, because in our tongue we do not use the singular of the present tense of this verb; we do not say *Ando, Andi, Anda*. Instead, we use *Vo, Vai, Va*. In this place, the poet imagines that Dante does not ask about the damnation of these people, but Virgil tells him without being asked. This is because original sin, which damns them, is not known to us through <term>natural science</term> <note>Knowledge gained through observation and human reason alone.</note>, which has its beginning in the understanding found in the senses and lower reason, but rather through theology. Therefore, human sensuality does not aspire to investigate this, nor does any doubt arise from it about which one might ask. **IT IS NOT ENOUGH BECAUSE** they did not have baptism: He identifies two types of unsaved men, even though they lived morally: those who lived after Christ but did not receive baptism—for "Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved" <note>Latin: *Quicunque crediderit & baptizatus fuerit hic saluus erit* (Mark 16:16).</note>—and those who lived before the coming of Christ, when baptism was not yet necessary. **THEY DID NOT ADORE God duly:** That is, they did not believe in the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—nor in the Christ who was to come. Among these, Virgil places himself. **FOR SUCH defects:** That is, for this lack of having true faith. **AND NOT FOR ANY OTHER evil:** Meaning, we have no penalty of the senses for committed crimes, but a penalty of the mind; for we live in desire, namely the desire for the glory of heaven. **WITHOUT Hope:** That is, without hope of ever attaining it. One who is in glory and enjoys God possesses the highest good. One who is outside of glory is either with the hope of going there eventually (like those in Purgatory) or is without hope. These latter are of two kinds: some are placed in eternal sensory pains (like those in all the other circles of Hell), and others are without sensory pain, like these here. These have no torments of the body, but of the soul. Their punishment is desire; and desire is nothing other than the longing to have present that which is absent, the absence of which continually torments the soul.

->Great sorrow took hold of my heart when I heard this,<-
->because people of much worth<-
->I knew were suspended in that Limbo.<-
->“Tell me, my master, tell me, my lord,”<-
->I began, wishing to be certain<-
->of that faith which conquers every error:<-
->“Did anyone ever go out from here, either by his own merit<-
->or by another’s, who was afterwards blessed?”<-
->And he, who understood my hidden speech,<-

He treats two things in these verses. First, he shows great compassion for these men who, having lived morally and being full of many virtues—and having, either through conscience or military discipline, performed many benefits for the human race or at least for their homeland—are nevertheless damned for not having had the Christian or Hebrew faith. In the second place, he wants Virgil to be his witness and make him certain of what he held by faith: that Christ, with his precious blood, ransomed those who, although they had followed a righteous religion, had died in original sin. **TELL ME MY MASTER, tell me my lord:** In the first chapter, we showed why he calls Virgil master, lord, and father; it is not necessary to repeat it here. **WISHING to be certain:** Although every believer believes what the Holy Church commands, nevertheless, every great mind, when able, willingly seeks knowledge and the confirmation of what it believes. **OF THAT Faith which conquers every error:** He said this to show that even if he lacked scientific knowledge, he nonetheless held the Christian faith to be most true and without error. **BY HIS OWN merit or by another’s:** Although no one can emerge from sin by themselves unless aided by divine grace, it is nonetheless necessary that we perform as much good as our fragility allows. Whence Augustine said: "He who created you without you will not save you without you." <note>Latin: *qui fecit te sine te non saluabit te sine te*.</note> Therefore, he wishes to show here that those who left Limbo did so not only through the merits of Christ’s Passion (without which no one is so perfect that they can be saved), but also through their own merits, because both are necessary. **MY hidden speech:** Because he did not explicitly express what he clearly wanted to say.

->replied: “I was new to this state<-
->when I saw a powerful one come here,<-
->crowned with a sign of victory.<-
->He drew forth the shade of our first parent,<-
->of Abel his son, and that of Noah;<-
->of Moses the lawgiver and the obedient;<-
->Abraham the patriarch, and David the king;<-
->Israel with his father and his offspring,<-
->and with Rachel, for whom he did so much.<-
->And many others, and he made them blessed;<-
->and I want you to know that before these,<-
->no human spirits were saved.”<-

Virgil understood that Dante desired to be certain of what he believed: that is, whether Christ drew the souls of the ancient fathers from Limbo, as Holy Church teaches. And therefore he responds: **I WAS new in this state:** Because I had arrived here only a short time before. For Virgil died in the twenty-sixth year of the empire of Octavian Augustus, who reigned fifty-six years; and Christ died in the eighteenth year of the empire of Tiberius, the successor of Augustus. Thus, Virgil had arrived in Limbo forty-eight years before Christ drew out the souls of the ancient fathers. **A POWERFUL one:** That is, Christ. And note that since Virgil was not a Christian, it did not seem appropriate to Dante that he should name Christ. Because he was not instructed in Christian doctrine, he did not know Christ as "the Christ," nor as the cause of the liberation of those souls, for he did not know by what reason He could do this; but he calls him "powerful" because of the effect he saw. Nor does this disagree with what is said...

...Ovid and Lucan <note>original: "uid & iob" — Likely a transcription error for Ovid and Lucan, the classical poets Dante meets in Limbo.</note>, and many others, as we wrote more extensively in the preface of this book. **WHO SOARS ABOVE THE OTHERS LIKE AN EAGLE:** <note>A reference to Dante’s description of Homer in Inferno IV, line 96.</note> The eagle has such strength that it gazes at the sun’s rays without being dazzled; likewise, <term>poetic fury</term> <note>original: "poetico furore" — Based on the Platonic idea of *furor poeticus*, a state of divine inspiration that elevates the poet's mind.</note> transcends even to divinity, as Plato shows when he writes of the four species of divine furies.

The greeting that the poets give to Dante, and making him the "sixth among them," signifies nothing else but that he became a poet by being drawn by the elegance and the learning of their works, and by having imitated them. Nor is it without reason that they spoke of things about which "silence is beautiful," just as it was "beautiful" to speak of them in that place. For it is reasonable that among them there was discussion of things pertaining to their learning. This fit well there <note>i.e., within the narrative of the poem</note>; but in the present work <note>the commentator refers here to the decorum of writing for his own audience</note>, it would not be appropriate.

Where it should be noted that it is not enough to reason about beautiful things, but it is also necessary that they be suited to the time, the place, and the subject matter being discussed. Furthermore, he shows that they lived in a "high castle," because they are placed in high fame and renown. <note>In Canto IV, the virtuous pagans dwell in a "noble castle" (nobile castello), which commentators often interpret as a symbol of human philosophy or secular fame.</note>

# CANTO FOUR. 38

**->We withdrew thus to one of the sides<-**
**->into a place open, luminous, and high,<-**
**->so that they all could be seen:<-**
**->There, directly upon the green enamel,<-**
**->were shown to me the great spirits,<-**
**->the sight of whom exalts me within myself.<-**

...but last things [are better understood] than first things. Whence the proverb is born: "he who wants to learn well must enter through the door," which means we must start from the beginning and not the end. WE CAME into a meadow of fresh greenery. He places them in a meadow because such a place, with its various flowers and herbs, is delightful. And we say that stable fame is "evergreen." Furthermore, he imitates Virgil, who says: <note>original Latin: "Devenere locos laetos: & amena vireta."</note> *They came to happy places and pleasant greenery.* And a little further down: <note>original Latin: "Pars in gramineis exercet membra palaestris."</note> *Some exercise their limbs on grassy wrestling grounds.* The meadow stays always green, and without being cultivated, it produces its fruit. Whence a meadow is called *prato*, almost like *parato* <note>Landino is using a folk etymology: "prato" (meadow) sounds like "parato" (prepared).</note>. For the fields of grain and the vineyards are not "prepared" to produce the utility expected from them without some cultivation; but only the meadow produces by itself. Thus fame, which is born from true virtue, always stays green and produces praise by itself. Afterward, he shows that he noticed by their manners and gestures that they were people of authority. Note that it rarely happens that gestures and outward appearance do not show the quality of a man. And especially the eyes are like windows through which we see the soul placed inside the body. SLOW and grave. He does not show them to be slow because their wit was slow (which the Greek calls <term>brady</term> and the Latin <term>bardo</term>, meaning a blockhead); but they were slow, meaning weighted and deliberate. For just as one easily recognizes a foolish lightness and frequent changeability without reason in the eyes, so conversely maturity and gravity appear there. Therefore, they were not slow as some blockheads and stupid, dazed people are, but as we see in grave, deliberate, and weighted men. Their eyes were slow and grave because in investigation, it is not necessary that the eye—that is, the intellect—run and judge before it knows. Rather, it is necessary that with a long duration of time it considers minutely and without lightness, and with gravity examines every part, both pro and con, if it wishes to find the truth. AUTHORITY: We call that by which reputation and estimation increase in a man, which is the reason why we often believe them, even though no reason is shown to us. SEMBIANTI: like gestures and acts, or to speak more expressly, in their outward demonstration. And it is a French word <note>Landino refers to the Old French "semblant."</note>, for they say *assemblare* for "to resemble," and from this word "example" is born. Whence we say someone shows goodness in their *sembianti* [appearances]. THEY SPOKE rarely. Which signifies maturity and wisdom. For as it is written: <note>original Latin: "In multiloquio non deest peccatum." A quote from Proverbs 10:19.</note> *In a multitude of words, sin is not lacking.* WITH VOICES sweet. Which signifies humanity and affability. And he placed this here so that one would not believe that their rare speaking proceeded from pride or austerity. Therefore, through rare speaking he shows gravity and modesty, and through sweet voices he denotes humanity and joyfulness. And certainly, it is perfect praise in a man when we see in him the highest gravity joined with the highest joyfulness. WE WITHDREW thus to one of the sides. Which is what anyone does who wants to see better. And he imitates Virgil, who said: <note>original Latin: "Et tumultu capit unde omnis longo ordine possit / Adversos legere: & venientum discere vultus." A quote from the Aeneid, Book VI.</note> *He took a spot from which he could scan the whole long line and learn the faces of those coming toward him.* And secretly it signifies that he who wants to know and speculate withdraws to one of the corners, that is, into solitude, because the crowd and frequency are enemies of speculation. And then he adds: IN A PLACE OPEN, luminous, and high. For just as he who wants to see with bodily eyes seeks an open place—that is, one not occupied by trees, nor mountains, nor obstacles that take away the view—and one that is luminous—that is, in pure daylight and without fog—and one that is high so that he stands above the thing he wants to see, like Zacchaeus who climbed the sycamore tree. So in speculation, it is necessary to remove and refute all obstacles and doubts that take away our view of the truth. Furthermore, we shall use luminous, conspicuous, and clear discourses, and we shall stay in a high place such as "First Philosophy" <note>Metaphysics.</note>, which is the source from which every truth derives. EXALTS me within myself: Because contemplating the egregious deeds of the magnanimous causes the soul of the considerer to rise and desire to imitate such magnanimity.

**->I saw Electra with many companions<-**
**->among whom I recognized Hector and Aeneas,<-**
**->Caesar armed with hawk-like eyes:<-**
**->I saw Camilla and Penthesilea;<-**
**->On the other side I saw King Latinus<-**
**->who sat with Lavinia his daughter:<-**
**->I saw that Brutus who drove out Tarquin,<-**
**->Lucretia, Marcia, Julia, and Cornelia,<-**
**->and alone, apart, I saw Saladin.<-**

He places first in this speculation of his the men who were excellent in the active and civil life. Afterward, those who were egregious in the contemplative life. Not because he prefers the active, but because, considering the nature of man—or insofar as he is a man—action occurs first, which consists in particulars, before contemplation, which consists in universals. ELECTRA: daughter of Atlas. <margin>C</margin> Atlas had seven daughters: Electra, <margin>H</margin> Maia, Sterope, Taygete, Alcyone, and Merope. Electra was the wife of Corythus, a king in Italy, by whom his principal city was named Corythus. Many believe this was the place they call Corneto today. Electra, however, not by her husband but by Jove, fathered Dardanus. Who, after the death of Corythus, coming into dissension with Iasius his brother (of the same mother and son of Corythus), deliberated to leave him alone in the kingdom and with part of the people sailed to Samothrace, and then to Phrygia where Troy later stood. And from him the Trojans had their origin. This was in the thirty-fifth year of Moses, and in the year of the world 3737. WITH MANY companions: as if to say either of the people who followed Dardanus, or rather of many kings who were excellent in the lineage of Dardanus. But because these were less famous, he shows he did not fully recognize them...
**E iiii** <note>This is a signature mark used by printers to keep the pages in order for binding.</note>

## Section D

Concerning **Hector** and **Aeneas**: because these were the most excellent of men. **Hector** was the son of **Priam**: and possessed such virtue that he was almost the sole reason that **Troy** defended itself for ten years. And after many most excellent feats of arms—according to **Homer** and the other writers who followed Homer—he was killed by **Achilles**. But **Dio Chrysostom** <note>original: "Dione chriſoſtomo," a 1st-century Greek orator and philosopher known for his "Trojan Discourse"</note>, a supreme philosopher and diligent investigator of antiquity, demonstrates—both through the histories of the **Egyptians** and by many signs—that it was not Achilles who killed Hector, but rather Hector who killed Achilles. Furthermore, he argues that Troy was not destroyed by the Greeks; rather, the Greeks were broken and for the most part consumed by the Trojans. Regarding **Aeneas**, we spoke of him above.

The following day, she summoned her father, Spurius Lucretius, and her husband. The former brought Publius Valerius with him, and the latter brought Lucius Junius Brutus. <meta>This page continues the catalog of famous figures from antiquity whom Dante encounters in Limbo—the first circle of Hell reserved for the virtuous who lived before Christ or without baptism.</meta>

->**INFERNO.**<-

...of whom little can be said: And certainly this is not the place to be able—I do not say to adorn—but even to briefly narrate his many great and divine virtues. For if we consider his governance in the Republic, it seems that nothing could have remained for his studies and learning; if, on the other hand, we take note of the things he wrote, we would judge that he never departed from his studies. Nevertheless, he perfectly served both the active and the contemplative life. <note>The "active and contemplative life" refers to the Renaissance ideal of balancing political duty with intellectual study.</note> Solely during the conspiracy of Catiline, he preserved liberty; at that time, Roman liberty was abandoned by all the nobles, had he not come to its rescue. For this reason, he earned the title of "Father of the Fatherland" <note>original: *padre de la patria* (Latin: *Pater Patriae*)</note> by public decree of the Senate and the Roman people. And Pompey the Great, returning in triumph, said that he owed everything to Cicero, because if he had not preserved the fatherland, Pompey would have had no place to hold his triumph. He was, therefore, the father of the fatherland. Nor was he any less the father of Latin eloquence, which he raised to such sublimity that since then no one has been able—I do not say to raise it higher—but even to maintain it where he placed it.

**D** **LINUS** was a Theban. Because of his supreme eloquence, some poets said he was the son of Mercury and Urania, and others said of Apollo. Among the Greeks, he was the first to discover melody and proportion in music, and he was excellent in the poetic arts. He translated the letters that Cadmus brought from Phoenicia to Greece into the Greek style of speech. He had many disciples, but the most excellent were Hercules, Thamyris, and Orpheus. He wrote of the deeds of the first Dionysus. They say that because Hercules was of a dull wit in learning to play the lyre—and for this was often beaten by his master with the instrument—he eventually killed Linus with the very lyre with which he was learning.

**E** **SENECA.** This was Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Spaniard born in Cordoba, who later became a Roman citizen. And from him was born the Seneca of whom we presently treat <note>The author follows a common Renaissance error of splitting Seneca the Younger into two people: a father who was a declaimer and a son who was the philosopher.</note>, an admirable man of doctrine, especially Stoic philosophy. He was no less laudable for his natural wisdom and sanctity of life. Because of these virtues, he was appointed as the tutor to the Emperor Nero, and in the beginning, he was highly honored by him. But later, as Nero's cruel tyranny became more displeasing to him every day, and as he many times endeavored to stand in the way of the Emperor's rages, he fell under suspicion. Furthermore, he was often bitten by many detractors in Nero’s presence, accused of being a man who sought to increase his great wealth beyond that of a private citizen, seeking to win the favor of the people, and almost wishing to contend with Nero in the magnificence of his villas and the beauty of his gardens. Seneca, therefore, under an honorable pretext, wished to free himself from such envy and return all these things to Nero, demonstrating that because of his old age he was no longer fit for the governance of so many things. But Nero, then feigning love for him, would not accept them. Later, no longer able to hide his hatred, Nero determined that he must die. But granting him the choice of how he wished to die, Seneca had his veins opened in a bath of warm water. He was a very close friend of Paul the Apostle, as is shown by several letters sent from one to the other. <note>This refers to a famous but forged correspondence between Seneca and St. Paul that was widely believed to be authentic in the Middle Ages.</note> This persuaded Jerome that he might be among the blessed. But Dante, as Seneca’s baptism does not appear, nor finding him in the catalog of saints, places him in Limbo.

**F** **EUCLID** was from the city of Megara, a most studious reader of the books of Parmenides. He became an excellent physicist and mathematician. <note>The text here confuses Euclid of Megara (a philosopher) with Euclid of Alexandria (the mathematician and author of the *Elements*).</note> For this reason, after the death of Socrates, Plato and his other disciples—out of fear of the thirty tyrants of Athens—fled to Megara to join Euclid.

**G** He believed that there is only one Good, and this he calls sometimes God, sometimes Mind, and sometimes Prudence.

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion of the Second Circle of Hell, where Minos judges the souls. This page begins the commentary on the punishment of the Lustful.</meta>

**HELL.**

**"Mute of all light"**: that is, deprived of it. The author uses a term belonging to hearing [mute] for something belonging to sight. The disturbances of the soul are of four types in general, but in species there are many more, as we shall demonstrate in another place. All these things extinguish the light of reason within us. But above all others, love makes a man entirely blind. <note>The commentator is referencing the Aristotelian/Scholastic view that passions "cloud" the intellect.</note> Hence the poets depict Love as blind. Likewise, he is depicted as a child to show that he lacks all mature judgment. Regarding this, Propertius wrote: <note>original: "Quicunque ille fuit puerum qui pinxit amorem / Nonne putas miras hunc habuisse manus? / Is primum vidit sine sensu vivere amantes / Et levibus curis magna perire bona."</note> *“Whoever he was who painted Love as a boy, do you not think he had wondrous hands? He was the first to see that lovers live without sense, and that great goods perish through light cares.”* And the author rightly compares this to the sea, which, as we demonstrated most excellently in Virgil's *Aeneid*, represents appetite and sensuality. For just as the sea is calm in itself, but when moved by winds—especially if they are contrary—it rises in a great tempest; so our appetite, quiet in itself, is disturbed by various passions. These are often contrary within the mind, as shown by Terence’s character Pamphilus, who is pushed on one side by love and compassion for Glycerium, and on the other is pulled back by respect for his father. These "contrary winds" make the sea bellow; that is, they move the lover's sensuality to bellows and woes. **"The hellish storm"**. They specifically use the terms *bufera* and *busea* in the mountains when the falling snow is whipped up and whirled around in ruin by shifting winds. <note>The commentator uses local mountain dialect to explain Dante's specific word choice for the storm.</note> He imagines, then, that those spirits were in the same way milled about and transported through the air. This signifies nothing other than the continuous instability, inconstancy, and sudden changes found in lovers. For as Terence says, all these things are in love. Therefore, this constant inconstancy and furious change ravishes the soul, turning it from purpose to purpose and striking it—that is, giving it heavy pains, molesting and afflicting it. And when they reach **"the ruin"**, that is, when they fall from the thing they loved and remain deprived of it, there are the shrieks, the weeping, and the lamentations, and they blaspheme divine power. This signifies the extreme fury which is common in lovers. It also demonstrates the perversion in their love, because they prefer such love to the love of God and of their father. **"Who subject reason to talent"**. That is, to appetite. <term>Talento</term> <note>In modern Italian, "talent" means ability, but here it refers to "desire" or "inclination."</note> is the inclination of the soul and the appetite toward pleasure and sensory delight. Hence, "to talent" means to consent. **"And as the starlings"** carry their wings. This is an excellent comparison of birds to souls because of their lightness. Because starlings fly quickly and in great throngs, it expresses the multitude and velocity of the spirits. **"Hither, thither, upward, downward"** it leads them. The lover is never in one state. Instead, he now rises into the grace of the beloved, and now falls into ruin through enmities and dissensions. **"No hope ever comforts them"**. Not of rest, but even of a lesser pain. Regarding the actual Hell, this is true of every person damned for any sin whatsoever. Therefore, the author placed this here at the first location of punishments so that it might be understood for all the others. But regarding the allegorical sense, it is specific to the lustful, because such disturbance is insatiable. The more it is exercised, the more it inflames the appetite. The poets intended nothing else by Tityus, the son of the Earth, who wished to do violence to Latona, the mother of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>. This represents lust, which is born from the desire for earthly things; although the vulture gnaws his liver, just as much grows back continually as the bird devours. Furthermore, the lover is never without pain. For if he is deprived of the beloved, he consumes himself with the desire to have them. If he possesses them, he is always in jealousy and in suspicion of losing them.

<margin>M</margin>
And as the cranes go singing their lays,
making a long line of themselves in the air,
so I saw coming, uttering woes,
shadows carried by the said strife;
wherefore I said: "Master, who are those
people, whom the black air so punishes?"

As he expressed the multitude and velocity of the spirits through the comparison of starlings, so through the **cranes** he signifies their lamentations. And he rightly said **"go singing their lays"**, that is, laments. <note>The word "lai" (lays) refers to a specific type of mournful song or poem.</note> For almost all the verses and songs of lovers contain complaints and regrets, and things that move one to commiseration. Hence the Greeks call such verses **Elegies**, because <term>eleos</term> <note>original: "elos"</note> in Greek signifies mercy and compassion. **"Making a long line of themselves in the air"**. He does not say that the spirits were flying in a long line, because he showed above that they flew in a throng like starlings. But he says they flew singing their lays like cranes do when, in flight, they form a long line. **"Who are those people?"** He does not ask about all the people in that circle, because he already knows what kind of sinners are tormented there. But specifically, he asks about those who are near him. And because they are names from ancient history, he asks Virgil. Throughout the poem, he almost always observes this rule: he has Virgil speak of ancient histories, while modern ones—those after Virgil's time—he has others recount.

<margin>N</margin>
"The first of those of whom news
thou wishest to know," he then said to me,
"was empress of many tongues.
To the vice of luxury she was so broken,
that she made 'pleasure' 'lawful' in her law,
to take away the blame into which she had fallen.
She is Semiramis, of whom it is read
that she succeeded Ninus, and was his spouse."

**Semiramis** was the wife of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. Regarding her origin, Diodorus Siculus records fabulous things. For he writes that she was born in a forest near a lake in the city of Ascalon. He names her mother as one who was worshipped there as a goddess, and her father as a youth who sacrificed to her. He says that after she was born, she was hidden in a cave and there nourished by doves with milk, which they took from shepherds while they were milking. Finally, she was found and given to Simmas, the overseer of the king's shepherds. She was then named Semiramis because she had been nourished by doves, for in the Syrian language, **Semiramis** signifies a dove. Growing up, she became of such marvelous beauty...

# **HELL.**

[Left Column]

...the manner: It does not offend him that you love, but that you love inordinately. **Caina** awaits: that is, it expects him who killed us. And Caina is a place that will be mentioned below where traitors and murderers are punished; named after **Cain**, who was the first murderer, as will be more fully discussed there.

Once I heard those wounded souls,
I bowed my face, and held it low
until the poet said: “What are you thinking?”
When I replied, I began: “Alas,
how many sweet sighs, how much desire
led these two to the woeful pass!”
Then I turned to them, and I spoke,
and I began: “Francesca, your torments
make me weep, sad and full of pity.
But tell me: in the time of sweet sighs,
by what and how did love concede
that you should know your dubious desires?”
<gloss>The lover does not dare reveal himself to the beloved while the desires are "dubious"—that is, not yet known. But once he understands that she desires the same thing, then he takes heart to reveal himself.</gloss>
And she to me: “There is no greater sorrow
than to remember happy times
in misery; and this your teacher knows.
But if to know the first root
of our love you have such great affection,
I will do as one who weeps and speaks.
We were reading one day for delight
of **Lancelot**, how love constrained him;
we were alone, and without any suspicion.
Many times that reading urged
our eyes to meet, and drained our faces of color;
but only one point was the one that overcame us.
When we read how the longed-for smile
was kissed by such a great lover,
this one, who shall never be divided from me,
Kissed my mouth, all trembling.
A **Galeotto** <note>original: "Galeotto"; This refers to Galahault, the intermediary who encouraged the affair between Lancelot and Guinevere. Francesca is saying the book itself acted as a panderer.</note> was the book and he who wrote it;
that day we read no further in it.”
While the one spirit said this,
the other wept so, that out of pity
I fainted, as if I were dying,
And I fell, as a dead body falls.

[Right Column]

This shows that the sensuality expressed by Dante moves toward compassion; and bowing the face to the earth signifies that the soul has more care for the bodily pleasures of which these souls are deprived than for true and immortal pleasure.

**SWEET sighs.** Certainly, bodily pleasure is very sweet to the senses; but if it is followed, it contains a hidden poison which leads us to extreme ruin. Wherefore the best Tuscan lyric poet <note>Petrarch</note> said: *I know how the snake lies hidden among the flowers.* <note>original: "So come sta tra fiori ascoso langue"</note> For this reason, we ought to do with pleasure what the Trojan elders said of Helen: "Certainly this woman is beautiful, but it is better she goes away than that Troy should perish." Pleasure is a very sweet thing and very delightful to the senses, but it should be abandoned rather than the soul perishing, because it leads us to the "woeful pass," which is not only the essential Hell <note>The literal place of punishment</note> but also the moral one, because no perturbation torments the soul more than this.

**THAT you should know your dubious desires:** that is, you reached the point where one manifested their desires to the other. For the lover...

**WHEN the soul leaves the body pure** and without any contagion of any sin, it remains simple in its own nature; nor does it think of anything except its happiness, which is to enjoy God; and because it is not weighed down by any earthly mass, it flies easily and with supreme desire toward that goal. But the soul that departs filthy and defiled by sins, in which it placed all its happiness, desires nothing else but to practice those same sins. Wherefore the **Apocalypse** <note>the Book of Revelation</note> says most excellently: *For their works follow them.* <note>original: "Opa eni illorū sequuntur illos"</note> And **Virgil**: *The same joy they had in chariots and arms while living, the same care to feed their shining horses, follows them when they are laid in the earth.* <note>original: "Quæ gratia currū. Armorūque fuit uiuis quæ cura nitētes. Pascere equos eadē sequitur tellure repositos"</note> And the thinking upon past pleasures in a time when they can no longer practice them is their great passion and no small torment. This, therefore, demonstrates a general sentiment by saying: "there is no greater sorrow than to remember happy times in misery." And he adds: **AND THIS your teacher knows**, because Virgil in the sixth book <note>of the *Aeneid*</note> signifies this same sentiment in the verses already mentioned. Others say: "your teacher knows this" because he is currently damned in **Limbo** and deprived of the glory he had near Octavian <note>The Emperor Augustus</note>. But the first interpretation fits better.

Then it follows: although it is painful to remember happy times in misery, nevertheless it is no small consolation to relate it to one who shows compassion. These first two stanzas <note>term: "ternarii"; three-line stanzas or tercets</note> serve as the introduction to her speech; in the first, she captures attention through the gravity of the rhetorical device called a "sententia" <note>a brief moral saying</note>, and also gains goodwill through commiseration. In the second, she makes the listener receptive. Then in the third, she begins the narration, which she makes brief because she puts nothing superfluous in it; it is clear and fitting because she observes the proper order and uses appropriate and believable words. She shows all the means were present that could lead to such an end: first, the reading of amorous things and a similar case, which could even make those who do not love fall in love. And everyone understands that an example easily moves one to do the same, especially when there is the authority of esteemed persons like **Lancelot** and **Guinevere**. Then, because they were alone; and finally, without any suspicion. These conveniences could make one sin who had not previously been inclined to it; for as the proverb says: *An open chest makes a just man sin.* And this serves as a demonstration of the art; but morally, it shows that idleness, lewd readings, the example of those who have done what we wish to do (especially men of authority), and finally the convenience of place and time easily induce men to lewd and forbidden love.

### CANTO SIXTH 45

**WE were reading one day for delight.** To read "for delight" means to be in a state of leisure. For whoever is occupied with work does not seek amusement, but seeks to finish his business. Thus, they were in leisure; and leisure, together with lascivious amusement, generates carnal love. Whence Petrarch says: *It is born of leisure and human lasciviousness.* <note>original: "E nato d'ocio & di laſciuia humana"</note> And Ovid: *If you take away leisure, Cupid's bows perish.* <note>original: "Otia si tollas periere cupidinis arcus"</note> And the Terentian character <term>Menedemus</term> <note>A character in Terence's play 'The Self-Tormentor' who represents the strictness of a busy life versus the idleness of youth.</note> shows to his son that leisure is what makes men fall into lasciviousness, just as, conversely, toil and occupations preserve chastity. On this, Juvenal writes: *Their humble fortune used to keep the Latin women chaste in former times, nor did it allow their small homes to be touched by vice: labor, and short sleep, and hands worn and hardened by the Tuscan wool, and Hannibal near the city.* <note>original: "Præſtabat caſtas humilis fortuna latinas. Quōdā, nec uitiis contingi parua ſinebat. Tecta labor ſonique breues & uellere tuſco. Vexatæ duræque manus & pximus urbi Hanibal." This passage argues that hard work and the threat of war (Hannibal) kept the Romans virtuous.</note>

**OF LANCELOT, how love constrained him.** In Dante's time, a book called *The Round Table* <note>Referring to the Lancelot-Grail cycle of French prose romances.</note> was held in high regard; in which it is written that Lancelot was in love with Guinevere, the wife of King Mark <note>The commentator here mistakenly names King Mark—the husband of Isolde—instead of King Arthur as Guinevere's husband.</note>:

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, moving into the Third Circle where the gluttonous are punished. The previous page likely concluded the discussion of the second circle (the lustful) and the transition into the circle of gluttony.</meta>

->**INFERNO**<-

...sweet; and exquisite costs; and he is called a glutton. Similarly, the species would not endure because every animal would move toward death if, while they are alive, they did not generate someone to succeed them. Nature, fearing that negligence or the labor of nourishing and raising children might impede such generation, placed pleasure in intercourse. Therefore, he who uses this not to seek pleasure, but to produce children—and uses it when, where, how, and with whom it is appropriate—does not sin. He who does otherwise, sins. The gluttonous are therefore punished in this third circle, and the poet shows that upon returning to his senses, he found himself among them. And regarding the essential Hell, he assigns a fitting penalty, because every sin must be punished by its opposite. Therefore, where pleasure had been found in excellent wines, the sweetest foods, and exquisite dishes, the penalty is cold and heavy rain; and stained water in place of wine, and in place of food, there is hail and snow. And as for the moral meaning, everyone understands that excessive eating and drunkenness cause various humors <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to control health and temperament.</note> and catarrhs to descend from the head, which induce strokes, tremors, coldness of the nerves, and stupor of the soul. And this is denoted by the "dark air," because they induce gloom and oblivion in the soul; and those humors, having fallen into the stomach, rot with an extreme stench. All of this generates pains in the head, stomach, and sides, and gout, which make men howl like dogs. And it is a true sentiment and a common proverb: "the throat kills many more than the sword." **Rule and quality**: because similar effects are always born. Therefore, it is never "new," that is, it is not unusual, because that rule and quality is always the same.

**V**

[Left Column]
**Cerberus, a cruel and monstrous beast,**
   **with three throats barks like a dog**
   **over the people who are submerged here.**
**His eyes are red, his beard is greasy and black,**
   **his belly is wide, and his hands are clawed;**
   **he clutches the spirits, flays, and quarters them.**
**The rain makes them howl like dogs;**
   **with one side they shield the other,**
   **the miserable profane ones often turn themselves.**

[Right Column]
**Cerberus the beast.** Hesiod, the Greek poet, writes that Cerberus was the dog of Pluto <note>The Roman god of the Underworld.</note> with three heads, the son of Typhon the giant and Echidna the serpent. He says that Orthos, the dog of Geryon, was born from the same parents, as was the Chimera, which had three heads: one of a lion, one of a dragon, and one of a goat. And we demonstrate in the allegories of Virgil that Cerberus is placed to represent the necessities of the body: food, drink, and sleep, without which three things the animal cannot live. Therefore, Dante has placed him most excellently in this spot, because gluttony consists of food and drink when we exceed in them, as has already been said. **Cerberus, a cruel and monstrous beast.** This serves the fictional narrative: he is "cruel" because of the pain he inflicts. **Monstrous** <note>original: *diuerna* or *diuersa*, meaning different or varied</note> from other beasts; or "varied" because he has different mouths. **Cruel**, because gluttony

[Full Width Paragraph]
consumes everything. Hence Juvenal: <note>original: "Quis enim te deficiente crumena: & creſcente gula manet exitus ere paterno. Atque rebus merſis i uentrē fenoris atque argēti grauis & pecorū agrorūque capace."</note> *For what end awaits you when the purse is failing but the throat is growing, consuming the paternal inheritance and sinking everything into the belly—interest, heavy silver, flocks, and fields?* He is "varied" because he is not content with a simple food but seeks a variety of them from the earth, the sea, and the air. **Barks**: *latrare* in the Latin language means to bark. **His eyes are red**: as for the fiction, he gives him red eyes to show the beast's rage, for every angry person’s eyes turn red; and as for the allegory, it shows that such an effect is caused by superfluous food and especially wine. **The beard is greasy**, which is characteristic of gluttons. The "greasy beard" signifies the greediness of one who stuffs himself too much while devouring, so that not only the mouth but the whole face is smeared. **The belly is wide** to show the engorging of food. Hence the Prophet: <note>original: "Quorū deus uēter e." from Philippians 3:19</note> *Whose god is their belly.* **Clawed hands**: this denotes rapacity and the greed for food, because he snatches what he devours. **Clutches, flays, and quarters**: This places before our eyes the voracity of gluttons, and on the other hand, shows the torments men suffer through the vice of the throat, through which they fall into various diseases where it is necessary to cut, to burn, and in many ways tear the body. And he adds that they howl, to show various pains. From this it happens that the stomach, sides, gout, and fevers give great pain. But they have a proverb: *One morsel and two woes.* **With one side they shield the other**: that is, defense. It shows that from the throat is born the illness which causes one to turn now on this side and now on that side. **Miserable profane ones**: "Profane" in the Latin language means *procul a fano*, <note>A common medieval etymology: "far from the temple."</note> that is, far from the temple and religious things. Hence they call a "profane" person one who is wicked and contrary to all religion.

[Left Column]
**When Cerberus, the great worm, perceived us,**
   **he opened his mouths and showed his fangs;**
   **he had no limb that he kept still.**
**My leader stretched out his palms,**
   **took some earth, and with full fists**
   **he threw it into the ravenous gullets.**
**As a dog that barks and hungers,**
   **and then grows quiet once he bites his food,**

No small impediment is given to the man who directs himself toward the contemplative life and the investigation of divine things by the necessity of the body; for without sustenance and without food, life cannot be maintained. And then it happens that upon this natural necessity, depraved and corrupt habit craves many more delicacies and varieties of food than nature requires, which is content with little. Hence Cicero: <note>original: "paucis minimiſque natura cōtēta ē."</note> *Nature is content with a few very small things.* Therefore, it is a great impediment for a man who wants to go toward contemplation to have to think about things for his sustenance, it being necessary for life; but the wise man realizes that Cerberus—that is, such necessity—can be satisfied with things of little cost. Returning therefore to the text: he calls Cerberus a **great worm** because a worm is born of putrefaction and feeds on earth, and by Cerberus is understood the appetite, which we have already said is for earthly things. **He opened his mouths**: which are three as we have shown; and it shows hunger and the drawing in...

They can, as one reads regarding the angels and of Christ: they will rise again as male and female with their proper sexes, not because they are to be used, but so that the body may be perfect. And by this, he wishes to express how ugly a thing it is to consider the human soul—born for the contemplation and knowledge of great things—being [reduced to] filth and rot, when its proper food is knowledge and doctrine. For just as the body, composed of the four elements, is nourished by foods made of a similar composition, so the incorporeal soul is nourished by incorporeal things. **WITH slow steps**, which demonstrates contemplation, for he who is deep in thought walks slowly and often stops. He expressed, therefore, what Virgil says of Aeneas and Achates: "His faithful Achates goes as his companion and fixes his footsteps with equal cares." <note>original Latin: *Cui fidus Achates It comes: & paribus curis vestigia figit*</note> **TOUCHING slightly upon the future life.** Reasoning, though with brevity of words, about the life that shall be after the Last Judgment. He speaks here of this natural perfection, which even the damned will have after the Judgment. And the text is ordered thus: **ALL**, that is, "although." **This cursed people**, that is, the damned, **never goes into true perfection**, meaning that supernatural state containing the four gifts already mentioned. Nevertheless, they **expect to be more perfect then**, that is, after the Judgment, because at least they will have that natural [wholeness] **than now**, meaning before the Judgment, where they have neither the natural nor the supernatural [perfection]. Then he concludes the Canto, showing that having departed from Ciacco, they followed the road, which was circular and round. And they circled all that place where the gluttonous were punished. Which signifies morally that in this vice they diligently contemplated the vice from every side. **WE CAME to the point where it steps down**, that is, where one descends. For he imagines that one always descends from the wider circle into the narrower one. And in truth, the more grave the vice is, the more it descends to the bottom and the further it is removed from heaven. **THERE**, that is, at the beginning of the next circle, **we found Pluto, the great enemy**, of whom we shall speak in the following Canto.

In this seventh chapter, the author places the fourth circle, and this he divides into two parts. In the first, he places the punishments of the avaricious and the prodigal; and in the second, those of the wrathful and the sullen. And at the entrance of the circle, he imagines the demon Pluto to be the guardian and lord of this circle. This fiction, so that it may be better interpreted, reminds us of how the ancient poets said Pluto was the son of Saturn and Rhea, and king of the underworld. There were four sons of Saturn who denote the four elements: Jove is fire; Juno is air; Neptune is water; Pluto is earth. By Saturn, they mean Time, and they imagine that he ate all his other children except these four...

# INFERNO.

...among the souls of the Greeks, he said: <note>original Latin: "Pars tollere vocem Exigua inceptus clamor frustratur hiantes." This is from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, describing the ghosts of Greek warriors who are so weakened by death they can only produce a thin, ghostly cry.</note> "Some raised a tiny voice: the cry they began mocks their gaping mouths." **AND THAT GENTLE SAGE WHO KNEW EVERYTHING.** <note>Dante, Inferno VII, 3. The "sage" refers to Virgil, Dante's guide.</note> This is great praise for Virgil and worthy of him: for whoever reads his poem attentively sees that it is filled with so many and such varied subjects that one easily understands him to have been universal in all the disciplines of the ancients, as I strove to recount extensively in a preface of mine at the start of my lectures on the *Aeneid*. 

And if one were to say it is impossible for any man—however learned—to know everything, I respond that the poet here uses a <term>rhetorical figure|A technique where language is used to create a specific effect, often moving beyond literal meaning.</term> called **hyperbole**: that is, a surpassing of the truth used not only by writers but also in everyday speech, such as when we say, "It has been a thousand years since I last saw you." Therefore, he "knew everything," meaning he knew a great deal, and as much as almost any human can know. But if Virgil is viewed allegorically as the human intellect filled with wisdom and accompanied by divine grace, then it can truly be said he "knew everything." **GENTLE**: Noble and generous, as if to say that he did not...

[Right Column]
And if future things were useful to us, God would have given them to us, because God wills every good, being the supreme goodness. **PERHAPS by the force of paralysis.** <note>The commentator is examining the medical possibility of such a deformity.</note> *Paralysis* in Greek is a disease: which, because it loosens the connections of the nerves, induces a tremor in the limbs or twists them. In our language <note>Italian</note>, a person so afflicted is called **paretic** <term>paretico: a person suffering from partial motor loss or tremors</term>. The author concludes, therefore, that although this disease twists the limbs, nevertheless it never twisted anyone into this specific form. One sees in some the neck twisted by palsy, so that he looks sideways; but no one is seen so twisted that he looks backward. And it is an excellent comparison: because just as the paretic always trembles, so these who seek future things always tremble.

[Full Width Commentary]
That is, they live with fear and anxiety as to whether or not what they have predicted will come to pass; they always vacillate and doubt, considering their "points" and moments, the songs of birds, alterations in the air (from which side it thunders or lightens), marks in the earth, or the movement of fire. And finally, even a simple sneeze often makes them change their purpose.

[Left Column]
So may God let you, Reader, gather fruit
from your reading, now think for yourself

so twisted that the tears from the eyes
bathed the buttocks at the cleft.

of the hard crag, so that my Guide
said to me: "Are you still among the other fools?
Here **piety** <note>original: *pieta* - a pun in Italian meaning both 'pity' and 'religious devotion'</note> lives when it is well dead.
Who is more wicked than he
who bears passion against God’s judgment?"

[Right Column]
**SO MAY GOD let you gather fruit from your reading.** He who learns by reading gathers fruit. Therefore, the fruit of this reading is to recognize the foolishness of those who wish to foresee the future. And not without cause does Dante show great compassion: for since he knows the supreme perfection of our soul, it seems that he who, by exhausting himself to know more, becomes more ignorant, deserves compassion. And some say he shows such compassion toward these people because he recognizes himself to have been in such error. But I do not believe this, because Dante was a true **mathematician** <note>In this context, meaning a student of the stars and the quadrivium</note>, a science which no wise man ever despised. **WHEN I SAW our image from up close so twisted:** that is, Dante perceived the human image, and then he saw that the image of these people was twisted when he was near them. Note that this vice is not well recognized if it is not considered closely. For at first glance, wanting to pursue this science seems to be a virtue and not a vice. But let us understand that foreseeing the future is not of human nature, but is proper to God. Hence Isaiah says: "Tell me the former and the latter things, and I will say that you are gods." <note>original: *Priora & nouissima nunciate mihi & dican quod dii estis*</note>

[Full Width Commentary]
And Lucan: "The mortal race is ignorant of the fate of the gods." <note>original: *Sortisque deorum ignare mortale genus*</note> And in the Book of Kings: "For man does not see except those things which appear; but God looks upon the heart." <note>original: *Non enim uidet homo nisi ea que apparent. Deus autem intuetur cor*</note> Dante wept, and Virgil rebuked him. This denotes that the sensitive part of the soul induces compassion for every pain, even if it is justly given. But Reason <note>represented by Virgil</note> forbids that a man be moved to pity by punishments justly inflicted by God; and therefore he says "Here," that is, in Hell where he who erred is punished, **PIETY REIGNS when it is well dead.** It is as if he said: in this place, it is a holy duty <note>*pieta*</note> to have no pity <note>*pieta*</note>. But it is to be noted here that "piety" among the Latins is a virtue by which one bears due affection toward one's country and those joined to us by blood. From this arise compassion and congratulation. Compassion is sorrow for a neighbor's ill, and congratulation is joy at a neighbor's good. Therefore, in this place, he used "piety" to mean "compassion." Furthermore, it seems to be the conclusion of the wise that in no way should we have compassion for the punishments of the sinner, but rather for his misery, grieving that he has fallen into such error. But although Dante—who signifies sensuality—has had compassion for the sinner in many places, nonetheless he has not been rebuked by Virgil as he is here. This shows us that in those who have sinned through frailty, there is some excuse; but the error of these [diviners] has always been mocked even in life.

->CANTO XXI 103<-

**his new wood in that stead:** <note>original: "in quella vece"</note> that is, in that exchange. **AND others twist shrouds:** that is, they make ropes which are created by winding and twisting hemp. **AND some patch the foresail and some the mainsail.** There are three sails on a ship: the largest is the <term>Artimone</term> <note>The mainsail, usually the largest sail on a medieval galley.</note>; the smallest is the <term>Terzeruolo</term> <note>The foresail or small sail used in high winds.</note>; and one in between the two which is called the <term>Mezana</term> <note>The mizzen sail, located toward the stern.</note>. **THUS, not by fire, but by divine art:** that is, by divine order. **THAT it was beliming the bank on every side.** The literal meaning is clear. But allegorically, "to <term>belime</term>" <note>From the Italian "invescare," referring to birdlime, a sticky substance used to trap birds. The author explains that corruption "sticks" to everyone involved.</note> the bank on every side means that both he who sells offices and judgments, as well as he who buys them, is "belimed"—that is, captured by greed. 

Therefore, the courts of republics and of princes—and especially the Roman court—are like an <term>arzana</term> <note>An arsenal or shipyard, specifically referencing the Great Arsenal of Venice.</note> where in the winter (that is, amidst the fluctuations and tumults of men) the **pitch** boils. This pitch represents greed, which belimes and inflames living souls with the desire to possess; through this greed, one bends to their power magistrates, high honors, judgments, and legal sentences; nothing is granted or judged without a foul price. Whereby it follows that the good are cast down and the wicked are exalted.

CANTO XXII 105

“Let these ones stay safe until the next ridge
which goes entirely over the dens.”
“O my master, what is this I see?”
I said, “Without an escort let us go alone
if you know the way, for I do not seek one for myself.
If you are as observant as you usually are,
do you not see how they gnash their teeth
and with their brows they threaten us with harm?”
And he said to me, “I do not want you to be afraid;
let them gnash away at their own whim,
for they do this for the suffering ones in the pain.”
They turned along the left bank,
but first each had pressed his tongue between
his teeth toward their leader as a signal.
And he had made a trumpet of his backside.

**Curly:** <note>original: "riccia"</note> that is, a curly beard. Because according to **physiognomy** <note>The medieval pseudo-science of judging a person's character from their physical features.</note> a frizzy and curly beard demonstrates fraudulence. The fifth demon represents the burning desire to bring <term>barratry</term> <note>The trade of selling public offices or taking bribes; political graft.</note> to perfection after receiving a bribe. He is called **Libicocco**, which means "boiling lust," signifying an unrestrained and burning desire. The sixth is the infection of vice, which with its terrible poison pollutes and stains others; he is called **Draghignazzo**, from the poison of the dragon. The seventh is the offense done to one's neighbor, for the grafter mauls and tears like a wild boar tears with its tusk. For this reason, he is called **Ciriatto the Tusked**. Because "Cyro" <note>original: "Cyro"</note>—not only in the rustic tongue of our people, but in the Greek language—signifies a pig. The eighth denotes the oppression of one grafter against another when the more powerful one tears at the less powerful. This one is **Graffiacane** (Dog-scratcher), because he scratches those who bite others. **Farfarello** is the ninth, by which is meant a deceiver and a chatterer. **Rubicante** (Red-faced) is as if on fire, furious and bold.

The nature of the demonic tempter always frightens the senses at the end, just as, conversely, an angel always brings comfort at the end. Therefore, Dante is frightened by the signals of the demons because they gnash their teeth like dogs eager to bite, and they threaten by moving their eyebrows. But the **higher reason** <note>Represented by Virgil.</note> comforts him so that he does not fear, asserting that such signals are made for the damned. This signifies that they cannot harm anyone except the vicious. **But first each [pressed] his tongue.** This passage seems to many to be without dignity or decency; but certainly, the poet wished to demonstrate how grafters, once they have cheated someone, mock and deride them. Pressing the tongue between the teeth signifies making such a noise with the mouth as the wind makes when it exits from the posterior. This is what impudent buffoons do when they mock someone.

->CANTO XXII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE<-

[Large initial I]
**I** have seen horsemen move camp,
begin the skirmish, and make their muster,
and sometimes retreat for their safety;
I have seen scouts through your land,
O Aretines, and I have seen raiding parties go out,
tournaments clashing and jousts run;
Sometimes with trumpets, and sometimes with bells,
with drums and with signals from castles,

nor ship by sign of land or of castle.

[Woodcut Illustration: On a rocky cliffside, Virgil and Dante (labeled 'V' and 'D') observe a group of winged demons. The demons are armed with long hooks and pitchforks, standing over a pit of boiling pitch where sinners are submerged. In the lower scene, the demons appear to be escorting the two poets along the bank of the dark, bubbling river.]

In this same ditch <note>original: "bolgia"</note> the same sin is still dealt with, and the same sin is punished. But in the previous chapter, he placed those grafters who sold their own Republic. In this twenty-second Canto, he places those who, having been placed in good standing by some lord, sold the favor of that lord. Continuing, then, to describe the form of the punishment of these ones submerged in the pitch, he then makes special mention of one. In the third part, he induces this soul to reveal others. And in the final part, he narrates the trickery that this spirit used to deceive all the demons. **I HAVE SEEN.** He shows that he has seen a troop of men-at-arms depart, which requires the highest prudence and caution; for it contributes much to safety and victory to properly position and move the camps—a virtue they say was supreme in Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes. **AND BEGIN THE SKIRMISH.** This is a multitude of fighting men-at-arms, perhaps named from the Latin word **turma** <note>A troop of cavalry.</note>. Or truly it is an onomatopoeia, that is, a name taken from the noise and din heard in fighting. **AND MAKE their muster: and sometimes retreat for their safety.** The meaning is: I have seen signals given to soldiers, either when they move camp, or when they fight, or when they hold a muster, or when they flee. But never with such a sound. **SCOUTS I have seen.** Here he touches upon, according to some, the expulsion of the Ghibellines from Florence, in which they were mocked. But it is difficult, amidst so many and frequent changes in those times in the city of Arezzo (by which it was desolated), to understand which one he is presently describing. **RAIDING PARTIES** <note>original: "gualdane"</note> was the specific name the ancients gave to riding out against one another, representing a kind of battle. **Joust** is when one goes against another, body to body.

...and represents a singular battle. With signals from castles made equally with smoke by day and with fire by night. But I never saw any move with such a diverse <term>shawm<gloss>a medieval reed instrument, here referring to the signal used by the demon Barbariccia</gloss></term>: that is, the author is using the specific term for the general category. Nor did I see a ship moved by a signal from land or castle. Sailors, when they can see land—that is, some promontory—navigate according to it; and when they cannot see land, they follow the North Star.

**P**erhaps through this passage the poet demonstrates that although we should always flee the comfort and company of the wicked <note>original: "captiui," referring to those 'captive' to sin</note>, nevertheless, sometimes the place, the time, or some other cause leads us to associate with them. Therefore, "in the tavern with gluttons," understand that this is not for the sake of greed, because it is never permissible to associate with the vicious to commit a vice. But rather it is to take necessary food: and so it is here. For since Dante was in Hell and had need of a guide, it was necessary that he follow the demons. And allegorically, wishing to know the malice and malignity of such a vice, it was necessary that he have knowledge of the things comprised under the names of the ten demons. And for this knowledge, he follows them. **STILL**, my intent was on the pitch. Dante had his intent—that is, his attention—on the pitch to see some of the submerged sinners: because the lower reason seeks the knowledge of particulars and not the universals. **AS** dolphins. As sometimes dolphins in the sea come so far to the surface that they show their backs. This is a sign that a storm is soon to arise. Wherefore sailors, by such a sign,

> We went along with the ten demons;
> oh, fierce company! but in the church
> with saints, and in the tavern with gluttons.
> Still, my intent was on the pitch,
> to see every feature of the <term>bolgia<gloss>one of the ten 'pouches' or circular ditches of the Eighth Circle of Hell</gloss></term>
> and the people who were burning within it.
> As dolphins, when they make a sign
> to mariners with the arch of their back,
> that they should prepare to save their ship:
> So now and then, to ease the pain,
> some sinner would show his back
> and hide it in less time than a flash of lightning.

immediately prepare for escape. Thus those sinners, to lighten their pain, sometimes pulled their backs out of the pitch. But for fear of the demons' hooks, they put them back in less time than a lightning flash. The dolphin, above all other fish, delights in the sight of man and loves him greatly. This is known from what writers show in many cases. But most aptly in the story of Arion. Arion of Methymna, a city in Lesbos, was a most skilled musician and, by this art, very welcome to Periander, king of Corinth. But desiring to see the world and to spread his fame (not without profit), he sailed to Sicily, and from there to Italy, where by his skill he accumulated great wealth. But after some time, desiring to return to Periander, he boarded a ship of certain Corinthians. These men, moved by greed and far from any humanity, agreed to throw Arion into the sea and take his money. Hearing this, the musician first turned to prayers and tried to buy back his life from them. Then, seeing that he prayed in vain, he asked for a space of time before they threw him over, so that he might sing with his <term>cithara<gloss>an ancient Greek musical instrument in the lyre family</gloss></term>, dressed and adorned in the most precious robes and jewels he had. This was granted to him, and he sang upon the prow; and after the song, he threw himself into the sea. And immediately, received by a dolphin, he was carried in safety as far as the island of Taenarum. And from there he went to Corinth. And by Periander, those who had wanted to drown him in the sea were summoned. They, stupefied by the unexpected presence of Arion, could not deny it. And Herodotus affirms that in Taenarum, where the dolphin landed him, there was his bronze statue placed upon a dolphin. Pliny also writes that a dolphin in the gulf of Baia became so tame with a boy who gave him bread every day, that finally, at any hour the boy called him, he came and carried him across the narrow gulf from Baia to Pozzuoli. And after several years, the boy having died, the dolphin stayed on the shore waiting for him, not without signs of sorrow; and finally, the boy not appearing, he died of grief. It would be very prolix to relate many other similar things written by Theophrastus, Aristotle, and other writers. 

**N**ow, the dolphin is of such speed that it surpasses in running not only other fish, but even birds and the arrow. Nor could any fish escape it, were it not that the dolphin cannot catch anything except when on its back. This is because its mouth is far from its snout and almost in the middle of its belly. And because it breathes like the whale and the <term>monk seal<gloss>original: "vecchio marino," literally 'old man of the sea'</gloss></term>, it is necessary that with incredible velocity it returns to the surface from the bottom where it follows its prey. It gives birth to young and not eggs, and nourishes them with milk. It carries the little ones on its back, and accompanies and escorts the youths. They live thirty years. Their voice is similar to a human wail. They love man greatly and delight much in music. If one dies, the others lead it out of the water. I have written these few things out of many, rather invited by the noble nature of the animal than because I judged it necessary in this place. And now I return to the text.

**H**ere no other allegory occurs. But to decorate the place, he only describes the place of punishment and uses the simile of the frogs. **I SAW AND ALSO**—that is, further—**TO THE HEART** where is the seat of the...
