### CANTO XXIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

**T**aciturn, alone, and without company,
we went on, one in front and
the other behind,
as **Minorite friars** <note>The Franciscans, known for traveling in pairs, one following the other in silence.</note> walk along the way.
My thoughts were turned toward **Aesop’s** fable
by the present brawl,
where he speaks of the frog and the mouse.
For *mo* and *issa* <note>Both are old Italian dialect words for "now"—*mo* from the south/Lombardy and *issa* from Lucca/Tuscany. Dante argues the fable matches the current event as perfectly as these two synonyms match each other.</note> are no more alike
than the one is to the other, if one couples
the beginning and the end with a steady mind.
And as one thought bursts from another,
so from that one another was born
which doubled my first fear.
I thought like this: "These demons through us
have been mocked, and with such damage and insult
that I believe they must be greatly annoyed.
If anger is joined to their ill-will,
they will come after us more cruelly
than a hound after the hare it snaps at."

[Woodcut illustration depicting Dante and Virgil walking, with demons and figures in a pit. Labels "CAIPHAS" and "D V" <note>Dante and Virgil</note> are visible.]

**T**he canto changes along with the punishment, because in this sixth ditch <term>bolgia|A "ditch" or "pouch" in the eighth circle of Hell.</term> he treats **hypocrisy** and the suffering and torment of it. But in the beginning, he describes their progress toward this ditch and the pursuit they endured from the demons, and how they were saved by **Virgil**. **SILENT**: which signifies that each was thinking of his grief within himself. **ALONE**: each by himself, which signifies the same. For when we wish to weigh something diligently, we separate ourselves from others. Hence the character **Simo** in the works of **Terence** said: <note>original: "Venit meditatus alicunde ex solo loco"</note> "He comes having meditated on something from a solitary place," that is, without the company of others. **ONE IN FRONT**: namely, Virgil. **THE OTHER BEHIND**: namely, Dante. And by this, he wishes to demonstrate that in the contemplation of difficult things, the **inferior reason** (which deals with specific details) cannot be equal to the **superior reason** (which has knowledge of universal truths). Therefore, the superior reason goes first as the more worthy thing, and the inferior follows it. **AS MINORITE FRIARS WALK ALONG THE WAY**: A fitting comparison both for the manner of walking and the silence. For these friars, when traveling, go one behind the other in silence and meditation. They were, therefore, alone in body, but the mind was accompanied by contemplation and investigation; these things proceed better and find the truth more easily when one is alone, for the soul can have no better company. Thus it happens to a learned man: the more the body is unaccompanied, the more the soul is accompanied. This is why **Scipio Africanus** used to say that he was never less alone than when he was alone, and never less idle than when he was idle. And **Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo**—a man of great eloquence and most adorned wit and well-lettered—when a certain citizen of ours (a man not wicked, but unlettered) wished to accompany him, saying "I do not want you to go so alone," responded: "I would be alone if I were with you." And **Seneca**, in an epistle, affirms that the wise man is never alone.

**TURNED TOWARD AESOP’S FABLE**: **Aesop the Phrygian** was a Greek poet who wrote "apologues," that is, fables, which contain within them moral lessons and hidden precepts for living well. One of these fables tells of a mouse walking through a field who came upon a ditch full of water. Not daring to cross, a frog offered to carry him across and tied the mouse to himself with the intent of pulling him under the water to drown him. But the frog pretended he was tying the mouse to him so that he would not fall. At that moment, a hawk, seeing the mouse and desiring to feed on it, swooped down and snatched him up; it carried off the frog as well because he was tied to the mouse. And so it happened that the fraud the frog had devised to harm the mouse resulted in his own death. Dante, therefore, remembered this because it was a similar case. Just as the frog, believing he would trick the mouse, was instead caught, so it happened to the two demons mentioned above. And it secretly demonstrates that similar things often happen among **barrators** <note>Those who trade in bribes or public office.</note>: while one seeks to trick the other, a third comes and tricks the tricker and the tricked.

**IN THE PRESENT BRAWL**: That is, in the current fight between **Alichino** and **Calcabrini**. He follows by saying there is no greater similarity than between *mo* and *issa*. For both these words in different parts of Lombardy signify what we call "now" and "just now." He is comparing the beginning (the motive that moved the frog and the demon, which in each case was to deceive) and **THE END**: that is, the effect that followed, which was that each remained deceived. **WITH A STEADY MIND**: that is, firm. **AND AS ONE THOUGHT BURSTS FROM ANOTHER**: that is, is born; this is a metaphor from flowers, which are not born unless the bud in which they are enclosed bursts open. **SO FROM THAT ONE ANOTHER WAS BORN**: from thinking about their fight, another thought arose, which was that they might want to take revenge on us and therefore pursue us. **WHICH DOUBLED MY FIRST FEAR**: the first fear he had when he saw...

And then he posits that, while thinking, he said to himself: “Since these <note>referring to the Malacoda's band of demons</note> have received harm and mockery on our account, they must certainly have conceived anger toward us.” And if this particular anger toward us **IS JOINED** <term>s’aggueffa: an archaic Italian term meaning to heap up or join together, specifically like adding a strand of wool to a bundle</term>: that is, it links and connects with the ill will of their evil intent. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s passage through the fifth ditch (bolgia) of the eighth circle of Hell, where the Barrators are punished. Virgil and Dante are currently attempting to escape the Malebranche demons who have turned against them.</meta>

**INFERNO.**

ours: Wherefore, although today I have judged that Antonio Canigiani and Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Two prominent Florentine citizens of the time, used here as an example of how the mind forms judgments of friendship.</note> are uniquely close friends and deserve to be loved, it would nonetheless be necessary to remake this judgment every hour were it not for the memory that preserves for us what has already been done. Returning, therefore, to what pertains to the present place: Dante saw the ten demons. <note>original: "la decima de demonii"; this refers to the troop of ten demons led by Barbariccia.</note> This was the task of the eye and the common sense; and not only did he see them present, but their images remained fixed in the imaginative faculty, <term>Imaginative faculty: The part of the mind that stores sensory images even when the object is no longer present.</term> whose office is to preserve them even in the absence of the thing itself. Wherefore his cogitative faculty, <term>Cogitative faculty: In medieval psychology, the "inner sense" that judges whether an image is helpful or harmful (e.g., a lamb instinctively fearing a wolf).</term> turning to the imaginative faculty, found these images there no differently than if he saw them in a mirror; and from the images, he drew intentions. For just as a dog, seeing its master, draws from that image the "intention" which is another, more incorporeal image—and this is benevolence—and seeing the wolf, draws from its image the intention which is enmity, and judges that it should celebrate the one and bite the other; so Dante’s cogitative faculty drew from the images of the demons the intentions which were cruelty, perfidy, malevolence, and the like. Therefore, he judged it useful to flee them. And the imagination was so powerful that he seemed to feel them coming. This judgment is proper to the senses, and because of this, it is found not only in man but also in other animals. But it is always concerned with particular things, because the senses cannot comprehend universals. Therefore Dante—that is, the sensitive part of him—judges from this particular judgment that at this time and in this place, these demons must be fled. Virgil—that is, the intellect—turns to this judgment and approves it because it is true; but he leads it from the particular to the universal. He judges that not only at this time and in this place should these demons be fled, but in every time and every similar place, all similar demons must be fled. Wherefore it is most true that reason, pouring itself over the senses, receives the judgment given by them no differently than a mirror receives the image of the body to which it is turned. And if such a judgment is well-given, reason immediately approves it. You, then, noting with diligence what we have said about the judgment of the senses and of reason, will easily understand the text to which I return. WE HAVE THEM ALREADY BEHIND US: Not that he saw them, but his imagination was so powerful that he seemed to see and hear them. Whence he says: I IMAGINE THEM SO—that is, so strongly—THAT I ALREADY FEEL THEM. And this we have explained just above. AND HE: Understand that Virgil replied: IF I WERE LEADED GLASS—that is, if I were a mirror, which is glass covered on the back side by a thin plate of lead. <note>Mirror-making in the 15th century involved coating glass with a lead or tin amalgam to create a reflective surface.</note> This plate is attached to the glass with certain liquids and herbal juices, which few people know how to do. It happens, then, that when a body is placed before the glass, because the glass is diaphanous—that is, transparent—it receives the image of that body into itself. But it does not retain nor multiply it within itself, because the image passes through it. But finding the lead on the other side, which is an opaque and shadowy body, the image cannot pass through and therefore remains in the glass and multiplies its rays there and becomes visible. And in this place, Dante has used periphrasis—that is, a circuitous way of speaking—because he has said in many words what he could have said in one. He could have said "mirror," and instead said "leaded glass," which is almost the definition of a mirror. THE IMAGE FROM WITHOUT—that is, the corporeal image—I would not draw to me more quickly than I IM-PRINT—that is, contain fixedly—THE IMAGE FROM WITHIN—that is, what you imagine and think. JUST NOW—that is, just a moment ago—your thoughts came among mine. For the senses and reason think upon the same thing. WITH SIMILAR ACT—that is, fearing as you do. AND SIMILAR FACE—that is, with a similar appearance, because that same thing represents itself to me as it does to you. But I, having taken your particular judgment, make it universal; and I judge that such things must always be fled. Nor does reason only judge what the senses judge; it transcends with its power and does what the senses could not do: for through the discourse of reason, it consults and investigates if there is any way to flee, and if there are multiple ways, which is the safest, and all the other things we treated extensively when we established the parts of Prudence. This discourse is the office of Prudence, and is proper to reason and not to the senses. Therefore, Dante, having led himself as far as the senses can go, then leads Virgil to investigate what is proper to reason. Wherefore follows:

<meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on Canto XXIII of Dante's Inferno, specifically focusing on the moment Virgil carries Dante to safety from the demons of the fifth ditch.</meta>

->CANTO&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;XXIII.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;109<-

...desire <note>The text begins mid-word: [ap]petito</note> more quickly than reason estimated, Virgil suddenly took Dante: and placed him on his chest and slid feet-first down that whole bank all the way to the bottom of the other ditch <term>bolgia</term> <note>The "bolge" are the ten circular trenches of the eighth circle of Hell</note>. This denotes that the departure from a vice already recognized must be swift and fast. And certainly, man slides to the bottom supine <note>lying on the back, facing upward</note>: because although he descends into the knowledge of another vice—and his feet, meaning his greed <term>cupidita</term>, carry us into it—nonetheless in going supine, the face looks upward. This is so that the recognition of the vice serves to raise one out of it, and not to remain submerged within it. And Virgil holds Dante to his chest, which is the seat of thought: to denote that the appetite <note>the "appetito" represents the human soul's natural desires or drives</note> should draw close to that which reason contemplates and considers. Reason, which with maternal love, seeing him in danger, leaves aside every other care and only attends to saving him. Nor can the demons stationed in the ditch of the barrators <note>corrupt officials who traded public office for money</note> follow Dante into the other ditch: because the temptations of the vice from which he has already departed cannot provoke him while he considers another vice. And it perfectly demonstrates that reason loves the appetite.

<summary>This page provides an allegorical interpretation of Virgil (representing Reason) carrying Dante (representing Appetite) into the sixth ditch to escape demons, symbolizing how reason protects the soul's desires during the transition between recognizing different vices.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a discussion on hypocrisy and moral pretense, likely transitioning from a previous analysis of sinners in Dante's Hell. The text relies heavily on Roman satirists and moral philosophers to define the nature of the "hypocrite."</meta>

->### INFERNO.<-

...spected. It is no wonder, then, if with such impetus and vehemence the Aquinian Juvenal <note>Aquinian refers to Juvenal’s birthplace, Aquino. He was a Roman poet famous for his biting satires on the corruption of Roman society.</note> thunders against them in his satire, the beginning of which is: *I feel like fleeing from here, beyond the Sauromatae <note>original: "Vltra sauromatas." The Sauromatae (Sarmatians) lived near the Black Sea; to a Roman, this meant the ends of the earth.</note> and the frozen ocean, whenever they dare to speak of morals—those who pretend to be like Curius <note>original: "Qui curios simulant." Manius Curius Dentatus was a Roman hero celebrated for his austerity and incorruptible virtue. Juvenal is criticizing those who look like moral heroes but act like libertines.</note> but live like Bacchanalians <note>Participants in the wild, often drunken festivals of Bacchus.</note>.*

And a little further down: *There is no trusting the face. For what street does not abound with grim-faced degenerates? You chastise shameful things when you yourself are the most notorious pit among those who claim to be Socratic!* <note>original: "Inter socraticos notissima fossa cinedos." A harsh critique of people who used the reputation of Socratic philosophy to mask their own moral failings.</note> And certainly, he who confesses his error while sinning and does not deceive you is worthy of excuse. Whence the same poet says: *Peribonius <note>A character in Juvenal's satires who openly displays his vices.</note> is more truthful and acts more ingenuously; I attribute his fault to the fates, for he confesses his malady in his face and gait. For such men, madness itself grants pardon. But they are worse who attack such things with the words of Hercules.* <note>To speak with the "words of Hercules" means to use the language of heroic virtue and strength to mask one’s own inner corruption.</note>

Of these, Cicero most wisely concludes in his book *On Duties* <note>original: "libro de officiis." A foundational text of Western ethics by Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> asserting that the worst kind of men is that of those who, when they wish to deceive, pretend that they are held to be good [men]...

CANTO                                        XXIII.                                        112.

In this, he imitates the Egyptians and those who, through mathematical doctrine, knew that the solar year is finished when the sun has completed its circle through all twelve signs <term>twelve signs: the constellations of the Zodiac</term>: which occurs in the number already written. Therefore, Caesar added to the year of Romulus <note>Romulus was the legendary founder of Rome; the original Roman calendar traditionally had ten months, starting in March.</note> January and February. And he ordered that the beginning of the year should be January; and for this reason, he named it after Janus <note>original: "Giano," the two-faced Roman god of transitions and beginnings</note>, whom the pagans believed to be the god of every beginning. And February he named from *februa*, which signifies purgation <note>original: "purgatione," referring to the Roman festival of Februa, a ritual of purification and atonement</note>. Because in this month they made sacrifices to purge the souls of the dead. For this reason, the Roman Church, following this order, also sets January as the beginning and start of the year. This moved the poet to say: **IN That part of the youthful year** <note>original: "In quella parte del giovanetto anno," quoting the first line of Dante's Inferno, Canto XXIV</note>, to denote that January is the first age of the year, in which, because it is the beginning, the year is still youthful. And so he lifts Dante, who represents the lower reason and sensuality. **TOWARD THE SUMMIT.** That is, toward the height which is speculation and contemplation. **OF ONE GREAT ROCK.** That is, of a piece of stone from the ruin. **HE SAW ANOTHER CRAG.** As if it were another rock. And so it happens: because the intellect not only considers the present, but also looks to the future, and foresees and commands the lower reason—which acts regarding specific details—as to what it must do. And it warns it not to set about doing anything that is beyond its strength. And therefore, while Virgil pulls sensuality toward difficult things, before the first place is considered, he warns that he should then grab onto another higher one. But before he trusts himself to it, he wants him to test if the crag can support him. The intellect excites the lower reason... |

Therefore, just as the physical body is burdened by breathlessness when going uphill, so too is our <term>sensuality</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "sensuality" refers to our lower, physical nature and desires, which resist the "upward" path of moral excellence.</note> troubled by the difficulty of embarking upon the steep path of virtue. But it is necessary...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XXIV, specifically focusing on the description of the Seventh Bolgia (ditch) of the Eighth Circle, where thieves are punished.</meta>

-># INFERNO<-

...red then they say red. AMONG this cruel & most wretched crowd. Among this abundance of cruel serpents and full of sadness & mourning, people were continually running, naked & full of terror, who were being seized by the serpents: and they did not hope to be able to find a <term>hole</term> <note>original: "pertusio", meaning a small opening or crevice to hide in</note>: that is, any hole to hide themselves from the serpents. NOR HELIOTROPE. That is, nor any thing which might make them invisible so that the serpents do not see them, as the heliotrope does. Solinus writes in the book *The Wonders of the World* <note>original Latin: "de mirabilibus mundi"</note> that the heliotrope is a stone which is found in Cyprus. But it is more noble in Ethiopia & in Africa: which is of a green color but clouded & distinguished by purple spots. But when placed in a copper cauldron, it causes the rays of the sun that reflect from it to become blood-red. And there is also a herb similarly called heliotrope: because it always turns toward the sun: and *helios* in Greek signifies "sun" <term>helios</term> <note>original Greek: "elios"</note> and *tropos* signifies "turn" <term>tropos</term> <note>original Greek: "tropo"</note>: The magicians write, therefore, that by anointing such a stone with the juice of such a herb, & consecrating it with legitimate prayers, the man who carries it becomes invisible. Therefore, these sinners do not hope to be able to find heliotrope by which they might be made invisible. WITH serpents their hands were tied behind. Because in this ditch the author places the punishment of the thief: We shall note that in two ways that which belongs to others is taken. Either openly: & with violence: as do the bandits & assassins & highwaymen: & anyone else who takes and plunders not by theft but by robbery: & often kills in order to plunder. Or indeed by theft & in secret with fraud & with deceit. The first are called *robbers* <term>robbers</term> <note>original Latin: "latrones"</note> by the Latins. The second are *thieves* <term>thieves</term> <note>original Latin: "fures"</note>. These second ones are called *fures* from this word *furvum*, which in Latin signifies "black" & "obscure": because he who wishes to commit theft seeks night & darkness & obscurity: Therefore, this seventh ditch being one of those where fraud is punished and not violence, it seems that here one should treat of thieves and not of robbers. Nevertheless, because also he who commits robbery with violence first uses fraud: & works with that more than with strength: as we see in the bandit who, before he assaults the traveler, hides himself in ambush: & uses many other frauds: for this reason, theft & robbery are punished together in a mixture. They stand, therefore, among the serpents which are animals full of craftiness & of cunning. To demonstrate that fraud & deceit are those vices with which they stain the soul: & with which they afflict & perturb the conscience: by which they are always bitten with remorse after the error is committed. They <note>the serpents</note> pass, then, through the loins and with the head and with the tail they fasten to the chest where the heart is, the seat of thought: because such fraud—with the head, that is, from the beginning before the sin is committed—brings great anxiety to the mind, thinking not only of the sin which one prepares to commit, but much more of the danger of infamy: & the harm that can result from it. And then with the tail, that is, after the end, rethinking that which he has done: & expecting every hour that such wickedness will be discovered. From which results infamy & punishment for him. This is the head: This is the tail of the serpent which, passing through the loins to the chest, pierces the heart: & knots itself in front: because such thought & such sting of conscience does not pass away: but remains tied in the mind: & always stays. Nor can they hide themselves nor flee such a sting of conscience: nor do they find any remedy for it: because as Juvenal says, "This is the first vengeance: that with himself as judge, no guilty person is acquitted." <note>original Latin: "prima haec est ultio quod se iudice nemo nocens absolvitur"</note> Therefore, no one who has committed any wickedness is acquitted by himself: because his conscience always judges that he deserves punishment for the sin committed: & as a witness of such wickedness, it stings him night and day.

It distinguishes between violent robbery and fraudulent theft, emphasizing that the "sting of conscience" is the primary inescapable punishment for the guilty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the punishments of the thieves in the seventh circle of Hell. Although the header in the original text reads "Canto XXIII," the content specifically covers the conclusion of Canto XXIV, where a sinner is incinerated and reformed like a phoenix, and identifies himself as Vanni Fucci.</meta>

CANTO XXIII. iis

**In the same way, the great sages affirm**
**that the phoenix dies and then is reborn**
**when its five-hundredth year approaches;**
**It feeds on neither herb nor grain in its life,**
**but only on tears of incense and amomum,**
**and nard and myrrh are its final swaddling bands.**
**And as one who falls, and knows not how,**
**by the force of a demon pulling him to the ground**
**or other obstruction that binds a man,**
**who, when he rises, looks around himself,**
**all bewildered by the great anguish**
**he has suffered, and sighs as he gazes;**
**Such was the sinner after he had risen.**
**O power of God, how severe you are,**
**that showers down such blows for vengeance!**

In no other way does this author affirm the rebirth from its own ashes than by using the example of the phoenix. They say this is a bird in Arabia, as large as an eagle; its neck is gold-colored, and the rest of its feathers are purple, except for the tail, which is azure, though distinguished with rose-colored feathers. They write that it lives five hundred and sixty years. <note>The author likely draws from Pliny the Elder’s Natural History here.</note> Manilius the Senator was the first of the Romans to write of the phoenix; and he said that no one ever saw it feed, but that in Arabia it is consecrated to the sun. When it is old, it makes a nest of twigs from the cassia tree and of incense, and fills it with fragrances, and in that it dies. From its marrow a worm is born, which afterwards becomes a phoenix; and immediately it performs the funeral rites for its already dead mother. It carries the entire nest to Panchaia <note>An ancient mythical island in the Indian Ocean, famous for its incense.</note>, a region of Arabia, to the City of the Sun, and places it upon the altar. Its death marks the revolution of the "Great Year," <note>The "Platonic Year," the time it takes for all the planets and stars to return to their original positions.</note> and that the qualities of the times and the stars return to their beginning; and this begins around the midday of that day when the sun enters Aries. Cornelius Valerianus writes that the phoenix once flew to Egypt and was brought to Rome in the time of the Emperor and Censor Claudius, and placed in the *comitium* <note>The political assembly space in the Roman Forum.</note> in the eight hundredth year since the founding of Rome. But no one doubts that this is false. Others write that the phoenix, when death approaches, turns toward the rays of the sun, and those rays, reflecting in its splendid feathers, create fire. Whereupon it burns together with the nest, and is reborn first as a worm, and after three days its wings grow. **HERB NOR grain does it feed on:** as other birds feed, but it feeds only on **TEARS:** that is, gums or resin of incense and <term>amomum</term> <note>An aromatic plant of the ginger family, used in ancient perfumes.</note>, which distills like tears from its trunk and then solidifies, as we see in the juniper and many other trees. Incense in Latin is called <note>original: "thus"</note> *incense*. Amomum, cardamom, and cinnamon are the same thing; it grows in Ethiopia in sterile places. It is a small tree that grows no higher than two cubits; they do not harvest it without the permission of Jove, and they obtain this with forty-four entrails of oxen, goats, and rams. When they have harvested it, they give half to the sun, and suddenly by itself it ignites and burns. Vespasian was the first who, in the Capitol and in the Temple of Peace, dedicated a crown of this wood ornamented with gold. **AND Nard and myrrh are its final swaddling bands:** that is, it makes its final nest of nard and myrrh in which it burns. Nard grows in India and produces spikes—wherefore it is called <note>original: "spigho"</note> *spikenard*. It also grows in Syria. It grows in Gaul, and this is better known to us; it even grows in Florence and is sown there; it also grows in Crete. Myrrh is a tree that grows in Arabia in the same forests as incense. Others hold that it grows in more regions of Arabia, whereas incense grows only in one called Sheba. This is a thorny tree and grows up to six cubits; the leaves are like olive leaves but curled and sharp. Others describe it as similar to juniper and of that flavor. **AND AS ONE who.** This is an excellent comparison by which he shows that after this man returned from ash into his first form, he became stunned, dazed, and senseless, just as happens to one who, by the force of incantations or some <term>obstruction</term> <note>original: "opilation"</note> <note>A medical term referring to a blockage of the bodily humors, believed to cause epilepsy or fainting.</note>, having been unconscious, comes to himself; but in that first moment, he is astonished and almost senseless. **BY THE force of a demon:** that is, by incantation, as we read of Simon Magus, who through magic arts made men faint in a form that they seemed truly dead, and afterwards, making them come to themselves, he led the common people to believe he had the power to resuscitate the dead. **OR OTHER obstruction that binds a man.** Such as the "comitial disease," otherwise known as the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>A historical name for epilepsy.</note>. It signifies allegorically that just as the one who faints, whether by diabolical incantation or by infirmity, remains stunned and marvels when he returns to himself because he does not remember what caused such an event; so when the sinner has fallen into theft, either by diabolical temptation or by the personal infirmity of his own sensuality, he then marvels within himself how he allowed himself to be overcome by such a sin. **O POWER of God.** With this exclamation, he admonishes the sinner that although God is full of mercy toward the living, nevertheless after death He uses nothing but severity, which is justice without any mercy. O how severe is the power of God! **THAT SHOWERS DOWN:** that is, with vehemence and great impetus He strikes such blows—that is, pains and punishments. Wherefore we say a "shower of water" <note>original: "croscia dacqua"</note> when the rain falls with great impetus. **FOR VENGEANCE:** that is, for punishment; because vengeance is sometimes taken as a judicial punishment and is a species of justice.

**The Guide then asked who he was;**
**Wherefore he replied: "I rained down from Tuscany**
**a short time ago into this fierce throat.**
**The life of a beast pleased me, not that of a man,**
**like the mule that I was. I am Vanni Fucci,**
**the beast; Pistoia was my worthy den."**

**I RAINED:** that is, I fell down damned, as is said of the demons who rain from heaven. **INTO THIS throat:** that is, into this...

CANTO XXV 116

"I have been cast down this far because I was
a thief in the sacristy of the beautiful ornaments.
And falsely it was once blamed on another;
but so that you do not enjoy such a sight,
if ever you shall be out of these dark places,
open your ears to my announcement and hear:
Pistoia first strips itself of the Blacks,
then Florence renews its people and its ways.
Mars draws a vapor from Valdimagra
which is wrapped in murky clouds,
and with a storm, impetuous and bitter:
it shall be fought over the Piceno field,
where it shall suddenly shatter the mist,
so that every White shall be wounded by it.
And I have said this so that it may cause you grief."

<note>Pistoia</note> was in great happiness. And in that great power, it had the Cancellieri family, in which there were more than a hundred men of military rank. Because of this, it was in great reputation and esteem, not only in its own homeland but in all of Italy. This family, by a wicked accident of which we will speak below in chapter 32, was divided by mortal hatred into two parts: one called the Whites and the other the Blacks. From this, a division arose in all the rest of the city, and then in a short time our Republic <note>Florence</note> became infected with the same disease, as we narrated more extensively in the sixth Canto. In the following year, and in the month of May, the Whites of Pistoia, with the help of the Whites of Florence, drove out the Blacks of Pistoia. Afterward, the Blacks formed an army, and they chose the Marquis Marcello Malaspina as their captain; the Marquises are in Valdimagra, today called Lunigiana, named after Luni, a very ancient city. And in the Piceno field, which is not far from Pistoia, they defeated the Whites. And therefore he says: **MARS draws vapors from Val di Magra**, because Mars is the signifier of war. **Draws vapors**, that is, causes which stir up war, just as terrestrial vapors drawn upward generate furious winds and sudden rains, to which the impetuous movements of wars are similar. **SHALL SHATTER the mist**, that is, it shall make a cruel battle. **WHICH will strike like lightning**, that is, it will act with great force, like a lightning bolt—that is, the heavenly arrow—which is born from the refraction of clouds, as we have shown elsewhere.

CANTO XXV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

At the end of his words, the
thief
raised his hands with both <term>the figs<note>An obscene gesture made by placing the thumb between the index and middle fingers; a profound gesture of contempt and blasphemy.</note></term>,
crying out: "Take that, God, for I square them at you!"
From then on, the serpents were my friends,
because one of them coiled then around his neck,
as if to say: "I do not want you to say more."
And another bound his arms behind him again,
clinching itself so tightly in front
that he could not give a single jolt.
Ah, Pistoia, Pistoia, why do you not resolve
to turn yourself to ash so that you last no longer,
since you surpass your own seed in doing evil?
Through all the dark circles of Hell
I saw no spirit so proud against God,
not even <note>Capaneus</note> who fell down from the walls of Thebes.

-> [Woodcut illustration: The thief Vanni Fucci makes the "fig" gesture toward the heavens while snakes coil around his neck and limbs. Other damned souls and hybrid creatures watch in the rocky landscape of the seventh pit.] <-

He continues to express the nature of Vanni, and demonstrates what great pride and impiety he used toward God, since out of contempt he showed Him his thumb between his fingers. But immediately, a rightful penalty followed the sin: because a serpent coiled around his neck, as if it wanted to squeeze his throat so that he could not speak; and another tied his hands behind him, and then clinched itself in front in such a way that he could not move. And by this, it is allegorically shown that it is no small torment to the wicked man who delights in sinning in words and deeds, that the power of speaking and doing be taken from him—of speaking, by binding his throat; of doing, by binding his hands. **AH Pistoia, Pistoia**: he uses an exclamation which stirs up indignation against Pistoia. Furthermore, he uses <term>congemination<note>A rhetorical device involving the repetition of a word for emphasis.</note></term> by doubling the name, which makes the oration more effective and more grave. **WHY do you not resolve**: that is, why do you not deliberate. **TO TURN YOURSELF TO ASH**: to burn and become ash. **SINCE in doing evil you surpass and conquer your seed**: that is, those who founded you, who were the seed from which you were born. And here many explain that the first founders of Pistoia were soldiers remaining after the defeat and death of Catiline, who, as Sallust writes, were full of wickedness and impious toward their homeland. But this cannot proceed, because it clearly appears that Pistoia existed before the conspiracy of Catiline. Therefore, we shall simply say: **YOUR seed**, meaning your ancestors. And he concludes that he has not seen in all the circles of Hell a soul more proud toward God. **NOR the one who fell from the walls of Thebes**: understand this as Capaneus, of whom mention was made above.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the thieves in the seventh circle of Hell, specifically focusing on the appearance of the centaur Cacus in Canto XXV of the Inferno.</meta>

-># **INFERNO**<-

Thus he fled so that he spoke not another word;
and I saw a centaur full of rage
come crying: "Where, where is the bitter one?"
I do not believe Maremma <note>A marshy coastal region in Tuscany, known in Dante's time for being infested with snakes and malaria.</note> has as many
snakes as he had upon his croup <note>The hindquarters of a horse.</note>
down to where our human form begins.
Upon his shoulders, behind the nape,
with open wings there lay a dragon
which sets on fire whomever it encounters.

Above, in the chapter where the tyrannical and violent men are punished, the poet placed the centaurs; and of those, enough was said there. Now he places Cacus here; who, although he is not the son of Ixion and the cloud as the centaurs are fabled to be, nonetheless the poet depicts him as half-man and half-horse and calls him a centaur because his habits were savage and bestial. However, he does not place him among the violent, but among the fraudulent, because in his thefts and robberies he mixed fraud with violence—and fraud is a graver sin than violence. He shows that Cacus is not only punished in this place but also punishes others. He accompanies him with Vanni Fucci because they were similar in committing not only theft but also sacrilege: Vanni in taking sacred things from a sacred place, and Cacus in taking the things of a god, Hercules being one of the gods of the gentiles. 

<margin>**V**</margin> Of this Cacus, Virgil said: <note>original: "Cacus aventine scelus atque infamia silve"</note> "Cacus, the crime and infamy of the Aventine forest." According to the fables, he was the son of Vulcan, the god of fire; they devise this because, being a famous thief and robber of all the surrounding countries, he laid waste to them with arson and fires. Whence they imagine that fire and smoke issued from his mouth. He inhabited the Aventine, one of the seven hills of Rome, and in it, he had a terrible cave, the entrance of which he closed with a very heavy stone; and there he led all his prey. Finally, as Hercules was returning from Spain and leading the herds of cattle which he had taken from Geryon, the king of Spain, Cacus, most greedy for new prey, stole four of them. He pulled them by their tails into the cave so that, by the sign of the tracks, it would seem they had not gone into the cave but had come out from it. Hercules searched for them for a long time, and finally, not finding them, he was already departing when he noticed their lowing. He ran to the cave; Cacus defended himself by sending out smoke and flame, but the strength of Hercules was greater, who lifted the stone that covered the cave. He leaped inside and with his club killed Cacus and led away the cattle.

**MAREMMA:** Every maritime place where the winter is less cold, and the grass lives for the sustenance of flocks and herds, we call "Maremma," as if "maritima" <note>Latin for "of the sea."</note>. This occurs especially in Tuscany because such marshes face the midday sun; and in that of Pisa, there is such an abundance of snakes that some places are uninhabitable because of them. **UPON HIS CROUP:** Because he is half-horse. **DOWN TO WHERE OUR HUMAN FORM BEGINS:** <note>original: "Insi no doue comincia nostra labbia"</note> That is, down to where the belly begins, which he calls "ours" because the centaur from the belly upward has human members. He calls the belly *labbia* because in it is the dregs and the filth, which in Latin is called *labes* <note>A Latin term for a stain, fall, or ruin, here used to create an etymological link between the face (labbia) and corruption.</note>. The snakes or serpents denote the frauds, which he places on the centaur's croup—which is his beastly part—to denote that the frauds were savage and cruel. **UPON THE SHOULDERS BEHIND THE NAPE WITH OPEN WINGS THERE LAY A DRAGON.** He places a dragon for that same reason, and puts it in the back parts to show that one uses cunning in vicious works. A man does not notice the cunning used against him except from behind—that is, after the deed is done. **WITH OPEN WINGS:** This demonstrates the vehemence and speed in doing evil. **WHICH SETS ON FIRE WHOMEVER IT ENCOUNTERS:** That is, whoever meets it; for every man who encounters fraud perishes by its fire.

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of Ovidian transformations, specifically the myth of Cadmus, linking classical metamorphosis to Christian virtue and civic life.</meta>

<margin>B</margin>

->### INFERNO<-

...to demonstrate that those men who are of long life and have experienced various and diverse events of fortune <note>In the Renaissance sense, "fortune" refers to the turning wheel of luck or fate.</note> become very prudent through experience; and they transform into serpents, because the serpent is a most prudent <term>prudent (prudentissimo)</term><note>Here, prudence refers to practical wisdom and the ability to judge the right course of action.</note> animal. And Ovid adds that such serpents harmed no one; they even looked upon men willingly. Which can mean nothing else than that within them was that prudence which is the virtue that governs us to live civilly, and to seek concord and tranquility, and to help ourselves and others, and to harm no one. And it was not a certain malice and wicked cunning which induces men to deceive other men. Therefore, the Sacred Scriptures, wishing to encourage us not toward vicious wickedness but toward virtuous prudence, said: **Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.** <note>original Latin: "Estote prudentes sicut serpentes & simplices sicut columbe" (Matthew 10:16)</note> It is as if to say: use serpentine prudence, but let it be simple, without concealment or deceit. And just as doves harm no one, so you should not harm anyone; but rather be helpful like Cadmus, who performed many beneficial acts...

<summary>This page provides an allegorical reading of the myth of Cadmus, interpreting his transformation into a serpent as a symbol of wisdom and civic "prudence" gained through long experience. It bridges classical mythology with the Gospel of Matthew to argue that true wisdom seeks the common good without deceit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous Canto, where Dante and Virgil observed the punishment of thieves in the seventh ditch. We now move to the eighth ditch, beginning with a famous rebuke of Florence.</meta>

**INFERNO**

**CANTO XXVI OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.**

[Large decorative initial G] **R**ejoice, Florence, since you are so great
that over sea and land you beat your wings,
and through Hell your name is spread.
Among the thieves I found five such
citizens of yours, from which shame comes to me,
and you do not rise to great honor thereby.
But if near morning the truth is dreamed,
you shall feel, before a little time has passed,
what Prato—not to mention others—craves for you.
And if it had already happened, it would not be too soon;
would that it were so, since it must be,
for it will weigh on me the more, the more I age.

[Woodcut illustration depicting Dante and Virgil standing upon a jagged rocky bridge, looking down into a valley filled with individual flames. Inside these flames, the souls of fraudulent counselors are hidden. Virgil points toward a specific double-peaked flame containing Ulysses and Diomedes.]

**IN** this 26th canto, Dante demonstrates how he arrived in the eighth <term>bolgia</term> <note>A "bolgia" is a ditch or trench in the eighth circle of Hell (Malebolge), where different types of fraud are punished.</note>: in which he places the fraudulent counselors, who are punished within most burning flames. And here he hears from Ulysses the account of his end. But in the beginning, with the gravest indignation, he reproves his fatherland for the wicked sin of theft; and he especially grieves that she [Florence] is so impudent that she is not ashamed; rather, it seems to her she is great. And here there are several rhetorical <term>colors</term> <note>In medieval rhetoric, "colors" refer to figures of speech or stylistic ornaments used to embellish a text.</note>. First is <term>apostrophe</term>, or rather exclamation: which is when we turn our speech to a person or thing absent as if they were present, as we see the poet turns his speech to Florence; and this is done for many reasons, and especially out of indignation and grave complaint and reprimand. Then there is another color called **irony**; and this is when the words have the opposite meaning to what we intend. Therefore he says REJOICE. And he means that she should be supremely saddened. THAT YOU ARE SO GREAT. THAT OVER SEA AND LAND YOU BEAT YOUR WINGS—that is, that your fame is spread over sea and land. And he said "beat your wings," meaning you fly; or truly because Fame is depicted with wings. Wherefore Virgil said: *She flies by night* <note>original: "Nocte volat" — a reference to the personification of Rumor/Fame in Virgil's Aeneid.</note>. AND THROUGH HELL YOUR NAME IS SPREAD. As if to say, your fame is spread everywhere, but it is much more noted for your vices than for your virtues. AMONG THE THIEVES. Every learned writer, after using irony, ought to place words that make clear what the irony had left in doubt. Thus, by saying he found five noble citizens, he shows that when he said "rejoice," he meant she should be saddened. FIVE. Gianfa Donati, Agnello Brunelleschi, Buoso Abati, Puccio Sciancato, and Francesco Guercio. SUCH—meaning so prominent and noble, which is the greater disgrace. For when the person is of greater authority, every vice in them is that much uglier. Just as when a garment is more beautiful, a stain is more unseemly upon it. BUT IF NEAR MORNING THE TRUTH IS DREAMED. He shows that through a dream he has foreseen the calamities and civil dissensions between the "Whites" and "Blacks" <note>The rival political factions of the Guelphs in Florence whose conflict led to Dante's exile.</note> that were to afflict Florence—which in truth had occurred before the poet wrote this work, but he feigns having written it before. Therefore he says: if my dream made <margin>C</margin> near morning is true (as it ought to be true). There are five species of dreaming: three true, and two false. The true ones the Latins call *somnium* [riddle-dream], *visionem* [vision], and *oraculum* [oracle]. *Somnium* is when we dream the truth, but it is obscure, nor is it understood without interpreters—as when the man who was in prison with Joseph dreamed he was pressing the grapes of three branches into Pharaoh's cup, and Joseph predicted to him how in three days he would be liberated and afterwards become the king's <term>pincerna</term> <note>A cup-bearer or butler.</note>, that is, his servant of the cup. And Polycrates, king of Samos, dreamed that Jove washed him and Phoebus, god of the sun, anointed him; and shortly after, the prefect of Xerxes had him crucified, and he remained on the cross so long that Jove (meaning the air/rain) fell upon him and washed him, and Phoebus (meaning the sun) liquefied and melted the fat of his body, whereby he became "anointed." An *Oracle* is when, while sleeping, it seems someone speaks to us, and what they say turns out true. A *Vision* is when, while sleeping, we seem to see something which later is exactly as we saw it. The two false species of dreaming are *insomnium* [nightmare/stress-dream] and *phantasma* [phantom]. *Insomnium* is when we dream false things, and it proceeds either from too much food taken—which, raising vapors to the head, makes us seem to fly or climb, or descending catarrh makes us seem to fall—or sometimes it comes from too little food, which makes us seem to be hungry. Sometimes it comes from corrupt <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed in medieval medicine to determine health and temperament.</note>: wherefore <term>cholera</term> [yellow bile] makes us see fire and similar things; <term>phlegm</term> makes us see water; <term>blood</term> makes us see cheerful things; and <term>melancholy</term> [black bile] makes us see black and terrifying things. It can also be born from the cares and thoughts of the mind; wherefore we often dream that what we were thinking about while awake has been given to us or taken from us. But when we have the mind free from every thought and the body not weighed down by food or humors, it happens that our soul through sleep is almost released from the body and returns to its nature, which is divine, and can foresee future things. And this happens especially toward daybreak because, having digested our food, we remain more unburdened and the mind is less weighed down by the body. And for this the poet said: BUT IF NEAR MORNING THE TRUTH IS DREAMED. Similarly Ovid said: *For near dawn, when the lamp was already flickering* <note>original: "Namque sub aurora iam dormitante lucerna" — from Ovid's Heroides, referring to the time when dreams are most prophetic.</note>.

And having fallen asleep, he was placed in a ship and finally brought back to his homeland. 

But all this is a fiction of Homer, who demonstrates nothing else by this except how a man, passing through many vices and afterward purging himself of them, arrives at the **Supreme Good**. In this, **Virgil** imitated him in the first book of the *Aeneid*; and **Dante** in these three canticles follows Virgil. In this place, he puts him [Ulysses] with **Diomedes**, tormented for those frauds that they committed together. First, when **Thetis** had hidden **Achilles** on the island of **Scyros** with the daughters of King **Lycomedes** in female dress, so that he was not recognized. And the Greeks, seeking him to lead him to the conquest of Troy, Ulysses and Diomedes by their cunning recognized him and led him to Troy, where he was killed by **Paris**. 

Afterward, with great cunning, they entered by night and took from the temple of Minerva the statue of this goddess, which was called the **Palladium**, without which the Greeks could not take Troy. And finally, they devised the **Horse** full of armed men with such fraud that the Trojans placed it inside the city. And so that they could enter, they broke down a gate and the tomb of **Laomedon** which was above that gate. The poet says, therefore: *The junction of the horse*; because with that junction, they deceived the Trojans who broke the gate. From which **Aeneas** then departed, from whom the Romans had their origin. And they [Ulysses and Diomedes] still weep for the trickery and the deceit they used in finding Achilles, for whom his wife **Deidamia** grieves, though she is dead. Deidamia was one of the daughters of Lycomedes, whom he [Achilles] knew when he was hidden among them, and from there he fathered **Pyrrhus**. Similarly, they are punished for the **Palladium** which they stole.

**B**ecause he has already imagined that within one and the same flame are Ulysses and Diomedes, <note>Diomedes was a Greek hero of the Trojan War who often conspired with Ulysses.</note> and for this reason it has two points, or if you will, two horns. He demonstrates now that the larger horn held Ulysses within it, and that one began to speak. He makes the horn of Ulysses larger because in him there was greater cunning and more fraud. Therefore, **THE GREATER HORN.** Where the spirit of Ulysses was. **FROM THE ANCIENT FLAME.** He said "ancient" because of the long time he had been in Hell until the time of Dante. **SHAKING ITSELF MURMURING.** An excellent poet: who, feigning an impossible thing—that a flame might speak—strives as much as he can not to depart entirely from the nature of flame, which is that although it does not speak, it nonetheless murmurs; and such murmuring arises when a certain wind coming out of the burning material strikes it. **TO SHAKE ITSELF.** To move with a murmuring sound. **LIKE THAT WHICH.** The which. **WIND WEARIES.** That is, beats and moves. **THEN THE TIP.** The summit. He [Dante] strives as much as the nature of the thing allows to make his narration plausible. **CAST OUT A VOICE.** As if to say he did not speak entirely like a human being.

<meta>This text appears to be from Cristoforo Landino’s famous 1481 commentary on Dante Alighieri’s Divine Comedy. It specifically addresses Canto XXVI of the Inferno, where Ulysses (Odysseus) explains that neither his love for his son, his devotion to his old father, nor his love for his wife Penelope could conquer his inward desire to gain experience of the world.</meta>

# INFERNO.

The love of a son for his father is called "pious." <note>The author is playing on the Latin term *pietas*, which in the Renaissance meant far more than religious "piety"; it referred to the fulfilling of duty toward one's family, country, and the gods.</note> This is because, as we demonstrated above, piety is a type of justice through which we love our homeland, our father, our mother, and our other blood relations. **OF THE old father.** He rightly added the word "old"; for although it is a duty of piety not to abandon one's father at any age, it nevertheless seems a lesser cruelty to leave them while they are still in their "green" and robust years than when they are oppressed by extreme old age. This is because at that stage, languid and without strength, they require from their son that which they cannot provide for themselves.

Therefore, we ought to take an example from the storks; <note>The "gratitude of storks" was a popular medieval and Renaissance moral image, based on the belief that young storks carried their elderly parents on their backs and fed them.</note> in the very same nest where they were fed and raised by their parents, they later nourish those parents in their old age. And finally, he calls the love toward a wife "joyful." This is because the highest joy and pleasantness is found in the company of a wife who is chaste and obedient. We are constrained by the debt of nature and by both divine and human precepts to love a wife in whom such qualities are found...

<summary>This page provides a moral commentary on the familial duties Ulysses abandoned, specifically defining "piety" as a form of social justice and using the stork as a symbol of filial debt.</summary>

# IV XX          INFERNO

Human life is like a voyage at sea. For in it, fortune varies so much, giving us now serene happiness and now cloudy adversity, just as the winds make the sea at one moment calm and tranquil, and at another turbulent and stormy. And our living is a way of sailing through this sea. And old age is like a port for this life. And therefore he says: WHEN I saw myself arrived at that part of my age—meaning when he had reached old age—WHERE every man should lower the sails and gather in the ropes.

This is expressed in the <term>metaphor</term> <note>original: "traslatione," a rhetorical term for the transference of meaning or metaphor.</note>. [The devil] was of the order of the **Cherubim**: of whom we will speak more fully in Paradise. **ONE CANNOT BE ABSOLVED WHO DOES NOT REPENT.** The reason the devil gives Saint Francis is: that the Count [Guido] cannot be saved unless he is absolved; nor can one be absolved who does not repent of the sin committed; nor can one at the same time want to commit the sin and repent of it; because wanting and not wanting are opposites. **AH, WRETCHED ME.** Then in great perturbation he [Guido] said what had happened to him. **TO MINOS HE CARRIED ME:** and that one coiled. Of Minos much has been said above in the 5th Canto: both in recounting the histories and the fables, as in demonstrating the allegorical sense. **AND THEN OUT OF GREAT RAGE HE BIT IT:** this is the end of those who are damned by their own conscience: who out of desperation become furious even against themselves. **THESE ARE OF THE CRIMINALS:** that is, of the damned [sentenced] to enter the flame: which covers and steals the soul, which cannot be seen inside; and so he said above: "And every flame steals a sinner"; and thus "clothed" in this flame. **I GRIEVE** <note>original: "mi rancuro"</note>: that is, I lament to myself and bear hatred toward myself: for "rancor" is hidden hatred. **UNTIL UPON THE NEXT ARCH:** until upon the bridge of the ninth ditch (bolgia). **WHERE THE FEE IS PAID:** <note>original: "el fio"</note> that is, the fief and tribute; as if to say: the punishment of those who, by sowing discord with false slanders, dividing and splitting those who were joined and friends, **ACQUIRE A BURDEN:** they acquire sin, which is a burden and weight upon the soul.

CANTO XXVIII OF THE FIRST
CANTICLE BY DANTE.

[Woodcut illustration depicting the ninth bolgia of Hell. In the center, a figure is split open from the chin to the groin, labeled "MAHOMET" <note>MAVMETH</note>. To the left, a demon with a sword stands over mutilated bodies. To the right, Dante and Virgil observe the scene. Various severed limbs and heads are scattered on the ground.]

[Bottom Section:]
In the two preceding cantos our author has treated fraudulent counselors punished in the eighth ditch. Now he places the **sowers of scandals and of schisms and heresies**: those who through their fraud have destroyed and separated those who previously lived joined and in harmony, deservedly are placed having their members separated and divided and torn, more or less according to whether they sowed greater or lesser discord; and in this place fits the saying of the Psalmist: <note>original: "Filii hoium dẽtes eorũ arma & sagitte. Ligue eorũ gladius acutus"</note> **"The sons of men, their teeth are spears and arrows; their tongue a sharp sword."** [Psalm 57:4]. Who could ever—as an excellent poet, having to treat great and tragic things, use such a beginning that makes the listener attentive, demonstrating that the greatness of the things cannot be found in suitable words. Similarly Virgil [says]: <note>original: "Non mi si linguæ cẽtũ sint oraq̃ cẽtũ: Ferrea uox oēs scele rũ cõprẽdere formas. Oia pẽarũ pcurrere noia possem."</note> **"Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, a voice of iron, could I encompass all the forms of crimes, or run through all the names of punishments."** [Aeneid 6.625-627]. He imitates Virgil then: and Virgil imitates Homer. Therefore **WHO COULD EVER**: as if to say, no one. **TELL OF THE BLOOD AND THE WOUNDS.** The quantity of the blood and the cruelty of the wounds. **FULLY:** sufficiently. **EVEN WITH UNBOUND WORDS:** with speech that is loose and in prose; because he who writes in verse uses words "congealed" with a certain measure. But he who writes in prose uses words free and untied from every measure and rhyme; and the meaning is this: No one could sufficiently tell of the horrible slaughter, even if one wrote in prose where it is easier to express what we want than in verse; or truly: **TO TELL IT MANY TIMES:** this text can be ordered in two ways: either truly "who could tell of the wounds which I saw by telling them many times," that is, I saw with the purpose of telling many times. Or truly we shall say: "Who could ever tell fully by nature many times," that is: although I told them not once, but many times. **EVERY TONGUE WOULD CERTAINLY FALL SHORT:** in telling. And he assigns the reason. **BY OUR SPEECH:** insufficient. **AND BY THE MIND:** insufficient. **THEY HAVE:** which speech and mind have. **LITTLE SENSE:** that is, they are a small receptacle, they have little capacity. **TO COMPREHEND SO MUCH:** that is, to understand such great things.

**CANTO XXVIII 127**

**[Left Column]**

If all the people were gathered together once again
who once lay upon that fortune-tossed land
of Puglia, grieving for their spilled blood
By the Trojans' hand, or in that long war
which made such a high heap of rings
as Livy writes, who does not err;
With those who felt the painful blows
for resisting Robert Guiscard;
and the others whose bones are still gathered
At Ceperano, where every Apulian
was a traitor; and there by Tagliacozzo,
where old Alardo won without weapons;
And one should show his limb pierced through, and another his lopped off,
it would be nothing compared to the foul fashion
of the ninth ditch.

Even a cask losing its middle-stave or side-piece
is not split open as I saw one soul,
ripped from the chin down to where one farts.
Between his legs hung his intestines;
the vitals were visible, and the dismal sack
that turns what is swallowed into excrement.
While I stood fixed on seeing him,
he looked at me and with his hands pulled open his chest,
saying: "Now see how I tear myself!
See how **Mohammed** is mangled!
Before me goes **Ali**, weeping,
his face cleft from chin to forelock.
And all the others whom you see here
were sowers of scandal and of schism
while they lived, and therefore they are thus split."

**[Right Column]**

<note>The commentator explains that the wounds seen in this circle of Hell far surpass the carnage of Italy's bloodiest historical battles.</note>

This means that even if the wounds given in all the battles fought at different times in various countries were combined, they would be as nothing in comparison to the wounds of those who were in this ninth ditch. And so he says: *If there were gathered together*—that is, if all the people were collected who once grieved for their blood spilled upon the fortune-tossed land of Puglia <note>Puglia is called "fortunate" (fortune-tossed) because Fortune showed her greatest variety of changes there.</note>. And he lists five wars. The first was between Aeneas and Turnus, about which Virgil writes most elegantly in the last six books [of the *Aeneid*], showing terrible slaughter and killing. *Or by the long war that made such a high heap of rings:* this refers to the conflict at Cannae in Puglia, and the great defeat that Hannibal, captain of the Carthaginians, dealt to the Romans because of the recklessness of the consul Marcus Varro. Varro, against the advice of Paulus Aemilius, insisted on joining battle when he could have avoided it and gradually worn down Hannibal’s armies. Hannibal could not find new soldiers every day, and he entered battle at an hour of the day when the sun struck the eyes of the Roman soldiers; likewise, the wind greatly hindered them, carrying dust from dry places against their faces. On that day, eighty senators were killed, along with two quaestors and twenty-one military tribunes. Some men had already been consuls, praetors, or ediles. Forty thousand infantrymen died, and two thousand seven hundred knights. From so many bodies, Hannibal had a bridge built for his army to cross. This so weakened the Roman forces that if he had known how to use such prosperous fortune and come immediately to Rome before the terrified people could recover or provide any defense, he would have taken Rome; but his delay robbed him of victory. Whereupon Maharbal the Carthaginian cried out in indignation: <note>original: "Vincere scis Hannibal, victoria uti nescis"</note> "You know how to conquer, Hannibal, but you do not know how to use your victory." Regarding this, Petrarch wisely said: <note>original: "Vinse Hannibal: ma non seppe usar poi ben la vittoriosa sua ventura."</note> "Hannibal conquered, but did not know how to use his victorious fortune well afterward."

*With those who felt the painful blows:* there was an ancient Duke of Normandy named Richard, and he had two sons: Richard, who succeeded his father, and Robert Guiscard. In the year of our salvation 1070 <note>AD 1070</note>, Robert came to Puglia to Robert the Apulian, who was then Duke there. He gave him great help in the wars against the Prince of Salerno. Finally, Robert [the Apulian], having no male children, made Guiscard his son-in-law and successor to the Duchy. Because of his military virtue, Guiscard conquered Puglia, Calabria, and the whole realm of Sicily, which Alexios, Emperor of the Greeks, had occupied. Later, he was in favor of Pope Gregory VIII against Henry III. His successors reigned until the time of Henry, father of Frederick II.

*And the other, whose bones are still gathered:* this refers to the war and defeat that Charles I dealt to Manfred, not without the prompt work of the Florentine Guelphs, as was said elsewhere.

*And there by Tagliacozzo:* this is the other battle that the aforementioned Charles fought against Conradin, nephew of Manfred, on the plain of San Valentino near Tagliacozzo. *Alardo:* this was a Frenchman <note>Erard de Valéry</note> who at that time was returning from the Holy Land, a baron of no small authority and already old. Seeing the small forces of Charles against Conradin, he advised him to trust more in counsel than in arms. This advice had such authority with Charles that he committed the entire care of the matter to him. Through his prudence, though nearly defeated in the battle, he recovered a most ample victory, but not without great slaughter on every side. The battle was in the year of our salvation 1268, on the twenty-fourth of August. Afterward, in memory of the event and for the salvation of the souls of the slain, Charles built an excellent abbey called "Victory."

<note>The commentator now explains the "contrapasso," or the symbolic nature of the punishment.</note>

He establishes a suitable penalty; for it is rightfully fitting that he who has divided man from man, or man from God—scattering scandal, discord, and schism—is himself opened and divided. Allegorically, this happens to such men because they always have a distracted and divided mind. He feigns, then, that the heretics are split down the middle even to the head, because they have divided the Church of God, which ought to be one body of which Christ is the head. He places first one who is opened from the thighs to the chin, and makes a comparison to a barrel from which either the <term>middle-stave</term> <note>original: "mezule"</note> or the <term>side-piece</term> <note>original: "lulla" or "tulla"</note> has been removed. And he says *Veggia*, that is, a barrel, which in Latin is called <note>original: "veges"</note> *vassis*. *Is not split open*: it is not pierced and opened as much as the one I saw, broken from the chin down to where one farts—that is, to the end of the [torso]...

**[Marginal Notes]**

<margin>Manfred was [defeated] at Benevento by Alexander IV and Charles [of Anjou], who stayed and was sent by the counsel of Pope Urban in the year of our Lord 1265.</margin>

# INFERNO

**torso** where the exit is at the rupture of the belly: and where the foul-smelling wind issues forth: which when it comes out with sound and noise, some call a <term>trulla<note>A vulgar Latin/Italian term for a chamber pot or a noisy discharge of wind; the commentator notes it is not "learned" or "literary" speech.</note></term>: though not learnedly. **The innards:** that is, the intestines. **He gasps:** he sobs.
That this narrative is **filthy with excrement**: nevertheless, the poet uses it not merely to show a natural thing: but allegorically it signifies that whatever enters the mouth of the schismatic becomes dung. That is, whatever he learns as doctrine becomes a corruption to other men: and certainly he was the greatest corruption among men: which not only is not extinguished: but God, the just judge, permits—to avenge himself and punish his enemies with his enemies—that such a religion expands its borders. Wherefore, in this year—to the supreme infamy of the Christian name, and no small ruin for miserable Italy—he has taken Otranto: anciently called *Hydruntum* in Calabria. I know not what will follow: but it is the sins of the princes of this age, of whom almost all are infected: and the discords of Italy place in us more fear than hope. **May God have mercy on us and cause his face to shine upon us** <note>original Latin: "Misereatur nostri deus & illuminet vultum suum super nos"</note>.

**WHile there I saw everything focused:** everything fixed: that is, I am entirely intent. **I rip myself:** I tear myself and open myself. We have said above that the author places here the punishments of the ninth species of fraud which is called scandal: or rather schism: and these sins are a species of envy. For it stands in opposition to the love contained under charity: to which envy is the contrary. These sowers of scandal and schism, under the appearance of good, commit fraud to the harm of their neighbor: but infidelity, schism, and heresy are different among themselves. **Infidelity** is opposite to the faith and is the not believing what the faith believes in every part and thing. **Heresy** is a tearing away from the faith in some part, or making some change in it. **Schism** is a tearing away entirely from the faith and from the union of it. And because this is greater than the first two: therefore the poet feigns that it is punished in this lower part. Schism, then, is the division and separation of the unity of faith and charity. But also the division within cities between faction and faction and among citizens: and also between man and man is comprised under this sin. Therefore, he who has committed heresy in the faith is divided entirely from the chin downward, because he has divided the body of the Church, of which Christ is the head: and those who have committed scandal among princes, who are heads of the people, have their wounds in the head: and those who have divided relatives have cut off their hands: and those who have divided a son from the father have cut off the head and carry it in their hand.

But because the history of **Mahomet** is not entirely to be passed over: we shall note how in the year of our salvation six hundred and ten, during the papacy of Boniface III and the reign of Emperor Honorius: there was in Arabia a certain Mahomet, a magician and of the highest cunning, and greedy for honor—not human, but divine. And in his youth he saw various lands and nations: and in Jerusalem he understood the Mosaic law: and elsewhere the Christian law. And thus instructed, with miracles that he performed with magical arts, he persuaded the impious multitude of Arabia that he was the Messiah come from heaven: and gave new laws, mixing therein many voluptuous things: by which he easily drew the crowd to his devotion: and with this favor he acquired lordship: and especially by feigning a most holy life and habits. And with supreme cunning he had accustomed a white dove to feed in his ears: in which he secretly placed millet and similar bait in a way that when he was preaching to the people, he would have the dove released: and suddenly it would come to his ears: and he would affirm that it was the Holy Spirit which was showing him what was good to do. To such great cunning was added another most pernicious plague. For **Sergius the monk**, falling into the Nestorian heresy, was cast out by the monks: wherefore he passed into Arabia: and joined himself to Mahomet: and because he was very learned and full of cunning, he...

...the more evil follows, the more their punishment increases. He describes the plain of Lombardy as far as Romagna. Mercabò <note>original: "Mercabo"; a former fortress located near the Po delta, significant as a strategic border post</note> is on the Po and at the edge of Romagna on the shore facing Venice; it was built by the Venetians and later taken by Roberto da Polenta. It was destroyed when the Venetians were defeated at Ferrara in thirteen hundred and eight. **TO THE TWO** best men of Fano: Malatestino <note>Malatestino dell’Occhio, the "one-eyed" Lord of Rimini described by Dante as a cruel tyrant</note>, the Lord of Rimini, under the pretext of an invitation to a banquet at La Cattolica <note>A coastal town between Rimini and Pesaro</note>, ordered two leading citizens of Fano to come and dine with him, pretending to want to discuss great matters with them. He says this because their souls will be driven out of their bodies, which are like the vessel of the soul.

Oh, how dismayed he appeared to me,
with his tongue cut out in his throat,
Curio, who once was so bold in speech!

And one who had both one and the other hand cut off

***

**[Commentary - Right Column and Surrounding Text]**

He places Cyprus as a very eastern island and very distant from Majorca, which is in the west. Cyprus was once joined to Syria, as Sicily was to Italy and as Euboea was to Boeotia. And this island is located to the east in the Pamphylian Gulf; to the west it is opposite Sicily <note>The text likely means Cilicia here, as Cyprus is near the coast of modern-day Turkey</note> and Syria. It was a very effeminate island, in which there was an ancient law commanding that every woman once in her life must go to the Temple of Venus, and not leave until she had known a stranger. Majorca consists of two islands near the shores of Spain, called the *Gymnasiae* by the Greeks, because the inhabitants there stayed almost naked in the summer; *gymnos* in Greek signifies "naked" <note>original: "gymnos i greco significa nudo"</note>. The Latins call them the Balearics because they skillfully use slings (*frombole*). The larger of these is called Majorca, and it is near Spain by a day's sail. Therefore, since Cyprus is very far east and Majorca very far west, by saying "between the island of Cyprus and Majorca," he wishes to encompass the entire sea from East to West.

NEPTUNE, being the god of the sea, should reasonably have seen everything that was ever done in the sea. In the genealogy of the pagan gods, Saturn was the lord of heaven, earth, and sea. Of him there remained four children: three males—Jove, Neptune, and Pluto—and one female called Juno. In the division, heaven fell to Jove by lot; Juno, whom he took as his wife, had the air as her dowry. Neptune was content with the sea, and Pluto with the underworld. The allegory of the fable is that the universe was created by God and placed in time; Saturn signifies nothing other than Time. Hence in Greek he is called *Kronos* from *chronos*, which is "time" <note>original: "cronos da chronos cioe tẽpo"</note>. They say that he devoured all the children born to him, except for those four whose allegory we showed above. In the verse, "Neptune" is written with a single 'n' for the sake of the rhyme.

NOT of pirates: meaning sea corsairs. NOT of Argolic people: Greek people, because Greeks are called "Argolics" from Argos, the principal city of the Greeks; they were for a long time masters of the seas. Alternatively, he said "Argolic people" to mean seafaring people, calling sailors "Argolics" after the *Argo*, the first ship, of which we will speak elsewhere.

THAT Traitor: namely Malatestino. WHO sees with only one: that is, he sees with one eye because he was blind in the other. AND HOLDS the land: Understand this as Rimini. THAT there is one here with me who would wish to be fasting from the sight of it: referring to Curio. This man was a Roman orator, very eloquent, of whom Cicero writes. He was restless and factious, and greatly favored Caesar's party in the civil war against Pompey. When Caesar was bringing his army from Gaul to Rome, he stopped at Rimini because, according to the laws, he could not cross the Rubicon river with an army. Curio came from Rome, where he was then a <term>Tribune of the Plebs</term> <note>A powerful elected official in Ancient Rome who protected the interests of the common people.</note>. With his eloquence, he so moved Caesar that where Caesar was still doubtful whether to pass or not, he resolved to cross. Appropriately, since Curio was a major cause of the civil dissensions—primarily through his eloquence—the poet depicts him without a tongue. Thus, he would wish never to have seen Rimini, because there he committed the scandal for which he is damned here.

HE WILL MAKE THEM come to a parley with him and then he will kill them: and because of this, they will not need to make vows or prayers to the wind of Focara. Focara is a place in the sea between Pesaro and La Cattolica, so dangerous due to windstorms that all sailors passing there make vows and prayers to God for their escape. But these men, being dead, will no longer have to sail through this place to return home.

**d** Dante asks who is "he of the bitter sight": that is, who is the one to whom it seems bitter to have seen Rimini, since he had said he wished to be "fasting" from seeing it <note>In this context, "fasting from a sight" means wishing one had never seen it at all.</note>. Then Pier, with his hand, opened the mouth of Curio, who was his companion in that place, and showed that his tongue had been cut out. This punishment was fitting for him, because having justly sinned with his tongue, he ought to be punished in it.

THIS Curio: DRIVEN OUT from Rome by the Pompeians. SUBMERGED, removed, and took away the doubt of Caesar. Even though Caesar, having reached the end of his province, was pushed by the desire for mastery to cross the Rubicon and make war on the Pompeians, nonetheless reverence for the laws restrained him. But Curio inflamed him to cross, affirming that "the man prepared always suffered harm from waiting." This is a verse taken from Lucan <note>A Roman poet whose epic "Pharsalia" depicts the civil war.</note>, where he introduces Curio persuading Caesar to undertake the enterprise against Pompey, especially since he was instructed and prepared with armies and everything else needed for war. Hence he says: "Remove delays; it has always injured those who are ready to defer" <note>original Latin: "Tolle moras semper nocuit differre paratis"</note>. Therefore Curio affirmed to Caesar that THE MAN PREPARED: the one who is ready: ALWAYS suffered harm from waiting: that is, from lingering. This means it is always harmful for those who are prepared to delay and hesitate.

OH, HOW DISMAYED HE APPEARED TO ME, Curio: A most fitting punishment, that he who had sinned with eloquence and audacity should be punished with their opposites, which are silence and dismay.

**f** And Curio, for having caused harm with his tongue, had been deprived of his tongue; it was fitting that Mosca should also... <note>The text cuts off as it begins to discuss Mosca dei Lamberti, another soul in this ditch.</note>

The commentary provides a wealth of geographical and mythological context regarding the Mediterranean and the nature of "Time" as Saturn.</summary>
