->**INFERNO.**<-

...like. **IN THE MANNER.** In the likeness and form **OF A LANTERN:** in this way he carried his head before him to see with its eyes; just as we carry a lantern when we wish to see in the darkness. **AND THAT** one: That head watched us and said, "Woe is me!" <note>original: "O mei"</note> **OF HIMSELF HE MADE** a lamp for himself: with his own eyes, although they were separated from the torso, he provided light for himself—that is, for his torso. **AND HE WAS** two in one. Because the head was separated from the torso. **AND ONE** in two. Because one and the same soul was in the torso and in the head. **HOW** this can be, He who governs above knows. <note>A reference to God, whose divine power allows for this supernatural state in the afterlife.</note> That one and the same soul should be in the head and the torso when they are joined together is natural and easily understood. But that it should be in both when they are separated is impossible according to the nature of a living creature. For although the soul in the body is "whole in the whole, and whole in every part"; <note>This phrase "tutta in tutto: & tutta in ciaschuna parte" refers to the Scholastic philosophical concept that the soul, being incorporeal, exists entirely within every part of the physical body simultaneously.</note> nonetheless, the origin and source of the <term>spirits</term> <note>In medieval physiology, "spirits" were subtle substances or vapors that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body, facilitating movement and sensation.</note>—which are the vehicle that carries the powers of the soul—is in the heart; and the place where the aforementioned spirits are generated, or at least where perfection is given to the senses and to motion, and from where the motor and sensory nerves arise, is the head. Therefore, since the heart cannot by itself...

<summary>This passage provides a philosophical and physiological commentary on the figure of Bertran de Born, who carries his severed head like a lantern. The author explains the paradox of how a single soul can inhabit two separated body parts through the lens of medieval science and divine will.</summary>

->CANTO XXIX 130<-

# CANTO XXIX OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE

**L**he many people and the diverse wounds
had made my eyes so intoxicated <note>original: *ebbiate*, literally "drunk," meaning his eyes were overwhelmed and clouded by the sight of so much suffering</note>
that they were eager to linger and weep.
But Virgil said to me: "Why do you still stare?
Why does your vision still linger
down there among the miserable and mutilated <note>original: *smozighate*, referring to the mangled bodies of the schismatics in the previous ditch</note> shadows?
You did not do this at the other ditches <term>bolge: the ten circular trenches that make up the eighth circle of Hell, where different types of fraud are punished</term>;
consider, if you think to count them,
that the valley winds for twenty-two miles.
And already the moon is beneath our feet;
the time now granted to us is short,
and there is more to see than you yet realize."

[Woodcut illustration: Dante and Virgil stand on a rocky ledge overlooking a pit of suffering souls. One soul is labeled "CAPOCCHIO" <note>Capocchio was an alchemist and acquaintance of Dante, burned at the stake in Siena in 1293</note>. Flames rise in the background.]

We have finally arrived at the tenth ditch <term>bolgia</term>, in which the falsifiers are punished. Falsity is the tenth species of fraud. Falsity cannot exist unless one thing is shown for another to the detriment of one’s neighbor <note>The original text uses the abbreviation *pxio* for *prossimo*, meaning neighbor or fellow man</note>; and it is generally to deny the truth or to pretend that the false is true. There are two types: in speech, and this is called a lie; and in deeds, and this is properly called falsity.

<summary>Dante lingers in grief over the mutilated souls of the ninth ditch until Virgil reminds him of their limited time, noting the vast circumference of the abyss. They then reach the tenth and final ditch of the eighth circle, where falsifiers are punished.</summary>

"We are Latins <note>original: "Latin sian noi"; in Dante's time, "Latino" referred to someone from the Italian peninsula, specifically those who spoke the vernacular derived from Latin.</note> whom you see so ravaged here,"
replied one of them, weeping,

and each, trembling, turned toward me
along with others who heard him by rebound.
The good master drew close to me,
saying: "Tell them now whatever you wish."

"So that your memory may not fade away
in the first world <note>The world of the living.</note> of human minds,
but that it may live on for many suns,
tell me who you are and of what people;

"I was of Arezzo, and Alberto of Siena,"

and he, who had great desire but little sense,

because I did not make him a Daedalus <note>The mythical inventor who fashioned wings of wax and feathers to fly.</note>, he had me

for the alchemy I practiced in the world,
I am condemned by Minos <note>The mythological judge of the underworld who assigns souls to their proper circle.</note>, who is not permitted to err."

**[Commentary - Right Column]**

...which mitigate the itching. The spirit responds and says that he and his companion were Latins, and in return asks Virgil who he might be. Virgil replied that he was one who leads his living companion through Hell, descending from ledge to ledge. In this place, no allegory occurs that cannot easily be drawn from those already stated. These words caused such great wonder in the two spirits, who were leaning one against the other, that they broke away from that leaning—which was a mutual support and reinforcement—because by leaning together, one sustained the other. Here is noted the misery of the alchemists, who, seeing that none of their experiments succeed, often seek help from someone who perhaps knows even less than they do.

**And trembling** with stupor. **With others who heard him by rebound.** This is a metaphor <note>original: "translatione"</note> from those who play ball; when a player does not hit the ball as it is sent, he hits it afterward when it bounces. Thus, they heard the voice which did not come directly to them. And that Virgil had Dante ask the questions signifies that the Higher Intellect finds universal truths, and then leaves the Particulars to be found by the Lower Reason, as we demonstrated more clearly above.

**THIS MAN WAS** Master Griffolino of Arezzo, who was a great alchemist. One day, for the sake of having pleasure with a certain Alberto of Siena, the son of the Bishop of Siena—who was a foolish man and very gullible—he said that he knew through magical arts how to make a man fly. For a long time, he kept Alberto in suspense with words, promising to teach him such an art, and extracted money from him. Hearing of this, the Bishop condemned him as a necromancer and had him burned. Wherefore he says, excusing himself, that he is in Hell not for magic (because he never practiced such an art), but for alchemy. **PUT TO THE FIRE**, that is, to be burned. **BUT WHAT I DIED FOR**, that is, the magic art, is not why I am in this part of Hell. **SPEAKING IN JEST**, that is, mocking him. **AND THAT ALBERTO**, who had desire, that is, a vain longing and little sense, had me burned only because I did not make him a Daedalus—that is, I did not make him fly, as the poets imagine of Daedalus, whose fable is told elsewhere. **BY THE ONE WHO HELD HIM AS A SON**, meaning the Bishop, who regarded him as his son. This is said as if to imply that, since he was not born of a lawful marriage <note>original: "eglyptio matrimonio," likely a corruption or specific reference to legitimate/Egyptian marriage rites in legal-historical commentary.</note>, it could easily be that he was not the Bishop’s son, for a woman who joins with a man not her husband rarely stays faithful to him; and if she gives birth, she most often gives the child to the wealthiest man, so that the son may have a better father. **BUT MINOS CONDEMNED ME** to the last ditch as an alchemist and falsifier of metals. **TO WHOM IT IS NOT PERMITTED**, it is not permitted to err.

The accompanying commentary explains the metaphors of physical support and the social scandals involving the Bishop of Siena's "son."</summary>

**CANTO 30, PAGE 14**

"I found them here, and they have not turned since,"

Thousands of years had passed before him. **The false woman who accused Joseph:** Twelve sons were born to Jacob, son of Isaac, from whom the twelve tribes of the Jewish people later descended. But of all of them, Joseph was most dear to Jacob, both because he possessed great intelligence <note>original: "ingegno"</note> and because he was born in his old age. However, because of the great love his father bore him, envy arose among his brothers. They eventually sold him for thirty silver pieces to merchants who were traveling to Egypt—a price that was, without fail, very small for such a great man, but one which was meant to be a prefigurement <note>original: "figura"</note> of the sale of Christ, who is both Man and God. The merchants then sold him in Egypt to Potiphar <note>original: "Sutifar"</note>, an official <term>eunuch: here used as a title for a high-ranking court officer</term> of Pharaoh the King, who was the commander of the army. Joseph, through his virtues, in a short time...

**CANTO XXXI 135**

We turned our backs to the wretched valley
up along the bank that rings it around,
crossing over without any speech.
Here it was less than night and less than day,
so that my sight went ahead but little;
but I heard a loud horn sounding.
It was so loud it would have made any thunderclap seem faint;
following its path against the wind,
it directed my eyes all to one place.
After the painful defeat when
**Charlemagne** lost the holy company,
**Roland** did not sound [his horn] so terribly.
<note>Dante refers to the Battle of Roncesvalles (778 AD). According to legend, the knight Roland blew his ivory horn (the Olifant) with such force to signal Charlemagne that he burst the temples of his head. Dante uses this famous literary moment to emphasize how loud the mysterious horn in Hell sounds.</note>

The sound was the reason I directed my eyes to one place from which it came. We should consider why in this place things could not be seen, but could be heard. In this location, the **giants** are placed because of **pride** <note>original: "supbia"</note>, which makes men so reckless that they wish to exceed their natural strength and possess more power than nature grants them. We will speak more of these giants further down. The author describes the darkness because pride is born from the ignorance of not knowing oneself. But it is heard because the actions of the proud are such that many people talk about them. **After the painful defeat.** This refers to Roncesvalles in the Pyrenees mountains, which divide Gaul from Spain. Here, through the treachery of **Ganelon** <note>The archetypal traitor in French epic poetry.</note> of Pontieri, the paladins were defeated by **Marsilio**, the King of Spain. And Roland sounded his horn so loudly after the flight of his men that he gathered a hundred of them, and with those he made an assault and killed Marsilio; however, we will speak more of Roland in the 19th Canto of *Paradiso*.

I had only turned my head a little toward there
when it seemed to me I saw many high towers;
whereupon I: "Master, what city is this?"
And he to me: "Because you travel
through the darkness from too far away,
it happens that you then go astray in your imagination.
You will see clearly, if you reach that place,
how much the sense is deceived by distance;
therefore, spur yourself on a bit more."

<gloss>One eye requires a certain distance, and another eye another, because they have different strengths; likewise, the same eye sees differently in greater light than in lesser light.</gloss>

Then he affectionately took me by the hand
and said: "Before we go any further,
so that the fact may seem less strange to you,
know that these are not towers, but giants;
and they are in the pit around the bank,
from the navel downward, every one of them."
Just as when a fog dissipates,
the gaze little by little reshapes
what the vapor that thickens the air conceals;
so, piercing through the thick and dark air,
approaching closer and closer toward the edge,
error fled from me, and my fear increased.
For just as on its round wall
**Monteriggioni** <note>A hilltop town in Tuscany. In Dante’s time, its circular walls were crowned with fourteen high towers, making it look like a crown from a distance.</note> crowns itself with towers,
so the bank that surrounds the pit
was turreted with the upper halves of their bodies—
those horrible giants whom **Jove** <note>The king of the gods in Roman mythology (Jupiter), who famously defeated the Giants when they attempted to storm heaven.</note>
still threatens from heaven when it thunders.

**WE TURNED OUR BACK:** We turned our shoulders to the valley of the tenth **ditch** <note>original: "bolgia," referring to the last section of the Eighth Circle.</note>. <margin>M</margin> **UP ALONG THE BANK THAT RINGS IT:** That stands around it: which was the boundary between the eighth and the ninth circle. **CROSSING OVER:** They had already turned to see the damned souls; now they were crossing through to leave them. **WITHOUT ANY SPEECH:** This shows they were moved away from the contemplation of this sin, as they had already understood it. **HERE IT WAS LESS THAN NIGHT AND LESS THAN DAY:** Not total darkness, but very little light. **AND FOR THIS:** **The sight sent [me] little forward:** as if to say: I saw only a little further than where I stood. **BUT I HEARD SOUNDING:** I did not see much, but I heard; because where light failed (by which we see), sound took over (by which we hear). And this was so great that a thunderclap would have seemed weak in comparison. And this sound, following its path toward him—that is, proceeding forward. **I DIRECTED...**

Hebrew, Greek, and Roman do not write <note>The author is likely referring to the lack of contemporary written records for these figures in standard histories</note>: such as were Nimrod <note>original: "Nebroth," the biblical figure often described as a giant and the builder of the Tower of Babel</note>, Hercules, and Antaeus <note>A giant in Greek mythology who was the son of Poseidon and Gaia</note>. And Aurelius Augustine <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), an influential Christian theologian and philosopher</note> claims to have seen on the shore of Africa, near the city of Utica, a molar tooth so large that from it one hundred of our teeth could have been made. For where the reasoning of the mind is joined to ill will and to power <note>This passage reflects a philosophical argument about the danger of intelligence when combined with malice and physical strength</note>. All brute animals of great strength have ill will when incited by anger or fear, or by hunger or jealousy, or for the safety of their young, and they come against man. But although they might wish and be able to, nevertheless, because they lack rational ingenuity and industry <term>industry: used here in the classical sense of purposeful skill or diligent activity</term>, they do not succeed. Hence man has that defense. But because in the giant, the reasoning of the mind—that is, industry and ingenuity—is added to his...

<gloss>not as proud as Neptune: that is, the sea moves them. <gloss>...as the same Psalmist [says]: *But you, O God, shall bring them down into the pit of destruction* <note>original Latin: "Tu vero deus deduces eos in puteum interitus" (Psalm 55:23)</note>. And elsewhere: *Let not the tempest of water drown me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor the mouth of the pit close over me* <note>original Latin: "Non me demergat tempestas aquæ neque absorbeat me profundum neque urgeat super me os putei" (Psalm 69:15)</note>. NO earthquake. He shows by comparison with an earthquake how strongly Ephialtes shook himself. And certainly no thing causes greater movement among men, nor induces greater fear, than pride. This gave so much fear to the poet that he feared death more than ever. And there was no need or necessity to make him die more than a *docta*: that is, a brief space, because whoever lets themselves be conquered by this vice dies in their sins. *Docta* in the Florentine language signifies a brief space of time. In essence: in any brief time that I stayed with such fear, I would have died. But the chains and bonds that I saw were not broken by his shaking took away my fear. Then they went to Antaeus, who, without his head, was five ells taller than the cavern. An *Ell* [Alla] is the name of an English measure of two braccia in the Florentine style.</gloss>

"O you, who in the fortunate valley

**G**rateful: <note>Refers to Antaeus</note> he fought with Hercules; and every time Hercules threw him to the ground, the earth renewed the strength of her son Antaeus. Pomponius Mela <note>A Roman geographer, c. 43 AD.</note> writes that he was king of the furthest part of Mauritania, and there he built the city of Tangier, where his shield made of very large ivory remained. Theodontius writes that Hercules with his army many times took the kingdom from him. But as soon as Hercules had departed, he [Antaeus] regained strength from his neighbors and reacquired the kingdom. But finally, pretending to flee, Hercules led him very far away and then, suddenly turning, defeated and killed him. This, according to Augustine, was in the times when Danaus reigned in Argos; and according to Eusebius, it was in the times when in Athens there were kings...

...they held in prison. But Juno had Mercury stealthily draw them out of prison. And they are sons of Neptune, because heavy movements and heavy tempests move... They conquer Mars, because they become victors in battles. By means of Mercury: which signifies that just administration and wisdom resist tyrants, and often take from them the victory already acquired...

To vary the narrative of these giants so that one same form would not generate boredom, he asks about Briareus. And Virgil answers him that Briareus is much further on; and because he is bound in the same form as Ephialtes, it is not worth the labor to see him, being made in the same way except he is more ferocious in the face. But he says he will see Antaeus, who speaks and is unbound. And by him they shall be placed in the bottom of every sinner: that is, of Hell, where there is every evil. Briareus, Cottus, and Gyges were sons of Heaven and Earth, and had a hundred hands and fifty heads. They were strongest and most warlike above all others. Here the poet follows the opinion of other poets, who place Briareus in Hell as an enemy of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. But Homer places him as a friend and tells the fable whose form is this: Juno, Neptune, and Pallas conspired near Nereus the sea god to manufacture a chain with which they would pull Jove out of heaven; which conspiracy Thetis the sea goddess revealed to Jove. And Jove, having called Briareus to his aid, so terrified them that they abandoned the attempt. And it accords with the Scripture, placing them bound, because the Psalmist writes: *To bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with manacles of iron* <note>original Latin: "Ad alligandos reges eorum in compedibus: & nobiles eorum in manicis ferreis" (Psalm 149:8)</note>. And similarly we will say of the pit...

Because he wishes to entreat Antaeus to put them down, he speaks to capture goodwill, saying: "O you Antaeus, who once brought a thousand lions as prey because you were of such strength that you could easily conquer them." IN the fortunate valley: Happy for Scipio because it made him the heir of glory. Since Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder, having been made consul against Hannibal, judged that the Carthaginians could better be defeated in Africa than in Italy. Wherefore he passed from Pisa to Sicily, and from Sicily to Carthage, and set his camps in the place that was formerly called the kingdom of Antaeus and was afterwards called Castra Cornelia after the same Cornelius Scipio. THE FORTUNATE valley for the Cornelian people, because Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder reduced Carthage to servitude. And later Africanus the Younger conquered and destroyed it. AND IF YOU HAD BEEN AT THE HIGH WAR: he calls it high because it was against the gods. He says this to capture goodwill. And here he follows Lucan, who in the fourth book puts a similar sentiment. Antaeus was the son of the Earth, strong and immeasurable...

->CANTO XXXII<- [right] 137 [top right]

[Ae]geon, the father of Theseus. <note>Aegeon was a mythological hundred-armed giant, often confused or associated with Briareus.</note> **Set us down.** This is his petition: where Cocytus <note>The frozen lake at the very bottom of Dante's Hell.</note> is cold, where this river mentioned above freezes. **And do not let it be loathsome to you.** Do not be indignant, because we are of much less weight than is appropriate for your arms. **Do not make us go to Tityus nor to Typhon.** As if to say, although these two could set us down, nevertheless <margin>R</margin> carry us yourself so that the gratitude for the favor may be yours. Tityus was the son of Jove and Elara, daughter of Orchomenus. But Jove, fearing that Juno would notice, hid her under the earth; therefore, they believed he was a son of the Earth. This man wanted to couple with Latona, mother of Apollo. For this reason, Apollo pierced him with his arrows and cast him into the underworld. Leontius writes that he was a prince in Boeotia; and trusting in his great strength, he wanted to take Delphi from Apollo; but Apollo slew him and cast him into the underworld: that is, he reduced him to a lowly and private life. Typhon <margin>S</margin> was one of the Titans who, fighting with his brothers against Jove, was struck by Jove’s thunderbolt and placed under Mount Etna. **This man can give of that which is craved here.** As if to say, in the place of damnation one cannot hope for salvation, but only for some fame; and Dante can give him that. **Do not twist your snout.** Do not hold us in disdain; because the Florentines say "to twist the snout" when someone refuses to do something; <term>snout</term> <note>original: "grifo"</note> as if to say he sharpens his muzzle in the likeness of a pig, which we call a "grifo." **Because he lives and still expects a long life.** He can therefore give him fame in the world, because he is alive and hopes to live for a long time. **Unless grace calls him to itself before his time.** That is, unless by divine grace he is called to the celestial life before the natural course of human life. For whoever dies before the natural course dies before their time. Wherefore Virgil says of Dido: *But the miserable woman, before her day and suddenly inflamed by fury.* <note>original: "Sed misera ante diem subitoq; accensa furore"</note>

Thus spoke the master, and he in haste
stretched out his hand and took my leader,
from which Hercules once felt a great squeeze.
Virgil, when he felt himself taken,
said to me: "Come here so that I may take you";
then he made himself such that he and I were one bundle.
As the Garisenda appears to the beholder
under its leaning side when a cloud passes
over it so that it hangs in balance;
So Antaeus seemed to me who stood at watch
to see him lean; and it was such an hour
that I would have wanted to go by another road.
But lightly at the bottom that devours
Lucifer with Judas, he placed us;
nor, thus bent, did he make any delay,
But like a mast in a ship, he raised himself.

The meaning of the text is clear. But allegorically it shows that descending to the contemplation of pride—not to fall into it, but to have knowledge of the vice—Antaeus (that is, such a vice) carries Virgil; he carries Reason. For by mounting upon the vice, it is recognized; and Virgil takes Sensuality, which without Virgil would be defeated by Antaeus. <margin>T</margin> **As the Garisenda appears to the beholder.** The Garisenda is a tower in Bologna, thick and not very high, but very tilted; so named after the Garisendi family; and it is near the Asinelli tower. Therefore, someone standing under this tower on the side where it leans, when clouds pass over it, the tower appears to be moving in the opposite direction and falling. In such a way, then, Antaeus appeared to him when he leaned down. **As the Garisenda tower appears to the beholder. Under its leaning side:** under the part from which it hangs. **When a cloud passes over it:** and the tower itself hangs toward the cloud. For the eye is deceived and it seems that the clouds do not move, but the tower moves; and because it is tilted on that side, it seems that in moving, it falls. **So Antaeus seemed to me. And it was such an hour that I would have wanted to go by another road** because of the fear I had. And allegorically it shows that Sensuality, in coming to know vice, goes at great peril of remaining ensnared there if it is not succored by Reason; because it is always prone to earthly things. **But lightly at the bottom he placed us.** Because he who resists the flatteries of sin, such knowledge places us lightly at the bottom; that is, it shows us the baseness and vileness of sin. **Which devours Lucifer with Judas** as will be understood below. **But like a mast in a ship, he raised himself.** Having placed us at the bottom without staying, he rose with that height and gravity with which a mast is raised.

to describe the bottom of the entire universe,

<note>Dante is beginning Canto XXXII. He warns that the center of the Earth—the lowest point of Hell—is too grim for the simple, "infant" language used to call for one's parents.</note>

...greatest heat. <note>original: "mo ardore"</note> Therefore, betrayal will be the contrary to that, situated in the deepest lowliness and in the highest ice, **where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.** <note>original: "ubi ē fletus & ſtridor dētiū," a common Latin biblical reference to the suffering of the damned.</note> The **gnashing of teeth** indicates the extreme cold, and **Cocytus** indicates the weeping, because *to weep* <note>original: "cocyzin," a transliteration of the Greek verb 'kokyein'</note> in Greek signifies "to wail" or "to weep." Therefore, as the author begins the narration of the things he finds in the ninth circle—because the gravity of the vice <term>gravity of the vice: the heaviness or seriousness of the sin</term> makes them difficult and almost unspeakable—he offers an excuse and shows himself to be insufficient for such great matter; these words make the listener attentive. Then he invokes the aid of the Muses so that what he cannot do by himself, he may achieve through their help. **IF I had the rhymes**—referring to the verses which are in rhyme—**Harsh and hoarse**... the true praise of the poet is that the verse... <note>Dante seeks "harsh and hoarse" rhymes to match the grim, frozen reality of the bottom of the universe.</note>

### CANTO XXXII. 155

...it had the appearance of glass and not of water. The first part, which is closest to the wall and is wider, is called **Caina**; the reason for this will be made known to you below. The second is **Antenora**. The third is **Ptolomea**. The fourth is **Judecca**. If we examine these types of betrayals closely, we will see that they contain not only pride but also envy, which has not been treated by name elsewhere because it is such that it flows into various vices. And because this envy comes from pride, the first proud and envious one was Lucifer. And because fraud committed against one who trusts—which is called betrayal—comes from pride and envy, it is punished here. 

If it is between blood relatives, it is punished in the first circle, which is called Caina after **Cain**, who out of envy killed his brother Abel <note>Cain and Abel are the biblical sons of Adam; Cain committed the first murder</note>. This is against natural loyalty. If it is against one’s country, where there is a bond of shared origin, it is worse because it is against many; this is punished in the second circle and is called **Antenora** <note>Named after Antenor, a Trojan who was believed in the Middle Ages to have betrayed his city to the Greeks</note>. Or truly, if the faith given to a friend is broken, and this happens in two ways: either against one whom we have seduced into giving us benefits, and then it is the third degree, which is worse than the second because the faith was not only given but earned. This is punished in the third circle called **Ptolomea** after **Ptolemy**, who invited priests to a banquet and killed them during the feast <note>Likely referring to Ptolemy, the son of Abubus, from the Book of Maccabees, who murdered his father-in-law Simon at a banquet</note>. Or it is committed against a friend who is a benefactor, which is a degree worse than the others; this is the fourth degree. This fourth degree is the worst because it is ingratitude. It is called **Judecca** after **Judas Iscariot**, who betrayed the humanity of Christ. In the center of this pit, as in the place furthest removed from heaven, Lucifer is punished, because his crime is above all others.

->**The Poem**<-

**The Danube in Austria never made**
**so thick a veil for its course in winter,**
**nor the Don beneath the cold sky.**
**As it was here; for if Tambernic**
**or Pietra Pana had fallen upon it,**
**it would not even have creaked at the edge.**
**And as the frog sits to croak**
**with its muzzle out of the water, when the peasant girl**
**often dreams of gleaning.**
**Livid, as far as where shame appears,**
**were the doleful shades in the ice,**
**setting their teeth to the note of the stork.**

->**The Commentary**<-

**The ice was so thick that the Danube in Austria.** Nor the Don <note>The Tanai</note> ice so strong. **Austria** <note>original: "Osterichi"</note> is the coldest part of Germany <note>In the 15th century, German territories often included parts of modern Austria</note>; in Latin it is called Austria, through which passes the Danube, the largest river in all Europe. It rises in the mountains of Germany, passes through Hungary, and enters the Euxine <note>Black</note> Sea with such force that for more than sixty miles into the sea it maintains its fresh water. In winter it freezes so strongly that entire armies pass over it with horses and carts. It is commonly called the **Danube**. The **Don** <note>original: "Tanai"</note> rises in the north <margin>Y</margin> from the Ryphean mountains where there are immeasurable colds; it divides Asia from Europe and enters the Euxine Sea near the city of Theodosia. The ice was so thick that if these very high mountains, **Tambernic** and **Pietra Pana**, had fallen upon it, the ice would not have broken, nor even moved enough to make the sound "creak" <note>original: "chrichi"</note> which occurs when ice moves. **Tambernic** is a very high mountain in Slavonia. <margin>Z</margin> **Pietra Pana** is in Tuscany in the Garfagnana region above Lucca; it is called *Pietra Apuana* by the Latins. And truly, there is a very great coldness in the heart of the proud and the traitor, as we said above. They stood with their heads out of the water, just as at the time of harvest frogs stand when the peasant girl **OFTEN**—many times—**dreams of gleaning**: of picking up and gathering the fallen ears of grain. He said "dream" because a person often dreams of doing what they intend to do. **LIVID**. This demonstrates great coldness and similarly applies a color suitable to envy. Whence the Latins say *livor* <note>meaning a bluish-black color or spite</note> for envy. **AS FAR AS WHERE SHAME APPEARS**. Up to the face, which shows itself when one is ashamed. In the same ice he places the betrayers of relatives, of friends, and of the fatherland. But those who are lower are always in greater cold because they are closer to the center. It is reasonable that he who has committed the greater betrayal should be further from the fire of charity. It is a greater betrayal when the path to one's country is broken because it is done against many rather than just relatives. And it is greater against friends, and greatest against God. **Setting their teeth to the note—the song—of the stork**: because trembling, they chattered their teeth, making with them that noise that a stork makes when it strikes its lower beak against the upper one. By this chattering of teeth, great cold is demonstrated. This is what the Gospel says: **Gnashing of teeth.** <note>original: "Stridor dentium"</note>

->**The Poem**<-

**Every one held his face turned down;**
**the cold is witnessed by the mouth,**
**and the sadness of the heart by the eyes.**
**When I had looked around a little,**
**I turned to my feet and saw two so close**
**that the hair of their heads was mixed together.**
**"Tell me, you who press your chests together,"**
**I said, "who are you?" and they bent their necks;**
**and after they had raised their faces to me,**
**their eyes, which before were only moist within,**
**gushed over the lids, and the frost froze**
**the tears between them and locked them up.**

->**The Commentary**<-

**Every one held his face turned down.** It is the nature of the traitor never to look anyone in the face. Furthermore, he is forced to feel shame because he remembers having always acted against that virtue which is proper to man. And certainly, traitors always turn their faces down and consider nothing other than earthly and base things. **WHEN I had looked around a little.** The first four stanzas are well enough known. But that the tears should freeze in a way that locked their eyes signifies that the envious person, although he sees misery, nevertheless the cold—that is, the lack of charity—does not let him see it or be moved to compassion. **AND ONE**. Not responding, those two, another shade responded **STILL with his face down as we said above**. **THE VALLEY of Bisenzio.** The Bisenzio is a river between Florence and Prato, and it enters <margin>A</margin> the Arno six miles from Florence. **ALL the Caina.** We said that he names this first circle after **Cain**, who was the son of Adam, the first man, and was a farmer. And he had Abel his...

->CANTO XXXIII 140<-

...because of jealousy over a woman whom each of them loved; the Archbishop <note>Ruggieri degli Ubaldini</note> planned to avenge this injury upon the Count <note>Count Ugolino della Gherardesca</note>. He therefore increased that suspicion and stirred up many enemies against him, especially three principal families: the Gualandi, Sismondi, and Lanfranchi. In short, they incited the common people against him, and the Archbishop in person, carrying a cross, led the people to the Count’s house. 

He was captured along with four of his sons <note>Historical records indicate they were two sons and two grandsons: Gaddo, Uguccione, Nino, and Anselmuccio</note> and imprisoned in the tower which stands upon the Piazza degli Anziani <note>The Square of the Elders in Pisa; the tower is now part of the Palazzo dell’Orologio</note>. The keys to the prison were thrown into the Arno river so that no one could open it, and food was denied to the prisoners. For this reason, from that time on, the tower was called the "Tower of Hunger." 

The poet <note>Dante Alighieri</note>, therefore, speaking in the person of the Count, narrates how they all died of hunger and describes the circumstances—details which, in truth, neither the poet nor anyone else could actually know. However, because it was common knowledge that they had died of starvation, he invents the details to make the scene believable, and introduces the Count, who says:

It also notes Dante's use of "poetic license" in imagining the private suffering of the prisoners within the Tower of Hunger.</summary>

->CANTO XXXIII.<-                                                                 190

...when he says: *And I heard the door below the horrible tower being nailed shut.* <note>Inferno XXXIII, 46</note> Whereupon, as in Virgil: *Nor have I any longer any hope of seeing my ancient fatherland.* <note>original Latin: "Nec mihi iam patriam antiquam spes ulla videndi," Aeneid 2.137</note> It stirs the emotions, then: if we grieve for one who weeps, how much more shall we grieve for one who, through pain, cannot weep? The father’s weeping was a great sorrow to the sons; it was a great sorrow to the sons that the father could not weep. The poet highlights the length of time in which they were afflicted by hunger. This device is often used by 
Virgil: *Where they say he wept for seven whole months in order.* <note>Georgics 4.507</note> And in the character Palinurus: *On the fourth day, uplifted by the high wave, I barely sighted Italy.* <note>Aeneid 6.355-356</note> He highlights their weakness, where he says: *Then I betook myself, already blind, to groping over each one.* <note>Inferno XXXIII, 73</note> Likewise Virgil says of Mezentius: *He raises himself on his wounded thigh.* <note>Aeneid 10.856</note> He highlights their youthful age, as Virgil does: *Unhappy boy, and an unequal match for Achilles.* <note>Aeneid 1.475</note> Also the sight of it: *As youths placed on funeral pyres before the eyes of their parents.* <note>Georgics 4.477</note> And because it is a greater sorrow to see calamity than to hear of it, **HE SAID** "as you see me": *I saw the three fall,* <note>Inferno XXXIII, 70</note> just as Virgil says: *And those most miserable things which I myself saw.* <note>original Latin: "Quaeque ipse miserrima vidi," Aeneid 2.5</note> I could show many more passages in this speech that are most suited to move one to compassion. But with these, we can investigate the supreme skill of the poet, both here and in many other parts of the work.

**When he had said this, with eyes askew,**                    Immediately after the count had finished his narration, he 
**he took up the wretched skull again with his teeth,**     returned to gnawing the skull of his enemy. The poet 
**which were as strong against the bone as a dog’s.**      imagines this because the one who has been wronged always has the injury before his eyes; the injury stays before the eyes of the one who was wronged, and day and night it goads him, and his conscience gnaws at him. **AH, Pisa, shame of the peoples** of the fair land where "sì" is heard: that is, the shame of the beautiful country of Italy in which one says "sì." For just as the Frenchman says *oy* <note>modern French: "oui"</note>, and the German *io* <note>modern German: "ja"</note>, and the Greek *ne* <note>Greek: "nai"</note>, so all of Italy says *sì*. And certainly, it is a shame for the Italians not to have punished such cruelty, a vice that is most abominable in the Italian nation, which more than others was always humane and merciful. 

**Ah, Pisa, shame of the peoples**
**of the fair land where the "sì" is heard,**
**since your neighbors are slow to punish you.**

**Let Capraia and Gorgona move**                                 **SINCE your neighbors are slow to punish you, let Capraia and**
**and make a hedge for the Arno at its mouth,**            <margin>N</margin> **Gorgona move.** These are two small islands 
**so that it may drown every person in you.**                 located in the sea not far from the mouth of the Arno. He wants these to block the mouth of the Arno so that, having no exit to the sea, the river swells up in Pisa, through which it passes, and floods it. Count Ugolino, to stabilize his state, married two daughters: one to Count Guido of Battifolle, and the other to Oldobrando, Count of Santa Fiore. To Guido he gave Ripafratta <note>a fortified village</note> as a dowry. **For if Count Ugolino was rumored**: that is, if he had the reputation. He speaks very skillfully here: first, that it was great cruelty to kill the count without having certainty of his treason; but let us concede that one should believe the rumor, and for this reason he should be punished. 

**For if Count Ugolino was rumored**
**to have betrayed you in your castles,**
**you should not have put his children to such a cross.**
**Their young age made them innocent—**
**a new Thebes!—Uguccione and Brigata**
**and the other two the song names above.**

Nevertheless, you should not have punished the children, especially with such a **cross**: that is, with such a heavy martyrdom. And he gives the reason: because their **young** and tender age made them **innocent**, for they were still so young that they did not think of matters of state, nor were they called to any council by their father. **NEW Thebes**: a city as cruel as Thebes was. In Thebes, the first founders, brothers born from the sown teeth of the serpent, killed each other; the mother and aunts killed Pentheus; Athamas killed his son Learchus and then lay with the mother; Eteocles and Polynices, brothers, killed each other for the desire to rule. <note>Thebes was the mythological archetype of civil war and family betrayal</note>. Next, he shows that the age of the children was still "new" (young) by naming Uguccione and Brigata, who were the two eldest, and the other two whom **THE SONG names above**: This chapter earlier named them as Gaddo and Anselmuccio. He arranges the text thus: "O new Thebes, the young age of Uguccione and Brigata and the other two whom the song above names made them innocent."

**We passed further on, where the frost**                       This is the third ring, and it is called **Ptolomea**. <note>Named for 
**roughly swathes another folk,**                                  Ptolemy, who betrayed his guests</note> Here the spirits 
**not turned downward, but all upturned.**                  stay in the ice backward [on their backs], and the tears, before they can exit, find no relief because they freeze in the hollow of the eyes and form a kind of **crystal visor**. Then those tears that follow, finding the exit closed, turn back inward and increase the agony. And the poet imagines this because here are punished those who betrayed under the guise of benevolence and love. They have, therefore, shown a sign of charity so that those they wish to betray might be less on guard. This is expressed by their staying **supine**, which is to look up toward heaven. But they do not stay in a way that the tears can exit, because such charity is fake. Therefore, the weeping does not let them weep and increases the agony, because that false charity increases the betrayal, which deserves greater punishment. **VISOR**: like spectacles. **ALL the hollow**: all the concavity that is beneath the brow, in which the eyes are located.

**The very weeping does not let them weep,**
**and the grief that finds a barrier on their eyes**
**turns inward to increase their agony;**

**for the first tears form a knot,**
**and like a crystal visor,**
**they fill all the hollow beneath the brow.**

**And although, as if from a callus,**
**because of the cold, every sensation**
**had ceased to have its dwelling in my face...**

**AND although**: although every sensation had thus **ceased**: that is, removed its **dwelling**: that is, its room from my face.

# **INFERNO.**

[Main Text - Top Left]
Already I seemed to feel some wind,
   wherefore I said: "My master, what moves this?
   Is not every vapor extinguished down here?"
And he to me: "Soon you shall be where
   of this your eye shall be the answer,
   seeing the cause which rains down the blast."

[Commentary - Top Right]
As if from a callus: <note>original: "cõe da un callo"</note> that is, my face had no more sensation in itself than a callus, which, being dead flesh, does not feel. And this happened to me because of the cold. In essence, although my face was so numbed by the cold that I felt neither cold nor heat, any more than a callus would, nonetheless I seemed to feel some wind, at which I marveled. For wind is born of hot and dry vapors raised by certain stars, and especially by the sun; the power of which does not seem able to penetrate down into the center <note>the center of the Earth/Hell</note> to resolve vapors into wind. **AND HE TO ME: Soon you shall be where**: because the causes of many things cannot be seen with the eyes, nor felt with any sense, it is necessary that they be demonstrated with natural reason. But where the sense perceives it for itself, reason is not needed. Therefore, the sense will demonstrate from where this wind is caused. And it is a most subtle fiction that just as in the supreme heaven the created spirit <note>the Holy Spirit</note> is born from the power and wisdom of God, which inflames charity—and for this reason is compared to fire and the southern wind—so from Lucifer proceeds the freezing wind of pride, which deadens every heat of charity, and hardens and freezes all human hearts.

[Main Text - Middle Left]
And one of the wretched of the cold crust
   cried out to us: "O souls so cruel
   that the last station has been given to you,
Lift from my face the hard veils,
   so that I may vent the grief that impregnates my heart,
   but a little, before the weeping freezes again."
Wherefore I to him: "If you want me to help you,
   tell me who you are, and if I do not rid you of it,
   may I be forced to go to the bottom of the ice."
He replied then: "I am **Friar Alberigo**;
   I am he of the fruits of the evil garden,
   who here receive a date for a fig." <note>A proverbial expression meaning to be paid back with interest; here, his punishment exceeds his crime.</note>

[Commentary - Middle Right]
<margin>Friar of the Jovial order</margin> While he was passing through the ice, **Friar Alberigo** begs him to lift the ice from his eyes. And Dante promises to do it with an oath of that which he intended to do anyway, which was to go to the very bottom of hell. **O CRUEL SOULS**: because you do not help my pain. **THAT THE LAST STATION HAS BEEN GIVEN TO YOU**: He believed that Dante and Virgil were also damned for treachery and, having newly arrived, were not yet placed where they were meant to stay. Hence he says: "Until you are given the last station," meaning the final place where you must stay forever. **LIFT THE VEIL**: that is, the ice covering my eyes, so that with tears I may vent the pain which, not being vented, fills my heart. It shows that although the damned, and those who have made a habit of treachery, sometimes wish to open the eyes of charity, the ice of pride and hatred does not allow it. **I AM FRIAR ALBERIGO**: This man was of the Manfredi family, lords of Faenza. In his later years, he became a <term>Jovial Friar</term> <note>original: "cavalieri gaudente," a member of a religious military order intended to keep the peace, but often seen as corrupt</note>. He was so cruel that, being in discord with his kinsmen and desiring to remove them from the earth, he pretended to want to be reconciled with them. After the peace was made, he invited them to a magnificent banquet, and at the end of the feast, he commanded that "the fruit" be brought. This was the signal given to those who were to kill them. Thus, they immediately jumped out and killed all those Alberigo wanted dead. Hence, even among us, it is a proverb when we want to show someone has been struck down, we say he has had "the fruit of Friar Alberigo." Therefore, he said "the fruit of the evil garden" because the garden that gave such fruit was wicked. **WHO HERE RECEIVES**: I receive a date in place of a fig: for just as the date is more excellent than the fig, so much greater is the punishment he receives here than the one he gave his kinsmen when he killed them.

[Main Text - Bottom Left]
"O," I said to him, "are you already dead?"
   And he to me: "How my body stands
   in the world, I possess no knowledge.
Such a 'privilege' has this **Ptolomea**,
   that often the soul falls here
   before **Atropos** gives it death. <note>Atropos is the Fate in Greek mythology who cuts the thread of life.</note>
And so that you may more willingly scrape
   the glazen tears from my face,
   know that as soon as the soul betrays,
As I did, its body is taken from it
   by a demon, who thereafter governs it
   until all its time has turned.
The soul falls into such a cistern,
   and perhaps the body still appears above."

[Commentary - Bottom Right]
**T**his "advantage" <note>the privilege of falling into Hell early</note> he spoke of with irony. For besides other evils, the traitor has this: that his soul comes to eternal pains before the time of his death arrives. And he feigns that a demon enters the body of the traitor and governs it until his appointed death. By this, he meant to signify that the obstinacy of the traitor is so great that he never repents. This is also shown by the Evangelist concerning **Judas**, saying that after the betrayal, the devil entered the body of Judas; and he, despairing, said: "My sin is greater than that I might deserve mercy." <note>original Latin: "Maius est peccatum meum quam ut veniam merear" — Landino attributes this quote to Judas in his despair, though it originates with Cain in Genesis.</note> Therefore, notwithstanding that he lives many years after the act of treachery, we can say the soul is damned, because it is obstinate in sin; and a devil—that is, such obstinacy—governs the body, so that it appears to be a living man. But as for his character, he is a devil. **PTOLOMEA**: Just as the upper circle was called **Antenora** after Antenor, so this is Ptolomea after **Ptolemy**. So that this may be better understood, we will repeat briefly from the Book of Maccabees how the Maccabees reigned in Israel after the times of Alexander the Great. There were three brothers adorned with most excellent virtues: Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan, and Simon...

...priests: and very strong in deeds of arms: and especially Simon, who with supreme justice and strength defended the liberty of the Hebrew people against many kings and renewed the confederation with the Romans. <note>This refers to Simon Maccabeus, a leader of the Jewish rebellion in the 2nd century BCE.</note> This man had a son-in-law, Ptolemy, son of Abubus, <note>original: "Ptolemeo da bobo"</note> who was in every way unlike such a good father-in-law, being wicked and impious against the one who had so honored him. Being then appointed by Simon as governor in Jericho, and trusting in his great treasures, he dared to attempt—with supreme wickedness—to seize the princedom and the high priesthood from his father-in-law. Simon came to Jericho with two sons, and Ptolemy received them most magnificently and with a splendid banquet; and at the end of it, he had the old man and his sons killed, along with all the others who had come with him. <note>This biblical betrayal from the Book of Maccabees is the namesake for "Ptolomea," the section of Hell for those who betray guests.</note> 

->ATROPOS<-

The poets posit three [figures], whom they call the Parcae <note>The Fates of classical mythology.</note>. Through them, they demonstrate the beginning, the progress or course, and the end of human life. Thus, the first, who signifies our birth, is called Clotho; she holds the distaff with the thread. The second is called Lachesis, because *lachein* <note>original: "lachão"</note> in Greek signifies "to allot" and "to distribute"; for to every person who is born, she gives their lot, that is, that portion of life which falls to them. Therefore, they imagine that she spins the thread that Clotho holds, because she produces the course of life. The third denotes the end of the course, which is death. Whence they imagine that she breaks and snaps the threads of Lachesis, and they call her Atropos; because in Greek *a* signifies "not" and *trepein* <note>original: "trepiti"</note> means "to turn"; because death does not turn or bend for anyone's entreaties and spares no one, but is immobile and inflexible. The ancient Latin poets called these three Parcae: Nona, Decima, and Morta. TIME...

<meta>This page continues the technical and allegorical commentary on Dante’s Inferno, specifically Canto XXXIV, following the description of Lucifer’s immense size.</meta>

...clinging to the hair of the thighs <note>original: "ſ appiccādōſi a peli dele coſcie"</note> and the legs of Lucifer. He posits that Lucifer—whose stature we have already discussed—is located in the lowest part of the world, which is the center of the earth. However, because the center is an **indivisible point** <term>indivisible point: in medieval Aristotelian physics, the geometric center of the universe where gravity converges from all directions</term> and is not large enough to contain such a massive body, it follows that his middle is positioned at the center. 

From his middle up to his head, he remains in our hemisphere. Therefore, it was necessary for the poets <note>Dante and his guide, Virgil</note> who were descending from the surface of the earth in our hemisphere to climb down along Lucifer’s body until they reached the middle, which was at the center. Then, having passed the center and wishing to move into the other hemisphere, they had to climb up the rest of his body until they reached his feet.

**PAY ATTENTION.** <note>original: "ATTIENti"</note> It is necessary that the appetite and the **inferior reason** <note>In medieval psychology, "inferior reason" manages practical, worldly affairs, while "superior reason" is reserved for the contemplation of divine truths</note> cling to the superior.

**Panting.** <note>original: "ANſado" (ansando); this refers to the physical exhaustion and "panting" described by Dante as they struggle to turn around at the center of the earth</note> This demonstrates that even the superior reason [is strained...] <margin><unclear>Illegible marginalia</unclear></margin>

<summary>This passage explains the physics of Dante’s transition through the center of the earth by climbing Lucifer's body, providing both a geometric and an allegorical interpretation of the "superior" and "inferior" reason.</summary>

and if I then became distressed,
let the common folk <note>original: *gente grossa*; referring to those who lack the intellectual or spiritual insight to understand the physics of the center of the world.</note> imagine it, who do not see
what that point was that I had passed.

"Rise up," said the master, to his feet,
"The way is long and the path is difficult,

"Before I tear myself away from the abyss,"

"to draw me out of my confusion, speak to me a little:
Where is the ice? And how is this one fixed

when I turned myself, you passed the point

**CROSSING** as was shown above. But here it turned around the pit for a while and sloped slightly, because it fell only a little from on high. **HIDDEN PATH**: dark because of the shadows. They returned to the bright world without caring to rest: the poet says this because without any interruption, once we have recognized our <term>vices</term> <note>original: "viti" — habitual sins or moral failings</note>, we must go toward the purgatorial virtues. **TO SEE THE STARS AGAIN.** To see the heavens again: because he who departs from Hell, that is from vice, returns to see the stars; that is, he departs from the "beastly life" and returns to the "human life," which is led by the contemplation of celestial things. Now, by the grace of God, the author returns from Hell, and here he describes the place where he exited and the manner of his exiting. **A PLACE IS DOWN THERE**: beyond the center. **REMOTE FROM BEELZEBUB**: distanced from Lucifer. **AS MUCH AS THE TOMB EXTENDS**: He calls the "tomb" the vacuum he has placed around Lucifer: that is, the ninth circle already called by him "the pit," which goes down to the bottom and the bank of which he made for the giants, and inside he placed the traitors. Now he shows how large this pit is. And there was just as much to climb in that hemisphere as there was in ours, where they had descended down to Lucifer. They went up, therefore, through this tomb to the surface; and there they emerged through a round hole onto an island surrounded by the ocean; and on that island he places a very high mountain in which, grade by grade, one finds Purgatory; and at the summit is the **PARADISE OF DELIGHTS** <note>The Earthly Paradise or Garden of Eden</note>.

# PROLOGUE

First, I say that Holy Scripture, many authorities of the saints, and various revelations establish the existence of purgatory.
And the Holy Church affirms it, especially with Christ saying through Matthew: "Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the future." <note>original Latin: "Qui dixerit uerbum contra spiritum sanctum non remittetur ei nec in hoc seculo neque in futuro." This refers to Matthew 12:32, a key verse used by theologians to argue that since some sins aren't forgiven in the "future" life, others must be.</note> Therefore, Christ demonstrates that in the other life, some sins are purged and forgiven. And Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), whose writings, particularly the *Dialogues*, were fundamental in shaping the medieval understanding of Purgatory.</note> demonstrates that in the other life there are certain faults which the fire purges. Nor do only Christians posit purgatory, but also Plato, who holds that the soul, once separated from the body, if it is defiled and stained with the most grave and nefarious wickednesses, remains in eternal punishments.
But if the sins are less grave, let it be purged and then return into other bodies. <note>The author is comparing the Platonic concept of reincarnation/purification to the Christian Purgatory to show a universal consensus among "wise" men.</note> And Virgil, in the sixth book <note>Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, which describes Aeneas's journey into the underworld.</note>, says in the same vein: "Until a long day, when the cycle of time is complete, has removed the ingrained stain and left pure the ethereal sense and the fire of simple air." <note>original Latin: "Donec longa dies pfecto temporis orbe Concretam exemit labe purumque reliquit Aethereum sensum: atque aurae simplicis ignem."</note> And let this suffice to demonstrate that purgatory exists. But wanting to understand according to the Christian religion where it might be located, it is the opinion of Richard of Middleton <note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1308) was a prominent Franciscan theologian known for his detailed scholastic maps of the afterlife.</note> that beneath the earth there are four places: and in the lowest part, which is the center of the earth, and where in perpetual...

# CANTO <unclear>1</unclear> 146

Well-instructed and learned in the poetic art, our author divides this second <term>cantica<note>The Divine Comedy is divided into three "cantiche" (plural): Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso.</note></term> into three parts, in imitation of Virgil, Ovid, Statius, and the other Latin heroic poets: the **proposition**, the **invocation**, and the **narration**. 

However, the first two—the proposition and the invocation—serve the purpose of a preface. Since the specific duty of a preface is to make the listener ready and fit to easily understand what follows, we shall make them well-disposed, attentive, and receptive. 

He thus captures this goodwill through his subject matter, promising to sing of Purgatory—a thing most excellent for human souls, as it is the only means by which they can attain divine knowledge, in which the <term>highest good<note>Original: "summo bene." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the ultimate state of happiness and union with God.</note></term> consists. He further captures goodwill through his own person, showing that he labors to write what is not only useful but necessary for the mortal generation. Furthermore, he makes the listener attentive through the greatness of the subject matter. Insofar as...

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the Inferno commentary into the opening of the Purgatorio. The translator continues the style of Cristoforo Landino’s famous 1481 commentary, which blends Platonic philosophy with Christian theology.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

Nothing remains of the sensory part of the body that can be purged. And the soul becomes worthy of ascending to heaven: because then, finally, the soul can rise to the contemplation and knowledge of divine things when it has been purged of its vices. Whence: **Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.** <note>Matthew 5:8</note> But because there is no stain that can make the soul filthy and ugly except vice, and nothing removes vice except virtue, it is not only useful but necessary for better understanding to narrate briefly that the moral virtues are divided—according to the Platonists—into four species: **civil**, **purgatory**, **of the already purged soul**, and **exemplary**. 

The **civil virtues** belong to man because, being an animal born not to be solitary but to live in congregation and company—from which cities are born—he uses these to administer the republic. With **prudence**, he investigates what is useful; with **justice**, distributing honors and duties equally, he preserves union and concord. With **fortitude**, he creates a frank and invincible spirit to endure every labor and danger to defend the fatherland. And with **temperance**, he desires nothing of which he must later repent; in nothing does he exceed the measure and the law. But these virtues are not perfect in the civil and active life, because the men who converse only in that life do not possess true wisdom. 

After the civil virtues follow the **purgatory virtues**, which do not fall within the civil life. Instead, they belong to the few men who are capable of divine things; such virtues expedite and free the soul of him who is disposed to purge himself from the contagion of the body and give himself entirely to divine things, fleeing human ones. He does not labor with Martha, but gives himself entirely to Mary; <note>In medieval thought, Martha represents the active life of work, while Mary represents the contemplative life of prayer and study.</note> that is, he leaves the active life entirely and follows the speculative life. 

Beyond these purgatory virtues are those **of the soul already purged**, which has remained without any stain. In this state is the office of **prudence**—I do not say to prefer divine things to human ones, as the purgatory virtues do, but to choose only the divine, as if nothing else existed but those, and to look only upon them. The office of **temperance** is not to restrain desires, but to forget them entirely. The office of **fortitude**—I do not say to conquer the fear of horrific things, but to not even know what fear is. And finally, they use **justice** in joining themselves with the divine mind in such a way that they never depart from it. 

The fourth are the **exemplary virtues**, which exist in God alone. Since the Platonists place the "ideas" of all things in the divine mind, the idea of virtue will be there most greatly. Here, then, **prudence** is nothing other than the divine mind itself. **Temperance** is that which totally turns toward itself with perpetual intention. **Fortitude** is that which is always the same and never changes. **Justice** is that which, by eternal law, never removes itself nor bends from the eternal continuation of its work. These are the four generations of moral virtues which, although they are all against the passions and perturbations of the soul, are nonetheless different in themselves: because the first do not take away the passions entirely but mitigate them; the second remove them; the third forget them; and in the fourth, it is a wicked thing even to name them. I have therefore treated them extensively so that the reader, should they occur in many other places, may refer back here.

**But here let dead poetry rise again**
**O holy Muses, since I am yours**
**And here let Calliope rise up somewhat,**
**Following my song with that sound**
**By which the wretched magpies felt**
**The blow such that they despaired of pardon.**

After the proposition follows the invocation. And he begins: *O holy Muses.* Look here: let **dead poetry** be resuscitated in this place. He says, as if to say: "I pray to you, O holy Muses, that you inspire in me the poetic faculty, which for a long time has been dead." For before Dante, for many centuries, Italy had been prey to various generations of barbarians, and afflicted and oppressed by so many wars and tumults that every liberal art had lain dormant. He was among the first who tried to draw this faculty called poetry out of the darkness. How perfectly he succeeded, we strive to express in his biography, and his present poem aptly manifests it. This is, therefore, the reason that led him to say: *But here let dead poetry rise again.* 

Or, truly, he wants dead poetry to rise again as if to imply: "Up until now we have treated of Hell, where everything is dead; but hereafter we shall treat of Purgatory, through which the soul is resuscitated." And certainly, the soul dead through vice rises again through purgation. *O holy Muses.* We spoke of the Muses sufficiently in the second canto of the *Inferno*; therefore, it would be superfluous to repeat here what we have already written. 

*Since I am yours:* Because I am a poet, and poets are dedicated to the Muses, being their priests. Whence Virgil says: <note>original Latin: "Me vero primis placeat ante omnia musae: quorũ sacra fero."</note> *But as for me, first of all, may the Muses, whose sacred objects I carry, please me above all things.* And he makes his petition honest, saying that it is right for the Muses to favor one who is theirs. 

*And here let Calliope rise up somewhat:* Let her lift herself up a bit, as if to say that, this being a higher subject, a higher style is appropriate. And certainly, to whoever offers attentive ears, it is easy to recognize that the style he uses in the *Inferno* is almost at the lowest level. For one beginning is: *In the middle of the journey of our life*; another is: *To run through better waters...* <note>Dante contrasts the "low" style of the Inferno with the "middle" style of the Purgatorio.</note> He invokes Calliope because she is the most excellent among the Muses, and her name signifies "good voice." And whoever invokes her, invokes all the others. Whence Virgil said: <note>original Latin: "Vos o calliope precor aspirate canenti."</note> *O Calliope, I pray, breathe upon the singer.* 

*Following my song:* Because he does not begin his work from Purgatory, but follows after Hell. Therefore, let Calliope rise—as if to lift the style—and make it more sonorous, following my work. 

*With that sound:* With that voice *by which*: from which *the wretched magpies*: that is, the wretched daughters of Pierus were converted into magpies <term>pice: magpies or jays</term>. And this is the blow which they felt from the voice of Calliope. These were nine daughters of Pierus from the city <margin>D</margin> of Pella, women certainly erudite in many arts. But because of their glory, they were so proud that they esteemed the Muses as nothing and presumed to surpass them in everything, and especially in song. Nor were they content not to go to Parnassus to find them near the Pierian spring, and there with villainous words provoke them to sing. The commission was given to Calliope, who after a long time defeated them and converted them into magpies. This bird is talkative and easily learns human speech. *Pica* in Latin signifies the jay, and also the magpie; but this...

It then transitions into the poetic invocation of the Muses, specifically Calliope, marking the transition from the "dead" style of Hell to the revitalized poetry of spiritual ascent.</summary>

->CANTO ONE. 197<-

Pliny, in the book of *Natural History*, calls it *pica caudata* <note>original: "pica caudata"; a long-tailed magpie</note> because it has a long tail. And therefore, the meaning is: Let Calliope rise, following my song with such a voice as that with which she conquered the magpies <note>A reference to the Pierides, daughters of King Pierus, who challenged the Muses to a singing contest and were transformed into magpies upon their defeat.</note>. This voice had to be so sonorous and excellent; otherwise, she would not have won. And through this, he demonstrates his petition to be modest: by the magpies who provoked the Muses, we shall understand every rash person who presumes to be able to conquer or be equal to the Muses—that is, to the divine doctrines. After the proposition and invocation are now completed and finished by the poet, the narration begins. And he intends that his beginning shall be to describe the time and the quality of the time.

**Sweet color of oriental sapphire**
**that gathered in the serene aspect**
**of the pure air, even to the first circle,**
**To my eyes restored delight**
**As soon as I came out of the dead air**
**which had saddened my eyes and breast.**

The meaning is that when he emerged into that hemisphere <note>The Southern Hemisphere, where Dante locates the Mountain of Purgatory.</note>, the sun was not yet born, but it was not far from its birth. This is because Venus already appeared in the East; and because she was in Pisces, and the sun in Aries—signs close together with little interval—she rose before the sun. Furthermore, he demonstrates that at that time the air had been most pure, and full of serenity and tranquility. Therefore, the color of the air, which was such as that of an oriental sapphire, restored delight to my eyes. 

**The beautiful planet that comforts to love**
**made all the east laugh,**
**veiling the Pisces that were in her escort.**

**SWEET**, that is, the suave and delightful color. And although sweetness is properly a matter of taste, nonetheless every other thing that delights any other sense is called "sweet." Hence Petrarch: *And how sweetly she speaks and sweetly she laughs.* And Horace: *I will love Lalage, sweetly laughing, sweetly speaking.* <note>original: "Dulce ridentem lalagen amabo dulce loquentem"</note> 

**Of oriental sapphire.** Pliny shows that there are sapphires of a purple color and of a blue color. The poet mentions the latter in this place, and says that the blue ones are called "male sapphires." 

**THAT gathered in the serene aspect.** For if the air were not serene, it would not be blue. And the poet takes great pains to show that the air in that place was pure and clear, and contrary to the foggy air of Hell. For just as vice generates obscurity, so the purgation of vice induces serenity. 

**OF THE pure air even to the first circle.** That is, up to the first sphere, which is the heaven of the Moon, from which downward mutable things begin. Therefore, the serene color of the air restored delight to my eyes. For Dante had such delight before he entered into Hell while staying in the serene air. Then, entering into the infernal shadows, he lost it. Now, having exited, it returns to him again. And although he appears to speak of the delight of the physical eyes, nonetheless understand it allegorically as the spiritual eyes. The eyes take delight in bright and beautiful things; and the beauty of a thing is good proportion with suitable color. Therefore, just as the physical eyes take delight in physical beauty and sensible light, so the eyes of the mind greatly delight in their own light, which is Reason, and in their own beauty, which is Virtue. Whence Plato writes that if we could see the beauty of virtue with the eyes of the mind as we see the beauty of the body with physical eyes, the love that would make us love them would be incredible and most ardent. 

**THE Eyes:** that is, the visual sense; and **THE BREAST**: the mind. 

**THE BEAUTIFUL planet that comforts to love.** The star of Venus. He says, therefore, that it was the time of morning and not much before the day. For the sun was in Aries; which sign begins to rise after Pisces has entirely left the East. Therefore, a good part of the sign of Pisces having already risen, Venus was seen, as she was in that sign. And we demonstrated in the first canto of the first canticle that in this he imitates Virgil. And as that poet establishes that Aeneas had Venus as his guide and leader—not the earthly but the celestial one—so too in that place and in this, Dante...

->### CANTO ONE 148<-

...mind, by following the virtues, serves God: whose service not only makes us free, but makes us reign <note>original: "regnare"; a common theological paradox stating that to serve God is to rule as a king</note>. Recognizing this, the Stoic philosophers in their paradoxes <note>A reference to the *Paradoxorum Stoicorum* by Cicero, which explores ethical truths that seem to contradict common opinion</note> write that all the wise—that is, the good—are free, and the foolish—that is, the vicious—are slaves. 

But returning to the text: he positions it toward the **north** <note>original: "septentrione"</note>, which is to say, toward the vices; for this supreme love of liberty rises within us as soon as we have recognized the misery that exists in the bondage of vices. And he does not wish to demonstrate here the "first liberty" that was in the soul before the transgression <note>original: "puaricatiõe" or *prevaricazione*, referring to the Fall of Man</note> of our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note> and before sin.
