->PURGATORY<-

...the laws of the abyss. As if to say the laws ordained by God for the abyss—that is, for the depths and the lower part of the world—which is called the abyss, a word that in the Greek language signifies "depth." <note>original: "abyſſo"</note> OR, **Has heaven changed?**; as if to say, where there is no change, but everything is stable.

**My leader then took hold of me,**
**and with words, and with hands, and with signs**
**of reverence, he made my legs and brow submissive.**
**Then he answered him: "I did not come of myself;**
**a lady descended from heaven, at whose prayers**
**I assisted this man with my company."**

It is a fitting thing <note>original: "Conueniente coſa"</note> that Virgil admonishes Dante: that is, that Reason admonishes Sensuality to show reverence to Cato. For if the appetite does not show reverence for the liberation of the soul, it will always be prone to vice. **My leader then took hold of me.** Because one cannot love liberty if Reason does not bring the appetite and sensuality under its power and make them bow and revere liberty. **And with words**, by persuading him; **and with hands**, by positioning him; **and with signs**, by showing him. Sensuality is admonished with words—that is, with manifest doctrine; with hands—that is, with excellent works which are examples for us to follow virtue; and with signs—which are more obscure meanings. **He made my legs reverent** by making me kneel. **And the brow** by bowing the head; and rightly so, because the knees are attributed to mercy. Hence, when we wish to move someone to mercy, we are accustomed to kneel and likewise embrace the knees of the one we wish to appease. And the forehead, where the eyebrows <note>original: "ciglia"</note> are, is attributed to shame. Sensuality, therefore, feels shame, which is a sign that it repents of its error and desires to amend itself and asks for mercy, without which—as we have shown elsewhere—man cannot be saved. 

Then he replied to what Cato had asked: what guide and what light had drawn them from Hell, and had marveled whether the laws were broken or the will of God changed. Therefore, Virgil responds, first stating that he has been Dante’s guide, requested by Beatrice. And we showed in the second canto of the *Inferno* how Reason, illustrated by natural and philosophical doctrine (which Virgil represents), became a guide to Dante to show him the vices at the prayers of Beatrice, who is "cooperating grace," sent by the Light and by another whom he does not name, who are "prevenient" and "illuminating" grace. <note>These are technical theological terms: prevenient grace moves the soul toward God before any human effort, while cooperating grace assists the soul in doing good works.</note> And he has satisfied the questions that were: "Who has guided you?" and "Who acts as your lantern?" Then he follows:

**"But since it is your will that more be explained**
**of our condition, how it truly is,**
**it cannot be my will that this be denied you.**
**This man never saw the final evening;**
**but through his folly he was so near to it**
**that there was very little time left to turn.**
**As I said, I was sent to him**
**to rescue him, and there was no other way**
**than this one upon which I have set myself.**
**I have shown him all the wicked people,**
**and now I intend to show those spirits**
**who purge themselves under your authority.**
**How I have led him would be long to tell you;**
**from on high descends a virtue that aids me**
**in conducting him to see you and to hear you."**

Virgil had already satisfied Cato's first two questions and shown him what guide and what light had conducted him; now he responds to the third, demonstrating that because they were from Hell, the laws were not broken. For neither of them was damned in Hell, as you will see in the progression of the text. **But since** <note>original: "Ma da che"</note> means "but after." **Your will**—that is, you wish. **That more be explained**—that it be further unfolded, that more of our condition be shown. It is a metaphor <note>original: "tranſlatone"</note> taken from things that are tangled and folded up, which cannot be clear to us unless they are unfolded. The meaning, therefore, is: "since it is your will that we reveal more of our condition to you." **How it is true**—that is, just. **It cannot be my will that it be denied to you**—that what you ask be refused. And just as your request is just, so it cannot be my will that what you ask be denied. 

And so that you may understand that the laws of the abyss are not broken, know that I was never damned to Hell, because I am in Limbo. Nor was this man yet damned there, since he is not dead, and there none are damned except the dead. There are two "Hells," as we have said above: the "essential" one, in which there are only the souls of those who died in mortal sin; the other is the "moral" one, in which is understood to be anyone who has formed such a habit of vice that they cannot leave it. But Dante was alive; and if he was entangled in some vice, he had not yet formed a habit. Thus, he had not descended into Hell as one damned, because such are not judged by Virgil (that is, by Reason), but by irrational and beastly appetite. But he had descended to have true knowledge of vices so that, knowing how harmful they are, he would wish to be free of them. 

Hence he says: **This man never saw the final evening**—that is, death, which is the final night and darkness of man. This signifies he is not yet dead—that is, he has not formed a habit of vice—and so with my guidance he was able to escape it. **But through his folly**—through his foolishness and ignorance, because through a lack of reason we fall into vice—**he was so near to it that very little time was left to turn**—that is, he had to leave. And he said "turn" <note>original: "uolgere"</note> because the revolution of the planets, and especially the sun, creates time. Wherefore Petrarch, wishing to describe the sun, said: "When the planet that distinguishes the hours..."—that is, when the sun, which by its revolution distinguishes the hours and every space of time. And he imitates Virgil, who said: "As the years turn." <note>original: "Voluentibus annis"</note> There remained, therefore, little time to be able to help him. This denotes that if he had persevered longer in vices, he would have formed such a habit that he could not afterwards escape. But Beatrice sent Virgil to him—that is, divine grace—and that awakened Reason in him, which made him recognize vice. And well...

The commentary by Landino interprets the physical gestures of kneeling and bowing as the triumph of Reason over Sensuality and explains the theological distinction between physical death and the "habit" of vice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, likely from the perspective of Cristoforo Landino, explaining the allegorical necessity of the descent into Hell before reaching Purgatory.</meta>

->### CANTO ONE. 19<-

...you: And there was no other way but this one through Hell. Because when vice has seized us, it knows how to flatter us so much with delights that if reason <note>In Dante’s allegory, Human Reason is personified by the poet Virgil, who guides Dante through the first two realms.</note> did not show us their ugliness and the punishments—which is what it means to lead us through Hell—we would never succeed in freeing ourselves from them. Therefore, Reason could not lead him to salvation without making the journey through Hell. And for this reason, he says he has shown him all the wicked people: that is, every generation <term>generation: used here to mean the various categories or families of sins</term> of vices; and now I intend to show him Purgatory. Because from the recognition of the malignancy of vices, the desire to purge oneself is born.

->**Under your authority.**<- <note>original Latin/Italian: "Sotto la tua balia." This refers to the guardianship of the soul's progress.</note>

Although everything is under divine power, one can nevertheless say that Purgatory is under the authority of Cato <note>Cato the Younger, the Roman statesman who chose death over tyranny, serves as the guardian of the shores of Purgatory, symbolizing political and moral liberty.</note>—that is, of liberty—because no one can enter Purgatory unless he repents of his errors. And no one repents of being a slave to vice unless he becomes eager and desirous of liberty.

<summary>This passage explains that the journey through Hell is a necessary psychological and moral realization of the ugliness of sin, led by Reason, which then inspires the soul to seek the liberty found in Purgatory.</summary>
<keywords>Reason, Hell, Purgatory, Cato, Liberty, Repentance, Vice, Allegory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Dante's Purgatorio, specifically focusing on the character of Cato of Utica and the symbolic transition from earthly concerns to spiritual ones.</meta>

-># **PURGATORY**<-

[Top Right Commentary]

Civil liberty lasts as long as that same civil life lasts. But once the contemplative life <term>contemplative life: a life focused on spiritual meditation and the study of God, as opposed to the "active life" of work and politics</term> has arrived, one must observe the law of that state. This is because the contemplative life is eternal. Hence, it says in the Gospel: *Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.* <note>original Latin: "Maria autem optimam partem elegit: quae non auferetur ab ea" (Luke 10:42), referring to Mary of Bethany who sat at Jesus's feet while her sister Martha worked.</note>

And then he adds: *But if a lady of heaven moves or rules you*, as if to say: "I am no longer bound to Marcia <note>Marcia was the wife of Cato the Younger. In this allegory, she represents the earthly, active life that Cato has left behind in the afterlife.</note>, but to a heavenly lady; and if she guides you, **AS you say, there is no need for flatteries**." He used the word "flatteries" most excellently. For men are led to do our will either by the reasons we put forward, or by flatteries. 

Reason leads toward what is true and just. Flattery, however, works through the pleasure it shows you; with fraud, it persuades you that something is good which is actually not. Therefore, to pray for the love of Marcia is a "flattery," because the active life labors among earthly goods, and these pull us to love them with their flatteries, showing in life...

<summary>This passage provides a philosophical commentary on the transition from the "active life" of earthly politics (symbolized by Marcia) to the "contemplative life" of spiritual pursuit (symbolized by the lady of heaven), interpreting Dante's encounter with Cato.</summary>

# CANTO XX [Page] 200

## CANTO XX OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE

[Woodcut illustration: A landscape depicting scenes from Purgatory Canto XX. In the center, several figures lie face down on the ground. Above them is the label "HUGH CAPET" <note>original: "VGO CIAPETA"</note>. To the right, two figures, Dante and Virgil, stand and observe. In the background, there are rocky hills and more figures.]

**C**ontra a better will, a will
fights poorly;
wherefore against my own pleasure, to
please him,
I drew the sponge from the water not yet full.
My leader moved, and I moved through
clear spaces along the rock,
as one goes along a wall close to the battlements.
For the people who pour out drop by drop
through their eyes the evil that occupies the whole world,
on the other side, approach too near the edge.
Accursed be you, ancient wolf,
who more than all other beasts have prey
because of your hunger, bottomlessly deep!
O heaven, in whose turning it seems believed
that conditions here below are transmuted,
when will he come through whom she shall depart?

The text continues by treating avarice <term>avarice: an insatiable greed for riches; one of the seven deadly sins</term>, and in the beginning demonstrates that although he was eager to hear more things, nonetheless he departed from the spirit to whom he had said farewell. **Against a better will, a will fights poorly.** When there are two different wills, that which is less good fights poorly—that is, it poorly combats and resists against the better one. And therefore he [Dante], whose wish was to know from the spirit that which did not matter much, wished to yield to the will of the spirit, which was better, because it desired to be purged from the vice of avarice. This precept follows: whenever we are conquered by better reason, we should always make our own will conform to the will of others. **I drew the sponge from the water not yet full.** This is an excellent metaphor to demonstrate that a man departs still thirsty for that which he desires to know. **I moved**, departing from the spirit. **My leader**, who waited for me and was before me, **moved**, proceeding ahead of me. **Through the clear spaces**, that is, areas not occupied by the souls who were lying there. **Along the rock**, along the stone mass. Close to this mass just as one goes close to the battlements who walks along the top of city walls. And they did this because the souls who wept for the sin of avarice—which occupies the whole world—approached, that is, they came too close to the edge. **Accursed be you, ancient wolf.** Avarice began in the world as far back as Cain. He, according to the "Master of Histories" <note>Likely referring to Petrus Comestor, a popular medieval historian</note>, invented weights and measures, and was more intent on gain than was required. And in the first fruits that he offered to God, his avarice was demonstrated. Therefore, avarice is ancient. We will not speak further of the wolf here, having said enough in the first canticle <note>referring to the wolf encountered in Inferno Canto I</note>, where it is shown that of the three animals—the Leopard, the Lion, and the Wolf—this is the worst and does the most harm. And for this reason, it has us as prey more than the other animals. **O heaven, in whose turning**, that is, in the celestial revolutions. **It seems believed.** Mathematicians <note>The author refers here to astrologers and astronomers of the time</note> hold that the celestial motions give movement and influence to all things created beneath them. However, our souls, created by God without the mediation of secondary causes, alone remain free from such influences. Nonetheless, celestial influences can incline us toward justice, and change kings and empires into the proper form of administration. **When will he come through whom she shall depart?** This refers to when the "Greyhound" <note>original: "Veltro," a prophesied savior or leader mentioned in Inferno Canto I</note> shall come to drive greed away.

We went with steps slow and short,
and I was intent on the shades whom I heard
pityingly weep and complain.
And by chance I heard "Sweet Mary"
called out before us in the weeping,
as a woman does who is in labor.
And following: "So poor you were,
as can be seen by that hostelry
where you laid down your holy burden."
Next I heard: "O good Fabricius..."

It is a **MOST CONVENIENT** thing that those who are eager to be purged of the vice of avarice—which is nothing other than greed for treasures—should hold in their minds the examples of those who have been content with little. Therefore, it first shows that the spirits of this place at the same time invoked the name of Mary, as does a woman who is about to give birth. And they remembered how cheerfully she endured poverty, and they said, "You were as poor as is shown by the hostelry <note>The stable in Bethlehem</note> in which you gave birth to our salvation." **O Good Fabricius.** <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman consul famous for refusing bribes and living in poverty</note> In all the purgings of these sins, the poet places examples not only of Christians but of pagans <note>original: "gentili"</note>, because morality is common to both our religion and theirs. Furthermore, the sinner might excuse themselves by saying a virtue is impossible to achieve, because not everyone is raised to the high state of grace to which Mary and many holy men were raised; such an excuse cannot be made regarding the example of the pagans...

Therefore you felt the earthquake and the pious
spirits through the mountain giving praise
to that Lord—may He soon send them above.
Thus he spoke to us; and because one enjoys
drinking as much as the thirst is great,
I cannot say how much good he did me.

The wise leader <note>Referring to Virgil.</note> said: "Now I see the net
that catches you here and how one is untangled,
why it trembles here and why you <term>rejoice together</term>.<note>original: "congaudete", a Latin-inflected term for collective joy.</note>
Now, may it please you that I know who you were,
and why you have lain here for so many centuries;
let the reason be contained within your words."
"In the time that the good Titus, with the help
of the highest King, avenged the wounds
from which issued the blood sold by Judas,<note>A reference to the Roman Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which Dante viewed as divine retribution for the Crucifixion.</note>
With the name that lasts longest and honors most,<note>The name "Poet."</note>
I was there," responded that spirit,
"famous enough, but not yet with faith.
So sweet was my vocal <unclear>voice</unclear>...

<meta>This page continues the encounter between Dante, Virgil, and the Roman poet Statius in the fifth terrace of Purgatory. Statius has just explained that the earthquake they felt was a sign of a soul’s purification and release. He now begins to identify himself and his debt to Virgil, unaware that the spirit standing before him is Virgil himself.</meta>

### CANTO XXI 204

[Left Column]

The sparks which warmed me from the divine flame,
from which more than a thousand have been lit,
were the seed of my poetic passion.
I speak of the *Aeneid*, which was my
mother and my nurse in poetry;
without it, I never achieved a dram's weight of worth.
And to have lived on the other side <note>In the mortal world.</note>
when Virgil lived, I would consent to one more sun
than I owe for my release from banishment. <note>Statius claims he would willingly spend an extra year in the suffering of Purgatory just to have known Virgil in life.</note>

He writes in his *Silvae* <term>Silvae: a collection of occasional poems by Statius</term> that his father was Neapolitan. I sang of Thebes: where he describes the discord born over the kingdom between Eteocles and Polynices, of which I made mention in the *Inferno*; and the war that Adrastus, King of Argos and father-in-law of Polynices, moved against Thebes; THE GREAT Achilles. Regarding whom you shall seek the history in the second canto of the *Inferno* <note>Dante likely refers to the mention of Achilles' death and his presence among the lustful.</note> concerning his death. But I fell on the way with the second burden. <note>Meaning he did not give perfection to his second book, the *Achilleid*, because it was interrupted by his death.</note> Wherefore Francesco da Buti <note>A 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> errs greatly, who reproves Dante for saying such a work is imperfect and insists it is finished. But if he had noted the beginning well, he would have clearly understood that poem to be merely commenced and not perfected. Furthermore, some say he did not fall with the second burden but with the third: because he had finished not only the *Thebaid* but also the *Silvae*. To those we answer: the *Silvae* are not laborious works of sleepless nights like the *Thebaid*. Therefore, the *Silvae* did not deserve to be called a "burden" like the *Achilleid*, which itself had no less difficulty than the *Thebaid*. **THE SPARKS WERE THE SEED of my passion.** He shows that the principle of his learning and fame was Virgil’s *Aeneid*, by imitating which he was able to become an excellent poet. Thus the text is ordered: the sparks of your genius, which warmed me with the divine flame of poetry, were the seed of my passion—that is, they were the cause of my excitement. **FROM WHICH.** From which sparks more than a thousand are lit: because Virgil has been the rule and example for all poets. **And to have lived over there.** That is, in our world; and he says I would "consent to one sun," which is a solar course of 365 days and six hours, to have lived with Virgil. The meaning is: I would consent to stay one more year before leaving banishment—that is, to leave the pains of Purgatory to which I was condemned—if I had lived together with Virgil. But there are some to whom it seems Statius shows little desire by offering only one year; however, if we remember the words of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, regarding the intensity of purgatorial cleansing.</note> on the pains of Purgatory, we will understand that one year in that torment is a very great thing.

[Left Column continued]

Virgil turned these words to me
with a look that, while silent, said "be silent";
but the power of the will cannot do everything.
For laughter and tears are such close followers
to the passion from which each one breaks away,
that they follow the will less in those who are most truthful.
I just smiled like a man who winks,
whereupon the shadow fell silent and looked me
in the eyes, where the expression is most fixed.
"So may you bring such great labor to a good end,"
he said, "why did your face just now
show me a flash of laughter?"
Now I am caught on one side and the other:
one makes me keep silent, the other conjures me
to speak; thus I sigh, and am understood
By my master; "Do not be afraid,"
he says to me, "to speak; but speak, and tell him
what he asks with such great care."
Wherefore I: "Perhaps you marvel,
ancient spirit, at the laughter I gave;

[Right Column]

<note>original: "me amice. thebaidos letam cum fecit statius urbē: pmisit que diem tanta dulcedine captos. afficit ille animos tataq̃ libidine uulgi Auditur."</note>
"My friend, when Statius made the city happy with his *Thebaid*, it promised a day [of fame], and it affected those minds captured by such sweetness and with such desire from the common folk it is heard." <note>A Latin commentary note discussing the popularity of Statius's work in Rome.</note> **That he was from Toulouse:** Because he was from Toulouse, which city is on the borders of Gascony toward Brittany; and through his learning and eloquence, he became a Roman citizen. **Of Myrtle** poets were crowned. Wherefore Petrarch says: "what longing for laurel or what for myrtle." **Statius:** It is no wonder if this poet, so occupied in things so lofty, so varied, so diverse, and so numerous, followed the common opinion held by all men of his times and did not investigate the homeland of Statius, as it served him nothing in this place. For such great genius did not esteem minute things, and he could well rely on the authority of Lactantius, <margin>D</margin> the commentator on his *Thebaid*, a man of much eloquence. But Statius...

[Right Column continued]

**Virgil turned.** That is, these words made Virgil turn to me with such a look that, by being silent, he signaled to me that I should be silent. **But the power of the will.** That is, that power which is called the "will" cannot do everything: because it often happens that a man, not wishing to cry, cries; and not wishing to laugh, laughs. Because every passion of the soul, such as joy and sadness and the like, has certain acts and gestures that follow said passions even though the man does not wish it. Therefore laughter follows joy, even if we did not want it to, and weeping follows sadness. **FOLLOW LESS.** They follow the will less. **IN THOSE WHO ARE.** In those who are less prone to feigning. **I just smiled.** Although by Virgil’s signs I did not want Statius to recognize Virgil yet, and for this reason I wanted to contain the laughter, nonetheless for the reason stated above, I could not contain it. **LIKE A MAN WHO WINKS.** Like one who makes a sign. **AND LOOKING ME IN THE EYES:** He looked at my eyes, seeing me laugh. **WHERE THE EXPRESSION IS MOST FIXED:** Where the image and likeness of the soul is most expressed and carved, because the eyes are like windows through which the soul is seen. **May you bring to a good end.** That is, if you lead such great labor as climbing to Paradise to a good end, tell me: why did your face show me a flash of laughter? **Now I am.** He was in difficulty on every side because Virgil signaled that he should not speak, and Statius prayed that he would. **WHEREFORE I sigh.** Because of such anguish; and by such a sigh I am understood by Virgil; but Virgil, seeing me in this ambiguity, gave me permission to speak.

[Bottom Section]

but I want a greater wonder to seize you:
This one who guides my eyes on high

There is little ambiguity in these tercets <note>original: "ternarii"; the three-line stanzas of Dante’s verse</note>. And therefore they require no exposition.

**CANTO XXII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.**

[Main Text - Left Column]
<term>G</term><note>Large decorated initial letter</note> Already the angel was left behind us,
the angel who had turned us to the 
sixth circle,
having erased a stroke from my face;
And those who have their desire set on justice

with "I thirst" <note>original Latin: "sitio"</note> without more, finished it.
And I, lighter than through the other passes,
went along so that without any labor
I followed up the swift spirits.
When Virgil began: "Love,
kindled by virtue, has always kindled another,

Wherefore from the hour that Juvenal <note>Decimus Junius Juvenalis, a Roman satirist who lived after Virgil but before Statius</note> descended

who made your affection clear to me,
my goodwill toward you was such
as ever bound one to an unseen person,
so that now these stairs will seem short to me.
But tell me—and as a friend forgive me
if too much liberty slackens my rein—
and as a friend now speak with me:
How could avarice find a place within your breast,
among so much wisdom
of which through your care you were full?"

[Right Column - Woodcut Illustration]
<note>The illustration shows the three poets—Dante, Virgil, and Statius—climbing the rocky path of the mountain. Statius is identified by name twice as he leads or follows through the terrain. Trees represent the entrance to the next terrace, where gluttony is punished.</note>

[Right Column - Commentary Text]
THE poet has already gone from the fifth circle to the sixth, where the soul is purged from the vice of gluttony. It deals with the conversion of Statius with great praise of Virgil. Starting then, he says: that they had already left the angel behind, who had shown them the sixth circle. Having erased from the face a bit, because he had erased the fifth sin <note>The 'P' for Peccatum (sin) carved on Dante's forehead by the gatekeeper angel</note> so that there remained to him only the sixth and the seventh. And "Those who have" shows that the souls who were purging themselves in the fifth circle, seeing Dante ascend purged of avarice, out of joy and congratulation sang: *Blessed are those whose sins are covered* <note>original Latin: "Beati quorum tecta sunt peccata"; a reference to Psalm 32:1</note>; and in the end turning to Dante as he was ascending, they said: *sitio*, that is, "I thirst" <note>An allusion to the Beatitude "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness"</note> for eternal salvation. AND I MORE LIGHT. He was lighter than in the circles below because he was purged of more vices, and by such lightness he could ascend as an equal to Virgil and Statius, who were swift spirits. LOVE kindled by virtue always kindled another. If one loves another for the virtue that he sees in him, it follows that the loved one loves the lover. PROVIDED that the flame, that is, that such love is known to the one who is loved. But it does not happen thus in carnal love, because often one is loved carnally who does not love the lover. Wherefore, by which thing it happened: that Juvenal descending into Limbo and telling me of your very great love toward me, I was bound to bring you such benevolence, which was...

->### CANTO XXII 206<-

There are seen there of your people
Antigone, Deiphile, and Argia,
and Ismene as sorrowful as she ever was.
There is seen she who showed the Langia,
the daughter of Tiresias, and Thetis,
and with her sisters, Deidamia.
<note>original: "Quivi si veggon delle genti tue..." These lines refer to characters from Statius's epic poems, the *Thebaid* and the *Achilleid*. Virgil is telling Statius which of his literary "people" are in Limbo.</note>

Of all the Romans, he was a most excellent poet and philosopher. Many learned men did not hesitate to equal him to Aristotle. He wrote forty-one books on antiquity, and these he divided into human and divine matters. <note>The commentator is likely referring to Marcus Terentius Varro, a massive figure in Roman scholarship.</note> There was another Varro, a contemporary of Virgil, of whom Virgil writes honorably in his *Bucolics*: *But I am not yet worthy to speak of Cinna, but rather to cackle like a goose among the tuneful swans.* <note>original: "Sed neque dicere cynam Digna. sed argutos interstrepere anser olores." (Virgil, Eclogue IX). The commentator is distinguishing between Varro Reatinus (the scholar) and Varro Atacinus (the poet).</note> To this man, along with Tucca, Octavian <note>The Emperor Augustus</note> left the unfinished works after Virgil's death. And because of this, Virgil left in his will that they should be burned; but Octavian would not allow it, so that the honor of the Latin tongue would not be extinguished. **THOSE PEOPLE.** Virgil my leader replied: those of whom you ask, and Persius and I, are with that Greek whom the Muses nursed more than any other poet—meaning Homer—of whom we spoke in the *Inferno*. Nor by these words does he place Homer above Virgil, but in bringing him to speak, he portrays him as modest. **PERSIUS WAS** a citizen of Volterra, whose genius his satires, though few, show as a manifest sign. **IN THE FIRST** circle: as was shown in the first canticle <note>The *Inferno*</note>: and there we often spoke together of the mountain. **WHICH.** That is, the one who has our nurses: that is, the Muses; in short, they speak of the Muses by whom poets are nourished. **EURIPIDES.** An excellent poet and writer of tragedies; he was a disciple of Anaxagoras and a fellow student of Socrates. He was very skilled at writing tragic things with compassion. **ANACREON,** a lyric poet, was born on the island of Teos. **SIMONIDES,** a poet from the island of Ceos. He was the inventor of the method of places and images belonging to artificial memory. <note>Simonides is credited with inventing the "Memory Palace" technique.</note> He had written hymns in honor of Scopas, a very powerful and wealthy man in Thessaly, in which he had interspersed many praises of Pollux and Castor, the sons of Jove called the Dioscuri. <note>The Gemini twins.</note> And he recited them at a banquet to which Scopas had invited many; after having recited them, Scopas said to Simonides that he would give him half the reward he deserved for the verses, and for the other half, he should ask the Dioscuri, whom he had equally praised. Simonides agreed, and a little later two young men dressed in white arrived. For a matter of importance, they had Simonides called out of the house; as soon as he had exited, the house collapsed, and the young men vanished. It was judged that those had been the Dioscuri come to save him from the ruin. **OF YOUR PEOPLE:** not "yours" because they are related to you by blood (because you are from Toulouse <note>A common medieval error; Statius was actually from Naples.</note>), but yours because you sang of them most ornately in your heroic verses and treated them in your poem. Antigone was the sister of Eteocles and Polynices. Deiphile and Argia were the daughters of Adrastus; Deiphile married Polynices and Argia married Tydeus. Ismene is a river in Boeotia <note>Ismene was also the sister of Antigone.</note>. **THERE IS SEEN** she who showed the Langia: she showed the fountain of Langia to the army of Adrastus, and in that moment Archemorus died from a snake bite. This was Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, of whom we spoke in the first canticle. The daughter of Tiresias: this was Manto. And her story is also told in the founding of Mantua. Similarly, we include the fabled history of Thetis, mother of Achilles, and how she hid her son on the island of Skyros with the daughters of Lycomedes; there was Deidameia, and by him she gave birth to Pyrrhus.

Both poets were now silent,
intent once more on looking around,
free from the ascent and from walls.
And already the four handmaidens of the day
remained behind, and the fifth was at the chariot pole,
directing its burning horn ever upward.
When my leader: "I believe that toward the edge
we must turn our right shoulders,
circling the mountain as we are wont to do."
Thus usage there was our guide,
and we took the path with less doubt
because of the assent of that worthy soul.
They went on ahead, and I alone
behind, and I listened to their speech,
which gave me understanding in poetry.

The poet feigns that they are attentive again because he will treat new material; "free from the ascent" because such material does not need greater speculation, and "from walls" because whoever climbs stairs has a wall on each side that blocks the view. But here there was no impediment to speculation. **AND ALREADY** the four handmaidens. Time: which the sun consumes to make one revolution—that is, from leaving the east until it returns there—is divided into twenty-four hours. And because of this, the poets feign that the hours are handmaidens of the sun, and they divide them into twenty-four parts, and station them at posts so that each guides the pole of the solar chariot for its own space of time. Therefore, when the fourth hour has led the chariot through its space, she remains behind, and the fifth succeeds her, and then the others in order. The poet wishes to show in this place that four hours had already passed and the fifth had come; and because of this he says that "already the four handmaidens remained behind and the fifth was at the chariot pole." **DIRECTING** its burning horn upward: because until midday the sun always rises, and he calls the tip of the chariot pole the "horn." **I BELIEVE THAT TOWARD THE EDGE:** because in all the other terraces he had seen that turning to the right side made them keep the right path; he estimates the same here. And therefore he says: "Thus usage was our guide," and shows that custom and experience generate doctrine. **BY THE ASSENT OF THAT WORTHY SOUL:** he means the soul of Statius, which, purged of sins, was truly worthy and should have greater knowledge of such a journey. **THEY WENT ON AHEAD:** because the intellect and...

[Illustration: A woodcut shows figures in a landscape with trees. Labels indicate "FORESE" <note>Forese Donati, a friend of Dante</note>, "V" <note>Virgil</note>, and "D" <note>Dante</note>.]

He shows in this 23rd Canto the penalty through which the gluttonous are purified in the sixth circle, and he recognizes a certain soul: and especially Forese, with whom he speaks. **While I fixed my eyes**: a comparison that he thus fixed his eyes through the green leaves of the tree as do those who waste all their time chasing birds <note>fowling or hunting</note>, and just as they lose time, so was I losing it. **My more than father**: if there can be an affection greater than the paternal. **He said to me, "Son"**: <gloss>original: "filiole", which is a Latinate name.</gloss> **Come now**: as a true father, he admonishes the reason and the senses that they must follow him, and demonstrates that nothing is more ruinous than to consume in useless things the time which we ought to spend usefully. **To distribute**: not just one single thing is required in human life, but many; therefore it is necessary that we distribute to each as much time as is required. **I turned my face**: to attend to that which I was warned of. **My step**: to put into practice that which he commanded me, which was that I should follow him. **Who were speaking so**: because as I have already said: "A pleasant companion is like a vehicle on a journey." <note>original: "Facundus comes pro uehiculo est in uia." A common Latin proverb suggesting good conversation makes travel feel faster.</note> Therefore, the walking was of no cost. **And behold, a weeping and a singing**: they wept for contrition and true repentance of the sin committed, and they sang for the hope of being able to purge it and, having purged it, to go toward salvation. **"O Lord, [open] my lips"**: This is in the prophetic psalm: "O Lord, thou shalt open my lips, and my mouth shall declare thy praise." <note>original: "domie labia mea aperies & os meum anunciabit laudẽ tuã" - Psalm 51:15.</note> Which prayer is appropriate for the gluttonous. So that the mouth—which in the past they opened for superfluous food—shall in the future open to sing divine praises. **In such a way that delight**: because I saw that those were to be saved. **And grief**: to see them in their present pain. **Perhaps loosening the knot of their debt**: <gloss>that is, untying the knot, meaning the obligation of their duty; that is, of that for which they remain debtors to God for the penalty they have to pay for it.</gloss>

Following on the path, he shows that a crowd was coming behind them, which, because it moved more quickly, reached them and stared at them and passed ahead, just as pilgrims do who travel not without suspicion, and reaching unknown people, they stare and pass by. <term>Pilgrim</term> <note>original: "Peregrino"</note> is a Latin name and signifies anyone who makes a journey outside of his own country. **In the eyes**: wishing to demonstrate that those souls, through long and great abstinence, were very exhausted; he provides the signs that we see in thin bodies. **First**: that the eyes are sunken inward. **The second**: that the color has faded. **The third**: that the skin is upon the bone; <gloss>that is, that between the skin and the bone there is no flesh.</gloss> **Erysichthon**: <note>original: "Herisithone"</note> He was an impious man in Thessaly who held Ceres, the goddess of grain, in contempt and prohibited sacrifices from being made to her. For this reason, the enraged Ceres placed an unheard-of hunger upon him, through which in a short time he consumed all his substance, and finally sold his daughter multiple times. And after this, he ate his own limbs. Under such a fable, Ovid expresses the nature of the glutton.

**PURGATORY INFERNO** <note>The header curiously mentions "Inferno," likely a printer's error or a reference to the whole work, as the text is clearly from Purgatorio.</note>

...all impregnated with herbs and flowers.
I felt a wind strike me in the middle of
my forehead, and I clearly felt the feather move,
so that I smelled the fragrance of ambrosia: <note>original: "ambrosia," the food/scent of the gods.</note>
And I heard it say: "Blessed are those whom the light
of grace so illumines that the love of taste
does not kindle too much desire in their breasts,
always hungering for what is just."

**CANTO 25 OF the second canticle by Dante**

<margin>r. obstacle</margin>

[Large woodcut initial O containing a figure]
**N**ow the hour was such that the climb brooked no
delay, <note>Literally "did not want a cripple," meaning they had to move fast.</note>
for the sun had left the meridian circle
to the Taurus, and the night to the Scorpio. <note>A medieval way of telling time: it is about 2:00 PM.</note>
Therefore, as a man does who does not stop,
but goes on his way, whatever may appear to him,
if the needle of necessity pricks him;
so we entered through the gap, <term>the gap<gloss>a narrow opening or path</gloss></term>
one before the other, taking the stairs
which by its narrowness unpairs the climbers.
And like the young stork that lifts its wing
with the desire to fly, yet does not dare
to leave the nest, and drops it down again;
so was I, with a desire both kindled and quenched,
coming even to the act that he does
who prepares himself to speak.

->**Commentary**<-
The scent: because it moves the new herbs and flowers. This makes one feel the fragrance, that is, the smell of ambrosia. Taken from the first book of Virgil <note>The Aeneid</note> when he imagines that Venus, in departing from Aeneas, spread a great scent, where he says: *And her ambrosial hair breathed a divine fragrance from her head.* <note>original Latin: "Ambrosieque comae divinum vertice odorem spiravere."</note> And I heard it say "Blessed." These words are from Matthew the Evangelist where he says: *Blessed are they who hunger and thirst after justice, for they shall be filled.* <note>original Latin: "beati qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam quoniam ipsi saturabuntur."</note> This voice was saying: "Blessed are those whom grace illumines," meaning they have so much of the light of God's grace that the love and greed for taste and gluttony does not "smoke"—does not evaporate or give off too much superfluous desire—and their appetite is "hungering" only for what is just and reasonable.

[Woodcut illustration: Three figures (Dante, Virgil, and Statius) climb a narrow, rocky path. To the right, souls are visible within flames.]

->**Commentary continued**<-
This present Canto describes how they climb to the 7th circle where lust is purged in fire. It describes the time and shows Dante having a desire to have a doubt clarified. Virgil comforts him to ask; having heard the doubt, Virgil solves part of it, and leaves part for Statius to solve, who demonstrates the creation of the fetus in the mother's womb and likewise the infusion of the soul. "Now it was the hour." He describes the time and shows that midday had passed. Because the sun was in Aries and was already declining toward the west, Taurus, which follows it, had risen to the midday point. Therefore, it was necessary that while Taurus was at the midday of the hemisphere of day, Scorpio was at the midday of our hemisphere of night, because these two signs are opposites. "Therefore as a man does who does not stop," meaning he does not stay still, but goes on with his life "whatever may appear to him," for whatever reason. "So we entered through the gap," meaning through the entrance of the stairs. One before the other—they did not all go together, but one by one. And this because the "narrowness" of the stairs "unpairs" the climbers. The meaning is that the stairs were so narrow that those who climb cannot go side-by-side; certainly, in such high speculation, sensuality cannot go side-by-side with intellect, but it is enough if it follows and goes behind it. "And like the young stork." A fitting comparison which expresses this: I had a great desire to ask Virgil about the doubt mentioned below, and I reached the point of speaking, but then shame did not let me send the word out. I acted like the stork which, wanting to leave the nest, begins to flap its wings but then, for fear of falling, does not dare to fly. With desire "kindled and quenched"—the desire to ask was kindled and inflamed, but shame quenched it.

**Dante's Speech**
My sweet father did not stop his pace,
even though it was swift, but said: "Release
the bow of your speech, which you have drawn to the iron." <note>A metaphor for being on the verge of speaking, like an arrow pulled back to the arrowhead.</note>
Then I confidently opened my mouth
and began: "How can one become thin
where the need for nourishment does not apply?" <note>Dante asks how spirits, who have no physical bodies, can look starved.</note>
"If you remembered how Meleager
was consumed as a brand consumed itself,
this would not be so bitter to you," he said. <note>Meleager’s life was tied to a piece of wood; as it burned, he wasted away, illustrating how a spirit can be affected by external things.</note>

->**Commentary**<-
"And if you thought how at your every quiver, your image quivers within the mirror, what seems hard would seem easy to you. But because you should rest within your will..."

<margin>To the prudence and doctrine that the man has is divine.</margin>

Therefore Virgil, through certain gestures in Dante, perceived that he was doubting. And remembering the thinness of the souls, he guessed his doubt by conjecture; to take away the shame that prevented him from speaking, he incited him to ask, saying: "Shoot the bow of speech which you have pulled to the iron." This is an excellent metaphor, comparing words to arrows. Then Dante safely opened his mouth. Reassured by Virgil, Dante spoke confidently and opened his doubt: which was how it could happen that the souls grow thin in Purgatory.

# CANTO XXV z ii

And if you thought how at your every quiver
your image quivers within the mirror,
what seems hard <note>original: "duro"</note> would seem easy <note>original: "vizo," meaning clear or easy to understand in this context</note> to you.
But so that your desire may rest <note>original: "adaghe," to find ease or settle</note> within,
here is Statius <note>A Roman poet whom Dante depicts as a secret convert to Christianity; he acts as a guide alongside Virgil</note>, and I call and pray him
that he may now be the healer of your wounds. <note>Virgil asks Statius to explain a complex theological point that Virgil, as a pagan, cannot fully resolve.</note>

...that thinness arises from a lack of nourishment. Therefore, when a man fasts and deprives himself of food, his body grows thin; but the souls <note>original: "laie," a transcription of "l'anime"</note>, which are incorporeal, have no need for food. And so he <note>Dante</note> asks how one can become thin in Purgatory, where it does not touch <note>physical matter</note> and there occurs no need for nourishment, that is <note>original: ".i.", the Latin abbreviation for "id est"</note> the need to feed oneself.
If you remembered Meleager <note>A hero from Greek mythology whose life was bound to a charred log</note>. Meleager was the son of Oeneus, king of Calydon. And his mother Althaea, when he was born, saw that the Fates <note>The three goddesses of destiny</note> placed a piece of wood on the fire, and said that Meleager would live as long as that wood lasted. His mother took it from the fire so that it would not burn. Meleager grew up, and having become a young man, it happened that a terrible boar was wasting the entire region of Calydon <note>The Calydonian Boar, sent by Artemis to punish the city</note>...

...that arrives via this path and that,
It operates so much that it moves and feels
like a sea sponge; and from there it begins
to organize the powers for which it is capable.
Now it folds, my son, and now it extends,
the virtue that comes from the heart of the progenitor,
where nature provides for all the limbs.

<note>This passage from Purgatorio 25 explains how the "active virtue" (the formative power) begins to shape the fetus into a living being, moving from the state of a plant to a "sea sponge" (an animal-like state) before becoming human.</note>

...stomach through a vein called the "great gate" <note>original: *gran porta*; this refers to the portal vein</note> to the liver; and it is cooked for the second time. And the superfluous and waste humor called urine is separated; and through the kidneys it distills into the bladder, and is pushed out through the neck of the same. The remaining chyle <term>chyle: a milky fluid produced in the digestive system from which blood is formed</term>, having been sufficiently purified and cooked by the liver, has taken on the color of the liver and becomes red. Then, in the third digestion <note>Medieval medicine taught that the body underwent four "cookings" or digestions to turn food into tissue.</note> which occurs either in the heart or in the liver by the power of the heart, it removes from itself the superfluous choler—which the Latins call bile—and the foam of the blood, and sends it to the gallbladder. It also removes the melancholic humor—which is the dregs of the blood, which the Latins call "atrabile" <note>original: *atrabile*, meaning "black bile"</note>—and sends it to the spleen. After the third digestion...

**CANTO [space] XXV. [space] 76-104**

**[Left Column]**

And so that you may marvel less at my words,
look at the sun’s heat which becomes wine
when joined to the sap that flows from the vine.

And when Lachesis <note>In Greek mythology, Lachesis is the Fate who measures the thread of life. Her "running out of flax" means the end of a person's life.</note> has no more flax <note>original: "lino"</note>,
the soul is released from the flesh, and in its power,
it carries with it both the human and the divine.
The other faculties—memory, intelligence, and will—
which were almost silent before,
are now much more sharp in action than they were.
Without stopping, the soul falls by itself
marvelously to one of the shores <note>original: "riue". This refers to the banks of the Acheron for the damned or the mouth of the Tiber for those destined for Purgatory.</note>;
there it first learns its destined path.
As soon as the space encompasses it there,
the <term>formative power: the soul’s inherent ability to give shape to matter</term> radiates around,
just as it did within the living limbs.
And just as the air, when it is saturated with rain,
becomes adorned with various colors
because the rays of another <note>The sun.</note> are reflected within it,
so the neighboring air here sets itself
into that form which the soul, having halted there,
imprints upon it through its own power.
And then, similar to the little flame
that follows the fire wherever it moves,
this new form follows the spirit.
Because its outward appearance is created from this,
it is called a "shade" <term>shade: the temporary "body" of a soul in the afterlife, made of air but capable of sensation</term>; and from this it then organizes
every sense, even including sight.
By this we speak, and by this we laugh;
by this we produce the tears and the sighs
that you may have perceived throughout the mountain.

<summary>Statius explains how the soul, upon death, retains its higher faculties and automatically forms a "shade" body out of the surrounding air, allowing it to feel and express emotion despite lacking physical flesh.</summary>

# CANTO XXVI 214

"My limbs are over there [on earth], but here I am with them,
with their blood and their joints.
I ascend from here so as not to be blind anymore;
a Lady above <note>Refers to the Virgin Mary, who initiated Dante's journey</note> has won grace for me,
which is why I carry my mortal frame through your world.
But—so may your greatest longing be satisfied
soon, so that the Heaven which is full of love
and spreads most widely might house you—
tell me, so that I may yet record it on paper:
who are you, and who is that crowd
that was moving away behind your backs?"

No differently is the bewildered mountain-dweller troubled,
falling silent as he gazes in wonder,
when, rough and rustic, he enters the city,
than each shade appeared in their countenance;
but after they were unburdened of their shock—
which in noble hearts is quickly stilled—
the one who had questioned us before began:
"Blessed are you, who from our borders
take experience on board <note>original: "in barche," literally 'in boats,' a metaphor for embarking on a spiritual journey</note> to die a better death.
The people who do not come with us committed the offense
for which Caesar, during his triumph,
heard himself called 'Queen' in mockery <note>A historical anecdote where Caesar was teased for a rumored affair with King Nicomedes of Bithynia; Dante uses this to identify the first group as those who practiced 'Sodomy' or same-sex lust</note>.
Therefore they depart crying out 'Sodom!',
reproaching themselves, as you have heard,
and they aid the burning <note>The wall of fire that purifies the souls on this terrace</note> with their shame.
Our sin was hermaphroditic <term>hermaphroditic: Dante uses this term to describe heterosexual lust—attraction to the opposite sex—that was 'natural' in gender but 'bestial' because it ignored human reason and law</term>;
but because we did not keep human law,
following our appetite like beasts,
in shame of...</note>

<summary>Dante explains his presence in the flesh to the souls in Purgatory, and the poet Guido Guinizzelli explains the two groups of the lustful: those who committed 'Sodomy' and those who followed 'hermaphroditic' (heterosexual) lust.</summary>

### PURGATORY

**n** Our acts, which were lustful, and the sin of which they are guilty, are being declared. The "guilty" is the one accused, just as the "actor" <note>The term "actor" here refers to the legal role of the "plaintiff" or accuser in a trial.</note> is the one who accuses others. There is no time to speak, because it is late and I would not know the others, for they are many and unknown to me. I will indeed satisfy your desire regarding myself; I will make it so that your desire to know me will be satisfied <note>The original uses "scemo" (diminished), meaning the hunger for knowledge is lessened by being fed.</note> and finished, because I will tell you: I am **Guido Guinizelli**.

**M** This man was our fellow citizen <note>Guinizelli was from Bologna.</note> and a knight; and in his time he surpassed all others in Tuscan rhyme. <note>Guinizelli is considered the father of the *Dolce Stil Novo* (Sweet New Style), the poetic movement that Dante himself followed.</note> "And already I purge myself": he says this although it has been only a short time since he died; nevertheless, I am already in Purgatory, and I did not have to wait in the outskirts <note>Referring to Ante-Purgatory, where those who delayed repentance must wait for a period equal to their life on earth.</note>.

# PURGATORIO

In these **seven circles** of Purgatory, **Joyful**. Although divine grace brings joy in every part: nevertheless, much [joy] appears here, being already led to the end of the purgation. **Blessed are the pure in heart** <note>original Latin: *Beati mundo corde*</note> because in truth, this being the last circle, whoever leaves from here is purged of every thing. **In a voice much more vivid than ours**. That is, in a voice much more alive than our own. And certainly, the voice of grace is more alive and has more efficacy than the human voice. **Then no further one goes**. These are the words the angel used, saying: "O holy souls, after this one goes no further forward unless first the fire bites you." Therefore, enter into it. **Wherefore I became such**. He says that no other color was in him than that which is in a dead man when he is buried. **Dante shows** fear of entering these flames, and he has never feared in the other circles. This silently tells us that he had almost no other punishment to receive but this one, which was against the sin of the flesh <note>The sin of lust, which is purged in this final circle by fire.</note>. **Upon my clasped hands I stretched out**: I made such a gesture as one does who has great pain, clasping the hands and interlacing one finger with the other, and I stretched out, almost throwing myself backward, and I imagined within myself that which happens to a human body placed in the fire.

PURGATORIO

Straight up the path climbed through the rock,
toward that direction where I blocked the rays
of the sun, which was already low, before me.

And we had climbed only a few steps <note>original: "levammo i saggi." In this context, Dante uses "saggi" to mean "samples" or "trials," suggesting they had tested the first few steps of the stair.</note>
when I and my sages <note>Referring to Dante's guides, the Roman poets Virgil and Statius.</note> felt the sun
setting behind us, because the shadow I cast had vanished.

And before the horizon, in all its vast reaches,
had become a single uniform color,
and night had spread all its darkness,

Each of us made a bed of a single step;
for the law of the mountain broke in us
the power to climb more than it did the desire. <note>In Purgatory, a divine law prevents any soul from ascending after sunset; the "nature of the mountain" physically saps the traveler's strength when the sun's grace is absent.</note>

<margin>He shows that the path climbed straight and toward the east, because the sun being in the west, the shadow of the one climbing appeared before his eyes. And therefore he says: "toward that part where I took away the rays before me of the sun which was low." He knew the sun had gone down when he no longer saw his shadow. He imagines, therefore, that the climb from this seventh terrace to the terrestrial paradise was along a bank of <unclear>stone</unclear></margin>

# CANTO XXVII. 217

Young and beautiful, in a dream, it seemed to me
I saw a lady walking through a meadow,
gathering flowers, and singing she said:
"Let whoever asks my name know
that I am Leah, and I go moving about
my beautiful hands to make myself a garland.
To please myself here at the mirror I deck myself;
but my sister Rachel never departs
from her looking-glass and sits all day.
She is as eager to look with her beautiful eyes
as I am to adorn myself with <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the full thought is "adorn myself with my hands; seeing satisfies her, as doing satisfies me."</note>

<margin>It happens that we demonstrate how by Leah is understood the active life, and by Rachel the contemplative life. <note>In medieval theology, the sisters Leah and Rachel from the Book of Genesis were standard symbols for these two ways of living: the "active" life of good works and the "contemplative" life of prayer and meditation.</note> We will not repeat at present what has already been said; but in this place I believe he <note>Referring to the poet, Dante.</note> places Leah to denote that man, having already been purged of his vices, exercises himself in the earthly paradise—that is, in mortal life—in the active life according to civic virtues and according to the Christian religion. This is done so that, having been a good citizen in this Jerusalem, the earthly city, we may ascend to Jerusalem, the heavenly city, where there is not Leah but Rachel—that is, the contemplative life. Through her, with lynx-like and eagle-like eyes, <note>Lynxes and eagles were famously believed to have the sharpest vision in the animal kingdom, symbolizing the intensity of spiritual insight.</note> we will be able [to see] into the primary source and mirror...</margin>

<summary>This page depicts Dante’s dream of Leah and Rachel, who represent the active and contemplative lives, serving as a transition into the Earthly Paradise. The accompanying commentary explains how a virtuous life on earth (the "Earthly Jerusalem") prepares the soul for the divine vision in heaven (the "Heavenly Jerusalem").</summary>

CANTO XXVIII                                                                                                                              218

->**CANTO XXVIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.**<-

[Large decorative initial 'V' containing a figure of a man's face]
**V**ery eager now to search within
and around
the divine forest, dense and
living,
which tempered the new day to my eyes,
Without waiting longer, I left the bank,
taking the countryside slowly, slowly,
over the ground that was fragrant on every side.
A sweet breeze, without change
within itself, struck me upon the forehead
with no harder a blow than a gentle wind.
By which the branches, trembling readily,
all bent together toward the side
where the holy mountain casts its first shadow;
Yet they were not so diverted from their uprightness
that the little birds among the treetops
would stop practicing all their art;
But with full joy, they welcomed the first hours of day,
singing among the leaves,
which kept a bass-note <note>The Italian word "bordone" refers to the steady drone or accompaniment of the wind in the trees, like the bass pipe of a bagpipe.</note> to their rhymes,
Just as it gathers from branch to branch
through the pine forest on the shore of Chiassi <note>referring to the Pineta di Classe near Ravenna</note>
when Aeolus <note>The Greco-Roman god of the winds.</note> releases the Sirocco wind from his threshold.

[A woodcut illustration depicting several figures in a lush, wooded landscape. On the left, two figures in robes, Dante and Virgil, stand near a tree. In the center, a woman, Matelda, stands near a stream. On the right, a group of figures are gathered among trees.]

Dante had now arrived from the final circle of Purgatory to the terrestrial paradise, which theologians call the garden of delights <note>original Latin: "delitiarum. i. de dilecti"</note>. This place, as we have said, represents the state of innocence. In it, he finds Leah, who is interpreted as the active life. This demonstrates that once a man is purged, he must exercise the active moral virtues according to Christian precepts; from this follows that happiness which can exist in the active life. Thus, having practiced this life as a citizen of this lower Jerusalem, he may ascend to contemplate the celestial Jerusalem. This will be the subject of the third canticle <note>Paradiso</note>. For this reason, in the following cantos, he will set forth the beginning of the new Church founded on the Evangelical law, which was previously signified in the ancient Mosaic law and in the synagogue of the Jews.

He first describes the most delightful greenery of the grass and trees, the sweetness of the flowers, the pleasant wind, and the most sweet melody of the birds. By the grass and flowers, he demonstrates the certain hope that, after that state of innocence, they will reach the true paradise. By the light wind without change, he signifies the tranquil and orderly movement in holy works, in which no perturbation can arise. He walked with joyful steps, because every thought and consideration of ours should be done with good maturity, and not thoughtlessly or precipitated with too much speed. He walked, therefore, because we must never cease from good works. But he walked with "joyful steps," meaning with mature consideration. After this, he describes Matelda, of whom we shall speak in the proper place, who asks what cause produces the wind and the river in that place. **EAGER NOW TO SEARCH WITHIN AND AROUND.** He was, therefore, desirous to search the divine forest, meaning the true active life: "within," as if to say its own essence, and "around," which denotes the circumstances. He wished, therefore, to search paradise through the middle and in a circle, meaning through its extremities.

We showed at the beginning of the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> that Dante finding himself in the dark woods signified nothing other than the troublesome prison of the body, in which the soul, enclosed by the contagion of the flesh, contracts various faults and stains itself with various sins. For this reason, he described it as dark and full of wild beasts that hindered the path toward the sun. Now, because he posits that after the knowledge of sins he has ascended through all the levels of Purgatory—that is, he is purged of every vice—his senses and appetite (which by the contagion of the body were previously rebellious against reason) are now so united with reason that they have almost become the same thing. Consequently, the forest which was previously thorny, dark, and full of beasts has become pleasant and delightful, full of lights and flowers. This denotes virtue, from which the best fruits emerge; for the flower first possesses the sweetness of beauty and scent, and finally produces the best fruit. **THE DIVINE FOREST**, that is, the divine woods made for the habitation of men, with every beauty contrary to that which is described in the Inferno. **DENSE** with trees and grass, and **LIVING** with lights. **WHICH TEMPERED THE NEW DAY TO MY EYES**: the greenery of the trees and grass tempered the splendor of the sun that had already risen. For it was now the fourth day that my eyes could endure it. This signifies nothing else but that the virtues of a man established in a state of innocence in the active life make his intellect capable of receiving the divine light. **WITHOUT WAITING LONGER**, neither for time nor a guide, **I LEFT THE BANK**, that is, the edge, and began to enter the middle as one can do who...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Purgatorio, specifically Canto XXVIII, where the Pilgrim enters the Earthly Paradise (the Garden of Eden). The commentator, likely Cristoforo Landino, explains the allegorical significance of the landscape, the breeze, and the river Lethe.</meta>

-># PURGATORY<-

the same and sufficient. **TAKING** the field: as if in wide and spacious contemplation. **SLOWLY**, slowly: to show that whoever wishes to acquire any doctrine must proceed with a slow pace. **OVER** the ground: that is, on the earth. **WHICH**, that is, which: **EMITTED A SCENT** through the herbs and through the flowers with which it was clothed. And certainly, the operations of the already purified soul emitted an excellent scent everywhere. **A sweet breeze was born from the eastern parts**: a sweet and temperate wind. This is the good will inspired by God; this was like a temperate wind. Because the will that moves toward good deeds is always temperate and is not impetuous, as are unbridled desires. It comes, therefore, from the East: that is, from God, the will directed toward the good; and such a wind bends the leaves toward the West: that is, toward mundane things. Because the active life consists in the prudent, just, courageous, and temperate administration of fleeting goods; nor does this active life last, except as long as this mortal life lasts. But the contemplative life is eternal, because it is concerned with eternal and celestial things. Therefore, the Truth in the Gospel said: "Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." <note>original Latin: "Maria autem optimam partem elegit quae non auferetur ab ea"</note>. Not however from their height being straight or scattered: They do not bend from their straightness so much that the birds, which are among the branches, leave off singing. This denotes that although the operations in the active life bend toward the administration of the body, nonetheless they do not depart from the birds that sing: that is, the man does not cease because of this to continually give thanks to God; but they sing their first hours: that is, the verses they sing in the morning among the leaves. Because nothing forbids us that among the leaves: that is, among civil cares and operations, we cannot praise God. **WHICH held the burden**: that is, the tenor. So sweet was the murmur of the breeze, which struck the leaves, that it provided a tenor accompaniment to the song of the birds. Because the movements of the already purified soul are without perturbation, and they help in the singing of divine praises. **SUCH AS** such was that sweet murmur in that forest, as is in the pine forest of Ravenna. **WHERE** Chiassi <note>Now known as Classe, the ancient port of Ravenna.</note> is, the land near Ravenna, on the shore where the Emperor Justinian built the church of Saint Apollinare, which land the Lombards later destroyed while besieging Ravenna.

**My slow steps had already carried me**
  **so far into the ancient forest that I**
  **could no longer see where I had entered;**
**And behold, a stream took away my further walking,**
  **which toward the left with its little waves**
  **bent the grass that sprouted on its bank.**
**All the waters that are clearest here**
  **would seem to have some mixture in them**
  **compared to that one which hides nothing,**
**Even though it moves dark, dark**
  **under the perpetual shadow that never**
  **lets sun or moon shine there.**

**ALTHOUGH** his steps had been slow, nonetheless they had carried him so far through the ancient forest that he did not see where he had entered; and he rightly said "ancient," because the Earthly Paradise was made by God at the beginning of the world. Furthermore, taking it for the state of innocence, no state is more ancient in souls, because in that state it was created by God. **COULD NOT** see where I had entered. Man entered into the state of innocence as soon as he was created, and of this entry we cannot remember, because no one remembers the entry the soul makes into the body; wherefore also in the first canticle <note>Referencing Inferno, Canto I.</note> he said: "I do not well know how to repeat how I entered." **AND BEHOLD** a stream took away my further walking. Just as Holy Scripture posits that from the Earthly Paradise come from the same source the Euphrates and Tigris, so the poet feigns that from the eastern part of this paradise and from the same source come two rivers: <term>Lethe</term> <note>From the Greek for "oblivion."</note> and <term>Eunoe</term> <note>From the Greek for "good mind."</note>. Lethe, of which he presently makes mention, flows to the left hand. This name Lethe signifies oblivion.

And whoever ascends from Purgatory to the state of innocence drinks of this water, and by drinking it, forgets all sins. Because he enters into the third species of virtues, which are of the soul already purified, through which he no longer fights against vices as he did in the <term>purgatory virtues</term> <note>The virtues practiced during the process of purification.</note>; but he makes such a habit of the virtues that he forgets the vices; whence Juvenal says: "Let him not know how to be angry, let him desire nothing." <note>original Latin: "Nesciat irasci cupiat nihil"</note>. And for this reason, he feigns that it flows to the left, which signifies a vicious thing, carrying away the memory of evil. The other he calls Eunoe: that is, "good mind," because nothing comes to his memory except the good and virtue. Which is the reason that from the state of innocence he may ascend to the contemplation of divine things. **ALL THE WATERS** the meaning of the tercet is that the water of this Lethe is clearer than any water that is in this world here. Which signifies that the soul, which in the state of innocence is so accustomed to virtue that it not only overcomes vice but forgets it, is most pure. **EVEN THOUGH it moves dark**. The water of Lethe is most clear; **BUT** [neither of sun] **NOR OF MOON**: it appears dark. We can say that such oblivion so removes from us the perturbations that in prosperous worldly things make us proud, nor do they make us elated. Nor yet do miseries hinder us from acting well. Which even the Psalmist expressed, saying: "The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night" <note>original Latin: "Per diem sol non uret te: neque luna per noctem"</note>; where he takes the sun of the day for burning desire in prosperous fortune, and the moon of the night for the passions that burn our mind in adversity.

**With feet halted and with eyes I passed**
**beyond the streamlet, to admire**
**the great variety of the fresh May branches.**
**And there appeared to me, just as appears**
**suddenly a thing that drives away**
**every other thought through wonder.**

**ARRIVED** at the river, he halted with his feet: because with his body he went no further forward; but with his eyes, that is, with his sight, he passed the river because he was drawn by the variety of the fresh <term>mai</term>. For with the greatest stupor he looked upon the varied abundance of the trees that were there, and these he calls *mai*. Because thus the Tuscan calls the green branches that by ancient custom on the first day of May we hang at the windows. **AND ALLEGORICALLY** he halted having reached the river. Because he could not pass to the active life and to virtuous actions unless he first drank of Lethe: that is, unless he is confirmed...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante Alighieri’s Purgatorio, Canto 28, following the poet’s entry into the Earthly Paradise (the Garden of Eden). It introduces the figure of Matilda, who represents the "Active Life."</meta>

# CANTO XXVIII. 219

->A lady all alone who went along<-
->singing and choosing flower from flower,<-
->with which all her path was painted.<-

She moves in such virtuous acts that she not only overcomes every vice but even forgets it. And nevertheless, although the poet could not yet "pass over"—that is, operate in virtuous actions for the reasons stated—nonetheless his eyes "passed over" with their sight, because he could begin to consider what those actions might be.

And not without reason did he see a variety of fresh blossoms. This is because the <term>active life</term> <note>The 'active life' refers to the medieval Christian ideal of serving God through good works and social responsibility, rather than through quiet meditation alone.</note> involves various and diverse actions that draw the soul in many directions. Thus the Gospel, which the author here attributes to Matthew <note>original: "matheo"; the quote is actually from Luke 10:41</note> regarding this active life, says: **"Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things."** <note>original: "Martha Martha sollicita es & turbaris erga plurima"</note> AND THERE, that is, on the other side of the river, there appeared to me a lady in that form which usually appears when something happens suddenly: something that brings such great wonder that it diverts every other thought from our mind. This lady went along alone, singing through a path full of flowers, and she chose flower from flower. By this lady, the poet understands the **Active Life**, and he calls her **Matilda**. She is named after the Countess Matilda <note>Matilda of Canossa (c. 1046–1115) was a powerful Italian noblewoman and a key supporter of the Papacy.</note>, a woman of the highest nobility and the greatest virtue in administration. She was the daughter of Beatrice. This Beatrice was the daughter of the Emperor of Constantinople <margin>T</margin>; she was captured by the love of an Italian lord of the House of Canossa and followed him to Italy secretly from her father. But finally, the Emperor endowed her with many lands in Italy, especially the "Patrimony." From them was born Matilda, a woman of most honest character, great spirit, and prudence in administering her lordship, and of the highest piety. For this reason, she gave great help to the Pope against the Emperor. She endowed many churches, and especially the Cathedral of Pisa, near which she was buried in the year 1060 <note>Landino’s date here is historically debated; Matilda actually died in 1115.</note> in the tomb of Beatrice, her mother. She built many churches and finally offered her lordship, which today is called the Patrimony <note>The "Patrimony of St. Peter" refers to the land holdings of the Catholic Church.</note>, to the Church of St. Peter in Rome. Therefore, just as our poet at the beginning of *Purgatorio* placed Cato as a man most loving of liberty, so at this beginning of the "Paradise of Delights" (Eden), in which he establishes the active life, he imagines finding Matilda: she who joined civic virtues with true Christian religion. He depicts her as being "alone," not because the active life is lived in solitude, but to demonstrate that even in this life there is <margin>X</margin> a need for constant meditation. And "singing": this demonstrates the eloquence with which the wise persuade others to good works and dissuade those they govern from evil ones. AND "choosing flower from flower": among the many actions that come with the active life, she chooses those which possess the most virtue.

->“O lovely lady, who with love’s own rays<-
->are warmed, if I am to believe your looks,<-
->which usually are witnesses of the heart,<-
->May the will come to you to draw forward,”<-
->I said to her, “toward this river bank,<-
->so far that I may understand what you sing.<-
->You make me remember where and what<-
->Proserpina was at the time she lost<-
->her mother, and she her springtime.”<-
->As a lady who dances turns around<-
->with feet close to the ground and to each other,<-
->and hardly places foot before foot,<-
->She turned upon the vermilion and upon the yellow<-
->little flowers toward me, not otherwise<-
->than a virgin who lowers her modest eyes;<-
->And she made my prayers satisfied,<-
->drawing so near that the sweet sound<-
->came to me with its meanings.<-

**O LOVELY lady.** These are the words that Dante used toward the lady to persuade her to approach the river so that he could understand what she was singing. He seeks her goodwill by using the word "O" and calling her "lovely." And certainly, civic actions performed with virtue are beautiful. He adds: **Who [warmed by love's rays]**. It could not be otherwise. Because the active life takes on many tasks for the homeland, for relatives, for friends, and finally for all men; and no one would want to weary themselves for others if they were not warmed by the fire and rays of love and charity. **"For charity seeks not its own."** <note>original: "Caritas enim non quaerit quae sua sunt"; from 1 Corinthians 13:5</note> **IF I AM to believe your looks**: Dante could not know if this lady was truly inflamed by the flames of love, having only just seen her. But he judged her by her "looks"—that is, by certain acts and gestures which bore the sign and likeness of love. And these gestures are most often certain and undoubted signs of the soul. **MAY THE WILL [come to you]**: He places his request, which is that she approach the bank of the river so that he can understand what she sings. **YOU make me remember where Proserpina was first**: The abduction of Proserpina <note>Proserpina (Persephone) was the daughter of Ceres; she was abducted by Pluto (Hades) while picking flowers in Sicily.</note> has already been described by us; she was in a most pleasant meadow in Sicily, adorned with herbs and flowers, when she was snatched by Pluto and taken to Hell, such that her mother lost her, and she lost the flowers of "springtime." He shows, therefore, that the meadow where Matilda was is similar to the one Ovid describes where Proserpina was abducted. **AS a lady turns**. He shows that she turns with her feet close to the ground and to each other, because a lady hardly lifts her foot from the ground and hardly moves from the spot when she dances. **VERMILION and yellow**: He mentions the colors of the flowers—vermilion to denote that virtuous acts in the active life must be full of fire (meaning charity), which the color vermilion signifies; and pure from every stain of vice, which is signified by yellow, the color of the purest gold metal. **AND she made my prayers satisfied**: because she approached so near that I not only heard the sound of the words, but I perceived their meaning.

She came right to the river with her eyes downcast, not looking at Dante. But having reached the bank, she raised them and looked at him. He imagines this because the doctrine of which we have already spoken does not shine in our soul until it is near the river Lethe <note>In the Earthly Paradise, the river Lethe washes away the memory of sin.</note>—that is, within the virtues of a soul already purified.
