# CANTO XXVIII. 220

He made man good, and for good, and this place
He gave to him as a pledge of eternal peace.
By his own fault he stayed here but a little while;
By his own fault, for weeping and for toil
He traded honest laughter and sweet play.
So that the disturbances which occur below—
The exhalations of the water and the earth
Which follow after heat as much as they are able—
Should not wage any war against man,
This mountain rose toward heaven so high
That it is free from them from where it is locked.

<note>original: "fe lhuomo bono abene..." This passage explains that God created humanity for a good purpose and intended the Garden of Eden as a foretaste of Heaven.</note>

They are in the third region <note>In medieval meteorology, the 'third region' of the air was the highest layer, believed to be above all weather and terrestrial disturbances.</note> which such vapors cannot pass through. Therefore, there can be no winds, rains, snow, hail, or lightning there. And allegorically, it demonstrates that those who dwell in the purgatorial virtues and in those of the already-purified soul feel no mental perturbation. THE SUPREME GOOD, which is God. WHO ONLY PLEASES HIMSELF: God alone, through Himself and not through any external thing, finds pleasure in Himself. The intention of the author <unclear>illegible</unclear> is that man, in the virtues of the already-purified soul, exercises himself in the active life according to our religion; and afterward in the contemplative life, hearing from Matelda (that is, from sacred theologians) that doctrine which is necessary for our salvation. And for this reason, he introduces her to teach him what the beginning of the human race was, and for what end man was produced, and in what place he was put; and how, for not being obedient, he was cast out; and afterward she will narrate the predictions—through figures—of his salvation made in the Old Testament, and afterward the coming of Christ, his salvation. And how through that we are led back to His obedience and finally to salvation, returning to innocence.

HE MADE MAN GOOD. Because every vice that is born in him is not from God, but from his own choice. TO GOOD: to the end that he might possess Him, who is the Supreme Good. AND THIS PLACE: that is, the Earthly Paradise. AS A PLEDGE OF ETERNAL PEACE. God intended that man in a state of innocence should inhabit this place for as long as it pleased God; and afterward, He wished to lead him to Heaven. Therefore, it was a pledge of eternal peace: that is, of Heaven, where there is supreme beatitude. BY HIS OWN FAULT: through his defect, a word derived from "to undo" <note>original: "diffalta... decto da diffare." The commentator links 'fault' or 'default' to the idea of 'un-making' or failing to act.</note>. Because he who sins does not "do." And sin is nothing other than the privation of good. Therefore, he "un-does" and does not "do." HE STAYED HERE BUT A LITTLE WHILE. They say that the first man was created in Damascus and from there translated into the Paradise of Delights at the hour of Tierce <note>Tierce is roughly 9:00 AM.</note>. And there He gave him the precepts he was to observe; and He presented all the beasts to him, and Adam gave them their names. Afterward, He put him to sleep and formed the woman from his rib; and afterward the serpent came and tempted Eve, and after the hour of Nones <note>Nones is roughly 3:00 PM.</note> they ate the forbidden fruit; and immediately the angel came and drove them out and put them into this world full of bitterness. From which it is gathered that he did not stay even three hours in Paradise.

SO THAT THE DISTURBANCES. He showed first how man was put in Paradise. Now he shows why such a place was more eminent above the earth than others. And he says that this mountain rose—that is, it raised and exalted itself—toward heaven so much that it is free from the exhalations and terrestrial vapors raised by the heat of the sun, so they would not wage any war against man by bringing winds, rains, hail, snow, and the like. But allegorically, it shows that he who is elevated from the earth—that is, from the thoughts of earthly things—and has pulled up his sensuality and made it obedient to reason and united with it in such a form that the flesh does not fight against the spirit, has a tranquil soul, outside the winds of appetite and the waters of sadness and every other perturbation.

<gloss>He has shown that Statius did not lie to Dante when he told him that this mountain was free from the previously mentioned alterations.</gloss> Now he demonstrates that, notwithstanding this, there is nevertheless a wind here that moves the leaves, which is born because the "first turn"—that is, the Primum Mobile, which in twenty-four hours turns from East to West and from there returns to the East—moves the air in the same circuit. And from this motion the wind is born, which can move the leaves; and he calls it "living air," that which is above the third region. AND THE STRUCK PLANT: that is, the tree struck by such a wind impregnates the air with its virtue, and the air, spinning, shakes it from itself, whereby it falls upon the "other earth"—that is, in this earth of our hemisphere. And such earth upon which such virtue falls conceives—according to whether it is fertile or by the power of the sky and the stars to which it is subject—and generates such a plant as that virtue desires. Because of this, we should not marvel if any plant is born here without a visible seed—that is, without us seeing it or sowing it—because it is born by the aforementioned virtue. And concluding, the countryside of the Paradise of Delights—which he calls "countryside" because it is level, and it is "holy" because it signifies innocence—is full of every seed. Because of this, it produces every fruit that is found here on our side, and even those that are not "plucked" here, meaning they are not gathered. Because there is the Tree of Life, and he who eats of that fruit does not die.

First, she sang like a lady in love because the true interpreters and doctors of our theology, with great zeal toward their neighbor—whether by preaching or otherwise warning and teaching—continually make us learned. Therefore, "singing like a lady in love," she continues with the end of her words; that is, once she had finished declaring to Dante what had already been said, she began without intermission to sing the psalm whose beginning is: *Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered* <note>original: "Beati quorum remisse sunt iniquitates & quorum tecta sunt peccata"</note>. And by this he demonstrates that little time is spent in the investigation of this doctrine and in the operations of these virtues of the already purified soul, for we are illuminated by the power of divine grace.

as a figure is stamped in wax.

Q Polyclitus <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE, known for his mastery of proportion</note> was the son of Ageladas and from the city of Sicyon, a sculptor much celebrated among the ancients, and especially for a statue which they call the <term>Diadumenos</term> <note>A youth tying a ribbon around his head</note>, valued at one hundred talents. He had a name appropriate to himself, because "Polyclitus" in Greek signifies a man of much fame. BUT NATURE WOULD BE SCORNED; that is, she would remain defeated. We properly say someone "receives scorn" when they presume or trust they will surpass another, but then the opposite happens. And one can speak of "scorn of honor." For just as we say a man "puts out his horns" when he exalts himself through victory and for having achieved what he desired, so by contrast we say one is "shorn of his horns" <note>The commentator plays on the word "scornato" (scorned/de-horned)</note>. THE ANGEL GABRIEL, who came to earth to announce to Mary. WITH THE DECREE: with the determination made by the omnipotent, triune, and unique God: that Mary should conceive by the power of the Holy Spirit the Eternal Word, who was to redeem the human generation. This Incarnation made Jesus our Redeemer and mediator between God and man, and reconciled us with God in a way that we regained peace, which for many years had been mourned; that is, desired with tears by the holy fathers. While they were in life, and after they were suspended in <term>Limbo</term> <note>The place where the righteous souls of the Old Testament waited for Christ</note>, they waited to be freed through the passion of God, which redemption opened the "long prohibition"—that is, it opened it for the human generation, to whom it had been forbidden for so long a time. For from the sin of Adam until Christ's descent into Limbo, five thousand two hundred and thirty-two years passed. BEFORE US IT APPEARED SO LIFELIKE. This is great praise for sculpture: that being before them where nothing should appear but a mute and inanimate image, it nevertheless showed itself speaking with supreme sweetness. And then he says: IT DID NOT SEEM; that is, it did not resemble a silent image, but an image that speaks. And this occurred because the image of the angel seemed to be speaking. And nearby was the image of Mary, and anyone would have sworn the angel said "Hail," as he said when he announced it to her. FOR THERE; because there was depicted that one—the image of Mary—WHO TURNED THE KEYS TO OPEN THE SUPREME LOVE, she who turned the keys to open the supreme love of God, which our sin had shut away from us. For the holiness and humility of Mary was the key that opened divine love to us. And just as the image of the angel was carved so skillfully that it seemed he said "Hail," so that of Mary seemed to consent to the divine command, and with supreme humility said: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord." <note>original: "Ecce ancilla dei"</note> He places here, then, the image of Mary as the singular and first example of humility. Of her, as the "historian of Carthage" <note>Likely referring to Sallust, though the sentiment is a common trope of the time</note> said, it is better to be silent than to say too little.

"Do not keep your mind only on one place," 
said the sweet master <note>Virgil, Dante's guide</note> who had me 
at that side where people have their hearts. 
Wherefore I moved, and with my eyes I saw, 
behind Mary, along that same cliff-side 
where he who was moving me stood, 
another history set into the rock; 
wherefore I passed Virgil and drew near, 
so that it might be laid out before my eyes. 
There, carved into the marble itself, 
was the cart and the oxen drawing the sacred Ark, 
because of which one fears an office not assigned. <note>A reference to Uzzah, who was struck dead for touching the Ark of the Covenant without being a priest</note> 
In front appeared people, and all of them, 
divided into seven choirs, made two of my senses 
say—one "no," the other "yes, they sing."

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

These examples are carved and not painted, because painting is easily removed, but not carving. And they are carved not in soft material, but in hard. This warns us: if we wish to completely drive pride from ourselves, it is necessary that we have humility sculpted and completely fixed in our minds. Furthermore, he uses white marble to denote that such humility must be pure and clean, and not spotted with any fiction or simulation. And as the color white is bright and shining, so should this humility shine. For "nothing is more proud than a feigned humility." <note>original: "nihil e [est] ficta humilitate supbius" (Latin quote from St. Jerome)</note> Furthermore, it shows that such images are so lifelike that not only Polyclitus or any other excellent sculptor, but Nature herself could not make them so realistic. This signifies nothing else but that such humility must be in its own proper image, in a form that neither human wit nor natural movement could make more lifelike.

Having placed the example of the humility of Mary, he places that of David the King. Nor should the admirable wit and absolute learning of the poet be overlooked in this place. He knew that man uses pride in three ways: either toward a superior, or toward an equal, or toward an inferior. Therefore, to these three types of pride, he judged it necessary to oppose three types of humility. Thus, for the example of humility toward a superior, he placed Mary. Toward an equal, David. Toward inferiors, Trajan. Mary humbled herself to God. David used humility with the priests, playing the lyre and dancing with them before the Ark, which humility was among equals. Trajan humbled himself to the widow, who was much inferior to him. But so that the humility of David may be known to us: it is in the Second Book of Kings <note>Known today as 2 Samuel 6</note> that after the death of Saul, a most proud king, David was elected in his place. He gathered all the clergy of Israel to transfer the Ark of the Lord with a most pleasing procession to his city, Zion. The Ark was in Gibeah and in the house of Abinadab, son of Saul. He then placed it on a new cart and accompanied it with a great celebration of sounds. Uzzah <note>original: "Oza"</note> and Ahio, sons of Abinadab, guided the cart. And as the oxen of the cart moved clumsily on the road and stumbled, and because of this the cart moved awkwardly, Uzzah came to the aid of the Ark which was wobbling, and reached out his hand to it...

### CANTO XXX. 275

That is, it never had any covering at all except for the sin that took it away from us; and which made everyone who followed the candlesticks in the earthly paradise <term>wise and instructed</term> <note>original: "accorto & amaeſtrato"; here referring to spiritual readiness and guidance</note>. Just like our own <term>septentrion</term> <note>original: "septentrione"; usually referring to the seven stars of the Big Dipper used for navigation, but here used metaphorically for the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit</note>, which is lower in the sky. **MAKES**: that is, it makes them wise and instructed to take a good journey. **AS**: that is, like anyone who turns the helm to reach port. # PURGATORIO.

The high virtue that had already pierced me
before I was out of my boyhood.
I turned to the left with the respect
with which a little child runs to its mother
when he is afraid or when he is afflicted,
To say to Virgil: "Less than a drop <note>original: "dragma," a small unit of weight, here meaning a tiny amount or drop.</note>
of blood remains in me that does not tremble;
I recognize the signs of the ancient flame."
But Virgil had left us bereft <note>original: "scemi," meaning diminished or emptied of his presence.</note>,
Virgil, sweetest father,
Virgil, to whom I gave myself for my salvation.

...from her <gloss>Beatrice</gloss> he felt again the ancient love. This indicates that from tender years man begins to love Beatrice—that is, the Supreme Good which makes us blessed. But we hardly recognize it then. Later, sensuality and appetite take over, which twist us toward the path of pleasures and the "goods of fortune," which we follow as if they were the supreme good. And in this way, we distance ourselves from Beatrice so that our eyes, guided by appetite, no longer recognize her; because seeing nothing but pleasure, the soul does not believe there is any other good but that. But after we are purged of vices and have come to the state of innocence, <term>prevenient grace</term> <note>Grace that "comes before" human action to predispose a person toward God.</note> breathes in us, which is called "hidden virtue." And this makes us recognize Beatrice, whom we loved from the beginning. And this grace inflames us with her love, she being the Supreme Good. **SOON.** Immediately that through this glory the high virtue—that is, celestial love—which had already pierced me in boyhood, now struck me. And certainly, the love of the true good is innate in men. But false good deceives us, which is why we are divided from it until reason begins to have more power in us than appetite. I turned to the left hand to Virgil, just as a child turns to its mother when afraid or hurt. But turning, I noticed Virgil had already departed from me. And he had left us—me and Statius—diminished, because the Virgilian number <note>The group of three poets: Virgil, Dante, and Statius.</note> was reduced. I say "sweetest father" to whom I had given myself for my salvation; and I wanted to say to him: "Not a drop of blood remains in me that does not tremble for love; and I know it proceeds from love because I recognize the signs of the ancient flame." This sentiment he took from Virgil, where he said: *I recognize the traces of the ancient flame* <note>original Latin: "Agnosco veteris vestigia flammae," from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 4.</note>. **He turned to Virgil.** This denotes that, struck by love, he turned to reason, which is in man to recognize such love and its cause. But Virgil had abandoned him; that is, human reason cannot by itself know the divine without divine grace. But Statius remained; that is, the intellect enlightened by Christian theology. Dante recognized her through prevenient grace.

Not all that our ancient mother <note>Eve.</note> lost
could keep my cheeks, once cleansed with dew,
from turning dark with weeping once again.
"Dante, because Virgil goes away,
do not weep yet, do not weep yet;
for you must weep for another sword."
Like an admiral who, at poop and prow,
comes to see the people who serve
on the other ships and encourages them to do well;
On the left side of the chariot,
when I turned at the sound of my name,
which of necessity is recorded here.
I saw the lady who first appeared to me,
veiled beneath the angelic festival,
directing her eyes toward me from across the stream.
All that veil which fell from her head,
encircled by the leaves of Minerva <note>The olive branch, symbolizing wisdom and peace.</note>,
did not let her appear clearly.

**The loss of Virgil** had such power over me that, although I was in the paradise of delights—which the ancient mother, Eve, the first woman, lost through her disobedience—and had my cheeks cleansed with dew, nevertheless they became dark and mournful and weeping. **ADRE** that is, *atre*; and *ater* in Latin signifies black, and consequently mournful and sad. **DANTE** because seeing Beatrice, and seeing Dante's grief at Virgil's departure, she turned to him with these words: "Dante, do not weep because Virgil goes away. Because you must still weep **FOR a greater sword**," that is, for a greater pain, as we shall see below. **LIKE AN admiral.** An excellent comparison in which he likens theology to the admiral of a fleet. Because just as the admiral, without leaving his own ship, but appearing now at the stern and now at the bow, comforts those on the other ships and encourages them to do well, so Beatrice on the left side of the chariot excited Dante to do what you will hear below. Thus theology, not leaving the chariot—which signifies the body of all Sacred Scripture—and from the left side, which signifies the Old Testament where the prohibitive and punitive doctrine of the Church is. For in the Old Testament, God made manifest and swift vengeance. And Beatrice here threatens Dante. And therefore she was not on the right, which signifies the New Testament, where the exhortative Church and the promiser of eternal life is. Because she does not yet promise him anything, but reproves him. And he turns at the sound of his name to denote that these words were against sensuality, which is signified by "Dante." And therefore he says that "of necessity it is recorded here" <note>Dante famously apologizes for naming himself in the poem, which was against medieval literary etiquette unless necessary.</note>. **I SAW THE lady.** Turning at the sound of the voice, I saw that she who spoke was the lady who had first appeared to me. **Veiled beneath the angelic festival.** Surrounded by the angels, who we said above were singing *Blessed art thou who comes* <note>original Latin: "Benedictus qui venis."</note>. And she directed her eyes to me from this side of the river. **ALL the veil.** We have shown above what the veil and the garland signify. But here he adds that he recognized her notwithstanding that the veil did not let her be seen clearly, to demonstrate that faith does not have [perfect] knowledge.

Regally, in her demeanor still haughty,
she continued like one who speaks...

**Regally:** that is, loftily and imperiously without regard, as kings are accustomed to do. **IN the act** in the sight of flowers. **STILL.** Here it says that although she had to be appeased, yet she was still haughty; that is, proud. **AS...**

<meta>This page continues the scene in the Earthly Paradise where Beatrice rebukes Dante. The commentary is by Cristoforo Landino, a famous Renaissance scholar, whose explanations help the reader understand the complex allegories of the poem.</meta>

# PURGATORY.

->Thus I was without tears and sighs<-
->before the singing of those who always tune<-
->their notes to the eternal spheres.<-
->But when I understood in their sweet melodies<-
->their compassion for me, more than if they had said<-
->"Lady, why do you so undo him?"<-
->The ice that was bound around my heart<-
->became breath and water, and with anguish<-
->through my mouth and eyes issued from my breast.<-

**[Right column commentary]**
...vegetative <note>The "vegetative soul" was a medieval psychological term for the basic life force shared with plants.</note> through which they are nourished by the moisture of the earth, sucking it up with their roots. **BY THE BACK OF ITALY.** He means the Apennine mountain range, which, as we said above, rises through the middle of Italy just as the back and spine extend through the middle of animals. **BY THE SLAVIC WINDS.** By northern winds, which he calls "Slavic" because Slavonia <note>Modern-day Croatia/the Balkans.</note> is to our north. **THEN LIQUEFIED.** **TRICKLES** <note>original: "trapela"</note> means it distills or drips. "To trickle" is when liquid drips out of a container that is not well-sealed. **AS LONG AS THE LAND THAT LOSES SHADOW.** This refers to the southern region near the equator where the sun casts very little shadow. **BREATHES** means to make wind. Just as the northern winds create ice and cold, those from the south are mild and melt it. **THUS WAS I WITHOUT TEARS AND SIGHS.** Because fear had chilled me, and the cold had so locked my pores that neither tears nor sighs could escape. **WHO ALWAYS TUNE THEIR NOTES TO THE ETERNAL SPHERES.** Just as a good musician follows the notes written in a book, the angels—by observing the influences and effects that proceed from the perpetual movements of the heavens—sing what they see marked in the fated order of divine providence. We have spoken of this before and will again. **BUT WHEN I UNDERSTOOD IN THEIR SWEET MELODIES**, that is, in the sweet song composed of various voices. **THEIR COMPASSION.** That is, they had pity on me, which I understood more through the singing of that psalm than if they had said to Beatrice, "Why do you distress him so?" And certainly, the office of <term>Theology</term> <note>Beatrice represents Divine Revelation or Theology in the poem.</note> is to rebuke sins with bitterness. But divine intelligences have compassion for the contrite and humbled heart, which God will not despise. **THE ICE THAT WAS BOUND AROUND MY HEART.** Fear, because the blood retreating to the heart induces a chill, and the cold of fear condenses. Afterward, the force of the warmth [of compassion] thaws the frozen thing and liquefies it, distilling it into tears through the eyes and sighs through the mouth; and this is why he says **BREATH AND WATER**, meaning sighs (which are nothing but wind) and water (tears). In short, he shows that after penance and purification, remembering how much the sacred scriptures threaten those who abandon them after starting to follow them, he nearly fell into despair; but the angels—representing divine grace—comforted him and brought him back to hope.

->She, still standing firm upon the right side<-
->of the chariot, then directed her words<-
->to those pious substances:<-
->"You watch in the eternal day<-
->so that neither death nor sleep steals from you<-
->one step that the world takes on its paths.<-
->Therefore my answer is with greater care<-
->so that he who weeps on the other side may understand me,<-
->so that fault and grief may be of one measure."<-

**[Right column commentary continued]**
**She, still standing.** This shows that she still persevered in her rebuke. **DIRECTED HER WORDS TO THE SUBSTANCES**, meaning the **PIOUS** angels, because in their song they had shown compassion to Dante. Here the poet uses a wonderful device. Since the angels had sung a psalm showing that mercy should be had toward Dante, it seemed reasonable for Beatrice to respond and give the reason why she continued her harshness. Her goal was not to harm him, but to help him by leading him to a contrition that was equal to his sin. On the other hand, it seemed unnecessary to explain this to the angels, since they already know all things. Therefore, the poet chose a middle path: she does not appear to be teaching the angels, but rather responding to their psalm and song, so that Dante might understand what he needed to do. **YOU WATCH IN THE ETERNAL DAY.** This is nothing other than contemplating all things as they are understood in God, as if in a most pure mirror and clearest light without any darkness. For God is the true light that illuminates the whole world, a light without end; therefore it can truly be called eternal. **SO THAT NEITHER NIGHT NOR SLEEP STEALS FROM YOU**, because you always contemplate that light in which all things are seen. Therefore, neither **NIGHT** (ignorance) nor **SLEEP** (laziness or bodily desire) takes any **STEP** (action or progress) from you that the **WORLD** (time) takes. **ON ITS PATHS**, meaning through its extensions and progress. No ignorance or earthly desire falls upon the angels as it does upon us, who are weighed down by sin and sensuality. But always contemplating God, they see all things in Him. **WORLD** <note>original: "seculo"</note> among the Latins most often refers to a space of a hundred years (hence the "secular games" <note>original: "sacri seculari"</note> of Apollo celebrated once a century). But in Holy Scripture, it signifies time, and time is born from the eternity of God, proceeding step by step from moment to moment. **THEREFORE MY ANSWER IS WITH GREATER CARE.** She says this as if to say: "You do not need an answer, but I have directed my words to you out of respect for the psalm you sang, so that he [Dante] understands through my careful response the danger he is in, unless he learns that the grief and contrition of the sinner must be as great as the fault committed."

->Not only by the operation of the great wheels<-
->which direct every seed to some end<-
->according to the stars that accompany them,<-
->but by the bounty of divine graces...<-

**[Bottom right commentary]**
**NOT ONLY BY THE OPERATION.** The poet grants that although all human souls are by nature similar and equal, the influences of the heavens (the "great wheels") have much power over the bodies to which the souls are joined. These influences affect the talents and abilities of men. But beyond these celestial influences, much is achieved by **GRACE**...

<summary>Dante describes his emotional breakthrough from frozen fear to weeping, prompted by the angels' compassion. Beatrice explains to the angels that her harshness is necessary to ensure Dante's repentance matches his sins.</summary>
<keywords>Beatrice, angels, contrition, divine grace, celestial influence, Apennines, Scholasticism, Landino commentary</keywords>

# CANTO XXIX 227
<note>While the header says Canto XXIX, the text actually contains the famous rebuke from Purgatorio, Canto XXX.</note>

[Left Column]

...that such high vapors then bring rain,
which our sights do not approach.
This man was such in his **new life**
potentially, that every right habit
would have made a marvelous proof in him.
But all the more malignant and wild
does the ground become with bad seed, uncultivated,
the more it has good earthly vigor.
For some time I sustained him with my face,
showing my youthful eyes to him;
with me I led him, turned in the right direction.

[Right Column]

...given by divine clemency; and concludes that Dante had favor from both the stars and from divine grace, in such a form that he could have made a marvelous proof <note>original: "pua" / "proua"</note> if he had followed the love of Beatrice, that is, the study of sacred letters. But as the bad seed becomes much more malignant in fertile ground than in sterile ground, so vice becomes greater in a sharp intellect than in a dull one. **NOT** only through the work of the **great wheels** <term>great wheels: the rotating celestial spheres that influence human temperament</term>, that is, through the revolutions of the heavens and the planets. The **Primum Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: the "First Mover," the outermost sphere of the universe in medieval cosmology</term> finishes its circuit in twenty-four hours, and draws with it all the heavens that are contained and included within it. But to report on the celestial motions would be too tedious at present; and in many places in this work a good part of them have been, if not clearly shown, at least not entirely obscurely hinted at. And if I do not err, the highest wisdom is observed here, just as elsewhere the poet concedes to the celestial flows as much as does not forbid our redemption and as much as is in truth; and nevertheless he does not take away, but rather affirms, the freedom of our...

[Full Width Commentary]

...**will** <note>original: "arbitrio"</note> and the help of divine grace. Beatrice concludes that none of these things were lacking to Dante, but his own incorrect will had distracted him for some time from the true way, along which he had proceeded from the beginning until a certain point. These wheels and revolutions direct every seed to a certain end. These rotations and revolutions make every seed that has generative power reach an effect which is the end of the thing, according to how the stars are companions—that is, according to various conjunctions of various planets; because the conjunction of Mars and Venus produces one effect, and that of Venus and Jupiter another. But by the **abundance of divine graces**, she shows that although the celestial influences can do much, nevertheless divine graces can, without comparison, do much more. "That such high vapors then bring rain": he uses an excellent metaphor, and the meaning is that just as copious rain descends when cold and humid vapors in the appropriate region are converted into water, so divine grace rains down abundantly. "Which our sights do not approach": because human sight and intellect cannot bring their knowledge close enough to understand the greatness of divine graces. **This man**: this Dante. **In his new life**: in his first age, potentially—that is, he had a natural disposition and aptitude such that if he had formed a **right habit**—that is, a virtuous one in the speculative virtues—such a habit would have made a marvelous proof. But all the more: in this metaphor, he uses the ground to represent the aforementioned aptitude, and the bad seed for the habitual vice. He says that just as bad seed, if it is not gathered before it falls to the earth, multiplies more in fertile ground than in sterile ground, so the seed of vice multiplies more in a great and sharp intellect than in a low, small, and dull one. **For some time I sustained him with my face**: I, by showing him my beautiful face and lovely eyes—which signifies that he was in love with the bark and surface of theology without tasting the marrow—for some time he followed the studies which led him in the right direction, that is, toward the virtues.

[Bottom Left Column]

As soon as I was upon the threshold
of my second age, and I changed my life,
this man took himself from me and gave himself to others.
When I had risen from flesh to spirit,
and beauty and virtue had increased in me,
I was less dear and less pleasing to him;
And he turned his steps along a way not true,
following **false images of good**,
which pay back no promise in full.
Nor did it help me to obtain inspirations,
with which, both in dreams and otherwise,
I called him back; so little did he care for them!
He fell so low that all arguments
for his salvation were now short,
except for showing him the **lost people**.
For this I visited the gate of the dead,
and to him who has led him up here,
my prayers were offered with weeping.

[Bottom Right Column]

**As soon as I was upon the threshold of my second age.** <margin>H</margin> There are two theological ages: the youthful and the mature. For we attend to theology in two ways: either according to the letter and morality, which serves the active and civil life—and this is the "new" or youthful age, and it is said that Beatrice (theology) is "in the flesh"; or truly we interpret the sacred letters allegorically and anagogically <term>anagogical: the deepest spiritual or mystical level of biblical interpretation</term>. This serves the contemplative life; it is the "second" and mature age of Beatrice, in which she is "without flesh," because she deals with incorporeal and eternal things—that is, she treats of God himself, who is entirely unknown to human sense and only comprehensible to the intellect in the smallest part. Therefore, "as soon as I was on the threshold of my second age," as we have explained above. **This man took himself from me**: because he left the studies of theology and **gave himself to others**, following other studies. **When I had risen to spirit from flesh**: I had turned from carnal to spiritual, and beauty and virtue increased because the allegorical sense is more beautiful and contains more virtue of intellect. **And he turned his steps**: he turned his affections. **Along a way not true**: along the left-hand path of vices. **Following false images of good**: he did not follow the virtues of the soul, which are the true good, but sought wealth, dignity, offices, and power; these are called "goods of fortune," and they are not true goods but only appear so because they have a false image of the true good; and they do not fulfill any promise because they promise true peace of mind and then do not give it. <margin>I</margin> **Nor did it help me to obtain inspirations**: an inspiration is a sudden and ardent will for virtue...

[Bottom Line]

### Commentary Column

The confusion and shame of the error committed and the fear of punishment pushed a "Yes" out of my mouth—that is, they forced me to confess. But my strength was so weakened that the sound could not be understood. But it was known by looking at my face. **As a crossbow:** as it often happens that pulling the crossbow too much breaks the string and the bow. Therefore, the bolt <note>The "asta" or "ghiera"</note> comes out with less force, wherefore its strike is almost in vain. So the poet broke under such spiritual disturbance, wherefore in pouring out tears and sighs, the voice slackened. **Wherefore she to me:** FOLLOWING this, Beatrice asks Dante: what trenches or what chains did you find? In my desires—that is, while you loved me: what desires led you to love the highest good? In short, while you were loving me and directed toward the highest good, what impeded you from passing forward and made you lose all hope? **Beyond which there is nothing to aspire to.** Because the highest good is God, and our ultimate end. For which pursuit we do all other things; and beyond Him there is nothing to aspire to, because after Him there is nothing. **And what attractions.** The meaning is: what induced you to leave me? Tell me if there were impediments you found on the path along which I was leading you, or indeed attractions and gains that the others whom you loved (leaving me) showed you on their "forehead"—that is, at first sight—for which you should stroll before them—that is, proceed forward and not depart from them. And she wants to conclude that everything else he has loved was unable to show him anything truly useful or honorable, but it only appeared so to his appetite.

The first tercet is easily understood with the explanations made above. **Weeping I said the present things.** He responds to Beatrice's question, saying that the cause that led him to love others was that as soon as her face was hidden from him, "present things" <note>Worldly distractions</note> turned him toward them by showing him "false pleasures," which is true. For as soon as we put into oblivion sacred letters and moral precepts by which we are directed toward honor, immediately the appetite turns to worldly things and, intoxicated by their pleasures, estimates nothing else to be good. **And she: "if you were silent or denied."** The author shows in this place that in divine judgment the confession of the sinner is not required so that the judge may be better instructed of the truth, because nothing is hidden from him; whether you deny or are silent, everything is known to God. But it is so that the sinner may humble himself and repent of the error. When he does this, he mitigates God's anger, just as the wheel <note>A grindstone</note> that sharpens iron: if it turns against the edge, it makes it thicker <note>meaning it blunts the sharpness of the punishment</note>.

**Nevertheless** <note>original: "Tuttavia"</note> sometimes means "always," sometimes "nonetheless." **So that you may bear shame:** so that you may more willingly feel shame; and so that another time you may be stronger against the "sirens" when you hear them—that is, against worldly pleasures. Through these, the sirens are described allegorically, which we have described extensively in this same canticle. **Lay down the seed of weeping:** put down the tears which weeping produces, just as every herb produces its seed, remembering the Psalm: "He who sows in tears..." <note>original: "qui seminat i lachrymis" from Psalm 126:5</note>. **And you shall hear:** and you shall understand how my buried flesh should have moved you in the opposite direction. As if to say: I will show you that my death should not have been the reason for you to follow others, but rather it should have moved you toward the...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, specifically Canto XXXII. The text focuses on the transition of the divine procession toward the Tree of Knowledge and the symbolic blinding of the pilgrim by Beatrice’s presence.</meta>

# LXXX PURGATORY

->This chapter discusses the Gryphon’s journey to the Tree of Knowledge. It represents the entire primitive Church. It describes how the Gryphon led the chariot back with all those who followed him, how the plant turned green with leaves again, and how Dante fell asleep and had a vision. Upon waking, he asks Matelda about Beatrice; she points her out to him and tells him to pay attention to the things that are about to happen.<-

**To long for:** to satisfy a longing, that is, a desire. *Brama* [longing] is a great desire for something; hence, to long for is to desire supremely. **Ten-year thirst:** a greed lasting ten years. <note>original: "decenne sete"</note> This implies that after he gained knowledge of the literal and moral sense of sacred letters—after which he abandoned those studies until he returned to gain an allegorical and spiritual understanding—ten years had passed in between. Therefore, he says he stayed ten years without Beatrice. **Because the other senses were extinguished:** I was so intent on seeing her that my other senses were extinguished and lulled to sleep. This signifies that he was so devoted to these studies that his mind was turned to nothing else. This happens naturally, as this same poet demonstrated above: when we are entirely turned toward one thing, all the other powers of the soul cease except the one we are exercising. **And they had on this side and that a wall:** his eyes were directed and fixed on Beatrice. **A wall:** that is, a barrier and obstacle on this side, namely the right and the left. Thus he demonstrates his constancy and perseverance in contemplation, such that neither prosperity (signified by the right hand) nor adversity (signified by the left) could remove him, because on the right he applied temperance, and on the left, fortitude. **To not care:** <note>original: "di non calere"</note> to not be concerned. This is a Tuscan verb and is only used impersonally, as in "I do not care for you." **In such a way her smile:** he provides the reason and says his eyes cared for nothing else, for in such a way her smile drew them to Beatrice. **With the ancient net:** with the ancient love, which captures the mind just as a net captures birds. **When by force my face was turned away from those goddesses:** that is, by the four Cardinal Virtues toward my left. And they turned it with words, which I saw them say, which were: "A gaze too fixed." <note>original: "troppo fiso"</note> He turned to the left where the Moral Virtues were. These goddesses made him turn his eyes away from Beatrice toward another part because he was looking too intently. For the Moral Virtues—and especially Temperance, advised by Prudence—demonstrate to us that we must do everything with moderation and measure. Hence the proverb of the learned: **nothing in excess** <note>original: "ne quid nimis"</note>. And Juvenal said: *the wise man imposes a limit even on honorable things.* <note>original: "imponit que modum sapiens & rebus honestis"</note>

# CANTO XXXII 231

[Left Column]

The beautiful lady who drew me to the crossing <note>Matilda, who represents the active life of the soul</note>
and Statius and I followed the wheel

the fault of her who believed the serpent—

Perhaps in three flights an arrow,
released from the bow, would have covered as much distance
as we had moved when Beatrice descended.
I heard everyone murmur "Adam";
then they circled a plant stripped
of flowers and other foliage on every branch.
Its crown, which spreads wider
the higher it rises, would be marveled at
for its height even by the Indians in their forests.

And Christian doctrine demonstrates the excellence of the Trinity in one God. **Adam**: they lamented the disobedience of Adam, through which the human race remained deprived of such a pleasant and joyous place. **A plant**: this is the tree of knowledge, which also represents obedience; by not observing this obedience, Adam contracted original sin, which took this paradise from us. **Its crown, which spreads wider**: This shows that the form of this tree was such that the higher the branches were, the more they spread out, which is the opposite of other trees. Additionally, this tree was so tall in form that even if it had been in the forests of India, where trees are tallest, its height would have seemed miraculous. It is reasonable that the tree of science <note>knowledge</note> should be the highest, because it proceeds step by step until the knowledge of God; and the higher it rises, the more it spreads and expands its branches, because the more we understand, the more remains for us to see. And this same tree also figures holy obedience, which is founded in humility, rises to God, and extends through infinite virtues.

"Blessed are you, Griffin <note>The Griffin represents Christ, having two natures: divine (eagle) and human (lion)</note>, who does not tear
with your beak from this wood, sweet to the taste,
since the belly is afterward twisted with pain."
Thus around the robust tree
cried the others; and the animal of two natures said:
"Thus is preserved the seed of all justice."
And turning to the pole that he had pulled,
he dragged it to the foot of the widowed branch,
and what came from the tree he left bound to it.

**Figures** <note>Interpretive explanation</note> that the pole <note>The pole of the chariot, representing the Cross</note> was made of the wood of obedience, because obedience is what guides and conducts the Church, and is linked with obedience. Therefore, the Griffin pulled the pole to the foot of the widowed branch. **Widowed**: deprived of leaves, and a "widow" because it was abandoned by the first man, who was disobedient to God.

As our plants, when the great light
falls down mixed with that
which shines behind the celestial carp <note>The constellation of Pisces; Dante refers to the sun entering Aries in springtime</note>,
swell up, and then each is renewed
with its own color, before the sun
joins its steeds under another star;
less than roses and more than violets,
the plant took on a new color,
which before had its branches so bare.

[Right Column]

**U**pon the Griffin turning the chariot—as said above—to the right hand, to assist with the synagogue of the Old Testament <note>The "Old Law"</note> denoted by the left wheel, he turned toward the Christian Church denoted by the right. Therefore, **the beautiful lady who was Matilda**: who drew me through the river Lethe to the crossing where I passed; and I and Statius followed the wheel, going behind the right wheel which made its orbit, its way, with an orbit—because in Latin *orbita* <note>original: "orbita"</note> signifies the path made by a wheel. **With a smaller arc**: with a smaller curve, referring to the right wheel. Since the chariot has two wheels, it must make two paths, and when it turns while moving, those paths remain curved in the shape of an arc, and the arc of the wheel on which the chariot turns is always smaller; therefore, turning to the right, the right wheel made a smaller arc. **The high empty forest**: the paradise of delights is empty because of the sin of the first man. **Through the fault of her who believed the serpent**: through the fault of Eve. **Perhaps in three flights**: perhaps as far as an arrow goes in three flights, that is, in three shots. And he said "three flights" because of the speed of the arrow and also because it has feathers. **Unbridled** <note>original: "diffrenata"</note>: as if exited from the string which acts as its brake; and the meaning is that they had already gone three arrow-shots when Beatrice descended. And he posits "three flights" because this number, as the Pythagoreans demonstrate, is perfect.

The first three heads were horned like oxen,
but the other four had a single horn upon their forehead;
a monster like this was never seen before.
Secure as a fortress on a high mountain,
there appeared to me, sitting upon it, a loose harlot
with eyes roving and ready.
And, as if so she might not be taken from him,
I saw a giant standing upright beside her,
and they kissed each other from time to time.
But because her greedy and wandering eye
turned toward me, that fierce lover
scourged her from her head down to her feet.
Then, full of contempt and cruel with anger,
he untied the monster and dragged it through the woods,
until the woods alone acted as a shield
between me and the harlot and the new beast.

<note>Dante uses this grotesque imagery to symbolize the corruption of the Papacy. The "harlot" represents the corrupted Church (specifically the Roman Curia), and the "giant" represents the French Monarchy (King Philip the Fair), who dominated the Papacy at this time.</note>

**[Commentary:]**
The sacraments are those administered by the prelates who are at the helm, that is, the government of the Church: which are Chrism <note>anointing oil</note>, Baptism, and Penance; and the other four [heads] he places at each of the four corners of the chariot. Return, then, to the place already mentioned in the Inferno, and you will have the full allegory of this chariot thus transformed. Now he adds the harlot and the giant, her lover. By the harlot, he means the Church and the Supreme Pontiff, specifically Boniface VIII; and by the giant, the King of France. Because the Church, which with the highest chastity should love her spouse Christ and never depart from spiritual things, became a prostitute; and for the hope of temporal goods, she loved the King of France, whom he calls a giant. Two things are in the giant: first, he is of great stature; second, "giant" signifies one generated from the earth. Similarly, the King of France was of very great power and lordship, and was "produced from the earth" because, scorning spiritual goods, he loved only earthly goods such as empires and riches. There sat, therefore, upon the chariot—that is, in the Apostolic See—a harlot: that is, Pope Boniface, who like a harlot corrupted by money and to acquire treasure, leaving his spouse, was given to the adulterer. **Loose:** free and without any restraint. **With eyes roving and ready:** just as a harlot draws a lover to her with ready and fickle eyes, so Boniface enticed the King with various promises. The giant was near her, fearing she might be taken from him: that is, the King continually maintained the Pope in his friendship through legates and orators, so that he would not turn elsewhere. **And they kissed each other from time to time:** by the "kisses," understand the affectionate offers and presents and gifts that they made to one another. But because this harlot turned her eyes toward me, the giant became jealous. The King saw Boniface was a vehement, eloquent man, and most greedy for honor; he was negotiating with various lords. For this reason, the King did not stop until he moved the Court to Provence <note>the Avignon Papacy</note> beyond the Alps. And therefore he says that the giant untied the chariot, which is the Church, and pulled it so far through the woods that the distance alone—that is, the terrain of the woods—became a shield between me and her: that is, it was an obstacle so that I could not see her. And he puts himself in the place of the other powers of whom the King was jealous, lest they take the Pope from him. **TO the harlot:** that is, to the Pope. **AND TO the new beast:** that is, to the Church which has become a new wild animal.

**CANTO XXXIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE**

This is the thirty-third and last canto, in which the poet, wishing now to exit Purgatory, follows the description already begun and demonstrates how, through the persecutions and transformations of the chariot and the helm—that is, of the Church and the prelates—the Virtues grieved. And Beatrice exhorted him to follow her and ask her about the doubts he had; and she absolves them, demonstrating that he who harms the Church shall be punished, and soon. Dante raises doubts and excuses his lowly wit, which Beatrice excuses by showing it to be sufficient now. Beginning, he shows that because of the disturbance of the chariot, the three Theological and the four Cardinal Virtues grieved and with sweet psalmody—that is, sweet song, and as if moved to mercy—they said: *Deus venerunt gentes in hereditatem tuam* <note>original Latin: "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance," from Psalm 79</note>. In this psalm, David laments the destruction that was to come to the Temple of God. This demonstrated that the enemies of the Church would use cruelty against her; and Beatrice, with tears and a piteous face, listened, her countenance changed almost as Mary’s was at the Cross.

*Deus venerunt gentes* <note>Latin: O God, the nations have come</note>
alternating,

she responded, colored like fire:
*Modicum, et iam non videbitis me; et iterum* <note>Latin: "A little while, and you will not see me; and again..." (John 16:16)</note> my beloved sisters.

For thirty-one <note>The text likely refers to the years of Christ's life or a specific theological calculation.</note> from the beginning of the world until the tenth, he says more than five thousand years <note>Medieval theologians often calculated the time from Adam to Christ as approximately 5,200 years.</note> he longed for the coming of Christ: who punished in himself the bite of Adam: because in restoration of the disobedience of Adam, Christ, God and man, having become obedient against that disobedience, suffered the penalty on the cross: which, as we said above, was made of that wood. **Your intellect sleeps.** If you do not consider that tree to be sublime for a singular reason: **And if they had not been the waters of the Elsa.** That is, if your vain thoughts and worldly things had not hardened your mind like the water of the Elsa—of which we said above that it hardens the things that enter it and turns them to stone: which the inhabitants near this river use in buildings. <note>The Elsa is a river in Tuscany known for its high mineral content, which "petrifies" objects by coating them in calcium carbonate.</note> This same thing happens with the water of the Farno river in Puglia: **And Albertus Magnus** <note>A famous 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> in the *Book of Minerals* <note>original: "libro de metalli"</note> writes that there is a spring in Boeotia which changes whatever is put into it into stone; which from white became black: and we told the fable in the twenty-seventh canto of the first canticle. <note>The myth of Pyramus and Thisbe, where Pyramus's blood stained the white mulberries dark red/purple.</note> **THROUGH SO MANY CIRCUMSTANCES** Beatrice says that if Dante had kept his thoughts fixed on God and they had not been hardened toward worldly things, he would recognize that God, by His justice, forbade man to touch that fruit according to morality, which was demonstrated by the circumstances of the tree: of which the first is that the tree was created by God and blessed so that man would render due worship to God, which is justice. The second is the long deprivation of Adam due to the transgression. The third is the satisfaction made through the passion of Christ.

She wants, then, since at present he cannot understand it for the reasons said above, that he at least carry its meaning in his heart: so that after he has been briefly purged of all vices, repeating it in his mind: listen then, she says, since you have made your intellect of stone—that is, you have made a habit of vice and are tinted in sin—because your mind is infected in such a way that the eye of the intellect, being sick, is dazzled by the splendor of my words, at least carry them with you: if not written, at least "sketched," although writing expresses it more and better than a picture. **For that reason that the staff is carried wreathed in palm:** the meaning is that even if you do not understand my words exactly, still carry away the sum of them so that this may be a sign that you come from me, just as the staff wreathed in palm is a sign that the pilgrim comes from the Holy Sepulcher <note>In Jerusalem.</note> where there is an abundance of palms: and for this reason she gives a precept that, notwithstanding that we have an infected mind such that in studying sacred things we cannot understand them because **"Into a malevolent soul, the spirit of wisdom shall not enter"** <note>original Latin: "In animam maliuolam non introibit spiritus sapientie." ### CANTO ONE 236

[Left Column]

# **THE GLORY**
**of him who**
**moves everything**
**through the universe**
**penetrates and re-**
**flects**
**in one part**
**more, and less**
**elsewhere.**

In the heaven that receives most of his light
was I, and I saw things that to repeat
he who descends from there knows not, nor is able.
Because, as it nears its desire,
our intellect goes so deep
that memory cannot follow after it.
Truly, as much of the holy kingdom
as I could treasure up within my mind
will now be the matter of my song.

[Right Column and Bottom]

[A woodcut illustration depicts the poet Dante looking upward toward a radiant, personified sun representing the Divine. The celestial sphere contains a crescent moon, stars, and various creatures including a lion, a ram, and fish, representing the zodiac and the created order.]

Because, as we have shown in the first canticle <note>The "first canticle" refers to the *Inferno*.</note>, all heroic poets divide their work into three parts: the **proposition**, the **invocation**, and the **narration**. These four tercets <note>A tercet is a poetic unit of three lines.</note> contain the **proposition**, in which the subject matter of the entire work is briefly stated. This subject is the treatment of the celestial kingdom—not according to its true nature (since this transcends our human intellect), but as much as his mind could grasp and, having grasped it, commit to memory. And because the proposition and invocation serve as a <term>proem</term> <note>A proem is a preface or introduction to a literary work.</note>, observe here what is proper to a proem and what its function is. Since we demonstrated this quite adequately at the beginning of the *Inferno*, I will not fatigue myself describing its parts here, but I will explain how the poet observes them at present. 

He captures **attention** by showing he has to speak of a thing so high that all others are far and incomparably inferior to it; for there is no comparison between the infinite and the finite—that is, between God and His creatures. He captures **goodwill** through his own person by showing that his labor in writing will be very useful to others. He captures **docility** <note>In classical rhetoric, "docility" refers to making the audience "teachable" or ready to learn the subject matter.</note> because he briefly demonstrates what he will treat throughout the whole canticle: the eternal kingdom. 

**THE GLORY.** Although "fame" and "glory" seem almost the same to many, nevertheless fame is a widespread report of something, while glory is a clear report of something accompanied by praise. Thus, fame can exist for something that brings neither splendor nor praise with it, but glory cannot exist without those. Therefore, it is defined by Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*: <note>original Latin: "Gloria est consentiens laus bonorum, incorrupta vox bene iudicantium de excellente virtute."</note> "Glory is the consistent praise of good men, the uncorrupted voice of those who judge rightly concerning excellent virtue." From this, it follows that all glory is fame, but not all fame is glory. Glory comes from a glorious work, and the universe is the work of God. 

**Of him who moves all things.** This refers to God. It is a rhetorical figure called <term>circumlocution</term> <note>original: "circuizione." This is the use of many words where fewer would do, often for poetic effect.</note>, which is when that which can be said in one word is said in many. **Moves all things**, whence Boethius says: <note>original Latin: "stabilisque manens das cuncta moveri."</note> "Remaining stable, You grant all things to be moved." He alone, therefore, is stable.

<summary>This page contains the famous opening tercets of Dante's Paradiso and the beginning of Cristoforo Landino's scholarly commentary, which explains the rhetorical structure of the poem's introduction.</summary>

otherwise distorted: because lines will show silver less than tin. Lead will show them confused. The wall will not show any line: but rather a shadow, and that will be distorted or larger or smaller. Nevertheless, all these images are from one and the same example. It is therefore no wonder that God, who is unique, is not the same in all things: because not every subject can receive Him in the same way as the nature of God himself, which is perfect; but rather according to its own nature and according to its capacity for more or less. God is in heaven for greater glory, as David says: *The heavens declare the glory of God* <note>original: "Cæli enarrant gloriam dei"</note> but virtually He is in every place. As Augustine says: *God is whole in heaven; whole on earth; and whole in both* <note>original: "Deus in cælo totus ē: in terra totus: & in utroque totus"</note>; and the Master of Intentions says: *Angels are circumscribed by location: God is uncircumscribed* <note>original: "Angeli circunscripti localiter: Deus incircunscriptus est"</note> but He shines more in heaven. And for this reason, the prophet Isaiah says: *Heaven is my throne: the earth is my footstool.* <note>original: "Cælum mihi sedes est: Terra autem scabellum pedum meorum."</note> IN the heaven that takes more of His light: this is the Empyrean heaven <term>Empyrean: the highest heaven, traditionally thought to be composed of pure light and fire</term> which is of pure light: and therefore it takes more of it than the others which are of light. But we shall say more things about light in a more convenient place. I was there: according to the fiction <note>The word "fiction" here refers to the literary construction or narrative frame of the poem</note> Dante ascended into heaven with his body; according to the allegory, he ascended there with the intellect: because through theological doctrine he reached as far as is permitted to man in the knowledge of divine things. AND I saw things that he who descends from there neither knows how nor is able to retell. Similar to that of Saint Paul: *And I saw things which it is not lawful for a man to speak.* <note>original: "Et uidi ea q̃ nō licet homini loq̃."</note> HE WHO descends from up there. While we are in heaven—that is, in the contemplation of celestial things—we cannot understand anything else; but when we descend to earth, we cannot retell anything. That is, we cannot, upon returning to earthly things, demonstrate the divine within them. Furthermore: while the intellect contemplates God and divine things, the memory fails and cannot retain them. And for this reason, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his eloquence</note> says on the epistle of Paul to the Hebrews: *Just as we understand many things about God that we are not able to speak, so we speak many things that we cannot understand* <note>original: "Sicut multa de deo intelligimus que loqui non ualemus ita multa loquimur que intelligere non possumus"</note>; and certainly we say many things of God which we both understand and do not understand: as for example, although we understand that God is infinite, and consequently He is uncircumscribed and is in every place: nevertheless our intellect cannot be capable of that infinity. Wherefore it can be concluded that we rather hear Him than understand Him, although in some way we do understand Him, but not sufficiently. Because approaching. He assigns the reason why he cannot retell: because the memory does not retain that which the intellect, plunging deep into Him, knew. The intellect, elevated to God, sees; but the memory does not retain it: therefore, the intellect having departed from God, we cannot retell what we saw. Truly as much as I from the holy kingdom: "Kingdom" because there the true King rules. "Holy": because it is consecrated to God; because it is firm, stable, and immobile; and lasts forever. "Holy" signifies a thing consecrated to God and also a thing firm and stable. AS MUCH AS: he does not promise to say absolutely everything: because the human mind cannot comprehend everything: and nevertheless it conceives much more than it can express. But as much as he could make a treasure. That is, to express as much as he committed to memory. They call "treasure" the place where we store our riches. And for this reason, Cicero and many other Latin writers call memory the "treasure-house" <term>Treasure-house: "Thesoro" in the original, a common Renaissance metaphor for the memory as a storehouse of knowledge</term> because that power of the soul has the quality of keeping for us what we have understood or learned.

...in the sun, which is not permitted to us in this state, that is, in the state of sin <note>The commentator explains that while humans are in a fallen state or "state of guilt," they cannot look directly upon the full light of God</note>. **I did not endure it for long, nor for so little.** The meaning of the poet is that once the sun had risen, he began to raise himself toward the heavens, that is, to contemplate. <margin>Z</margin> <note>This margin note likely serves as a reference marker for the definition of contemplation that follows.</note> **Contemplation is the free and clear-sighted gaze of the mind upon the exploration of wisdom, suspended in wonder** <note>original Latin: "Contemplatio est libera mentis perspicatio in sapientiae speculatione cum admiratione suspensa," a definition often attributed to the theologian Hugh of Saint Victor</note>. Nevertheless, he did not endure it for long, because if his eyes—that is, the sharpness of his <term>intellect: the faculty of the soul used for understanding spiritual realities, often described as having its own "sight"</term>—had endured the light for a longer time, he would have been able to discern the entire solar body; that is, he would have had true knowledge of the divine essence. But he did not have such a powerful eye. Nevertheless, for that short time that he did endure it, he saw the sparks and flashes that were born from the solar body, in the same form that they are born from...

And she began: "You make yourself dull <note>The original 'groſſo' literally means 'fat' or 'thick,' but here refers to being intellectually sluggish or thick-witted.</note>

# PARADISE

**V**ou who are in a tiny little
boat,
eager to listen,
following
behind my ship that sails on singing,
Turn back to see your own shores again;
do not trust yourselves to the open sea, for perhaps,
losing me, you would remain lost.
The water I take up has never been sailed before;
Minerva inspires me, and Apollo leads me,
and nine Muses show me the Bears <note>original: "lorse"; referring to the constellations Ursa Major and Minor, used for navigation.</note>:
You other few, who craned your necks
early on for the bread of angels <note>A metaphor for divine wisdom or theology.</note>, upon which
one lives here but is never sated,
You may well set your vessel upon the deep salt sea,
keeping to my furrow
before the water returns to its level.
Those glorious men who crossed to Colchis <note>Referring to the Argonauts, the first sailors in Greek mythology.</note>
were not as amazed as you shall be,
when they saw Jason turned into a plowman <note>An allusion to the myth where Jason had to yoke fire-breathing bulls to plow a field.</note>.

->[Illustration: Two figures in a boat on the water. One figure rows, the other points to the moon, which contains a face. The sky is filled with stars.]<-

The poet has already ascended to the first <term>sphere</term> <note>In the medieval geocentric model, the universe was composed of nested celestial spheres; the first and closest to Earth is the Moon.</note>. FOR WHICH REASON, in this his second canto, he describes how he entered the lunar body; and being asked by Beatrice the cause of the darkness and shadows which appear on the moon, he gives his opinion. BUT Beatrice refutes him and afterwards demonstrates the truth to him. As for this beginning, he admonishes the common crowd—those who are learned only in the minor sciences <note>basic secular education</note> and not learned in sacred things—who have been able to follow him until now: that they should come no further because, not being capable of such high matter, they might become lost, especially because he treats that which has never been treated by anyone else. On the other hand, he encourages those learned in sacred theology, of whom there are few, to follow him, promising them that they will marvel more than the companions of Jason marveled in Colchis. O YOU who are in a tiny little boat. It is a metaphor used by many poets to use the "sea" for the subject matter and the "ship" for the intellect or for learning. Therefore: *O you who are in a little boat*, that is, with little learning or intellect, EAGER to listen to my poem: FOLLOW behind my ship, come behind my style and my teaching. *Which sails on singing*, because every poet is said to "sing." HENCE in the first <term>canticle</term> <note>The *Inferno*.</note> [he said]: *I was a poet and I sang of that just [son of Anchises]* <note>original: "POETA fui & cantai di ql iusto"; a reference to Virgil's Aeneid.</note>. RETURN to see your shores, from which you departed—as if to say, "stay there"—that is, with low subject matter suitable for your weak intellects. DO NOT SET OUT upon the open sea, that is, into such profound and difficult matter, for perhaps, LOSING ME, you will remain lost; just as one who, not knowing the route, follows a guide, and if he loses that guide, he becomes lost. So too, he who follows an author writing of high and difficult things can understand something at the beginning, but when he arrives where he does not understand, it can be said that he has lost the author and remains lost. *Losing me*, losing my method, which is not common among other poets. THE WATER I run was never run before. By a wealth of eloquence, he says now "sea," now "deep," and now "water" for the same thing. And it stands in the metaphor, and the meaning is that the sea he sails was never sailed before—meaning by other poets or other writers. He does not deny that many have written most learnedly of the things he writes about, but no one ever wrote poetically and in an allegorical sense, adorned with poetic faculty, such high matter. *Minerva inspires*. It might have seemed the poet...

CANTO TWO: 240

[He] gave to man a sublime face: and ordered him to gaze at the heavens and to lift his upright countenance toward the stars. <note>original Latin: "Os homini sublime dedit: coelumque tueri iussit: & errectos ad sydera tollere vultus" — a famous quote from Ovid’s Metamorphoses describing the creation of man.</note> **BY time.** As if to say, from your youth, signifying by this the difficulty of divine doctrine: which we cannot well acquire if from our earliest years we do not give ourselves to the study of the liberal arts. **TO the bread of angels.** Just as the body is fed and lives by corporal food: so the intellect is nourished by divine fruit and knowledge: which he calls the "bread of angels": because they enjoy this: and in this alone do they find life. **OF that river.** That is, among us mortals: because the soul, while it is in the body, sustains itself with this doctrine. **BUT one does not come away sated.** Because we cannot have so much knowledge of it that it satiates us and is enough for us on earth. But it is so in heaven. **YOU may well put forth through the deep salt.** That is, through the high sea. That is, you can follow me into this profound subject matter. **KEEPING to the furrow.** He wants them to follow him so closely that the furrow made by his ship does not close up on them: which, once closed, the water returns to being level: for the furrow in the water creates a distinction. He warns those who follow him not to wait until such distinction no longer appears. For when they do not recognize the distinction between the allegorical and literal sense, and between the fictional thing and the truth, they will not be able to understand it. **THOSE glorious ones.** An excellent comparison by which he shows that the Greek Argonauts did not marvel so much when in Colchis they saw Jason become a plowman <note>original: "bifolco"</note> of the teeth of serpents: from which armed men were born: as much as you will marvel at what I shall say: and not without reason, for if that was against nature: this is so hidden in the secrets of nature that it does not seem natural. **GLORIOUS.** Desirous of glory. Or truly glorious: because they held great fame among the Greeks. **AT Colchis.** A city in Pontus where the Golden Fleece was. **PLOWMAN.** <term>Arator</term>: which in Latin is <term>bubulcus</term>. I do not tell this fable at present: because we have told it elsewhere. <margin>1 **To Thirst.** That is, the great desire. **Inborn.** Created together with us.</margin>

->for the god-like kingdom carried us<-
->swiftly, almost as you see the heavens.<-

->and perhaps in as much time as a bolt rests,<-

->"Direct your mind to God in gratitude," she said,<-
->"Who has joined us with the first star."<-

Because God created, together with our soul, a supreme desire in her to go to the Supreme Good: which is God himself. And not only did he create this desire in us: but he created it so that it always lives in our soul perpetually. Therefore he says they were carried by the thirst: the inborn and perpetual one they had. **OF the god-like kingdom.** That is, of blessedness and the Supreme Good: of which God is the form: for the Supreme Good is nothing other than God himself. **Beatrice looked upward.** This sentence is declared above: **and perhaps in as much...** shows that the interval of time was no more than the resting of a "quadrello" <note>A square-headed crossbow bolt.</note> or arrow upon a loaded crossbow: and **released from the notch.** That is, to release the crossbow and the arrow flies to the mark. And it is from the earth <margin>C</margin> to the heaven of the moon, ascending in a straight line, one hundred forty-eight thousand and five hundred forty miles. <note>The commentator is calculating the literal distance to the Moon based on medieval cosmology.</note> **I saw myself arrived.** He saw himself arrived in a marvelous place: and Beatrice, who knew his marvelling: and that he did not understand what place that was: because nothing that was in Dante could be hidden from her: since Theology knows what our already-purified soul desires: said, "Direct your mind in gratitude to God: because he has joined us with the first star." That is, with the Moon: which is the first star and planet above the elements. Nor for any other reason does Beatrice admonish him to direct his mind in gratitude to God for having arrived at the first star, except to show that every good work of ours and every piece of knowledge and intelligence comes from divine help. For which reason we must not glory in ourselves: but give glory to Him and be grateful for the gift received. Furthermore, he said **as glad as she was beautiful.** Theology is always beautiful: because it always tells true things: which are always beautiful. But when it tells of punishments and threats to the sinner, it does not show itself glad: but when it gives us knowledge of celestial things: it always appears beautiful to us and gives us joy.

<margin>d Describes the nature of the lunar body: which is lucid.</margin>
**IT seemed to me that a cloud covered us, dense,** solid and clean. And the moon is seven times larger **lucid, thick, solid and polished.** than the earth. **A lucid, thick cloud appeared the body of the moon.** **Almost like a diamond that the sun might strike.** And here note that some bodies are luminous naturally, like **Within itself the eternal pearl** the sun. Some in part, like a mirror. Some are transparent **received us, as water receives** like glass and water. **ALMOST like a diamond.** Because the lunar body **a ray of light, remaining united.** being by its nature dark, shines when the sun strikes it **If I was a body—and here it is not conceived** as a diamond does. **WITHIN itself the eternal pearl:** he calls **how one dimension could tolerate another,** the moon a pearl: that is, a "perla": and declares the same thing: that is, **which must be if body enters into body—** that the lunar body has no light of its own, but is lucid, that is, a recipient **the desire should more kindle us** of light: as are the diamond and the pearl: which, if they had **to see that Essence in which is seen** their own light, would shine at night. Therefore they have none: but **how our nature was united to God.** are receptive of it. **Received us.** It shows that they entered **There will be seen what we hold by faith,** into the lunar body: which is solid and thick without dividing **not demonstrated, but it shall be known of itself,** it: just as the sun enters water without dividing it. Which naturally **in the manner of the first truth that man believes.** cannot be that a thick and solid body: and that which receives it remain united. And therefore he says that **WHICH among men.** **IS NOT conceived.** It cannot be understood how **one dimension.** That is, a body which has its dimensions: that is, measurements: because it has length, height, and depth. **Tolerate.** That is, suffer another dimension. That is, another...

->CANTO SECOND 241<-

If it happens that this <term>rarity</term> <note>In medieval science, "rarity" refers to a substance being thin or less dense, as opposed to "density."</note> does not pass all the way through the Moon, there must be a limit beyond which its opposite <note>The dense, solid part of the lunar matter.</note> allows no further passage. From that point, the ray of light from another source <note>The Sun.</note> is reflected back, just as a color returns through a glass which hides lead behind itself <note>Dante is describing a typical medieval mirror, which consisted of glass with a lead backing to create a reflective surface.</note>.

Now you will say that the ray shows itself to be darker there <note>in the "spots" of the Moon</note> than in other parts because it is being reflected from further back <note>Dante's logic was that light reflected from deeper inside a "thin" part of the Moon would be weaker by the time it reached Earth.</note>. From this objection <note>original: "instantia"</note>, you can be freed by experiment—if you should ever try it—which is the usual source for the streams of our sciences <term>arts</term> <note>Dante uses "arts" (arti) to refer to the branches of human knowledge and scientific inquiry.</note>.

You shall take three mirrors; place two of them at an equal distance from you, and let the third be further removed, but positioned so that your eyes find it between the first two. Turning toward them, see that a light is placed behind your back that illuminates all three mirrors and is reflected back to you from all of them. Although the reflection that is further away may not appear as large in its size <note>original: "nel quanto," referring to the quantity or area of the light</note>, you will see that it must shine with the same brightness as the others.

Now, just as the ground beneath the snow is left as a bare subject, stripped of its previous color and its cold by the blows of the warm sunbeams, so I wish to shape your intellect, which remains <note>Beatrice is metaphorically "melting" Dante's cold, incorrect assumptions to prepare his mind for a higher truth.</note>...
voglio <insert>informar</insert> di <note>The OCR "uoglon formare di" likely corresponds to "voglio informar di," meaning "I wish to inform [your mind] with..."</note>

<summary>Beatrice uses a scientific experiment involving three mirrors to disprove Dante's theory that the Moon's spots are caused by light reflecting from different depths. She argues that distance affects the size of a reflection but not its inherent brightness.</summary>
