# PARADISE

Beatrice, speaking as a <term>theologian|In Dante's Divine Comedy, Beatrice transitions from being a figure of earthly love to a symbol of Divine Revelation and theological truth</term>, presents this argument: All the celestial bodies produce different effects in lower things <note>referring to the earthly, sublunary realm</note> according to their own power and the <term>virtue|In this context, 'virtue' refers to an inherent power or spiritual influence</term> of the <term>Intelligences|Angelic beings believed in medieval cosmology to govern and move the celestial spheres</term> infused within them. This is proven by the influences that lower bodies receive from them. He <note>Dante</note> says then:

->**"Within the heaven of divine peace."**<-

This is the <term>Empyrean heaven|The highest heaven in medieval cosmology, which was believed to be motionless and the direct dwelling place of God</term>. Because it is immobile and does not rotate, he calls it the heaven of divine peace; in this heaven is the celestial kingdom, where souls enjoy eternal peace.

->**"A body revolves."**<-

This is the <term>Primum Mobile|The 'First Moved,' the ninth heaven which rotates at a dizzying speed and imparts motion to all the lower spheres</term>, the ninth heaven; it is called the Crystalline heaven, and it is contained within the immobile Empyrean heaven.

->**"In whose power."**<-

Meaning within the motive and effective power of that Crystalline heaven.

->**"The being of all its content."**<-

The preservation of the existence and the motive and effective power of everything contained within it. This ninth heaven, which is the Primum Mobile—that is <note>original: "i:", abbreviation for the Latin 'id est'</note>, the first that is moved by the Empyrean—embraces all the other heavens, which are the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the Fixed Stars</note> and the seven planets. The heavens of the seven planets are not of [the same] material <note>the sentence breaks off here</note>

## CANTO TWO 24.ii

The heaven that so many lights make beautiful,
from the profound mind that wills it,
takes the image and becomes its seal.
And as the soul within our dust,
through different members and conformed
to diverse powers, unfolds itself,
so the Intelligence displays its goodness,
multiplied throughout the stars,
circling upon its own unity.

<note>The commentator explains that the "Intelligence" (an angelic mover) works through the stars much like the human soul works through different organs of the body.</note>
...various members demonstrate various powers according to the nature of the member. Inasmuch as in the heart it gives life, in the liver it nourishes, and in the brain it feels; so the intelligence, which is one in the eighth heaven <note>The sphere of the Fixed Stars</note>, extending itself into all the stars with various influences, operates according to the various powers of those stars. It pours itself into Saturn, which is cold and dry, and gives it influence according to the nature of Saturn; and so it does in the others.

Diverse virtue makes a diverse alloy
with the precious body that it quickens,
in which, just as life in a man, it is bound.
By the joyful nature from which it derives:
the mixed virtue shines through the body,
as joy through a living pupil.
From this comes that which from light to light
appears different, not from "dense and rare";
this is the formal principle that produces,
conforming to its goodness, the dark and the clear.

<note>The poet concludes that the brightness or dimness of stars comes from divine "virtue" rather than physical density.</note>
...insofar as it performs its operation successively. It is therefore a mixed nature that gives life. Whence Boethius: <note>original: "tu triplicis medium naturam cuncta moventem: Convertens animam per consona membra resolvis. Quae conserta duos motus glomeravit in orbem. In se met reditura meat mentemque profundam Circuit: et simili convertit imagine coelum."</note> "You, through the middle of the threefold nature that moves all things: turning the soul, you distribute it through harmonious members. Which, joined together, has gathered two motions into a circle. It moves to return into itself and circles the profound mind: and turns the heaven with a similar image." Or rather, let us understand the virtue mixed with the body and infused by the movers. **Light.** It shines through the divine nature, as joy through a living pupil; as through the eye of light, revolving and flashing, the joy of the heart extends. Therefore, from the divine light proceeds every difference that is from light to light; that is, from star to star: and not from "rare to dense" as you believed.

[Right Column]

...or a sword for the combatant; nevertheless, such motion is from the smith <note>An analogy explaining that while the sword does the cutting, the power comes from the blacksmith</note>.
**The heaven which.** That is, the one which. **So many lights.** So many stars make beautiful. This is the eighth heaven <note>The Sphere of the Fixed Stars</note> where the fixed stars are, and he says that this heaven, from the profound virtue—that is, infinite divine virtue—which turns it by means of its Cherubim <note>The order of angels associated with the eighth heaven</note> as to its multiform motion; and as to its natural and uniform motion by means of the first heaven <note>The Primum Mobile</note>, it takes the image—that is, the virtue imprinted in it—just as the image of a seal is imprinted in wax: **And becomes its seal.** Because it then imprints, according to its power, into the lower things the virtue first imprinted in it. **Profound mind** is the divine mind which is infinite. Whence Boethius: "And it circles the profound mind: and turns the heaven with a similar image." Then to better explain, I say that as the human soul, which is one, extending itself in various members...

**Diverse virtue** is the conclusion of the things said above, and by those terms is understood this place: "diverse" with binding and mixing; as we say that brass is made of diverse alloys. **With the precious body.** These are celestial bodies and heavens: but of more precious matter than other bodies. **To the Divine.** Because He makes it live and operate its effects. The Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy</note> maintain that all stars are animated; and Augustine in his *Retractations* <note>original: "retractationi"</note> writes that he has not found in Holy Scripture how one can either prove or refute that the world is animated. But if it has a soul, he affirms that it is not God, but made by God, in which body it is bound as vegetative life in the human body, and such connection creates the diversity of effects according to the diversity of the celestial bodies. **By the joyful nature.** Since God is simple form and immutable, from which the angels are created; and from the natural joy—that is, from God the highest good—derive the angels, a mixed virtue because it is...

[Woodcut illustration depicting Dante and Beatrice standing before a large moon with a human face, surrounded by stars. Below them is a landscape with a city labeled "PALERMO" and "ISLAND OF SICILY".]

**T**wo doubts had been born in the mind of the poet. And these doubts were so equal that he did not know where to begin. But Beatrice, who perceived them without him speaking, resolved them. And therefore, in this opening, he uses appropriate comparisons, saying that if a person's appetite were equal for two different foods, and he had the freedom to take whichever he pleased, he would never move more toward one than the other. Similarly, a lamb placed between two wolves, fearing them equally, would move no more this way than that. And likewise, if a dog were in the middle of two <term>does (daini)</term> <note>The original uses "dama," which Landino explains below.</note> and desired them equally, he would not follow one more than the other. **Between two foods distant**—that is, far apart. **And enticing the appetite.** **In one way**—that is, equally: meaning that one was no closer than the other. **That a free man**—meaning one who was at liberty to choose and take whichever he pleased. **So would he stand**—that is, in this way and similarly he would stand. Having placed the simile regarding *desire*, he now places it regarding *fleeing*, and says that a **lamb**—that is, a young sheep—which in the midst of two wolves feared one as much as the other, would stand between the **two cravings of fierce wolves**—that is, between two greedy and fierce wolves. <note>original: "bramare"</note> <term>To crave (bramare)</term> in the Florentine tongue means to desire exceedingly. **Between two does.** <term>Dama</term> in Latin is a wild animal not much different from a roe deer, and we call them <term>fallow deer (daino)</term>. **Therefore**—he arranges it thus. **Therefore**—that is, for the reasons said above: I neither blame myself—because as a man moved by his senses I deserve some excuse—nor do I commend myself. Because although my appetite, pushed equally by my doubts, moved me in equal measure, nonetheless reason ought to have considered which was of greater importance and preferred that one. **Since it was necessary**, lacking the free will to choose. **I was silent**, but my **desire**—that is, my wish—and the **questioning** together were **painted on my face**. In the face of a man appear various signs according to various affections of the mind.

The wise men were ready to interpret the dream, but they excused themselves for not knowing it. The King became angry and commanded Arioch, the prince of the military, to have them killed. Daniel, hearing of the King’s wrath, reported it to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azaria, his companions; and having turned to prayer for the safety of the wise men, Daniel received in a vision the revelation of the dream and the interpretation. And immediately he reported it to the king, which resulted in the liberation of all. I do not narrate the dream here because we narrated it in the *Inferno*, where Dante gives the description of the statue made of different metals with a foot of baked clay. <note>This refers to the "Old Man of Crete" in Canto XIV of the Inferno.</note> **You argue.** Your first doubt is: if a nun like Piccarda <note>Piccarda Donati, a woman Dante meets in the Moon who was forcibly taken from her convent.</note> was always of good will to remain in her religious order and never changed, how could the violence done to her by others—when she was taken by force from the cloister—lessen her merits and cause her not to merit as much as she would have merited staying in the cloister? **Also to doubt.** The second doubt is that, having seen these spirits in the lunar globe, Dante is almost inclined toward the opinion—

<margin>n</margin> Dante does not affirm this: but says it could be that the opinion of Plato is not exactly as the words sound. Rather, he means not that the soul returns to the stars: but denotes that influence is attributed to the stars: which inclines one either to virtue or to vice: whence comes either honor or blame. Although such an inclination can be resisted both by our free will and by divine grace: which is given to those who duly ask for it. <gloss>Because the wise man shall rule the stars. <note>original: "quia sapiens dominabitur astris"</note></gloss> And if this is his opinion, it does not deserve to be derided, that is, mocked as false, because his bow strikes some truth: that is, his intention is directed toward some truth. **This principle** which Plato posits, that every soul returns to the star from which it departed. **Badly understood.** Because it was understood according to the words and not according to the sense which we have stated above. **Twisted.** Removed from the true way of worshipping one God. **Almost the whole world.** Because, except for the people of God, all nations through idolatry worshipped the stars, or Jove, or Mercury, or Mars, or other stars.

<margin>f</margin> **This was the first doubt of Dante:** which Beatrice, for the reason already given in responding, made the last. The doubt was: if the good will lasts, the force used by others cannot diminish its merit: since it is our will that merits and demerits. But Piccarda and Costanza <note>Two women forced from their convents against their will, discussed earlier in the poem.</note> persisted in the good will to stay in the cloister. Therefore, the violence of those who forcibly removed them should not have diminished their merits: for if they had not left the cloister, they would have ascended to a higher heaven. Whence follows: **The other doubt that moves you.** **With less poison:** because it does not make you a heretic: which poison kills the soul and removes it from the faith held by holy theology. But this is not a doubt that can remove you from Beatrice: that is, from our faith. Inasmuch as doubting whether that which our faith holds is a just thing, he affirms the faith to be true. Therefore, this doubt is an **argument**, that is, a demonstration of faith.

<margin>e</margin> **Dante's argument was** that if the good will lasts, the violence done to it should not diminish the merit. In responding to this, Beatrice divides the will into two species: absolute and relative. Absolute will is that which, having once willed the good, always wills it. For example: <term>Lawrence the Martyr <note>St. Lawrence, who was executed by being roasted on a gridiron.</note></term> wants to stand firm in the Christian faith. Therefore, although he was roasted on the gridiron, he always willed that same thing, notwithstanding the great pain of the fire he suffered. And when this will is in our soul, no violence can diminish our merit: but rather increases it for us. The other species of will is called **relative**: and this wants either the greater good or the lesser evil. Therefore, if violence is when he who suffers—that is, undergoes and is forced—contributes nothing—that is, does not incline the will in any part toward that which is forced—it is why Piccarda and Costanza are not entirely excused: because the violence was not such that it could prohibit them. And they could, after they were taken out, have returned there. Nor could they be...

which would have caused them distress, even though they were forced into marriage multiple times against their will. # PARADISE

Absolute will does not consent to the harm,
but it consents to it insofar as it fears,
if it draws back, to fall into greater distress.
Therefore, when Piccarda expresses these things,
she means the absolute will, and I
the other; so that we speak the truth together.
Such was the rippling of the holy stream
that issued from the fountain from which all truth derives;
thus it put both one and the other desire at peace.
O beloved of the first lover, O divine one,
I said then, whose speech cleanses me
and warms me so that I am more and more alive,
my affection is not so deep
that it would suffice to render you grace for grace,
but let Him who sees and is able respond to this.
I see well that our intellect is never satisfied
unless the Truth illustrates it,
outside of which no truth expands.
It rests within it like a wild beast in its lair,
as soon as it has reached it; and reach it it can,
otherwise every desire would be in vain.
Because of that, doubt springs up like a shoot
at the foot of the truth; and it is nature
which pushes us toward the summit from peak to peak.

<margin>Greater. First, because Piccarda, with her absolute will, desired and chose the virginal life; but when a greater evil—death—seemed to follow from keeping that life, she chose marriage with her relative <note>or 'respective'</note> will. Therefore, when Constance affirms she wanted the monastic life rather than marriage, she means the absolute will. But when Beatrice says she did not want it, she means the relative will. Similarly, when we say that Alcmaeon wanted to kill Eriphyle, we mean the relative will. Because, having weighed that it was evil to kill his mother and evil not to avenge his father, he judged—though falsely—that it was a lesser evil to kill her than not to avenge Amphiaraus. And thus his will in the mother-killing was not absolute, but relative.</margin>

<margin>r In gratitude to Beatrice: who, being Sacred Theology and Divine Wisdom, is most excellently called the "beloved of the first lover," that is, of God, who is First Love—as we shall show in a more appropriate place. "O divine one," or O goddess, because divinity is power, wisdom, and love, and she is "divine" because she makes us divine. "Whose speech cleanses me": whose speaking—that is, the speaking of her who cleanses me—brings me near to God. For wisdom alone is what takes away ignorance, which is the root of every vice. "And warms," that is, sets me on fire and makes me alive in seraphic love. "Affection is not": he excuses himself because his internal affection for her cannot be deep enough to correspond to her favor "grace for grace," that is, love for love. "But let Him who sees and is able respond": and this is God, who, because He sees (that is, knows) what wisdom is, loves it; and because He can do whatever He wills, He loves as much as He wills, and wills as much as He can. "I see well": as if to say, you have opened my eyes in a way that I clearly recognize that our intellect is never satisfied and never rests; because truth feeds the intellect just as food feeds the body. It is not satisfied, then, unless that Truth "illustrates," or illuminates it, outside of which no truth "expands" or extends. And this is God, who, as He said Himself, is the Way, the Truth, and the Life; and He is True in such a way that no truth expands or extends outside of Him. "It rests in it like a wild beast in its lair": <term>*lustrum*<gloss>den</gloss></term> in the Latin language means the den of wild beasts. Therefore, just as the beast rests inside its den and desires nothing else, so our intellect, having arrived at God, rests there and desires nothing further. "And reach it it can": as if to say, it is not from God that man cannot arrive at this truth, for nature would have given us such a desire in vain. And as <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> the "Aquinian" says in his book *Against the Gentiles*, the ultimate and highest happiness of man consists in contemplating God. "Because of that, it is born": man, because he has a natural desire to find the truth, goes investigating with his reasoning and discourse; and in such discourse, various doubts often arise where we weigh which of many plausible reasons occurring to the mind is the truth. And such doubts are like "shoots" or suckers which grow at the foot of the tree. "And it is nature": that is, a natural thing in man which pushes him to the summit of truth, from one truth already found to another, just as a man climbs from hill to hill to the highest peak and ridge of the mountain.</margin>

This invites me, this gives me confidence
with reverence, Lady, to ask you
about another truth that is obscure to me:
I wish to know if man can satisfy you
for failed vows with other goods
so that they are not light on your scales.
Beatrice looked at me with eyes full
of sparks of love, so divine
that my vanquished power turned its back <note>fled</note>.
And I almost lost myself with eyes cast down.

<margin>q "This invites me": As if to say, I would not dare to ask you things instituted by nature (that is, by God) which ought not to be denied; therefore it seems permissible to ask you, but with reverence for that which I doubt. And he warns that we should use no arrogance or impudence, but the highest veneration in questioning those more learned than ourselves. "I wish to know": The doubt is this: Constance and Piccarda having made a religious vow and then broken it, can one satisfy God with other goods equivalent to that vow, in such a way that they are equal on the divine scales? And finally, he asks about vows in general. "Beatrice looked at me": All this signifies that other insights of theology, when they come to our mind, inflame us with an immeasurable love; and they are so divine that our intellect loses itself in them, just as eyes do in too much light.</margin>

<summary>Dante explores the distinction between absolute and relative will regarding broken vows, concluding that the human intellect can only find rest in the ultimate Truth (God). He then asks Beatrice if other good deeds can compensate for unfulfilled religious vows.</summary>
<keywords>absolute will, relative will, Piccarda Donati, Alcmaeon, Thomas Aquinas, divine wisdom, religious vows, satisfaction, intellect, truth</keywords>

# CANTO FIVE 249

Beatrice made the heaven of Mercury shine. **And if the star changed and laughed:** if the immutable and incorruptible star changed, laughed, and glowed. We often say a thing "laughs" when it glows and shines. How much more ought I to have changed, I who, because I am human, am by nature transmutable in every way—that is, in all modes—because not only is the body mutable, but also the soul through various disturbances.

This first comparison is very appropriate, but so clear that it required no explanation. If you, reader, wish to understand how much I desired to hear from those spirits about their state, consider if I did not continue immediately in saying what follows: that is, if it begins, how great would your desire be for me to speak? But Dante feigns having this grace above all others who are still living; that while in the militant life, he could see the eternal glory which is seen only by those who, after death, are in the triumphant life.

### CANTO II 150

...to generate in us the light of reason. And for this reason he said: "The sun shows you that it is rising." Because the light of reason, which had been submerged in the past <note>referring to the darkness of Hell or the state of sin from which the pilgrim has emerged</note>, may be recovered; and it shows us the way of purging oneself. 

**TAKE TO THE mountain** at a more gentle ascent. The way which leads to virtue is difficult and steep. Wherefore he admonishes here that we should always take the path that has less harshness, provided that it is capable of leading us to our goal. He wants us to climb. But because until we are well-confirmed in a good purpose, we must begin with the easier things, so that they do not lead us into despair. And then, once we are accustomed to such difficulty, the labor will seem less hard. 

**THUS he vanished**: this is intended to denote that it was not the actual essence of Cato <note>Cato the Younger, the Roman statesman who serves as the guardian of Purgatory; here the commentator treats him as an allegorical figure</note>, but an image placed there to signify liberty. And I rose up without speaking. In this consultation <note>the process of deciding on a moral course of action</note>, reason alone must be employed, and the <term>appetite|In Renaissance philosophy, the "appetite" refers to the part of the soul that experiences desires and impulses, which must be respectfully submissive to the higher faculty of reason.</term> with reverence.

Having washed his face, they came to the shore, which never saw any man navigate its sea who afterwards returned back. This, understanding it in terms of the dead, makes it manifest that no one goes to Purgatory who then returns back; rather, they proceed forward, ascending to heaven. But it is also true for the living. For whoever passes from vice to purgation does not then return back, but goes from the purgatorial virtues <note>The active process of cleansing one's sins</note> to those of the soul already purged. He says then: "We arrived at the desert shore," abandoned and solitary, as he said above regarding the path. "Which shore never saw a man navigate its waters"—which man was thereafter experienced, that is, had tried and attempted to return back. And poetically he gives sense to an inanimate thing <note>the literary technique of personification, where the shore is described as "seeing" the sailors</note>. Just as Virgil says: "And now they were climbing the hill which..." <note>original Latin: "Iamque ascendebant collem qui"</note>

sun arrives, it makes mid-day, because it is as distant from the east as it is from the west. Therefore, it is called the **meridian circle**. 
Thus, the sun was at the horizon, western to us and eastern to the other hemisphere. But the meridian of this horizon
in our hemisphere **covers**—that is, it stands above **Jerusalem** with its highest point—that is, when it is at its
greatest height—which follows that Jerusalem is in the middle of the world. <margin>F</margin> **JERUSALEM.** Isidore writes <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose encyclopedias were vital to medieval knowledge.</note>

east. Therefore, it is opposite to him, and thus, being opposite, it goes circling the heavens. **EXITING the Ganges**: just as the Ebro is a river
in Spain because it runs to the west, so the Ganges is a river in India because it runs to the east, and is called the eastern
mouth. The Ganges is a river in India named after Gange, an ancient king of India. Its origin is not well known.
Many say it is born in the highest mountains of Scythia and falls with a great roar to the plain into a lake. <margin>G</margin> **FROM there it exits**
and runs placidly and quietly. Nineteen large and navigable rivers enter into this one. Where it has the least
width, it is eight miles wide; where it has the most, a hundred. In no place is it less than twenty feet deep. Many
believe that this is the river the Holy Scriptures call the **Pishon**, <note>One of the four rivers flowing out of the Garden of Eden.</note> which signifies "inundation." **EXITING with the scales.** It was shown above that the sun was in Aries; <note>The Ram, the zodiac sign of Spring.</note> in which, because it creates the equinox, it stays as long in
our hemisphere as in the one below. It follows that when the sun is at the setting point, **Libra** (the Scales)—which is the sign opposite
to Aries—rises in the east. And therefore he said "with the scales," that is, with Libra, which **fall from her hand when she surpasses** [the day]—that is, when the night increases. The meaning is this: that there being two equinoxes in which the night is
equal to the day, when the sun is in the first point of Aries, it is the vernal equinox. But when it exits the first degree,
the day begins to increase. Wherefore Petrarch says: *It was in the season when the equinox makes the day the victor.* And the
contrary effect is made by the sun in the autumnal equinox, when the sun is in the first point of Libra. **SO THAT the white and the vermilion cheeks.** The poets feign that **Aurora** <note>The Goddess of the Dawn.</note> is a very beautiful goddess who resides in the east. Because
this time of day appears in the east a little before the sun. Wishing therefore to demonstrate that the sun was

We were still on the shore and stayed like one who
thinks to find the way and the journey, and not knowing it
yet, does not move the body, but the soul has set out on the way. And
standing in such thought, Dante saw a light in the sea very far
from himself, which was of that fiery color that is usually in
Mars when it happens that he is opposite to the sun
in a way that, as the dawn arrives, he is near the setting. Then,
since this planet is red by its nature, it happens
that in the thick vapors exhaling from the sea—already reddened by
the dawn—it appears redder and larger. And he arranges it thus: "We
were along the shore," etc., "and behold, a
light appeared to me such"—that is, of such a color—"as Mars glows red,"
not only by its nature, but also through the thick vapors.
**AT THE APPROACH**—at the time near the morning of the dawn. Of Mars
we will speak in the *Paradiso* when we come to its heaven. But
following the text: the light came so fast that when I turned
my eyes to Virgil, it had already approached, in a way that it seemed
brighter and larger. **THEN ON EACH SIDE.** This demonstrates what
happens to the sight, which from a distance sees nothing except confusedly
and without distinction. Drawing closer, therefore, he
began to discern the white wings; but first he discerned the color rather than the wings,
and therefore he said "a whiteness" and "he knew not what." And from beneath, little by little...

CANTO [PURGATORIO] THREE. 15q:

**that: but he turned his face toward it: because he was walking toward that.** WHICH TOWARD the highest sky spreads out: that is, it expands. For we say "to flood" (allagare) when standing water spreads out. THE SUN which behind. Dante, in his walking, turned his back to the sun; therefore he saw his shadow in front of himself. And not seeing that of Virgil, he doubted whether he had been abandoned. The sun which was flaming behind me was broken before me: it made a shadow in front of me: which shadow is because the sun, finding a support—that is, opposition and an obstacle—IN ME, that is, in my body, is broken and does not penetrate. ALONE In front of me the dark earth: shadowed. When we begin to climb toward purgation, the sun—that is, illuminating grace—accompanies us. But its rays penetrate Virgil in such a way that he leaves no shadow of himself. But they do not penetrate Dante, because he has a dense body which holds back the rays and does not let them pass through. From this it happens that his shadow is seen ahead. Virgil is <term>Higher Reason</term> <note>In the allegorical tradition, Virgil represents human reason at its highest potential.</note>, which is entirely penetrable by light; indeed, it is almost that light itself. Therefore, no darkness or ignorance proceeds from it. But Dante—that is, <term>Sensuality</term> <note>In this context, 'sensuality' refers to the physical senses and earthly appetites.</note>—has a dense body, not penetrable by rays. Therefore, it makes a shadow, like ignorance. Reason is entirely illuminated and has light within itself like the sun. The senses and the appetite are like the moon, which has no light of its own, and that which comes from the sun illustrates the surface but does not penetrate; therefore, on the side where the sun does not strike it, it remains dark. Thus, appetite and sensuality have no light except what they receive from reason, and that light does not penetrate them. Therefore, the other side remains shadowy. This is, therefore, the reason why Dante sees the shadow—that is, ignorance—in himself and not in Virgil.

Virgil realized that Dante suspected he had been abandoned by him; and therefore, turning entirely toward him, he said: Why do you lack faith? Do you not believe I am with you? And that I guide you? And then he adds: if you do not see my shadow as you see yours, know that this happens because I do not have my body with me as you have yours. Because I left that one at my death in the other hemisphere, where it is already <term>Vespers</term> <note>Vespers refers to the evening hour, roughly 6:00 PM; Dante uses the geographical positions of Jerusalem, Italy, and Purgatory to track time.</note>, that is, evening, because in this place it is morning. NAPLES has it, and from Brindisi it was taken: because the poet died in Calabria. But the body was later transferred to Naples, where his epitaph is: <note>original Latin: "Mantua me genuit calabri rapuere. tenet nunc parthenope cecini pascua rura duces."</note> <gloss>Mantua gave me birth; Calabria snatched me away; now Parthenope [Naples] holds me. I sang of pastures, fields, and leaders.</gloss> And this is according to the history. But allegorically, the soul that has put down the body—that is, the vices which proceed from the contagion of the flesh—makes no shadow, because only light remains. And being entirely illuminated, no ignorance remains in it. NOW If no shadow is cast before me. If the sun, which strikes my back, does not make a shadow in front of me as it does for you, do not marvel; for I do not have a dense body like you, but a rare one, like the celestial bodies. Therefore, do not marvel at these any more than at the heavens. For although those of the planets are seven, and the eighth where the fixed stars are, and one includes the other, nevertheless, because they are of a <term>rare body</term> <note>In medieval physics, 'rare' means thin or transparent, as opposed to 'dense' or opaque.</note>, and clear, and diaphanous, and transparent, they give way to their rays so that they penetrate even to the earth and to our eyes, so that we see all the way to the fixed stars. And this is because one does not block the ray of the other. TO Suffer torments, and heat and frost. He solves a question which could arise here: for it seems very doubtful whether souls, once stripped of their bodies (which, being composed of the four contrary elements, can feel pain), can suffer as they do. To which he responds: that divine power, which serves every nature, wills that they suffer; and it does not want it to be known to us how they can suffer. And therefore he said: "it reveals itself." And this place is much debated by theologians. Because all natural reasons seem to conclude that, the soul being incorporeal, it could not be afflicted by corporeal fire. Therefore, Thomas Aquinas holds that they suffer by means of the body; for notwithstanding that they remain stripped of their own bodies, God can nonetheless link them to some body in the manner of a "form," just as he links them to their own bodies to give them life. Or truly, without this, he can link them, just as necromancers, by the power of demons, link spirits to some image.

Until Quintus Marcius Philippus, who was censor with Lucius Paulus, placed another more orderly one near it. This was very pleasing to the people. And this was five hundred and ninety-six years after Rome was built; nor do I find that the Romans or other peoples in those times had bells, either for timepieces or for anything else. I have said this briefly about the quadrant that shows the hours. The material sphere <note>Also known as an armillary sphere, a skeletal model of the celestial globe.</note>, which shows the whole sky and its circles. The second is the round Astrolabe, but flattened in the shape of a platter, in which the entire position of the heavens is shown. The third is a quad...

# Observations on the Nature of Light and Color

-> **Recorded in the Winter of 1704** <-

It has been observed by many <term>Natural Philosophers<note>A historical term for people who studied the physical world and nature, the predecessors of modern scientists.</note></term> that the light of the sun, when passed through a triangular glass prism, produces a variety of colors. This phenomenon, which the ancients called the "rainbow" <note>original Greek: "iris"</note>, is not merely an illusion of the eye but a fundamental property of the light itself.

<margin>Compare this to the earlier experiments by Mr. Isaac Newton at Cambridge.</margin>

I have found that "the truth is found in the simplest things" <note>original Latin: "veritas in simplicitate penderet"</note>. When the beam of light is narrowed by a small hole in the shutter, the separation of the <insert>vivid</insert> colors becomes more distinct to the observer. If one color, such as the red, is separated from the rest and passed through a second prism, it does not change its hue; it remains red.

### Data of the Refraction Experiments

| Material Tested | Angle of Incidence | Observed Effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Clear Spring Water | 30 degrees | Slight bending of the ray |
| Venetian Flint Glass | 30 degrees | Significant separation of colors |
| <unclear>Essential Oil</unclear> | 30 degrees | *Inconclusive due to cloudiness* |

<gloss>Ensure the glass is wiped clean of all dust before the sun reaches its zenith.</gloss>

The <term>Refractive Index<note>A measurement of how much a substance, like glass or water, bends light as it passes through.</note></term> varies significantly between these substances. As the great scholars once wrote, "the nature of things is hidden" <note>original Greek: "φύσις κρύπτεσθαι φιλεῖ"</note>, yet through diligent measurement and the use of the mathematical arts, we may begin to uncover these secrets of the created world.

<summary>This page describes experiments involving prisms to understand how sunlight splits into colors, confirming that individual colors cannot be further divided and noting the different refractive properties of water and glass.</summary>
<keywords>optics, light, color, refraction, natural philosophy, 18th-century science</keywords>

->PURGATORY<-

First it is necessary that the heavens revolve around me
outside of the gate as much as they did in life,

Unless a prayer first aids me,
one that rises from a heart living in grace;

<gloss>As if to say nothing, and the reason is that the Bird of God <note>original: "uccello di dio"</note>—that is, the Angel who sits upon the gate of Purgatory, of whom more will be said below—would not let me enter. For it is necessary that the heavens revolve just as much time outside that gate of Purgatory as passed during one’s life. And this is according to the fictional premise made above: because I delayed my good sighs until the end of life. These are "good" because they are helpful and make the one who uses them good. Note the author's opinion here: that the prayers of those in mortal sin do not help those in Purgatory.</gloss>

<gloss>Reason <note>The commentator identifies Virgil as "Reason."</note> did not wish to delay further in laziness, and therefore he admonished Dante to rise. "See that the meridian"—that is, the circle of the fourth hour—"is touched by the sun." Therefore, if the sun had arrived at this circle, it signifies it was midday. "And already night covers Morocco with her foot from the shore"—that is, coming from the sea near Morocco or Mauritania, a region of Africa located in the West. The meaning is this: while it was noon in the hemisphere where Dante was, night was rising from the shore of Morocco, which is West to us but East to them. From this, he infers that neither day nor night is equal in all parts of the hemisphere, for it is morning in the East before it is noon, and noon before it is evening in the West.</gloss>

# CANTO FIVE OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

<note>Large decorated initial letter "I" containing two figures.</note>

**I** had already departed from those shades
and was following the footsteps of my leader,
when one behind me, pointing his finger,
cried out: "See how the ray does not seem to shine
on the left of the one below,
and he seems to behave like a living man!"
I turned my eyes at the sound of these words,
and I saw them staring in wonder,
at me, only me, and at the light that was broken <note>Dante’s physical body blocks the light, casting a shadow, which is impossible for the translucent "shades" or spirits.</note>.

[Illustration: A woodcut showing figures in a rocky landscape. Labels: PIA, BUCONTE, VIRGIL, DANTE]

<gloss>In this fifth canto, he places those who were engaged in military discipline <note>Soldiers and those who lived by the sword.</note> and delayed their repentance until the moment of death. He finds these on the third ledge. He had departed from those described above when an opening was shown to him; he was noticed because he was there with his body, for he made a shadow and the sun did not penetrate him as it does incorporeal spirits, but remained "broken." Many in this <term>Antipurgatory</term> <note>The outer region of Purgatory where souls wait before beginning their formal purification.</note> note with wonder that Dante is there with his body. This demonstrates the great leisure of these "lazy" ones; if they had been in an army, they would have turned their thoughts elsewhere.</gloss>

"Why is your mind so entangled,"
said the Master, "that you slow your pace?
What do you care what is whispered here?
Follow behind me and let the people talk;
stand like a firm tower that never shakes
its summit at the blowing of the winds.
For the man in whom thought sprouts upon
thought always moves his goal further away,
because the force of one weakens the other."
What could I say, except "I am coming"?
I said it, flushed somewhat with the color <note>Dante is blushing with shame after Virgil’s rebuke.</note>

<gloss>Reason <note>Virgil</note> reproves Sensuality <note>Dante</note>, which is eager to stop among the negligent. He warns that he pays too much attention to what is whispered—that is, the murmuring talk—and encourages him to follow Reason. Just as a tower does not move or bend for the blowing of the winds, so the one who wishes to climb to the purgatorial virtues must remain firm in their good purpose. No rumor heard from those who do not climb due to negligence should cause one to abandon the enterprise. "The tower does not move its summit"—that is, he who has made a firm resolution to climb should not change his mind because of the "blowing of the winds," meaning the vain reasons of others. "For the man in whom thought sprouts..." A man, after making a good resolution, should not go wavering in his mind with various thoughts and cogitations. Because the one who wanders in a diversity of thoughts "moves further from the mark," which is the end goal he had proposed to reach, and begins to be ambiguous and perplexed because...</gloss>

->CANTO FIFTH. 160<-

...which sometimes makes a man worthy of pardon; the subsequent thought **renders it vain** <gloss>that is: it makes it void</gloss> and annihilates the first. And just as when a crossbowman distances himself from the target more than he ought, the shot he fires **becomes hollow** <gloss>that is: it vanishes</gloss> because his crossbow does not carry that far; so it happens to this man. We specifically use the term "hollow" <term>insolla: used here to describe metal that is not properly condensed or solid but remains porous or empty inside</term> regarding iron. **SPRINGS FORTH:** this is a metaphor taken from trees, which are always putting out new branches. Therefore, a "sprig" <note>original: *rampolla*</note> signifies a new branch born upon the old one. **WHAT COULD I SAY.** When sensuality and appetite are made obedient to reason, and reason then shows them the truth and follows it, what can one respond except "I follow you"? And this is what Dante shows he has done. But his face was covered with a **vermilion** <note>a bright red pigment</note> color, which signifies feeling shame. And he adds that feeling shame makes a man worthy of pardon. He says "sometimes" because shame does not always deserve pardon, but only when it is the cause either of us not beginning to err, or if we have already begun, it takes us away from it. Whence **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher, whose ethics heavily influenced Dante</note> says: that shame is good in children, but not in the elderly. In children, it is a hope that they will refrain from error; in the elderly, it is not, because they have already made it a habit.

My master: "You may go your way
and report back to those who sent you
that the body of this man is true flesh.

# PURGATORIO

<margin>Marzucco's snake</margin>

Marzucco of the Scornigiani <note>A prominent Pisan nobleman mentioned by Dante</note> from Pisa, a knight and doctor <note>Likely a doctor of laws, a common title for high-ranking officials</note>, while riding one day from Suvereto to Scarlino <note>Coastal towns in the Maremma region of Tuscany</note>, a snake
of stupendous size crossed his path in the road. He was so terrified by it that he vowed to become one of the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans, known for their vow of poverty</note> if he survived. Having
become a friar, his son Farinata was killed. In this calamity, he showed such constancy <note>Historical term for stoic fortitude and the refusal to seek vengeance</note> that, together with the other friars, he celebrated
the funeral rites and accompanied him to the burial. Afterward, turning to his relatives with a long and most appropriate oration, he led them
to peace. And he kissed that hand of the murderer with which he had killed his son. He was like another Anaxagoras <note>A Greek philosopher often cited for his emotional detachment</note>, who,
having heard of the death of his son, was not at all disturbed. Instead, he said to the one who brought the news: "You tell me nothing new, for I
knew that I had fathered a mortal." And Cato <note>A Roman statesman famous for his rigid morality and stoicism</note> in a similar case said: "My son has satisfied nature because
he was mortal." But so as not to leave behind the story of the snake, they say that it fed on...

**Haughty and disdainful.** 

In our language, we call "haughty and disdainful" one who, through excellence of soul, does not look upon nor give thought to vile things, nor deems them worthy. # PURGATORY

**My Caesar, why do you not accompany me?** <note>original: "cesare mio". Dante is addressing Albert I of Austria, the Holy Roman Emperor, criticizing him for neglecting Italy.</note>
**Come to see the people, how they love each other,** <note>original: "quanto s'ama" (OCR: "fama"). Dante uses bitter sarcasm here to describe the civil strife and hatred between Italian factions.</note>
**and if no pity for us moves you,**
**come to feel shame for your own reputation.** <note>original: "fama". Dante implies that the Emperor's "fame" is being tarnished by his inaction.</note>

There: <note>This begins the explanation of the verse.</note> because since the Emperor is the King of the Romans, Rome, when deprived of the Emperor, remains a widow and alone. And finally, "come to see how much the people love each other," and you will see, in place of love, hatred and enmity. And if you have no pity for Italy, come to be ashamed of your own infamy. And certainly every prince should be ashamed who does not rule those who are under his protection with supreme justice and the most <term>humane mercy</term> <note>original: "humanissima clemētia". A key Renaissance virtue for a ruler.</note>. For as Plato writes, and as all the philosophers affirm, and the sacred theologians command: the king and all other princes have not been raised to such high dignity for their own personal profit or leisure, but for the peace of all.

<meta>This page contains the conclusion of Dante Alighieri’s famous political invective against Florence from Canto VI of the *Purgatorio*, followed by the opening of Canto VII. The right column provides a scholarly commentary, likely by Cristoforo Landino, explaining the poet's use of irony.</meta>

CANTO VII 165

[Left Column]

My Florence, you may well be satisfied
with this digression, which does not affect you,
thanks to your people, who are so resourceful.
Many have justice in their hearts, but they shoot late,
so as not to come to the bow without counsel;
but your people have it at the tip of their lips.
Many refuse the public burden;
but your people respond eagerly
without being called, and cry: "I’ll shoulder it!"
Now make yourself glad, for you have good reason:
you who are rich, you at peace, you so wise!
If I speak the truth, the facts will not hide it.
Athens and Lacedaemon <note>Lacedaemon is the ancient name for Sparta.</note>, who fashioned
the ancient laws and were so civilized,
made but a small hint at living well
compared to you, who make such subtle
provisions that what you spin in October
does not last until mid-November.
How many times, in the time you remember,
laws, money, offices, and customs
have you changed, and renewed your members!
And if you remember well and see the light,
you will see yourself like that sick woman
who cannot find rest upon the feathers,
but fends off her pain by tossing and turning.

[Horizontal line]

By changing government, one should leave injustice behind; if injustice persists within them, it happens that such a change does them no good.

[Right Column]

**Digression** is a tool used by writers when, for a specific purpose, they depart from their main subject. Here, the poet has departed from his path to rebuke the civil discords of Italy, and especially those of our republic. He speaks through **irony**—that is, by saying the opposite of what is meant—when he says Florence can be "content" because what he said in this digression does not "touch" her; he means that it touches her more than any other. **THANKS** to your people: read this also with irony, for he damns the people who do not "resourcefully" rise against the tyranny of the powerful. **Many have justice in their heart**: [but they shoot] "late," meaning they do not take action without careful counsel, as if they were unable to act. The meaning is: many would like to live justly, but they do not want to reveal themselves until they see they can achieve something, so they do not harm themselves to help others. Therefore, it "shoots late." Thus Sallust says: "To strive in vain, and to tire oneself for no other end than to earn hatred, is the height of madness." <note>original Latin: "Frustra autem niti: nec aliud se fatigando nisi odium querere extreme dementie est."</note> **BUT your people have it at the tip of their lips**: as if to say they reveal their will before considering or seeing how they might bring that will to perfection. **MANY refuse the common burden**: Many refuse the government of the republic. But the Florentine people are so prompt that every day one sees new changes. Hence he says with irony: "You who are rich, you at peace, you so wise." Athens was made noble first by the laws of Draco, then by the laws of Solon. The laws of Solon were admirable, among which were these: Whoever does not nourish his father and mother shall be treated with infamy. He who lives in idleness may be accused by anyone. The children of those who die in battle shall be nourished by the public. He who gouges out one eye shall have two of his own removed. Lacedaemon, through the laws imposed by Lycurgus, was reduced to such severity of life and customs that, with their incredible justice and invincible strength, they obtained rule over all of Greece and part of Asia. **LIKE that sick woman**: The nature of the sick person is to be eager to change places frequently to find rest. If she could leave the illness in the place she departs from, it would benefit her. But because she carries it with her, she must suffer wherever she moves. So too the people, if they could [find] peace; but because whatever magistrates they create are always in...

<margin><unclear>scribbled gloss</unclear></margin>

CANTO VII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE <note>The *Purgatorio* is the second "canticle" or book of the *Divine Comedy*.</note> OF DANTE.

**P**ost-haste, after the greetings, honest and glad,
had been exchanged three and four times,

"Before the souls worthy of ascending to God
were turned toward this mountain,
my bones were buried by Octavian.
I am Virgil, and for no other sin
did I lose heaven than for not having faith."
Thus my leader then replied.
As one who suddenly sees something
before him and marvels,
who believes and does not, saying: "It is not so,"
Such did that man seem; and then he lowered his brow,
and humbly returned toward him,
and embraced him where the inferior takes hold <note>Sordello embraces Virgil's knees or feet as a sign of respect.</note>.

...of gold, [comes from] the solidity of the sulfur, which does not produce the airy, watery quality of quicksilver <term>quicksilver: also known as mercury</term>. It is very healthy for the human body; and taken as food, it strengthens all the limbs. The soul alone, adorned with four powers <note>the four cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance</note>, directs its free will toward the good; it is immediately aided by divine grace and lives according to the virtues. # CANTO VIII 168

And the others then sweetly and devoutly
  followed her through the whole entire hymn,
  keeping their eyes upon the celestial spheres.

<note>original: "superne rote" (heavenly wheels), referring to the rotating spheres of the heavens in the Ptolemaic system.</note>

They praised her beauty and took the highest pleasure in it; but finally concluded it was much better that Helen <note>The commentator here uses Helen of Troy as a symbol of worldly pleasure or vice.</note> should depart so that Troy would not be lost through the desire to keep her. Thus a man, though he is enticed by the pleasure of the senses, prefers that Helen—meaning those pleasures—depart from him, because they are pernicious and lead us to vices; they do not want Troy—meaning their soul—to be ruined. When I began to burn <note>The commentator is likely interpreting the spiritual "burning" of the soul's desire for God.</note> they were already silent, they who previously sang "Hail, Queen." <note>original: "salve regia" (Salve Regina), a traditional Catholic hymn to the Virgin Mary.</note> And I began to wonder—that is, to perceive. **AROSE** <note>original: "SURTA," from the Latin *surgo*.</note> standing on her feet, **WHO ASKED** to be heard: she asked to be listened to, as if to say she asked for silence not with words but with her hand, making signs with her hand. **AND SHE LIFTED** both palms toward heaven, as one does who adores, **FIXING** her eyes—looking intently toward the East, because our religion has the custom of turning toward the sunrise when adoring. Hence ancient churches always have their altars facing that way. **AS IF SHE SAID TO GOD**: she watched so intently and devoutly that she seemed to say: **NOTHING ELSE MATTERS TO ME.** <note>original: "ALTRO non calme."</note> And she began to sing the hymn which is found in the office of Compline, <note>Compline is the final prayer service of the day in the Christian liturgy.</note> the beginning of which is: *To you, Creator of all things, before the end of the light.* <note>original: "Te lucis ante terminum rerum creator." This hymn asks for God's protection during the night.</note> So sweetly, that that sweetness drew all my senses to itself so that I did not remember myself. And this shows that in praying we must lift the eyes of the mind to heaven and have the mind entirely turned to God, in such a way that we remember nothing else.

**Sharpen your eyes well here, reader, to the truth:**
  **for the veil is now indeed so thin**
  **certainly, that passing through is easy:**

He admonishes the reader to sharpen their intellect to understand the allegorical sense of this fiction; and he shows that the "veil" of this allegory is not obscure, but is so transparent that it will be easily seen. Then he presents the fiction, saying that the host—that is, that multitude—sang the hymn. But note: "host" <note>original: "exercito," literally "army."</note> signifies a multitude of men who fight, or who are prepared to fight if necessary. Therefore this word fits well in this place: because those who exercise themselves in the purgatorial virtues are always ready to fight against temptations and overcome them. **SILENT**: he shows the prayer of these spirits, and said "silent" because God understands the heart and does not desire prayer of the mouth, although sometimes affection sends forth words. Hence the Psalmist: *With my voice I have prayed to the Lord.* <note>original: "Voce mea ad dominum deprecatus sum."</note> And elsewhere: *My heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced.* <note>original: "Letatum est cor meum: & exultavit lingua mea."</note> Saying therefore that God does not desire the words, Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an influential theologian.</note> says prayer is when our intellect is directed toward God. And for this reason Augustine says: *What profit is the noise of labors if the heart is hardened?* <note>original: "Quid prodest strepitus laborū: si induratum est cor."</note> And Solomon: *The prayer of the humble will pierce the clouds.* <note>original: "oratio humiliantis se penetrabit nubes."</note> This hymn is

well suited because in the Christian church it is sung at the beginning of the night; and the Lord is prayed to guard us from every nocturnal phantom and from every harmful thing, and to remove from us every temptation. These spirits, therefore, having finished the hymn, looked in silence at the heaven awaiting help. **PALE** from fear of the serpent and **HUMBLE** so that the prayer would be more acceptable to God. But so that we may understand the allegory of this text, there is no doubt that with the departure of light for the coming night—that is, our losing reason and divine grace through ignorance and sin—we are tempted by the devil and the flesh. Therefore the grace of God is necessary to us, without which our strengths would not be enough to defend us. And so these souls ask for it in that verse of the hymn. This grace is signified by the angels. And because temptation comes in two ways—either by negligence, leaving aside meritorious acts and works, or by suggestion, which is when the devil tempts us suggesting things that lead us to vice—therefore he places two angels, meaning the double grace of God, which defends us from the two temptations. One is placed on the right side of the valley to guard us from negligence. The other on the left, and this is against suggestion. The two swords are justice, which are blunted <note>original: "spunctate."</note> because such justice is mixed with mercy. He uses two swords because Paul also said *by the weapons of justice on the right and on the left.* <note>original: "per arma iustitie a dextris & a sinistris."</note> The fire denotes charity. Therefore the immeasurable charity of God sends the angel—that is, the defense—and sends him with justice, because he makes us worthy of it with "prevenient grace" <note>Prevenient grace is a theological concept referring to grace that precedes human decision.</note> which induces us to ask for illuminating, cooperating, and conserving grace. Hence the Psalmist: *May God have mercy on us and shine His face upon us and have mercy on us.* <note>original: "Miserereatur nostri deus & illuminet vultum suum super nos & misereatur nostri."</note> Therefore prevenient grace makes us turn to God to ask for mercy and light, so that we may perform meritorious works. But because our just works are not enough, it is necessary that the mercy of God supplies the rest. The angels have wings and green garments because the grace of God always keeps itself green <note>Symbolizing hope and life.</note> in us and never dries up, provided we wish it. The garment defends us from heat and frost. The wings lift us above the earth and raise us to heaven; and we can take the two wings to be justice and religion, as according to Plato you will find in the preface to the third canticle.

**THEY STAND ABOVE** because grace comes from heaven, and they place themselves in the middle because grace is needed on the right and on the left—that is, in prosperity and in adversity. **BLOND HAIR** signifies incorruption. **AND THERE WAS SUCH RADIANCE** that my eye could not endure it, so that I was dazzled. -># **PURGATORY**<-

<note>The text begins by calculating the time elapsed in the journey.</note> ...consumed part until the center: part from the center until the surface of Purgatory was double. Since, leaving our hemisphere in the sixth hour of the night—where day was already coming—it follows that in the other hemisphere one would find a new night. **OF THE cold animal.** <note>original: "fredo animale"</note> This seems contrary to Virgil, who said *now the burning scorpion contracts its arms*; <note>original Latin: "iam braccia contrahit ardens scorpius"</note> but Virgil had respect for the nature of Mars, the lord of this sign, which is a burning planet. And Dante refers to the proper nature of the sign, which is cold, fixed, and nocturnal. **WHO with its tail strikes the people** is well-deserved because astrologers call this sign the house of death, fear, toil, loss, and contention; and as the scorpion is an animal that stings with its tail, so the sun, when it is in that sign, is the cause of injury and stinging in the human body. Because it begins to decline, it warms the air less, which is why the air, distempered by cold, soon offends and stings bodies, as Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville, an influential medieval encyclopedist.</note> writes. And by **the steps with which the night rises**, he means the hours of the night. Therefore, it was already two hours into the night in the place where we were, which was the hemisphere over there; the day had already dipped its wings downward. Understand that in the same hemisphere as that of Adam, he had a body; and as far as the body is concerned, we are all descended from Adam, but the soul is entirely from God.

[Left Column]
In the hour when the swallow begins
her sad lays near the morning,
perhaps in memory of her first woes,
And when our mind, a pilgrim
further from the flesh and less seized by thought,
is almost divine in its visions,
In a dream, there appeared to me, suspended,
**A**n eagle in the sky with golden feathers,
with wings open and intent on descending.
And I seemed to be in the place where
his own were abandoned by Ganymede,
when he was snatched to the highest consistory. <note>The "highest consistory" refers to the assembly of the gods on Olympus.</note>
Within myself I thought: perhaps this one strikes
only here by habit, and perhaps from another place
it disdains to carry anyone up in its feet.

[Right Column]
The author, having already passed so much of the night in sleep that day was approaching and the dawn was beginning—the time when the swallow, in the season of spring, begins to sing—it appeared to him in a vision that he was in the forest of Ida, which is near Troy. This is where the poets feign that Jove, in the form of an eagle, snatched Ganymede. And in the sky, he seemed to see an eagle with golden feathers, ready to swoop down to make its prey. Whereupon he said to himself: perhaps it is the habit of this eagle to sit in this forest, and it does not deign to carry anyone to heaven except from here. **In the hour that the swallow begins her sad lays:** At the time of morning when the swallow begins. Her "lays" are her laments, which touches upon the fable, which is this: Pandion, King of Athens, had two daughters, Procne and Philomela. At the same time, there was Tereus, King of Thrace, who, being allied with Pandion, was of no small help to him in a war waged against him. Therefore, after the war, to confirm and establish their friendship, Pandion gave him Procne as his wife. Tereus took her to Thrace; and after some time, urged by his wife who was eager to see her sister, he returned to Pandion and obtained permission to take Philomela to Procne. But on the journey, seized by the beauty of the girl, against her will he took her honor; then, fearing the wretched girl would reveal such an injury, he cut out her tongue.

[Bottom Section]
And he left her in the woods. But Philomela, deprived of speech, helped herself with industry: she embroidered the whole story and sent it to her sister. Procne, moved not so much by pity toward Philomela as by a doubled hatred toward the adulterer, her husband, and the breaker of faith to two sisters, fixed her will to celebrate the sacrifices to Bacchus, which were done by night and in the woods. She went where her sister was and stealthily led her into her palace. She killed Itys, the son she had by Tereus, cooked him, and served him as food to his father; and after he had finished, she placed before him the head and feet of the son he had eaten. I do not recount how much cruelty the infuriated father prepared to use against her who had made a sepulcher of his own flesh. But the commiseration that the gods had for them transformed them all. Tereus became a <term>bubbula</term> <note>Likely referring to the Hoopoe, a bird with a crest or "crown."</note>, a foul-smelling bird but with beautiful feathers and a crown, so that it seems he retains his Attic dress. Itys became a pheasant. Philomela became a nightingale, which lives in the woods, and one does not see its tongue when it sings. Procne became a swallow and has remained red on her breast from the blood of her son with which she was stained. **And that our mind, a pilgrim further from the flesh.** At this time, the soul is more of a "pilgrim"—that is, further from the body. It is as if he says it is more disentangled and more free from the contagion of the body; and above, in the first canticle, we demonstrated by philosophical reasons why, at this hour more than others, dreams are more true. **IN A DREAM it appeared to me.** He feigns this vision: that it seemed to him he saw an eagle with golden feathers suspended in the sky with open wings, which seemed continually wanting to descend. Allegorically, according to Francesco da Buti <note>An early and famous commentator on Dante.</note> and several others, by the eagle is understood **Divine Charity**. Charity is always ready to snatch human souls to God, and the golden feathers demonstrate the rays of charity, shining and pure like gold. Then the author adds that he seemed to be in the forest of Ida, where Jove, in the form of an eagle, snatched Ganymede. Francesco, as already mentioned, understands by this that holy men who perform penance in the forests are more easily snatched by divine charity. And by this, the author wishes to say that he was disposed to purge himself like such men. This exposition I in no way reject, for it is pious and suited to the Christian religion. Nevertheless, when I consider the depth of the poet's genius, I judge that he wishes to show that while sleeping, there came to him that species of dream which the Latins call <term>somnium</term> <note>A dream that requires interpretation to reveal its truth.</note>, which predicts true things but obscurely and under a veil, in a form that cannot be understood without an interpreter. Therefore Dante—who is the sensitive soul—dreams, and then the higher reason interprets the dream for him. Because of this, we will say that Dante falls asleep in the valley, exhausted by the steep journey—that is, having begun to rise toward contemplation. And being exhausted in that human...

**[Left Column]**

...which opened heaven after its long prohibition.
Before us he appeared so lifelike,
carved there in a gentle pose,
that he did not seem a silent image.
One would have sworn that he said, "Hail," <note>original: "ave"</note>
for there she was imaged,
she who turned the key to open the supreme love.
And in her gesture she had these words impressed:
"Behold the handmaid of God," <note>original: "ecce ancilla dei"</note> as clearly
as a figure is stamped in wax.

**Polyclitus** <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE, known for his idealized proportions.</note> was the son of Ageladas and from the city of Sicyon, a sculptor much celebrated among the ancients, especially for a statue they call the *Diadumenus* <note>A youth tying a victory ribbon around his head.</note> valued at one hundred talents. He had a name suited to himself, because "Polyclitus" in Greek signifies a man of great fame. **BUT NATURE WOULD BE PUT TO SHAME**, that is, it would be surpassed. We properly say someone receives "shorn-scorn" <note>The author uses a wordplay on "scorno" (shame) and "corna" (horns).</note> when they presume or trust they will excel, but then the opposite happens to them. And one can speak of a "shame of honor." For just as we say a man "puts out his horns" when he exalts himself for a victory or for having achieved what he desired, so by contrast we say one is "shorn" or "de-horned." **The Angel Gabriel**, who came to earth to announce to Mary. **WITH THE DECREE**: with the determination made by the omnipotent, triune, and unique God: that Mary should conceive by the power of the Holy Spirit the eternal Word, who was to ransom the human race. This incarnation created Jesus our redeemer and mediator between God and man, and reconciled us with God so that we regained peace, which for many years had been mourned—that is, desired with tears by the holy fathers. While they were alive, and after they were suspended in Limbo, they waited to be freed by the passion of God, which redemption opened the **long prohibition**, that is, opened it to the human generation, to whom it had been forbidden for so long a time. For from the sin of Adam until the descent of Christ into Limbo, five thousand two hundred and thirty-two years passed. **BEFORE US HE APPEARED SO LIFELIKE.** This is great praise for the sculpture: that standing before a thing that should seem nothing more than a mute and inanimate image, it nonetheless showed itself to speak with supreme gentleness. And then he says: **HE DID NOT SEEM**, that is, he did not resemble, **A SILENT IMAGE**, but an image that speaks. And this occurred because the image of the angel appeared to speak, and nearby was the image of Mary, such that anyone would have sworn the angel said "Hail," as he did when he announced the news. **FOR THERE**, because in that place, **SHE WAS IMAGINED**, there was the image of Mary. **WHO TO OPEN THE SUPREME LOVE TURNED THE KEYS.** She turned the keys to open the high love of God, which our sin had shut away from us. Because the holiness and humility of Mary was the key that opened divine love to us. And just as the image of the angel was carved so skillfully that it seemed to say "Hail," so that of Mary appeared to consent to the divine precept, and out of supreme humility said: "Behold the handmaid of God." He places here, therefore, the image of Mary as the singular and first example of humility. Of her, as the historian of Carthage <note>Likely referring to Tertullian or Cyprian, though Landino often references classical brevity.</note> said, it is better to be silent than to say too little.

"Do not keep your mind only on one place,"
said the sweet master, who had me

**[Right Column]**

These examples are carved and not painted. Because a painting is easily removed, but not a carving. And they are carved not in soft material, but in hard. This admonishes us that if we wish to entirely drive pride away from us, it is necessary that we have humility sculpted and entirely fixed in our minds. Furthermore, he uses white marble to denote that such humility must be pure and clean, and not spotted with any fiction or simulation. And as the color white is bright and shining, so should this humility shine. For **nothing is more arrogant than a feigned humility** <note>original: "nihil est ficta humilitate superbius"</note>. Furthermore, he shows that such images are so life-like <note>term: *proprie* (accurate/lifelike representation)</note> that not only Polyclitus or any other excellent sculptor, but Nature herself could not make them so accurately. This signifies nothing else than that such humility must be in its own proper image, in a form that neither human wit nor natural movement could make more true.

Having placed the example of the humility of Mary, he places that of **King David**. Nor should one overlook in this place the wonderful wit and absolute learning of the poet. He knew that man uses pride in three ways: either toward a superior, or toward an equal, or toward an inferior. Therefore, against these three types of pride, he judged it necessary to oppose three types of humility. Accordingly, for the example of humility toward a superior, he placed Mary; toward equals, David; and toward inferiors, Trajan. Mary humbled herself to God. David used humility with the priests, playing the lyre <note>term: *citharizando* (playing the cithara or lyre)</note> and dancing with them before the Ark, which humility was among equals. Trajan humbled himself to the widow, who was much inferior to him. But so that the humility of David may be known to us: it is in the Second Book of Kings <note>Known as 2 Samuel in modern Bibles.</note> that after the death of Saul, a most proud king, David was elected in his place. He gathered all the clergy of Israel to transfer the Ark of the Lord with a most pleasing procession to his city of Zion <note>original: "Gyon"</note>. The Ark was in Gibeah, in the house of Abinadab, son of Saul. He placed it, therefore, on a new cart, and accompanied it with a great celebration of sounds. Uzzah <note>original: "Oza"</note> and Ahio <note>original: "achio"</note>, the sons of Abinadab, guided the cart. And as the oxen of the cart stumbled on the road and kicked, and because of this the cart moved awkwardly, Uzzah came to the aid of the Ark which was wavering, and placed his hand upon it...

A famous quote from St. Augustine’s Confessions regarding the soul finding peace in God.</note> *Entoma* <note>original Greek: "ἔντομα"</note> in Greek and in Latin *insects* <note>original: "insecta"</note> are all those "worms" <note>in this period, "worms" was a general term for small crawling creatures or larvae</note> that do not have all their limbs distinct, such as bees, ants, and similar things.
The great weights which these souls carried made them bow and crouch so that the chest touched the knees. Because of this, they appeared like certain **wooden corbels** which are placed in the wall under the beams of roofs or floors, or indeed ceilings; these are often carved in the shape of a man who supports the beam, and the great weight causes him to bend and crouch, and these supports...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XI, focusing on the paraphrasing of the Lord’s Prayer (the Pater Noster) as recited by the proud on the first terrace of Purgatory.</meta>

**CANTO XI. 177**

has an end. The finite is, without comparison, smaller than the infinite: and the smaller thing cannot contain the larger within itself: therefore God is not contained by the heavens. But he is said to reside in the heavens: because he has more love for the heavens, because the heavens and the angels are the first effects that he, the **First Cause** <note>In medieval philosophy, the "First Cause" is God, the uncaused cause of all existence.</note>, produced: and these are then the **Secondary Causes** for the inferior effects. For every superior thing is the cause of the movement of its inferior: as we shall declare more clearly elsewhere. He has, up to this point, said: **Our Father who art in heaven** <note>original: "pater noster qui es i cœlis"</note>: which words are the prologue of this prayer. Now he comes to the petitions: which are seven. And the first is: **Hallowed be thy name.** Wherefore he says: **Prais-ed be thy name and thy value.** In the first petition, he asks for the honoring of the Father. This signifies love with obedience and veneration toward the Father. And if it should seem superfluous to say "hallowed be thy name"—because one cannot hallow him who is the Holy of Holies—we shall say "hallowed," that is, "made firm": because "holy" <note>original: "sancto"</note> signifies "firm." **Value**: that is, virtue. **Vapor**: grace. **BY EVERY** creature. Whatever is produced by God, the First Cause and Creator, is called a "creature." But these are divided into six species. For some have only being: like stones. **X** <note>This "X" appears in the original transcription, likely a placeholder or marginal marker.</note> Some have a **vegetative soul** <term>vegetative soul: the most basic level of life in Aristotelian biology, responsible for nutrition and growth</term>: by which they are nourished and grow and produce seed to generate one like themselves: such as herbs and trees: and every other plant. Some, beyond the vegetative, have some sense: but do not have local motion: such as the **shellfish** <note>original: "calcinegli," small mollusks or barnacles</note> stuck to the rock. Some have a more perfect sense: and local motion: such as all the brute animals. Some, beyond the vegetative, sensitive, and motive, have reason: such as man. But above man is the angel: of whom we shall speak in another place. Every creature praises its creator as much as is in itself: that is, God: in whom, wishing to express the **Trinity**, he placed three names: namely **Name** for fame and wisdom: in which he expresses the **Son**. And **Value**: that is, power, for the **Father**. And **Vapor**: that is, heat, for the **Holy Spirit**. And this is the first request we must make: that every creature recognize its creator. **Come to us the peace of thy kingdom.** **Thy kingdom come** <note>original: "Adueniat regnũ tuũ"</note> is the second request. For in saying "thy kingdom come": it is nothing other than asking for the peace of eternal life: which is different from this of the world. And having rightly praised the Father, we ask for the paternal inheritance: which he left to us in his final testament when he said: **My peace I leave with you.** <note>original: "Pacẽ meã relinquo uobis"</note> **FOR we cannot reach it by ourselves.** Such tranquility man cannot acquire with all his ingenuity: because by himself he cannot have true knowledge of God, in which the soul finds rest. **UNLESS it comes to us**, that is, if by divine grace it is not poured into us. **AS of his will.** This is the third petition, which is: **Thy will be done.** <note>original: "Fiat uolũtas tua"</note> Therefore, as your angels: who, after the ruin of those who rebelled against God: although they remained in their free will, were confirmed in grace. Therefore the angels make sacrifice: that is, they offer to you their good will: that is, they dedicate their every will. And this place is explained in diverse ways. Some take "heaven" for the "just" and "earth" for the "sinner." Some by "heaven" understand the "spirit," and by "earth" the "body." Some by "heaven" mean "Christ," and by "earth" the "militant church." And these three opinions are posed by **Augustine**. **Jerome** says that as the angels serve you, God, in heaven: so also do we on earth. This opinion is followed by **Aquinas**. And our poet follows this same one. **Singing Hosanna.** **Hosanna** in the Hebrew language signifies "make safe" or "vivify" or "save us" or "our salvation." **GIVE today to us the daily manna.** This is the fourth request. **Give us this day our daily bread.** <note>original: "Panem nostrũ quottidianum da nobis hodie"</note> By this he understands the grace of God: which is spiritual food by which the soul is nourished: and therefore he said "ours," because it is proper to man as a rational animal and not to the brutes: one can also understand "bread" as necessary corporal food. For while we are joined with the body: it is necessary to sustain it, and to call it "ours" according to **Gregory**; for—
