# CANTO XI. 178

[Left Column]
...he twisted himself under the weight that hindered him.
And he saw me and knew me and called out,
keeping his eyes fixed with difficulty 
upon me, as I went along all hunched over with him.
"Oh," I said to him, "are you not Oderisi,
the honor of Gubbio, and the honor of that art
which in Paris is called 'illuminating'?"
"Brother," he said, "the pages smile more
under the pen of Franco of Bologna;
the honor is now all his, and mine only in part.
Truly, I would not have been so courteous
while I lived, because of the great desire
for excellence upon which my heart was set.
For such pride, here the fee is paid;
and I would not even be here, were it not
that, while still able to sin, I turned to God.
O empty glory of human powers!
How little does the green last upon the peak,
unless it is followed by an age of decline.
<note>Oderisi suggests that fame only lasts if the following generations are "dull" or "thick-witted" (etati grosse) and fail to produce someone better.</note>
Cimabue thought to hold the field 
in painting, and now Giotto has the cry,
so that the other's fame is obscured.
So has one Guido taken from the other
the glory of the language; and perhaps he is born
who shall chase both one and the other from the nest.
<note>The "two Guidos" are the poets Guido Guinizzelli and Guido Cavalcanti. The one "born to chase them away" is widely understood to be Dante himself.</note>
Worldly reputation is nothing but a breath 
of wind, which comes now from here and now from there,
and changes name because it changes direction."

[Right Column]
...to others: as he used to do when he was occupied in such vice. But he is content to yield to Franco of Bologna as a greater master than himself. And then he said: *the pages smile more*: as if to say they are better illuminated than those Franco "penned," that is, those he painted with the brush. 
**Franco:** This man was from Bologna and was a better miniaturist. <margin>A</margin>
**The honor is now all his:** as if to say that before he arrived as a good master, I held the first place, nor was there anyone who compared to me in value. But afterward, I was conquered by him in such a way that the honor is entirely his. Nevertheless, because after him I was ahead of the others, I am not left without some share of honor. Nor is it pride that makes him say *and mine in part*, because having placed the Bolognese master before himself, he can freely speak the truth about himself. 
**Truly I would not have been so courteous:** When I was in the sin of vainglory, I would not have been so liberal in praising Franco. And certainly, this vice exists in men who have some excellence in themselves, that they cannot praise another who possesses the same virtue. It seems to them that whatever praise they give to the other, they take away from themselves.
**The great desire:** for great greed. **For excellence:** of surpassing and conquering others. Whence I pay the *fee* here: the tribute, that is, the penalty. 
**And I would not even be here:** If he, while he was alive, had always practiced vainglory, it would be necessary that after death he go to damnation. But he shows that he turned to God, that is, to penance, while *able to sin*, meaning while he was in the life in which one can earn merit or demerit. 
**O empty glory of human powers:** that is, the glory which men take in their virtues. <term>Vanagloria</term> is called <term>Cenodoxia</term> by the Greeks, which is the same as *vanagloria* in Latin. 
<note>original: "Cenodoxia"</note> 
Concerning this, Isaiah says: *The flower of the glory of exultation falls.* 
<note>original: "Flos cadens gloria exultationis"</note> 
And the Psalmist: *A thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday which has passed.* 
<note>original: "Mille anni ante oculos tuos sicut dies hesterna que periit"</note> 
**With little green upon the peak:** that is, how little the "green" (vitality) lasts at the summit of its excellence. 
**Unless it is followed:** if it is not helped by "thick ages." The meaning is: if it is not "found" (invented), then although someone may be the first in a science, virtue, or art, nevertheless they remain first for only a short time, because someone else more excellent follows. Unless it is helped by "thick ages," meaning that an age follows him which produces men of "thick" (dull) intellect. And he proves this by the example of Cimabue, who obtained the honor and the first place in painting until Giotto...

[Middle Section]
...Giotto became such a master that he surpassed and outlived Cimabue; so perhaps in another time, someone will come who will conquer Giotto. Therefore, no one should take vainglory in their own powers. 
**Cimabue:** This man, while painting was in obscurity, brought it <margin>B</margin> into good fame. Giotto became a greater and more noble master than Cimabue. 
**To hold the field:** to remain the victor; this is a metaphor from the military. 
**So has one Guido taken from the other:** just as Giotto took the glory of painting from Cimabue, so Guido Cavalcanti took the glory of the language from Guido Guinizzelli of Bologna. 
**And perhaps he is born:** Many understand that he hints at himself; but he cannot be reproached for arrogance, because he does not state it convincingly of one more than the other. And he affirms nothing. 
**Worldly reputation is nothing but a breath:** fame, glory, the "cry," and noise—he takes these to be the same thing. Worldly "noise" is the fame of mortal things. 
**Nothing but a breath:** because it flies and spreads everywhere in a short time. Whence Virgil: *Fame, an evil than which none is swifter; she thrives on speed and gains strength as she goes.*
<note>original: "Fama malum quo non aliud velocius ullum Mobilitate viget viresque acquirit eundo"</note>

[Bottom Section]
What greater voice will you have if you shed <margin>S</margin> 
your flesh when old, than if you had died 
before you left behind "pappa" or "dindi," 
<note>Dante uses "pappa" and "dindi" as medieval baby talk for bread and money.</note>
before a thousand years have passed? Which is a shorter 
span to the eternal than the blink of an eye 
is to the circle that turns slowest in the heavens.
He who takes so little of the road 
ahead of me was famous in all Tuscany, 
and now he is hardly whispered of in Siena.

Oderisi continues by showing that before a thousand years pass, you will have no more fame. **If you shed:** if you cut and separate the old flesh from yourself—that is, if you die old—rather than if you had died before you left behind *pappa* or *dindi*. That is, before you left your first years, when small children, not yet knowing how to speak, wanting to say "bread" and "money," say *pappa* and *dido*. And if anyone should say a thousand years is a great span of time, he shows that a thousand years, in comparison to eternity, is a shorter space than the blink of an eye is in comparison to the movement of the eighth sphere, which moves one degree every hundred years.
**And turns:** that is, it is revolved and circled. 
**He who takes so little of the road ahead of me:** This was Master Provenzan <margin>C</margin> Salvani of Siena, who was the lord of Siena. And he was the victor at the...

He famously cites the transition from Cimabue to Giotto and the rise of a new poet (likely Dante himself) to surpass the Guidos.</summary>

| **Of which he was lord when the Florentine rage was destroyed**, which was at that time as proud as it is now **corrupt**. <note>The "rage" refers to the Battle of Montaperti (1260), where the Sienese Ghibellines defeated the Florentine Guelphs. Later, in 1219 <note>Historical records usually cite 1269</note> with 1,400 cavalry and 8,000 infantry, he besieged Colle. But the Florentine army came to its aid and broke the Sienese: and many were killed in revenge for our people slain at Montaperti. Provenzano was captured; his head was cut off and fixed upon the point of a lance and carried throughout the camp. Therefore, to demonstrate how quickly fame fades, it is said that this man, who was shortly before his death in great fame throughout Tuscany, is now hardly whispered of in Siena. **Of which he was lord:** referring to the city of which he was master. **When the Florentine rage was destroyed:** when the Guelphs were defeated at Montaperti, a history we treated in the first Cantica <note>Inferno</note>. **Which was proud at that time** and ambitious. **And now is corrupt:** that is, a harlot; as if to say that in those days the citizens were proud, but now they are greedy, and for greed they sell the public interest. This is similar to that line of Sallust: <note>original: "O urbem venalem & cito perituram: si emptorem inveneris."</note> "O city for sale and destined to perish quickly, if a buyer can be found." I cannot help but grieve in this place, for I wish so great a poet, of such miraculous genius and learning, had not let himself be carried away by the perturbation of his spirit toward his homeland. But the verse of Homer is true: that God never gave everything to a single man. |
| **Our renown is the color of grass**, which comes and goes, and it is discolored by the same sun <note>Referring to Time</note> that makes it spring from the bitter earth. | **Our renown is the color of grass:** our fame is like grass which remains green for a short time and then dries up. The poet stays within this metaphor because he said above: "it lasts with little green upon the peak." **And that which discolors it:** the sun, which signifies Time, is that which makes the grass grow and that same sun dries it; thus Time produces fame and then consigns it to oblivion. |

| **That is, he replied, Provenzano Salvani**; and he is here because he was **presumptuous** in bringing all of Siena into his own hands. | **Presumptuous** is he who attributes to himself what is not his, or what does not belong to him. He is the same as an arrogant man. |
| He has gone thus, and travels without rest since he died; such coin he pays **to satisfy the debt for one who was too daring** in life. | **One who was too daring:** one who had too much audacity. |
| And I: **if that spirit who waits** to repent until the edge of life stays down there <note>In Ante-Purgatory</note> and does not ascend here, | **And I, if that:** The text is ordered thus: And I, Dante, replied to Oderisi by raising this doubt. If that spirit, who before he repents—that is, returns to penitence—**waits**—that is, lingers—at the **edge**—the end of life—stays down there outside of Purgatory for as much time as he lived, and does not ascend—that is, does not rise up here into Purgatory proper. |
| **unless good prayers aid him**, until as much time passes as he lived, how was this coming granted to him? | **Unless good prayer aids him**, before a time equal to his life passes, how was his coming up here granted to Provenzano? Because it has been less time since he died than the time he spent alive, this contradicts what was said above <note>The rule that those who delay repentance must wait outside the gates</note>. |
| **When he was living most gloriously, he said,** he freely stationed himself in the **Field of Siena**, setting aside every shame. | Oderisi answers the doubt raised by Dante, saying that the great humility he used in **begging for money** to draw a friend from prison shortened the time he had to stay outside Purgatory. They say that King Charles had captured a friend of this Provenzano in the rout he gave to Conradin, and set a ransom of ten thousand florins under penalty of death if it were not paid in a short time. And Provenzano so humbled himself for his friend that he placed a carpet in the **Field of Siena** <note>The Piazza del Campo</note> and begged with every kind of plea for the prisoner's redemption. The words of the text are ordered thus: Oderisi said, responding to Dante's doubt, that when Provenzano lived in his most glorious and greatest state, he freely stationed himself—firmly in the Field of Siena, as the Sienese call their plaza—setting aside all shame. |

| I will say no more, and I know I speak darkly; but little time will pass before your neighbors act so that you will be able to interpret it. | And because this sentiment is stated **obscurely**, he says that in a short time your neighbors—that is, your fellow citizens—will act so that you can interpret it. In this way, he predicts Dante’s **exile**, in which he will understand that he who goes to the mercy of others trembles when he makes his request. |

# CANTO XII 179
## CANTO XII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE

**D**ust as the oxen who go 
under the yoke, 
I went along with that 
burdened soul,

->[Woodcut illustration showing figures in a landscape with carvings on the ground. Labels: NIMROD, LUCIFER, HOLOFERNES, VL.]<-

as long as the sweet pedagogue <note>The "pedagogue" refers to Virgil, acting as a teacher or guardian.</note> allowed. 
But when he said, "Leave him and pass on, 
for here it is good with sail and oars 
that each should push his boat as much as possible." 
Straight, as one wishes to walk, I rose again 
with my body, although my thoughts 
remained bowed down and diminished. 
I had moved and followed willingly 
the steps of my master, and both of us 
already showed how light we were. 
And he said to me: "Turn your eyes downward; 
it will be good for you, to calm the way, 
to see the bed beneath your feet."

Having departed from the souls who were purging their past pride, he shows that many stories are carved into the ground over which he passed, as an example and admonition for the proud. Virgil, therefore, let him go with Oderisi <note>Oderisi da Gubbio, a manuscript illuminator whom Dante meets among the proud.</note> until they reached where such sculptures were. Then he exhorted him to pass onward. He went side by side with Oderisi. And he names Virgil a **pedagogue** <note>The text notes that in Greek this means a guardian of children.</note> not without reason. Because in Greek this word signifies one to whom children are given into custody. He wishes then to signify that he—that is, the sensuality—is a child, because it easily allows itself to be conquered by appetite like a child; and the intellect is its guide. **FOR here it is good with sail and oars to push the boat.** This in summary means they should hasten in passing. Many refer this to the idea that we must use speed in penance, and rightly so. But it also signifies that there is no vice we should leave behind more quickly than pride, because it is the greatest of all and most ruinous of all. **STRAIGHT as one wishes.** Because in the company of the soul I had gone bowed down, at present I made myself straight as one ought to walk, although my thoughts remained bowed out of compassion for the soul, and also for the humility with which he purged his pride. **I had moved and followed willingly the steps of my leader.** Because having sufficiently contemplated pride, and <term>per consequens</term> <note>Latin: "consequently"</note> purged myself of it, I followed reason and doctrine willingly, and remained lighter than usual. But Virgil admonishes him that, while walking, he should look at the sculptures which were on the ground. All these, as you will see, were stories and fables of men in whom there had been much pride. The reason it was ordained that they should be sculpted on the ground was because they do not deserve any other place—those who raised themselves higher than nature, condition, or doctrine allowed—than to lie in the lowest place. And here the intellect <note>Virgil</note> admonishes the sensuality <note>Dante the traveler</note>, so that it does not become more elated than justice requires, to look at these sculptures—that is, to bring to memory such examples. And in his mind he considers with what justice God <note>original Latin: "Deposuit potentes de sede"</note> **put down the mighty from their seat**, and in how little esteem they remained in the memory of men. The proud sought height; now they lie in the lowest grade. They sought fame; now they are in infamy. They sought divine honors; now they are deprived of all human glory. This is what the man who wishes to purge himself thinks upon. This he continually considers. This day and night he has fixed in his mind.

**A**s, so that there may be memory of them, 
above the buried are the ground-tombs 
bearing marked what they were before. 
Wherefore many times people weep there 
due to the prick of remembrance, 
which only to the pious gives its heels. <note>An idiom meaning the "sting" of memory only spurs those who are compassionate to tears.</note>
So I saw them there, but of better likeness 
according to the figured craftsmanship, 
as much as the path jutted out from the mountain.

He demonstrates that he saw those stories sculpted on the ground in this way, which he will write about shortly after; just as one sees sculpted the images of men already dead upon their tombs, so that such images may bring back to our minds the memory of them. Whence he says, **like the ground-tombs**, that is, the tombs placed in the ground over the buried—that is, over those who are buried there—**bearing marked what he was before**, that is, they bear sculpted the buried man in that form he had before he was dissolved and returned to ash. And these images are carved so that there may be memory of them. Whence it happens that **there**—that is, over those images—people often weep. Because friends and relatives passing there weep. **BY the prick of remembrance**, that is, because the memory of the dead friend or relative pricks and torments the soul. But such a prick **does not give of its heels**—that is, it does not spur any but the **pious**—that is, the compassionate; because he who is not compassionate does not...

<summary>This page describes Dante and Oderisi walking bowed like oxen before Virgil instructs Dante to stand straight and look at the ground. The ground is revealed to be covered in intricate carvings of historical and mythological examples of fallen pride, compared to floor tombs in a church.</summary>

# PURGATORIO

| **PURGATORIO** | <margin>[Right column commentary]</margin> |
| :--- | :--- |

"So I saw there." Thus I saw that place represented—that is, carved and sculpted with a better appearance, meaning with a better image according to craftsmanship, following the rules of art. **SEE THERE AN ANGEL** who readies himself, who hurries and prepares. This angel is that **divine grace** of which we have already spoken so many times. We turned our bodies there;
"Blessed are the poor in spirit" <note>original: "beati pauperes spiritu"</note>

Ah, how different are these openings
from the infernal ones! For here one enters
amidst songs, but down there through fierce laments.
Already we were mounting up the holy stairs,
and I seemed to be much lighter
than I had seemed before on the level ground.
And I asked: "Master, what heavy thing
has been lifted from me, so that almost no
fatigue is felt by me as I walk?"
He replied: "When the sins remaining
still upon your face—which are fading—
shall be totally erased like the first one,
your feet will be so conquered by good will
that they will not only feel no fatigue,
but it will be a delight for them to be pushed upward."
Then I did like those who walk
with something on their head unknown to them,
except that the signs of others make them suspicious.
Because the hand helps to make certain,
and searches and finds, and fulfills that office
which cannot be accomplished by sight.
And with the fingers of my right hand spread out,
I found only six of the letters carved
by the one with the keys <note>The Angel at the Gate of Purgatory, who carved seven 'P's (Peccata/Sins) on Dante's forehead.</note> upon my temples.
At which my teacher, looking on, smiled.

[Right Column]

<margin>Souls who were purging themselves of pride showed their joy at Dante's ascent by singing; because here there is no envy of another's good, but charity. They sang: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" <note>original: "Beati pauperes spiritu: quoniam ipsorum est regnum celorum"</note>. Nor is it anything else to be "poor in spirit," except to lack pride. Therefore, those spirits rejoiced that Dante had already been purged of such a vice.</margin>

<margin>d. This shows Dante having become very light. To which Virgil responds, explaining that this lightness comes to him because one of the seven sins has already been cancelled. But when all shall be cancelled, not only will the climb not be a struggle, but it will be a supreme delight. And note that Virgil says the first sin was already completely extinguished, and the others nearly extinguished, to indicate that once the vice of pride is entirely purged, the others remain for the most part already purged.</margin>

<margin>n. The poet was not aware that one of the seven sins was already completely removed, and the others greatly diminished. Therefore, moved by Virgil's words, he searched with his fingers "spread"—that is, simply—and found only six. And it happened to him as to one who carries something on his head and does not know it; but seeing those around him laugh, and the eyes being unable to perform their office because they cannot see the top of the head, the hands compensate. And through them, man becomes certain of what he did not know. These words signify that the senses cannot be a true judge if the soul is still being purged of some vice. But reason shows it. Nor does a man notice the sins he has in his head, except after he is purged of the pride that makes us so swollen and bloated that we seem to ourselves to be virtuous. But once pride is discarded, then we begin to notice our errors. Virgil smiled: because the intellect laughs at the ignorance of the senses, and almost becomes another Democritus <note>Democritus was a Greek philosopher known as the "laughing philosopher" because he mocked the vanities of mankind.</note>.</margin>

# CANTO XIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

**N**ow we were at the top of the stairs
where for a second time
the mountain is cut back—
the mountain that "un-evils" <note>original: "dismala." A term created by Dante to describe the process of the mountain removing the "mal" (evil) from the souls.</note> those who climb it.
There, a terrace circles

No shadow is seen, nor any sign that appears;
the bank appeared bare, and the path appeared plain,

[Bottom Commentary]

<margin>Having left the first ledge where we saw the punishments of the proud, we now enter, having climbed the stairs, the second; in which envy is purged. Envy is a mutual torment of the soul, which consumes us for the good of others, and such pain returns upon itself. And Augustine said envy is pain taken from another's happiness. Wherefore Horace says: "The envious man is burned by envy inside and out" <note>original: "Invidus invidia comburitur intus & extra"</note>. Also: "The envious man grows thin at the fat success of another" <note>original: "Invidus alterius rebus macrescit opimis"</note>. And Solomon, wishing to show how much torment the Envious man gives to himself, said: "He who rejoices in the ruin of another will not go unpunished" <note>original: "Qui in ruina letatur alterius non erit impunitus"</note>. We were therefore at the...</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante Alighieri’s *Purgatorio*, specifically moving from the first terrace (Pride) to the second terrace (Envy).</meta>

# 181

->PURGATORIO<-

Now at the top of the stairs that lead onto the second terrace: which "un-evils" <note>original: *dismala*; a term used by Dante to describe the process of purging or removing evil</note>, that is, it removes the evil and the sin from those who climb it. This terrace encircles and surrounds the mountain, creating a level path around it; but it bends its arc more sharply, that is, it makes a smaller circuit: because, as we have said above, the more the mountain rises, the more it tapers, and for this reason the circle of the terrace comes to be smaller. And thus the sins decrease in degree <note>literally "step down" or diminish in gravity</note>. And the greater sins are always the lower ones. Therefore, the punishments likewise taper and diminish.

No shadow <note>meaning a soul or spirit</note>, nor sign, nor painting, nor sculpture is seen there, as there was on the ledge below <note>referring to the first terrace where examples of pride and humility were carved into the rock</note>. Instead, the path and the bank remain bare and simple. And the stones of which the terrace is made are of a livid <term>livid: a bluish-gray or leaden hue, which in the Middle Ages was associated with the color of bruised flesh and the "black bile" of envy</term> color. He indicates by this lack of painting or sculpture that envy does not manifest or appear openly except when mixed with some other sin. Or indeed, he said "shadow," meaning any soul: because the envious do not walk along the terrace <insert>in plain sight</insert>, and they were in a place further off. The livid color is appropriate to envy.

<summary>This page describes the transition to the second terrace of Purgatory, where Envy is purged. The commentator explains the physical narrowing of the mountain and why this level lacks the artistic reliefs found in the previous circle.</summary>
<keywords>Purgatory, Second Terrace, Envy, Dante Alighieri, livid color, symbolism of sin, mountain architecture</keywords>

From above I heard this person say:

And the shade who was asked this question

[Top Center Column]
"For from its beginning, where it is thrust forth

Because of this, the inhabitants of that miserable valley
have so changed their nature
that it seems Circe <note>The mythological sorceress who turned men into beasts</note> had them in her pasture."

[Middle Commentary Block]
**And was never worthy:** because it has no inhabitants adorned with any virtue; and to demonstrate this he begins to describe it: and he places its birth in Falterona, which is part of the Apennines. He says, therefore, that from the beginning of the Arno, which is born where the rugged mountain—that is, the Apennines—which is like the Alps, and is so "pregnant"—that is, so swollen and high, or truly pregnant with waters, because in a small space it produces both the Arno and the Tiber. **Which in few places passes beyond that height:** although the Apennines are very long, nevertheless in few places are they higher than at Falterona. **From which Pelorus is cut off:** it was the opinion of the ancients that the Apennines, of which we spoke in the *Inferno*, reach not only as far as Reggio, but also anciently went into Sicily; and its final part was that which since remained a mountain in Sicily, and is called Pelorus.

[Bottom Left Column]
"Among foul pigs, more worthy of acorns <note>original: "galle"; gall-nuts or bitter oak-apples</note>
than of any food made for human use,
it first directs its poor path.
It finds curs <note>original: "botoli"; small, yapping dogs</note> then, coming further down,
snarling more than their power warrants,

It goes on falling, and the more it swells,

Bloody he emerges from that dismal forest."

**Before we explain the words spoken of the valley:** understand that of these two spirits, the one speaking is Sir Guido del Duca of Brettinoro in Romagna. And the other to whom he speaks is Sir Rinieri da Calboli of Forlì. **Pigs** he calls all of Casentino as far as Arezzo, and especially the counts of the Guidi family, who were very luxurious men. **Poor path:** because it has little water. **Curs:** these are the Aretines; he equates them to "botoli," dogs of small body, and wants to show that the Aretines have much disdain but little strength; **disdainfully turning its snout away:** because once the river is near Arezzo, it turns to the right and leaves Arezzo behind. **The more it swells** through the rivers that flow into the Arno, **the more it finds that the dogs become wolves:** the cur snarls and barks, but the wolf is placed for the greedy, the predator, and the raptor; and this he intends for the noblemen and counts who were in the Valdarno, and partly for the **Florentines**. **Descending then through deeper hollows:** he places those of the lower Valdarno, and finally the **Pisans**, whom he calls **foxes** to denote that they are full of fraud and deception. **I will not stop:** he places three things in this tercet. First, he shows he does not care about being heard, which signifies that his conscience is now clean; he speaks not out of envy or hatred, but out of just indignation. Second, because he hopes to be useful to Dante by making him cautious. And in the third place, he shows that having to speak of future things, he will tell the truth, since he has heard it from a "true spirit" <note>A divine revelation</note>. **I see your grandson:** This was Sir Fulcieri da Calboli of Forlì, of whom he predicts that he will become the <term>Podestà</term> <note>A high-ranking judicial official or governor</note> of Florence, and for a price will kill many. We wrote in the sixth canto of the *Inferno* that in 1302 the Blacks <note>The Black Guelph faction</note> were restored to Florence by Charles of Valois. These men, fearing greatly the power and favor the Whites <note>The White Guelph faction</note> had in Florence, corrupted Sir Fulcieri to seize many of the White party, among whom were Sir Betto Gherardini, Masino and Donato Cavalcanti, Sir Neri Adimari, and Sir Tignoso de' Macci; and as men who wished to disturb the tranquil state of the...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XIV, where the spirit of Guido del Duca laments the moral decay of the Romagna region. The text provides historical context for the noble families and individuals mentioned in the poem.</meta>

CANTO XIV. 165

...for cultivating them now fewer would come.
Where is the good Lucio and Arrigo Mainardi,
Pier Traversaro and Guido di Carpigna?
O you Romagnuols turned into bastards!
When in Bologna a blacksmith <term>si ralligna</term> <note>Literally "takes root again," referring to a commoner establishing a noble lineage.</note>,
When in Faenza a Bernardin di Fosco
comes forth noble from a tiny weed.

**IN BOLOGNA.** Of the good sought for truth and for pleasure. According to the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "peripatetici"; followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> there are three species of good: the **honorable**, the **useful**, and the **delightful**. But the honorable is the true good. Therefore, he spoke of "truth" regarding the goods of the soul, which is honor; and of "pleasure" regarding the goods of the body and of fortune, which are the useful and the delightful. He concludes therefore that all of Romagna is made barren and poor of the "good sought for truth"—that is, the honorable good, which is the true good—and of the "good sought for pleasure"—that is, for delight and luxury. This signifies that it is void of virtue, which creates the honorable good, and of concord and peace, which create the delightful. Afterwards, he adds that everything within these boundaries—meaning all of Romagna—is filled with poisonous brushwood; and he says this as a metaphor. Because our souls are likened to the earth. For if the earth is not cultivated, it quickly becomes wild and fills with thorns, burrs, and every wicked weed. But if it is cultivated with diligence, it remains purged of those things, and good trees and every grain produce excellent fruit. So too human souls: if they are not exercised in the virtues, they become savage and beastly, producing the actions not of a man but of wild and cruel beasts. But if they are cultivated with excellent laws and institutions, and with civil and moral precepts, they produce every virtue. But here he shows that the "weeds"—that is, the vices—have so multiplied that they cannot be extinguished. This signifies that there are so many more wicked people than good ones that it is impossible to wipe them out, especially because they have formed a firm habit of vice. **O WHERE IS THE GOOD LUCIO.** <margin>X</margin> This was Messer Lucio da Valbona, a man of excellence and full of virtue. His daughter, Caterina, overcome by love, secretly joined herself with Riccardo, a noble youth; and Messer Lucio, with his prudence, had them marry, as our **Boccaccio** narrates at length in one of his novellas <note>A reference to the *Decameron*, Day 5, Novel 4.</note>. **ARRIGO MAINARDI** <margin>Y</margin> of Faenza: some say he was from Bertinoro, and a great friend of the one who speaks here. **PIER TRAVERSARO** <margin>Z</margin> was the Lord of Ravenna, magnanimous and highly reputed, who married one of his daughters to Stephen, King of Hungary. His power flourished in the times of Frederick II, against whom he eventually rebelled. But after his death, Frederick besieged and conquered Ravenna. **GUIDO DI CARPIGNA** <margin>A</margin> was a nobleman from Montefeltro, to whom none was equal in liberality. **A BLACKSMITH TAKES ROOT.** That is, when a craftsman of lowly condition makes himself great and causes a lineage and nobility to be born from him, as did Lamberta the blacksmith, who rose to such a state that he was almost the lord of Bologna; and from him descended Messer Fabbro de’ Lambertacci. **BERNARDIN DI FOSCO.** <margin>B</margin> This was the ancestor of Messer Bernardino who ruled Faenza, a man of low fortune but of most excellent wisdom and counsel, so much so that he came into great esteem among his fellow citizens.

Do not marvel, Tuscan, if I weep
when I remember, with Guido da Prata,
Ugolin d’Azzo who lived among us.
Federigo Tignoso and his company,
the house of Traversara and the Anastagi,
and both the one and the other family now heirless.
The ladies and the knights, the labors and the leisure
that love and courtesy once inspired in us,
there where hearts have now become so wicked.
O Bertinoro, why do you not flee away,
since your noble family has departed,
and many people, to avoid becoming corrupt?

**DO NOT MARVEL, O TUSCAN.** <gloss>i</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Guido del Duca in the Second Terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of Envy is purged. Guido has been lamenting the decline of noble families in the Romagna region.</meta>

->PURGATORIO:<-

[Left Column - Main Text]

...may no testimony of them ever remain.
**O Ugolino de’ Fantolini**, <note>Ugolino de' Fantolini (d. 1278) was a noble of Faenza known for his integrity. Since he died without male heirs who could ruin his reputation, his name remains "safe" or "pure."</note> your name is secure, since no one is expected to make it obscure by straying from your virtuous lineage.
But go your way now, for it pleases me more to weep than to speak, so much has your discourse <note>original: "ragione"</note> constrained my mind.

<margin>D. Ugolino de' Fantolini. This man was also a gentleman of Faenza, full of virtue and good manners. After these words, Guido gives Dante leave to depart, showing that it pains him greatly that virtue is extinguished in Romagna. **SO MUCH HAS YOUR DISCOURSE CONSTRAINED MY MIND**: I take pleasure in weeping because your discourse—that is, human reason, which induces every man toward charity (which is the proper virtue of man)—moves me to compassion.</margin>

We knew those dear souls heard us going; therefore, by staying silent, they made us confident of the path.
After we were alone, proceeding on, a flash appeared like a bolt that cleaves the air; a voice struck against us, saying:
"**Whoever finds me will slay me!**" <note>Genesis 4:14. These are the words of Cain after murdering his brother Abel, fearful of retribution.</note>
And it fled like thunder that dies away if the cloud suddenly bursts.
As soon as our hearing had a truce from it, behold, another voice came with such a great crash <note>original: "fracasso"</note> that it resembled thunder following quickly:
"**I am Aglauros, who became stone!**"
And then, to press closer to the poet <note>Virgil</note>, I stepped backward rather than forward.

[Right Column - Commentary]

...father of Mainardo. These men ruled over Imola and Faenza. They were called the power of the Pagani. Of them, Mainardo was the lord of Imola and Faenza, a man outstanding for the beauty of his body and military virtue. He is called a "demon" <note>Guido del Duca calls him "il demonio" earlier in the Canto.</note> because he was very astute; in Tuscany, he held the Guelph side because the Guelphs ruled there, but in Romagna, he favored the Ghibellines, as they were powerful in 그 region. It will be useful that a testimony of their true praise remains, despite what we have said regarding Mainardo’s cunning. But of him it is said...

<margin>B. Although we did not ask for the way, nor did the souls see if we were keeping the right path, nevertheless we trusted that since they heard us, they would have corrected us if we were not going well. **AFTER WE WERE ALONE**: We had already passed the souls and remained alone when we heard two voices. Here it should be noted that just as above he placed three voices exhorting one to charity, so here he places two which, by example, can draw us away from envy. The first three voices were heard while still among the souls to show that for those entering the purgatorial virtues, such exhortations are helpful. But because there is no further need for examples to restrain them from envy <note>once they have passed the terrace</note>, he states that these last two voices were heard after he had departed from the souls. **WHOEVER FINDS ME WILL SLAY ME**: Abel and Cain were brothers, as we have shown elsewhere. Abel was a shepherd, a just man full of religion; whenever he sacrificed to God, he offered the best lambs of the flock, wherefore he prospered more every day. Cain, on the contrary, was a wicked man without religion, and from his farming, he always offered the saddest ears of grain from the field. Because of this impiety, he fell into greater poverty. Moved by envy, he killed his brother Abel. God, being angry, cursed him. And he, turning to God, said: "My iniquity is so great that I do not deserve...</margin>

[Bottom Block - Commentary]

...pardon. Behold, you shall drive me today from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face, and I shall be a fugitive in the world; therefore, everyone who finds me will kill me." And God replied that they would not. Therefore, Dante, wishing to recall men from envy, uses these words. **AND IT FLED LIKE THUNDER**: Because such an example should fill every man with terror, so that he guards himself against envy and flees such a vice in his soul. **IF THE CLOUD SUDDENLY BURSTS**: This shows that thunder is nothing other than the refraction of condensed clouds. **AS OUR HEARING HAD A TRUCE FROM IT**: i.e., I heard it no more; behold, the other voice was heard by us with such a great crash <note>original: "fracasso"</note>, i.e., with such a great noise. He spoke well because "crash" signifies what in Latin is called *fragor* <gloss>a breaking sound</gloss>, which signifies a sound made by broken things, like thunder. It resembled thunder that follows the flash quickly and suddenly, because the thunder that comes immediately after the flash is always greater. In truth, the flash and the thunder happen at the same time, but because the sense of sight is faster than hearing, one sees the light of the flash before hearing the thunder. It should be noted that exhortation to virtue should be gentle, like the three voices heard above. But dehortation <note>warning away</note> from vice should be terrifying. **I AM AGLAUROS WHO BECAME STONE**: The poets feign that there were three daughters of Cecrops, King of Athens: Herse, Pandrosos, and Aglauros. Mercury saw them during the sacrifices of Minerva and fell in love with Herse, the most beautiful of the three sisters. Wanting to go to Herse's chamber, he had to pass the place where Aglauros was. She wanted to know the reason for Mercury's coming. Mercury revealed his desire to her and, with many prayers, comforted her so she would lend him secret help. But the very greedy and envious sister refused to favor him or keep his secret unless she received a great sum of money from him. Minerva was offended by Aglauros because shortly before she had dared to uncover the basket under which Erichthonius, born of Vulcan, was hidden. Therefore, moved to anger, she incited Envy to goad Aglauros so that she would envy Mercury's love for her sister and not give Mercury passage. Consequently, when Mercury could not persuade her with prayers or promises, he turned her into stone. Thus, the Poet uses this example to terrify men away from this vice. The description of the House of Envy also fits in this place, which Ovid describes with no less learning than eloquence. **AND THEN TO PRESS CLOSER TO THE POET**: This shows that he was walking ahead of Virgil, but then, out of fear, he drew back to stay close to him. This demonstrates that often the senses overreach through overly ardent desire, but when such examples terrify it, the sense restrains itself and submits to reason.</margin>

<summary>Dante hears the terrifying "claps of thunder" representing examples of envy—Cain and Aglauros—serving as warnings to the souls. Landino's commentary explains the mythological and biblical origins of these figures and discusses the psychological transition from desire to reason through fear.</summary>
<keywords>Ugolino de' Fantolini, Cain and Abel, Aglauros, Mercury, Envy, Mainardo Pagani, Virgil, Purgatorio Canto 14, Human Reason</keywords>

# CANTO XII 186

Already the air was quiet on every side
& he said to me: "That was the hard <term>bit</term><note>The original word *camo* refers to a bit, muzzle, or halter used to control a horse; here it signifies the harsh warnings that restrain human sin.</note>
which should hold man within his right goal.
But you take the bait, so that the hook
of the ancient adversary <note>The "ancient adversary" is a traditional name for Satan.</note> draws you to him,
& therefore little avail the bridle or the recall.
The heavens call to you and circle around you,
showing you their eternal beauties,
& yet your eye looks only at the ground;
wherefore He who discerns all things strikes you."

**T**his which Virgil says at present, he had already promised to say when he said: **THE BRIDLE** <note>In the previous Canto (XIII), Virgil explains that the spirits are restrained by "bits" (examples of punished envy) and encouraged by "reins" (examples of generosity).</note> should be of a contrary sound. I believe you will hear it, in my opinion, before you reach the pass of pardon. And he said to me: **THAT WAS THE HARD BIT**. That is: the voice of Cain; and that of Aglauros was the hard bit, that is, the hard bridle. Whence the Psalmist says: *With bit and bridle bind fast their jaws* <note>original Latin: "In camo & frẽo maxillas eorũ cõſtrige," from Psalm 32:9.</note>; because such examples ought to restrain everyone, so that they do not lapse into this vice <note>The vice of Envy.</note>. <meta>This page provides a linguistic and allegorical commentary on the opening of Canto XV of Purgatory, specifically focusing on the Pilgrim’s encounter with the blinding light of the Angel of Mercy.</meta>

# PURGATORY

...by the splendor: the splendor of the sun, which hit him from the front, first weighed upon his brow; but then the splendor of the angel appearing weighed upon him much more than before. Wherefore he wondered at things not counted <note>original: *cose non conte*; meaning things that are unfamiliar or have not been experienced before</note>, that is, because the appearance of the angel had never happened to him before. **Wherefore I raised.** Seeing myself dazzled by the excessive splendor, I placed my hands above my eyebrows and made a roof over my eyes so that the rays of the splendor would not strike them. **I made for myself a sunshade** <note>original: *solecchio*</note>—that is, I diminished the intensity of that sun for my eyes. *Solecchio* means a "little sun." Hence, when the sun strikes us in our eyes and we remove those rays from our eyes with some obstacle <note>such as shading one's eyes with a hand</note>, we call such a removal a *solecchio*, because it diminishes the sun. **WHICH**—that is, the sunshade—**FILES AWAY**—that is, removes and lessens—**FROM THE EXCESSIVE** visible: that is, from the too-much light.

->As when from water or from a mirror<-
->the ray leaps to the opposite side<-

# CANTO XV 187

...the leader when he said: "O human race, why do you set your heart where it is necessary to exclude partnership?" <note>original: "O gente humana: perche poni il cuore dove è mestiere di consorto divieto." [A] sentiment certainly appropriate for the intellect wishing to instruct sensuality. For it shows him the origin of envy, so that he may guard against it. And he responds that Guido <note>Guido del Duca, a nobleman of Romagna whom Dante encountered among the Envious in Canto XIV.</note> now knows in Purgatory the harm that follows from his greatest flaw—that is, the sin of envy—and therefore he should not wonder—that is, he should not be amazed. Because since charity is absent, he responds [against] the others. And certainly envy always carries its own punishment with it, because other sins have some pleasure <note>original: "voluptà"</note>. It is sweet for the proud man to obtain lordship. It is sweet for the greedy man to accumulate gold and silver. The lustful man rejoices to enjoy the thing he loves. But envy always torments its possessor. This is in proportion to the ardor and charity that they have within themselves toward God and their neighbor <note>original: ".pximo" (proximo). In this theological context, it refers to the Christian duty to love one's fellow human beings.</note>. Their eternal worth, eternal goodness, and glory increase as their charity becomes greater. <meta>This page serves as a reference key for deciphering specific scribal abbreviations, archaic spellings, and key names encountered in the manuscript's transcription.</meta>

# Manuscript Reference and Abbreviation Guide

*   **For** or **Through** <note>indicated in the text by a 'p' with a stroke</note>
*   **And** or **That** <note>indicated by a 'q' with a stroke, a common shorthand for the suffix '-que'</note>
*   **Christ** <note>original: "xpo", a traditional abbreviation using the Greek letters Chi and Rho</note>
*   **First Martyr** <note>original: "ptomartyre", referring to Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr</note>
*   **Which** <note>appears in the script as "ilche", though it may be misread as "llche"</note>

<meta>This page continues the introductory commentary or prologue to Dante's Purgatorio, specifically discussing the etymological and astrological origins of the names of the months in the Roman calendar as established by Romulus.</meta>

**PURGATORIO**

And from Homer, the "man-slayer" <note>original: "adriphonte," a corruption of the Greek *andriphontes*, meaning man-slayer or homicide</note>, he wanted the second month to take its name from Venus, a benevolent planet suited for procreation and for mitigating the malignancy of Mars. From this, we see that nature has ordained that even in the twelve signs of the <term>zodiac|the belt of constellations through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move</term>, after Aries—the house of Mars—follows Taurus, the house of Venus. And similarly, before the Scorpio of Mars comes the Libra of Venus, so that the martial fury may be tempered by the houses of the benign Venus. Others say that the month is not called *Haprile* <note>referring to the Greek name for Venus, *Aphrodite*</note> after Venus, but *Aprile* without the 'h.' This is because in that month the earth, which was previously frozen and constricted by the cold, knows how to open itself <note>referring to the Latin *aperire*, meaning "to open"</note> to produce new flowers and foliage. For this reason, the Athenians call it *Anthesterion* <note>an Ancient Greek month name</note>, which is as if to say "powerful in flowers," because at that time everything blooms. 

Later, after Romulus had divided the people into two parts—the <term>maiores|the elders or senior citizens of Rome</term> and the <term>iuniores|the youth or those of military age</term>—the third month was called May after the elders, and the fourth was called June after the youth. The other months were named by their number; and after June, the fourth month, follow <term>Quintilis|the fifth month, later renamed July</term>, <term>Sextilis|the sixth month, later renamed August</term>, September, and October.

<summary>This page explains the naming conventions of the Roman calendar months, linking April to either Venus or the "opening" of the earth, and May and June to the social divisions of the Roman people under Romulus.</summary>
<keywords>calendar, etymology, Romulus, Venus, Mars, zodiac, April, May, June, Anthesterion, astrology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of free will and the soul's origin, following the previous discussion on why the world has fallen into corruption.</meta>

-># PURGATORIO<-

**[Main text]**

You lie free, yet subject to a greater force
And a better nature; and that creates
The mind, which the heavens do not have in their care.
Therefore, if the present world goes astray,
The cause is in you, and in you let it be sought;
And of this I will now be a true scout for you.

From His hand, who gazes upon it with love
Before it exists, like a little girl
Who goes weeping and laughing in her play,
Comes the simple little soul, which knows nothing
Save that, moved by a glad Creator,
It willingly turns to what delights it.
At first, it tastes the flavor of a small good;
There it is deceived, and runs after it,
Unless a guide or a curb turns its love aside.
Thus it was necessary to set up laws as a curb;
It was necessary to have a king who could discern
At least the tower of the true city.

**[Commentary]**

<note>This commentary explains Dante's argument against "astrological determinism"—the idea that stars force us to sin.</note>

**YOU** who live. This is the reasoning: it shows that men are blind because they attribute every cause to the heavens; that is, they attribute every cause of our actions to celestial influence, as if the heavens by necessity pushed us to act or not act, to do evil or good according to the nature of such influence, and we could not defend ourselves against it. If this were true, **Free Will** would be extinguished in us. Not only do theologians posit Free Will, but all the most excellent philosophers confess it. Nor would there be **virtue**—which is a choice-based habit—nor **vice**, if it were not in our power to choose between good and evil. 

The Heavens initiate our movements, according to theologians, philosophers, and astrologers; but the celestial bodies have no influence that necessitates the rational soul in its intellect or its will, nor its Free Will. This is shown by **Ptolemy** in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note> and by **Aristotle** in the first book of *On Interpretation*. And **the Aquinan** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, writing against the heathens, affirms with the authority of Aristotle in the third book of *On the Soul* that the heavens are not the cause of our wills and choices directly. But they can make an impression upon the first movements of the soul, which we can resist with **reason** and with Free Will. If we choose well through these, we deserve merit; if poorly, we deserve blame. This is not the case with the "first movements," because they are not in our power. The stars influence bodily movements, and these can incline the soul. But they cannot necessitate it. In short: **Mars** incites anger, and this moves the soul. But the soul, through its Free Will, can resist. Similarly, the **sun** with the seed of man generates the human being. But it cannot pour in the rational soul, which comes solely from God without intermediary. The soul is more noble than the entire sensible world, and the stars are merely corporeal. Therefore, the heavens do not necessitate the soul. If they did, Free Will would perish. 

In summary, there is in us first the **appetite** <note>The raw desire or instinct</note>, then the **rational will**. The appetite has its first motion and inclination from the external constellations. The will has its motion and inclination internally from reason. And it comes into action through Free Will. This "second will" is what makes us deserve merit or blame.

**BUT SUPPOSE I SAY**, even if all our inclinations and soul-movements proceeded from the heavens, nevertheless **Light** is given to you—that is, **reason** and **intellect** are given to you, by which you know good and virtue, and evil and vice. And certainly, Free Will is in you, and it is in your power to choose what you want. Therefore, if it struggles to resist those first movements that the heavens begin, and **endures hardship**—that is, it resists in the first battles between the inclination given by the heavens and reason—reason, knowing that thing to be evil, desires to flee it. **THEN** it conquers everything. Because if it resists the first impulse, it becomes continent and wins against a **Greater force and a greater nature**. The human soul is subject not only to God, who is a greater force and greater nature than the "secondary causes" <note>Natural forces like the stars</note>, but it is also created directly by Him and remains free through God. 

**AND THAT GREATER FORCE CREATES** the human mind, which **the heavens do not have in their care**. Because God does not create the soul through secondary causes, but creates it immediately. **THEREFORE**, he concludes that **IF THE PRESENT WORLD**—that is, the false opinions and the depraved and corrupt appetites you have in your faculties because of the contagion the body gives to the soul—**LEADS YOU ASTRAY**, taking you off the right path and away from reason, **THE CAUSE IS IN YOU**, since you have Free Will. **IN YOU LET IT BE SOUGHT**, let it be requested and searched for within yourselves.

**THE HUMAN SOUL**, of which we have spoken, **COMES FROM THE HAND** and is produced by the power **OF HIM**, of God Himself, who **GAZES UPON IT** and considers it with pleasure. As it says in *Genesis*: <note>original: "Vidit que deus oia q̄ fecerat: & erāt ualde bona"</note> **"And God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good."** <note>Genesis 1:31</note> For God in His eternity sees everything that He shall later produce successively in time. I say, then, that the human soul comes from the hand of God; that is, it is created by Him. And not without reason does he say "it comes out," because it departs having been created, not bound in a form such that it cannot go where it wants, but with the Free Will to be able to return or not return to Him. **LIKE A... LITTLE GIRL**; that is, in the likeness of a small child who **PLAYS**—meaning it shows its childish and tender age, now weeping and now laughing. Because just as the tiny little girl, lacking prudence and moved by appetite rather than reason, cries and laughs over a small thing, so it shows that our soul is naturally disposed toward passions and disturbances. 

**THE SIMPLE LITTLE SOUL WHICH KNOWS NOTHING**. According to the opinion of **Aristotle**, who holds that the soul is like a **blank tablet** <note>Tabula rasa</note> capable of receiving whatever is imprinted upon it. **SAVE THAT, MOVED BY A GLAD CREATOR, IT WILLINGLY TURNS TO WHAT DELIGHTS IT**. In every created thing, there is born a supreme desire to return to its origin, which is its Creator, the supreme good. Therefore, our soul, created by God—in whom there is supreme joy because He is the supreme good—naturally desires to be joined with God. But being eager and desirous of this supreme good, it is often **DECEIVED** because, having newly arrived in the body, it cannot yet exercise reason, which could recognize the true good and discern it from the false. It uses, therefore, only the senses and the appetite, through which it cannot taste the flavor of the supreme good, which is God. Instead, it **TASTES THE FLAVOR OF A SMALL GOOD**, that is, temporal goods, and in these, it is deceived. Because the senses are lured by the lusts and pleasures of earthly things, the soul thinks that something is supreme which is either not good at all or is very small...

<margin>
small brief...
good of...
youth
many the...
mind the...
judgment...
intellect...
invited...
reins of things
</margin>

<summary>This page features Dante's explanation of Free Will, arguing that while the stars may influence human impulses, they do not dictate human destiny because God grants each soul reason and moral agency. The commentary draws on Aristotle, Ptolemy, and Thomas Aquinas to support the idea that the soul is created directly by a "glad Creator" and must be guided by laws to avoid being deceived by worldly pleasures.</summary>
<keywords>Free Will, astrology, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Creation of the Soul, Reason, Appetite, Law, Tabula Rasa, Purgatorio Canto XVI</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XVI of Purgatorio, specifically addressing Dante’s discourse on the causes of human corruption and the necessity of law and leadership.</meta>

# CANTO XVI. 191

with the good. Aristotle writes most correctly in the third book *On the Soul*: "The good of the intellect is the ultimate happiness." <note>original: "Bonum intellectus est ultima beatitudo"</note> And if the good of the intellect is indeed happiness, it follows that it is God. Therefore, this is what our intellect seeks, provided it is not deceived in its choice by the senses and by appetite. I know that to explain this passage, it would be useful to refer to many things which I narrated in the second book of our *Camaldolese Disputations*. <note>Cristoforo Landino, the author of this commentary, refers to his famous work *Disputationes Camaldulenses*, a philosophical dialogue on the active vs. contemplative life.</note> But such a large volume does not permit me to be overly wordy in every detail. **OF A LITTLE good:** since reason has not yet been awakened, the sense follows, which falsely judges that earthly goods—where there is some amusement—are the highest good. **IT FOLLOWS:** if our intellect is awakening; if the doctrine or precepts of a more learned man are warning us; if the grace of God is illuminating us. **OR THE RESTRAINT or divine and human law:** does NOT twist its love, does not turn back the love that it has placed in earthly and fleeting things toward the celestial and highest good. **THENCE it was fitting to set law as a curb.** It was a necessity: since men allowed themselves to be transported by appetite and were not ruling themselves according to reason, it was necessary to restrain their pride, ambition, greed, and lust with laws. This was so that those who did not abstain from vice for the love of virtue might abstain out of fear of punishment. For: "The wicked shrink from sin through fear of punishment; the good shrink from sin through love of virtue." <note>original: "oderunt peccare mali formidine penæ. Oderunt peccare boni uirtutis amore."</note> As Horace learnedly writes. **It was fitting to have a king.** It is not enough to have laws if there is no King, Prince, or Magistrate to defend them and see them observed. And this person must be of such life, doctrine, and prudence that, if he does not know the true city of eternal life, he at least discerns the tower—that is, the guardianship of that city, which is justice.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| The laws exist, but who puts a hand to them? | **THERE ARE** certainly laws. But there is no one to put a hand to them. For natural law is innate in our minds. But concupiscence <term>concupiscence: strong desire or lust, often specifically for earthly rather than spiritual goods</term> conquers reason. Nor was there ever a nation or religion that had divine and human laws so ready as the Christian one has. The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> had Lycurgus. The Athenians had Draco and Solon. The Cretans had Minos. Their laws were much regulated toward justice as far as human prudence could allow. But Christian laws have their origin in divine truth. But what does it profit if the administrators of such laws are the first to corrupt them? **THEREFORE, who puts a hand to them?** Who rules them? **NO ONE.** For neither do the popes put a hand to ecclesiastical laws, nor do the princes and lay magistrates defend the temporal ones. **To PUT a hand** means to operate according to the laws. For no one can correct others if they do not first correct themselves. |
| No one; because the shepherd who goes before | |
| Can ruminate but does not have cloven hooves; | |
| Because the people, who see their guide | |
| Reach only for that good for which they are greedy, | |
| Feed on that, and ask for nothing further. | |
| Well can you see that bad leadership | |
| Is the cause that has made the world wicked, | |
| And not nature which may be corrupt in you. | |

**THE shepherd.** Correctly he calls every prince a shepherd, according to what we have said in another place. **CAN ruminate but does not have cloven hooves.** We read in Leviticus that God commanded Moses that they should eat the meat of every animal that had cloven hooves and ruminated. <note>Landino is citing the dietary laws of Leviticus 11, which Dante uses as an allegory for spiritual discernment and the separation of powers.</note> Therefore, one of the two is not enough. And for this reason, the meat of the pig and the camel was not permitted, because they do not ruminate, even though they have cloven hooves. These two things are necessary for whoever governs. By **ruminating** we understand diligent examination and consultation in whatever they have to do, in the likeness of the ox and the sheep, which swallow grass without chewing it, and then, searching for it again with diligence, return it to the mouth and chew it part by part, ruminating. Hence there is a Florentine proverb: "he has well ruminated on this thing," meaning he has well-considered and thought about it. Therefore, first, every governor—whether cleric or lay—must consider well and understand what he has to do. Then he puts **cloven hooves** for discretion, which distinguishes temporal things from spiritual ones. And the prince should not confound them together. Rather, let the prelate care for the spiritual and the prince for the temporal. These two princes, as is written in the decrees, are from Christ as the mediator between God and man. For Christ did certain things as an Emperor—such as when he drove from the temple those who sold and bought. Others he did as a Priest—such as when he offered himself as a sacrifice. But they must be distinct persons. This is shown in Chronicles <note>original: "paralipomenon"</note>: for when Uzziah <note>Ozia</note> wished to approach the altar with incense, the priest forbade him. But as he persisted in his purpose, God suddenly covered him with leprosy. **BECAUSE the people, who see their guide.** It is a marvel how much the example—both good and bad—of princes can do in those who have to obey them. Therefore the poet concludes that seeing the people and the shepherds (who should guide them to the right end) direct themselves to worldly things, they also give themselves to those, because appetite pulls them. So the people being prone to this, and finding those who lead them, it is inevitable that they fall into a precipice. **WELL you can see.** He concludes: that bad conduct—that is, bad guidance—is the cause why the world (meaning men) are made wicked, and not nature.

| :--- | :--- |
| Rome, which made the world good, used to | **HE PRAISES** the time in which the Christian Republic was ruled by the Pope in the spiritual and by the Emperor in the temporal. Because everyone cared for the part committed to him, and attending to only one thing, he could do it with greater diligence. **ROME USED TO:** the Christian republic, of which Rome is the head. **Two suns:** two princes: the Pope, Bishop of Rome, and the Emperor, King of the Romans. **And the one and the other road / they made visible:** just as the sun shows all the ways and regions of the world, so these princes showed both roads. That of the world was shown by the Emperor. That of God by the Pontiff. **ONE has extinguished the other.** Because the Emperor wanted to occupy the spiritual jurisdictions... |

I know him by no other surname, 
unless I were to take it from his daughter Gaia. 
God be with you, for I come no further with you. 
See the light that rays through the smoke 
already whitening; and I must depart— 
the Angel is there—before the day appears." 
Thus he turned back, and would hear me no more.

[Right Column]

He approves Marco’s sentence: that priests ought not to entangle themselves in temporal affairs, and he produces as testimony the example from the Bible. There, by the laws of Moses, the sons of Levi (one of the sons of Jacob), because they were ordained for the priesthood and the administration of sacred and divine things, were deprived of temporal goods so they would have no other care than for sacred things, living instead off the tithes. 

**YOUR SPEECH:** When he says, "since you are Tuscan, it cannot be that you do not know the fame of such a great man." Therefore, in your denying that you know him, either you deceive me by telling a lie, or you test me. But because it often happens that we do not know someone by their proper name, but by being named by some nickname, I do not know how I could name him to you as a more well-known thing than to say: he was the father of Gaia. She, for being both most beautiful and most virtuous, was famous throughout all Italy. 

**GOD BE WITH YOU:** He takes his leave because they had gone so far together that they had reached where the thick smoke ended, and the dawn was already beginning to be seen. And he [Marco] could not exit the darkness. He arranges the text: **SEE THE DAWN** which rays, <note>original: "i." (id est)</note> that is, shines and radiates, already whitening. And I must depart before the day appears, that is, before the light is seen. 

**THE ANGEL IS THERE:** when he says, "do not fear losing the way," for the Angel is there at the end of the smoke and he will show it to you. The allegory of the Angel is already known, and the interpretation does not change. But note that in every entrance where one removes a layer of purgation, divine grace shows us the true way.

->**CANTO XVII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE**<-

[Large initial R]
**R**emember, reader, if ever 
in the <term>Alps</term><note>In the commentary below, it is noted that while "Alps" refers specifically to the mountains between Italy and France, Tuscans used the word for any high, rugged mountain.</note> 
a mist caught you, through which you saw 
no differently than moles see through their skin: 
How and when the thick, moist vapors 
begin to thin, and the sphere 
of the sun enters through them feebly. 
And let your imagination be light 
in reaching to see how I saw again 
the sun at first, which was already at its setting. 
So, matching my faithful steps 
to those of my master, I came out of such a cloud 
to rays already dead on the low shores.

[Woodcut illustration: A scene from Dante's Purgatorio. Two figures in long robes, representing Dante and Virgil, stand in the foreground of a rocky landscape. Other figures are visible in the background, some emerging from or entering a dark, smoky area. The sky above is filled with stars, indicating the transition of time.]

Our author exits from the circle of Wrath in this 17th Canto, and mounts to the fourth terrace, where <term>Sloth</term><note>Accidia: spiritual apathy or laziness in pursuing the good.</note> is punished. But first he imagines that certain visions appear to him; once these have departed, he finds the Angel, who leads him to the stairs of the fourth terrace. 

**REMEMBER, READER:** if in the Alps—meaning in any very high mountain. The "Alps" specifically are the mountains that divide Italy from France. But from these, all high mountains in the Tuscan tongue (though not in Latin) are called "Alps." 

**A MIST CAUGHT YOU:** a very thick mist reached you, which is usually thicker in the mountains because it is drawn upward by the sun, and not rising above five miles, it condenses there. 

**THROUGH MOLE'S SKIN:** because the mole always lives underground. And certainly, it has eyes, but they are covered by a thin skin. Because of this, it sees very little. But that it sees something is manifest. First, because nature would have made eyes in vain, and nature does nothing in vain. Secondly, because as soon as it comes out of the earth and sees the air move, it reacts. Of this creature, Pliny says that it is condemned by nature in many ways, living buried in perpetual darkness. 

**HOW AND WHEN:** He admonishes the reader first to remember the thick mist of the Alps. Afterward, he wants the reader to imagine the vapors: which, because they were first condensed by moisture, could not be penetrated by the rays of the sun. But then, as the sun dissolves the moisture that made them dense, it makes them thin, and the rays begin...

# PURGATORIO

...began to penetrate: but weakly. Imagining then these things: the reader should first understand: what the darkness of the smoke was like: and how afterwards, as he approached the exit, he began to see a faint glimmer of light as the smoke ended. And **if your imagination is nimble**: let your fantasy be ready to understand this. Let this power be "light," meaning quick to grasp and connect ideas.
**I SAW AGAIN the sun at first** <note>original: "RIVIDilo sole ĩ pria"</note>: that is, before I was entirely out of the mist. **DYING**: because as the sun was already setting, its rays began to fade. **SO EQUALING**: Thus matching my steps with the faithful steps of Virgil.

**O imaginative power that steals us**
**sometimes so far from the world that one notices nothing**
**though around us sound a thousand trumpets**
**Who moves you if the senses provide you nothing?**
**A light moves you that takes form in the heavens**
**by itself, or by a divine will that guides it down.**
**Of the impiety of her who changed her form**
**into the bird that most delights in singing**
**the trace appeared within my imagination.**
**And here my mind was so drawn in**
**within itself, that from the outside there came**
**nothing that could then be received by it.**

**IMAGINATIVE that steals us**: The poet wished to describe a state of imagination and the vision that appeared to him; and he raises a philosophical question. The "lower powers" of the mind include the common sense. The **Imaginative** power, **fantasy**, the **cogitative** (thinking) power, and **memory** are usually moved by the exterior senses: which are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Other philosophers <note>Referring to the Aristotelian tradition common in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> posit three interior senses. In the first part of the head, they place a power which they call the **apprehensive**, or **fantasy**, or **common sense**. In the second part, they place the **imaginative**, the **cogitative**, or the **estimative** <note>The "estimative" power is the faculty that allows an animal or human to instinctively "estimate" or judge if something is helpful or harmful</note>. The third is **memory**.

In this passage, the poet uses the term "imaginative" to represent the **estimative** faculty, whose job is—aided by reason—to consider the things that the common sense has received from the outside world and placed in the imagination (the "second sense"), and to judge if they are true or false, or good or evil. Such a judgment is then stored in the memory, as I demonstrated more extensively in my third book *On the Soul*.

The poet demonstrates that although the imaginative (that is, the estimative) power usually receives its data from the exterior senses, it nonetheless sometimes gathers the entire soul into itself so completely that the senses "fall asleep"; in this state, the senses cannot provide the mind with anything. Then, either through celestial influence <note>Astrological influence from the stars</note> or, more likely, through a light sent by God, the mind considers and judges things without any help from the senses, provided by that divine light.

This is clearly manifest because we see people become so deep in their imaginations that, even though they are in the presence of various people and where many sounds and noises are made, they nonetheless see and hear nothing. This happens for the reason already mentioned, and is especially aided by the **fantasy**, whose job is to "compose and divide" <note>To combine different images or separate them</note>.

**WHO moves you if the senses provide you nothing?**: If the natural order of the senses is that a stimulus must first come from the outside—for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, the eye sees an enemy and provides that vision to the common sense, which then stores it in the imagination—then the **cogitative** power (which he here calls "imaginative"), turning to the imagination as if looking in a mirror, sees the image and judges that it is necessary to flee. Once this judgment is made, the "appetite" <note>The impulse to act</note> is suddenly awakened and moves the person to run away. Therefore, the poet asks: if the exterior senses are asleep and provide nothing to the thinking mind, who provides the image? He answers as we have already stated:

**AND THERE MOVES YOU a light**: understand this as the **active intellect**. **WHICH in the heaven takes form**: that is, it takes its being from celestial influences which distribute activity and operation to this light from above; or it comes directly from the divine will; or from the will of the angels, who are free and confirmed in grace. **WHICH**: referring to that divine power or angel which **GUIDES IT DOWN** <note>original: "GIV LO sporge"</note>: directing the activity of said light downward. Although the human intellect is passive...

<summary>This page explores the philosophical nature of imagination (imaginativa), explaining how the mind can experience vivid visions—like Dante’s visions of the "impious" Philomela—even when the physical senses are completely blocked or "asleep."</summary>

**CANTO XVII** [Page number] **194**

...from pride. But briefly repeating as much as is sufficient for a perfect division, there are two species of love and of desire.

One is natural: which is innate in all creatures: through which they desire that good through which they preserve themselves in their being <note>This refers to the instinct for self-preservation and the natural inclination toward one's proper place in the universe.</note>. THE OTHER is animal <note>original: *aiale*, a contraction of *animale*. In this context, it refers to the "sensitive" soul or the power of the mind/soul (*anima*) to perceive and choose, distinct from mere instinct.</note>: and this proceeds from the will: in which there is choice and <term>free will</term> <note>The power of the intellect to choose between different objects of desire.</note>. Natural love never errs.

The animal love can err in three ways: 

First, by the object: which is when the appetite, not guided <note>The OCR reads *corropto* (corrupted), but contextually in Landino's commentary, this is *scorto* (guided/conducted) by the light of reason.</note> by the light of reason, loves that which is evil instead of good. 

Second, by too little vigor: which is when that which deserves to be loved supremely and above all other things is loved little and coldly—such as God, the supreme good, and moral goodness <note>original: *lhonesta*, referring to *honestas* or moral integrity</note>, which contains all the virtues. Hence, in the commandments given by Moses—or rather by God through Moses: "Love the Lord your God" <note>original Latin: *Dilige dominum deum tuum*</note>. 

OR BY too much: when temporal goods—which either should not be considered true goods, or...
