# **PURGATORIO**

...and for this reason it loves its own evil. And so he demonstrates: that the love of evil is the cause of **pride**, **envy**, and **wrath**. Through all these things it is known that the will cannot simply love evil for its own sake. Rather, it loves the evil of its neighbor as a means to its own good. <note>Dante’s philosophy, following Thomas Aquinas, suggests that no one desires evil itself; they desire a "good" (like status or revenge) through an evil act.</note>

[Column 2]
After he has treated the love that turns toward the harm of one’s neighbor—which was divided into three parts: pride, envy, and wrath—he introduces the love that moves toward the good with less vigor than it ought. The first type, which is tripartite, is punished in the three circles already mentioned. This second type, because it lacks its proper fervor, creates **sloth** <note>original: "accidia," a spiritual apathy or "tristitia de bono spirituali" (sorrow in the face of spiritual good)</note>, and is purged in this fourth circle. This "triform love" is wept for below in the four circles already passed. THE OTHER love runs toward the good with a corrupt order. The superior tripartite love turned toward evil; the other—that is, this one—does not turn toward evil. Instead, it runs toward the supreme good, God, and toward the virtues with a corrupt order, because it does not love Him as much as is fitting, and puts utility and pleasure before that love. EVERYONE confusedly apprehends a "good." In the mind of every man, there is an innate desire to know the supreme good, which is found as the ultimate end; therefore, toward that end every mind **CONTENDS**, that is, it exerts itself.

[Middle Section - Verse]
> This triform love that down below
> is wept for; now I want you to understand the other,
> which runs toward the good with a corrupt order.
> Everyone confusedly apprehends a good
> in which the soul may rest, and desires it;
> because of this, everyone contends to reach it.
> If a lukewarm love draws you to see it
> or to acquire it, this terrace, <note>original: "cornice," meaning the ledge or level of the mountain</note>
> after just repentance, martyrs <note>meaning "punishes" or "disciplines"</note> you for it.

[Middle Section - Commentary]
It satisfies and contents itself in such a way that it does not seek to join itself with that [Supreme Good]. **IF A LUKEWARM LOVE draws you to see or acquire it**: if love lacks its required fervor, from which sloth is born, **THIS terrace**—this circle—martyrs you, that is, it punishes you after a just repentance. How the lack of love toward the supreme good causes sloth.

[Middle Section - Verse 2]
> There is another good that does not make man happy;
> it is not happiness, it is not the good
> essence of every good's fruit and root.
> The love that abandons itself too much to this
> is wept for above us in three circles;
> but how it is reasoned as tripartite,
> I remain silent, so that you may seek it for yourself.

[Middle Section - Commentary 2]
Likewise, excessive love toward worldly goods creates **avarice**, **lust**, and **gluttony**, and these three sins are purged in the higher circles. **ANOTHER good there is that does not make man happy.** This encompasses all created things, which are good, but are an imperfect good, and are not the "good essence," because that is God, who is the fruit of every good. For the fruit and the reward of our good works is to enjoy God Himself, who is the root of every good.

[Bottom Left Commentary]
...every good: the love that abandons itself to it—that is, which runs toward it abandonedly, meaning without the restraint and measure of reason. For this reason, it is "too much" and exceeds the proper mode through three circles. In the first of these (which is the fifth in order), **avarice** is purged, which is the disordered love toward the goods of fortune. In the second (which is the sixth), **gluttony** <note>original: "golosita"</note> is purged. In the third (which is the seventh), **lust** is purged. **I REMAIN SILENT, so that you may seek it for yourself.** Virgil has demonstrated the supreme and perfect good, which falls only within the intellect. Now, regarding "sensible" <note>pertaining to the five senses</note> goods, Dante can proceed by himself, and therefore Virgil leaves such inquiry to him.

[Bottom Right Commentary]
This chapter follows by declaring what Love is and then demonstrates how Sloth is purged. But that "father" demonstrates what a teacher ought to be toward a disciple. And similarly, how the intellect stands toward sensuality; but we have already spoken of this many times. Not without reason does he call him "exalted doctor" and later "father," and similarly "master." He calls him "exalted doctor" to show that he can explain every great thing; "master" because he is accustomed to showing it; "father" because, since Dante was the "son" of a timid speech that did not open itself, Virgil encouraged him. Because I was fearing I might be bothersome in speaking, I did not open my will, and he with his words gave me the courage to speak. "My vision was clarified in your light"—through this he shows that the sensitive part and the lower reason take strength and become intelligent through the light of the intellect.

CANTO XVIII 195

| [Left Column - The Verse] | [Right Column - The Commentary] |
| :--- | :--- |
| But that truthful father who perceived<br>the timid wish that did not reveal itself,<br>by speaking gave me the courage to speak.<br>Whereupon I: "Master, my will is so enlivened<br>in your light that I clearly discern<br>all that your reasoning brings or defines.<br>Therefore I pray you, sweet father dear,<br>that you demonstrate love to me, to which you reduce<br>every good work and its contrary."<br><br> "Direct toward me the sharp eyes,"<br>he said, "of the intellect, and the error of the blind<br>who make themselves leaders shall be manifest to you.<br>The soul, which is created ready to love,<br>is moved toward everything that pleases it,<br>as soon as it is awakened into action by pleasure.<br>Your perceptive faculty <note>Original: *appresiua*—the power of the mind to take in images from the senses</note> draws an intention<br>from a real existence, and unfolds it within you,<br>so that it makes the soul turn toward it.<br>And if, being turned, the soul inclines toward it,<br>that inclining is love; that is nature,<br>which through pleasure is bound anew within you.<br>Then, just as fire moves upward<br>by its form, which is born to climb<br>to where it lasts longest in its own matter,<br>so the soul, once captured, enters into desire,<br>which is a spiritual motion that never rests<br>until the thing loved makes it rejoice.<br>Now it may appear to you how hidden<br>is the truth from the people who insist<br>that every love is in itself a praiseworthy thing.<br>Because perhaps its 'matter' always appears<br>to be good, but not every seal<br>is good, even if the wax itself is good." | ...of the intellect. And Virgil is ignited to teach: because the more easily the disciple learns, the more willingly the generous teacher shows. **Brings** <note>Original: *Porti*</note> in knowing things formerly unknown. And **defines** <note>Original: *discriua*</note> in defining and dividing. Because of this, **I pray you demonstrate to me** what love is, from which you say proceed both virtue and vice. Whereupon he narrates thus: **Demonstrate** what love is, and he refutes those philosophers who want every love to be praiseworthy. **Direct the sharp eyes of the intellect**: because such science requires sharpness of wit and diligence. **The error of the blind who make themselves leaders** is the error of those who do not see the truth and do not know, and nonetheless want to give doctrine. Thus they lead the disciple no differently than a blind man leads those who follow him. These people say that every love is praiseworthy, which is false. **The soul, which is created ready to love**: Because the human soul is created by God with the <term>concupiscible power</term> <note>The faculty of the soul that desires what is perceived as good or pleasurable</note>; which power can quickly be brought into action. Because when either the sense (which is called the "cogitative" faculty), or reason, or the intellect, has judged a thing to be good, immediately after such judgment is given, the concupiscible power is awakened and desires it. For example <note>Original: *uerbi gratia*</note>: the eye sees a horse; the sense receives this form from the sight and, once received, places it in the imagination. And the cogitative faculty considers it in the imagination and judges it to be good and beautiful. Which judgment, once made, suddenly excites that power of the soul which we call "appetite" to love and desire it. **Your perceptive faculty draws an intention from a real existence**: This "perceptive" power <note>Original: *appresiua*</note> which judges what ought to be chosen, draws the intention—that is, it pulls the appetite toward it—from that which is truly good, and loves it as a good thing. And if it is not good, yet the soul loves it anyway, it is because it remains deceived; it does not love it except because it believes it to be good. **And unfolds**: it opens and demonstrates this "intention" to the soul (that is, to the will) in a form that makes the soul turn toward it. **And if**, in turning, it begins to bend and incline toward it, such an inclination toward the thing that pleases is love and nature (that is, it is natural love). Therefore, we shall say that love is an inclination of the soul toward the thing which pleases it, once it is offered. **Which through pleasure is bound anew within you**: Because such an inclination, newly made by the soul toward the thing that pleases it, is a binding of the soul with the pleasing thing, and from this is born concupiscence and desire. **That inclining** (that is, that inclination) **is LOVE; that is nature** (that is, it is natural love). **Then, just as fire**: Every created thing was produced by its Creator with an innate inclination toward that which is its highest good. It never rests until it follows it. But such an innate inclination in the creature comes from nature, or from sense... |

[Bottom Section - Commentary Continued]

...or from reason. From **nature**, it exists even in inanimate things, as we shall say of fire. From **sense**, we see it not only in humans, but also in brute animals; for example, seeing the bait, the bird moves to feed on it. The inclination of **reason** is in man alone, as when we see <note>Cato the Younger, a Roman statesman famous for his commitment to liberty</note> Cato seeking perils to liberate his fatherland. Thus, just as fire has from its specific form (that is, from its being distinct from other things) the property of mounting upward as a light thing, and never rests unless it is hindered, until it returns to its proper region (which is above the element of air), **WHERE IT LASTS LONGEST IN ITS MATTER**: so our soul, captured by that which it judges to be good and beautiful, **ENTERS INTO DESIRE**: into the wish to attain it. **Which is a spiritual motion**: which desire is a spiritual motion and not a bodily one. Because desire moves the spirit and not the body. Nor does such a motion of the soul ever rest **until the thing loved makes it rejoice**: that is, until it obtains the loved thing with joy. **Now it may appear to you**: He concludes that by what has been said above, one sees that those who held (that is, affirmed) that every love is praiseworthy, were in error. And the error is born because they argue in this form: the perceptive part does not put anything before the will except that which it judges to be good; and the soul and the will do not incline except toward that which the perceptive faculty already judged to be good. But this argument would follow of necessity if... <note>The text cuts off mid-argument; it likely goes on to explain that judgment can be mistaken</note>

Form is that which gives being to a thing. Therefore, the form in man is the rational soul: because only by reason are we different from other animals. And the body is the matter. Therefore he says "every substantial form," which is the soul. "Which is distinct": <note>original: "secta," meaning cut or divided</note> that is, divided from matter, meaning it has its own being. Because it is separate from its matter, which is the body. AND it is also united with matter. In short, every soul has its own being: both in the body and when it shall be separated from the body. This is not the case with the souls of brutes <note>animals</note>, because once separated from their bodies, they have no being. Therefore the human soul is pure form, because it is divided from matter. And because of this, it has in itself a power different from all other species: which constitutes its own nature. THIS power is not seen nor known except by its effect: just as in a plant it is not known to be alive except by the green leaves. And because of this, man does not know where the understanding of "first ideas" comes from; that is, where the first knowledge in a small child comes from, such as recognizing the father and other similar things, and other general things in grown men. Nor does he know where the "affection" <note>desire</note> proceeds from, that is, the love for the "first object of desire," which is the Highest Good, which is God, whom every man desires. BUT he does not know why it is naturally in the soul, just as in the bee is the desire to make honey. This first desire is attributed neither to praise nor to blame, because as Aristotle says, the "first movements" are not in our power. But afterward, in the second and third movements, and in all others, reason itself is there. For despite the fact that every other following desire gathers around this first will—that is, although subsequent desires are directed toward these first movements—nonetheless they have merit and demerit <note>blame</note>, which the first ones did not have. Because they have innate in them the "virtue that counsels," that is, Reason, which is given to us by God so that it may "hold the threshold of assent"; that is, be the master of consenting or not consenting. And from this reason, which can consent or resist as it pleases, is the principle from which our merit is born: if it consents to the good AND does not consent to the evil. And thus demerit is judged in the contrary.

**Beatrice understands the noble virtue** <gloss>as much as reason dictates to us, both to restrain and contain the appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to human desires or impulses.</note>. **THEY PERCEIVED**, that is, the philosophers [perceived] this innate liberty—that is, free will. **THEREFORE** they left morality to the world: by restraining free will so that it would not decline into vice; they discovered a way of living honestly according to the moral virtues, and they wrote such precepts to benefit those who were to follow after them.</gloss>

**PURGATORY**

And in the sacrifices, the women were filled with fury. And not in the temples, but along the rivers <term>Asopus and Ismenus</term><note>Two rivers in Boeotia, Greece, associated with the ecstatic rituals of Bacchus.</note> they ran with lit torches and with staffs wrapped in vine leaves, calling out with great shouts the names of <term>Bacchus</term><note>The Roman god of wine and religious ecstasy.</note>, of which there were many. Therefore, these souls who were purging their sloth did so with speed; because they had previously been in the highest state of laziness, they now ran, and spoke loudly through the silence. *They had need.* They were in need of his help. *His stride falters.* His stride bends. Because they did not leave the circle, but circling around continually, they bent and twisted their path. *Falcare* means to bend, a word derived from *falce* <note>original: "falce"</note> (sickle), which is bent and curved. *Whose good will.* That is, those whose just love is driven by a good will; as if to say, they are carried by a righteous love.

<margin>Z</margin>
**Soon they were upon us, because running**
**came all that great crowd,**
**and two in front cried out while weeping:**
**“Mary ran with haste to the mountain,**
**and Caesar, to subdue Ilerda,**
**struck Marseille and then rushed to Spain.”**
**“Quickly, quickly, lest time be lost**
**through little love,” cried the others following,**
**“for zeal in doing well makes grace go green again.”**

<margin>Right Commentary block:</margin>
Not without great prudence does the poet introduce these two in front using examples that encourage speed, and then those behind to demonstrate how much delay causes harm. For the first ones ensure that, by leaving laziness behind, a person returns to study and fervor. And the last ones restrain us, so that we do not fall again into somnolence, weariness, and sloth. Therefore, weeping—which signifies repentance for past sloth and slowness in acting virtuously—they cried out. This signifies the spurring of the mind. For whoever wishes to return to true fervor, or to lead others back to it, reproves and awakens them by proposing and bringing to memory all the examples that can spur us on. *MARY ran with haste to the mountain.* When Herod, in order to kill Christ (whom he had heard from the Magi was born), commanded that all newborns from two years and under should be killed, Mary—warned by the angel to flee to Egypt—carried her son Jesus with the greatest speed upon an ass, running toward the mountains and passing through them immediately. *AND Caesar* departed with the greatest speed from Rome. Caesar, to crush the armies of Pompey in Spain, whom he had already broken in Thessaly and turned to flight toward Egypt. And although <term>Marseille</term><note>A city in southern France.</note> a city of Provence, tried to delay him, he nevertheless did not tarry, but left Brutus there to besiege it. And he rushed to Spain where he defeated Afranius, Petreius, and a son of Pompey. <term>Ilerda</term><note>The modern city of Lleida in Catalonia, Spain.</note> is a city in Spain. *Quickly, quickly.* This shows how much efficacy a good example has, seeing as through the words of the first two, all the others cry "Quickly, quickly, lest time be lost." Our life is short; therefore it is necessary to compensate for its brevity with our speed. *THROUGH little love.* Through the slowness of sloth, which is nothing other than a lack of love, as shown above. *FOR zeal in doing well.* That is, the solicitude and speed of doing well "makes green" in us—that is, it renews and causes to be reborn and return—the grace of God, which through sin was dried up within us. And certainly, the more a person strives to do good, the more God is inclined to help him.

**“O people in whom a keen fervor now**
**perhaps compensates for negligence and delay**
**put forth by you through lukewarmness in doing good,**
**this man who lives—and I certainly do not lie to you—**
<margin>A</margin> **wants to go up, provided the sun shines on us again;**
**so tell us where the opening is near.”**
<margin>B</margin> **These were the words of my leader;**
**and one of those spirits said: “Come**
**behind us, and you will find the gap.**
**We are so full of the desire to move**
**that we cannot rest; therefore, forgive us**
<margin>Handwritten note: 1154 and refers to the city of Milan in the year of our Lord 1164.</margin>
**if you take our justice for rudeness.**
**I was the Abbot of San Zeno in Verona**
**under the empire of the good Barbarossa,**
**of whom Milan still speaks with sorrow.**
**And one already has one foot in the grave**
**who will soon weep for that monastery,**
**and will be sad to have had power there,**
**Because his son, deformed in his whole body**
**and worse in his mind, and who was ill-born...”**

<margin>Bottom Right Commentary block:</margin>
*THROUGH lukewarmness.* Through sloth, which is nothing other than a lack of burning charity. *I DO NOT lie to you.* <note>original: "Non vi bugio"</note> I do not tell you a lie. *PROVIDED the sun shines on us again.* Because, as we have shown, without the sun one can only turn back and wander in the same place, but not go upward. *I WAS the abbot.* This man was a contemporary of Dante named Alberto, a man of good character but very remiss. <term>Zeno</term><note>The patron saint of Verona.</note> was the eighth bishop in Verona, a man of holy life, of excellent character, and of profound theology, as clearly appears in many volumes.

### CANTO XIX 197

...has placed in the stead of its true pastor.
I do not know if he said more or then fell silent,
so far had he already moved past us;
but this I heard, and it pleased me to remember.

"I shall trample underfoot the lion and the dragon" <note>original: "conculcabo leonem & draconem"; a reference to Psalm 91:13, historically associated with Pope Alexander III literally stepping on the neck of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa</note>. To which words Frederick replied: "Not to you, but to Peter." The Pope said: "To both me and to Peter." After this reconciliation, Frederick, as satisfaction for the injuries done to the Church, passed with his armies into Syria against the infidels. But being in Antioch and, in the great heat, bathing in the river, he drowned. Milan remained destroyed for five years. **And such a one has already.** This proverb is used for those who are already close to death. And it refers to Master Alberto della Scala, Lord of Verona: who more by force than by direct means <note>meaning legal or rightful procedure</note> made his son the Abbot of the aforementioned monastery (deformed and of bad character: hence it says: "ill-formed in body and worse in mind"). And he was "ill-born" because he was born of adultery. **Has placed in the stead of its true Pastor**, because the Abbot should be the true pastor of the monastery. But he, being greedy and rapacious, was not.

[Woodcut illustration depicting a man (Dante) lying in bed dreaming, with a woman (the Siren) standing before him, and other figures including Virgil and a lady (Lucia or Beatrice) appearing to expose the Siren's belly.]

He <note>Referring to the commentator, likely Cristoforo Landino.</note> has treated until now four spiritual and diabolical vices: those which proceed from malice. These are Pride, Envy, Wrath <note>Original: "uanagloria" (vainglory), often grouped with Envy/Pride.</note>, and Sloth. Now follow three which spring more from the senses than from reason; they are bodily and voluptuous. But in this nineteenth canto, the poet presents a vision that appeared to him in a dream; and then he reaches the stairs that climb to the fifth circle, where Avarice is purged. But first he describes the time, saying: *At the hour when the day’s heat can no longer warm the cold of the moon.* Here it is to be noted that the reflection of the sun’s rays, striking the earth, reverberates upward and heats the air. Later, when night comes, the air begins to turn cold because of the sun's departure and because of the moon's rays, which are cold. For the moon has no light of its own, but receives it from the sun; and it reflects downward the rays received from the sun, and every downward reflection creates cold, just as upward reflection creates heat. Nevertheless, until midnight, the air retains the heat of the day; but afterward, the moon’s rays overcome the heat, so that the further the night goes, the more the cold increases, because the day's heat has no more power. The moon is also aided by the earth, which is cold and dry, and sometimes it is aided by Saturn. For when Saturn gives its vigor to the moon—being a cold and dry planet—it greatly increases the lunar cold. Thus, the astrologer Alanus <note>Alanus de Insulis (Alain de Lille), a 12th-century scholar.</note> writes of Saturn: *With his chill he steals the joys of spring; he steals the beauty from the meadows and the stars of the flowers.* <note>original Latin: "hic algore suo furatur gaudia ueris. Furaturque decus pratis & sydera florum."</note> He describes, therefore, the morning time close to day, in which—as shown in the first canticle—dreams are true. *When the geomancers:* He describes the same time in another way. For geomancers perform their art in the morning time when dawn comes, because at that time the human mind and body are more obedient to celestial inclinations. And here we must understand that man can be moved by three causes: first, by his own will, which is born from the choice of free will; second, by a will moved by some passion, such as from a stomach too full or too empty, or from an excess of humors, or a lack of vital spirits; third, by natural inclination, which is caused by the movements of the heavens. And this last one alone contains divination. Therefore, the geomancer, wishing to exclude the first two, wants the points to be made without counting or thinking about them, so they are not by our choice but according to celestial inclination. And against the second, he chooses the time of the morning, in which the soul and body are sober—neither too full nor too empty. Geomancy is a type of divination which the Easterners especially practiced around the dawn in their lawsuits. They make sixteen rows, not of lines, but of chance points not numbered by the person making them. Then they are divided into four parts, so that each part has four rows; they pair the points of the row so that in the end, it remains either even or odd. And from every four, they derive the final parts and make a figure. The names of the figures are: Joy, Sadness, Greater Fortune, Lesser Fortune, Gain, Loss, White, Red, Conjunction, Cancer, The People, The Way, The Boy, The Girl, The Head, The Tail. <note>These are the traditional 16 geomantic figures, translated here from Landino's Latinate Italian.</note> *THEIR GREATER fortune:* This figure mentioned above is similar to a configuration of stars which forms the end of Aquarius and the beginning of Pisces. Therefore, if the sun was then rising with Aries, it follows that the figure of Greater Fortune, which is at the beginning of Pisces and rises about an hour before Aries, would appear in the east at dawn, which is about an hour before the sun. *THERE CAME TO ME in a dream a stuttering woman:* Because the three vices that follow are for excessive and immoderate love of temporal goods—and not truly goods, but false ones—the poet wishes through this vision to demonstrate the false happiness that comes from them. He portrays a woman who has five defects: she speaks distortedly, for she is a stuttering stammerer; she sees distortedly, for she is cross-eyed; she walks with a limp; she performs manual works imperfectly, for she is handless; and finally, she is of a hideous color. False happiness consists in these...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical analysis of the "Stammering Woman" (Femmina Balba) from Dante's Purgatorio, Canto XIX. This figure appears to Dante in a dream as a distorted hag who transforms into a tempting siren, representing the three sins of the flesh: Avarice, Gluttony, and Lust.</meta>

### CANTO XIX. 198

...five things: Riches, Lordships, Honors, Fame, and bodily pleasure. And so she is stuttering, stammering, and does not speak clearly, because the fame of such things is imperfect and is rather "infamy" than fame. By being distorted <note>The transcription reads "quercia" (oak), but in the context of Dante’s poem, the word is "guercia," meaning cross-eyed or distorted; the commentator is explaining why the woman's sight is flawed.</note> she signifies the imperfection of honors. Wherefore this is contrary to that Virgilian verse: *And had breathed the joyful honors upon his eyes* <note>original Latin: "lætos oculis afflarat honores." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book I, where the goddess Venus grants her son Aeneas a divine, beautiful appearance.</note>. And she is crippled <term>sciancata: literally "hip-shot" or lame</term> to show that those men who sustain themselves by leaning upon riches are like those who support their body on a lame foot. And because temporal lordships involve imperfect and vicious actions, she is maimed <term>mōca: missing a hand or part of an arm</term>, because we have previously stated that the hands signify "operations" <note>human deeds or actions</note>. The dull and pale color demonstrates carnal pleasures, which consist mostly of surface colors and beauties.

This section treats, therefore, of immoderate love toward "false goods." In this state, there is either only the desire—and then comes **Avarice**—or there is both the desire and the act. It should no longer seem difficult to you
when it is said that a just vengeance
was later avenged by a just court.
<note>Beatrice explains the paradox: the Crucifixion was a "just vengeance" for Adam's sin, but the later destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans was a "just punishment" for the Jews who killed the innocent Christ.</note>

<summary>Beatrice explains the theology of the Fall and the Atonement, clarifying how Christ's death was simultaneously a just punishment for humanity's sin and an unjust crime against his divine person.</summary>

# PARADISO 1

[Left Column]

But I see well now how your mind is restricted,
from thought to thought, trapped within a knot
<note>original: "drẽto aun modo" (dentro a un nodo). Dante uses the "knot" as a metaphor for a complex intellectual or theological problem that needs unravelling.</note>
from which, with great desire, it awaits to be loosed.
You say: "I clearly discern what I hear;
but why God willed only this manner
for our redemption is hidden from me."
This decree, brother, remains buried
to the eyes of everyone whose intellect
has not matured within the flame of love.
<note>Beatrice explains that the reason for the Atonement can only be understood by those whose "ingegno" (intellect) is refined by "caritas" (divine love).</note>
Truly, however, because at this target
many gaze and little is discerned,
I will tell why such a manner was most worthy.
The Divine Goodness, which spurns from itself
all envy, burning within itself, so sparkles
that it unfolds the eternal beauties.
<note>original: "liuore." In medieval theology, God is described as being without "envy" or "spite," meaning He does not begrudge sharing His existence; thus, His love overflows into creation.</note>
Whatever distills from it without intermediary
<note>original: "senza mezo." This refers to things created directly by God—such as the first humans, the angels, and the human soul—rather than through secondary causes like the stars or nature.</note>
has thereafter no end, because its imprint
does not shift when it sets its seal.
Whatever rains down from it without intermediary
is entirely free, because it is not subject
to the power of the new things.
<note>"The new things" (le cose nuove) refers to the influence of the celestial spheres and changing nature. Direct creations of God are not bound by these temporary physical laws.</note>
It is more conformed to Him, and therefore pleases Him more;
for the Holy Ardor, which radiates through everything,
shines most in what is most like it and most alive.
In all these things [the human creature] has the advantage...
<note>The text cuts off here: "sau" is likely the beginning of "s’avvantaggia" (has the advantage).</note>

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s explanation of the Atonement. She moves from explaining why the human race was punished to why God chose the specific method of the Incarnation for humanity's rescue, focusing on the legal and theological necessity of a "satisfaction" that man could not provide alone.</meta>

CANTO SEVENTH 215

Your nature, when it sinned entirely
in its first seed, was removed from these dignities
<note>original: "nel seme suo" (in its seed). This refers to Adam, the biological and spiritual ancestor of humanity. The "dignities" are the state of grace, immortality, and free will lost at the Fall.</note>
just as it was removed from Paradise.
Nor could these be recovered, if you look
very closely by any path,
without passing through one of these ways:
Either that God alone, by His own courtesy,
had forgiven; or that man, by himself,
had made satisfaction for his folly.
<note>In medieval theology, "satisfaction" is a legal term meaning to make amends or pay a debt for an offense to restore the balance of justice.</note>
Fix your eye now within the abyss
of the eternal counsel as much as you can,
fixed closely on my words.
Man could never, within his own limits,
ever make satisfaction, for he could not go as low
in humility and subsequent obedience,
as he had intended to go high in disobedience;
<note>Beatrice explains a logical paradox: because Adam's sin was pride (trying to be like God, an infinite height), man would have to perform an act of infinite humility to balance it, which is impossible for a finite being.</note>
and this is the reason why man was excluded
from being able to make satisfaction for himself.
Therefore, it was necessary for God, by His own ways,
to restore man to his full life—
I mean by one, or indeed by both.
But because the work is so much more pleasing
to the worker the more it represents
the goodness of the heart from which it issued,
the Divine Goodness, which imprints the world,
was pleased to proceed by all its ways
to raise you up again.
<note>The "two ways" are Mercy and Justice. While God could have simply forgiven man (Mercy), He chose to involve Justice as well by becoming man in Christ, which more perfectly demonstrates His love.</note>

Nor between the final night and the first day
has there been, or will there be, so exalted
and so magnificent a process,
whether by the one way or the other.
<note>The "final night" is the end of the world, and the "first day" is Creation. Beatrice asserts that the Incarnation is the greatest event in the entire history of the universe.</note>

<summary>Beatrice explains that humanity was unable to atone for the Fall because no human act of humility could match the scale of Adam's pride. Consequently, God chose to use both Mercy and Justice through the Incarnation to restore mankind, an act she describes as the greatest in history.</summary>

PARADISE

[Left Column]
And these things were also created beings,
because if what has been said is true,
they should be secure from corruption.
<note>Beatrice refers to the elements (earth, air, fire, water). Dante is confused: if God created them, why do they decay? She explains that while the universe is divine, the basic elements are shaped by "secondary causes" (the stars), not directly by God's hand.</note>
The angels, brother, and the pure land
in which you are, can be called "created"
just as they are in their entire being.
But the elements that you have named,
and those things that are made from them,
are informed by a created power.
<note>term: "informed" (Italian: *informati*). In medieval philosophy, this means giving "form" or essence to raw matter.</note>
The matter they have was created;
the informing power was created
in these stars that go around them.
The soul of every brute and of the plants
is drawn from a potential complex
by the rays and the motion of the holy lights.
<note>This refers to the "sensitive" and "vegetative" souls of animals and plants, which medieval thinkers believed were generated by the influence of the stars on physical matter, rather than being immortal.</note>
But your life is breathed without intermediary
by the Supreme Goodness, who enamors it
of Himself, so that it always desires Him.
And from this you can further argue
our resurrection, if you reflect
how human flesh was made then,
when both the first parents were formed.
<note>Beatrice argues that because God created the bodies of Adam and Eve directly ("without intermediary"), human physical nature has a claim to immortality, necessitating the Resurrection.</note>

<column-break/>

[Right Column]
**To be:** because God created matter and form at once, and created them for Himself without the intermediary of secondary causes. But the elements and bodies composed of them were created by a "created power" which God placed into the elements when He created their matter from nothing; and thus their form is from God by means of that created power. Because their natural form, although it issued into being from the potentiality of matter, and therefore can be said to be made of something, is nonetheless the light that is said to be the principle before every form and matter. Therefore it cannot be perpetual nor free, because the form that the elements currently have was not created by God immediately <note>original: *imediate* (directly/without anything in between)</note>, but by means of the created power that God put into the first matter in that state of formlessness in which it was created. Matter was created by God without intermediary, and therefore it is perpetual and free; and it is subject to none but God. The informing power was created, which brings "elemented" things <note>Things made of the four elements.</note> into being, and this power is in the stars which revolve around the elements. **The soul of every brute:** the sensitive soul in beasts and the vegetative soul in plants is not perpetual, because it is made from a potential complex, a material composition of the simple formal elements purified by the influence of the heavens; and therefore it is temporary and subject to the influence of the heavens. And because it is drawn out by the influence of the stars above with their rays and motion, he said "the rays and the motion of the holy lights." **But your life:** the human soul. **Breathes:** lives without intermediary, because as soon as the body is organized, God at once creates our soul without intermediary, and in creating it, pours it into the body. Therefore the **Supreme Goodness** (that is, God’s goodness) creates the soul and enamors it of Himself because He places in it a natural desire to achieve the Supreme Good, which is God Himself. **He offers a conclusion:** that the reason already stated proves that we must rise again with our own flesh, because God made the body of the first man without intermediary, and for this reason, He will make it perpetual; and from that He made the first woman. Therefore, it must be perpetual, and so must ours which come from them. Thus the death of such bodies must be only for a time; but concerning the resurrection of bodies, we have spoken sufficiently in another place.

He has finished treating as much as was appropriate concerning the second heaven of Mercury. # PARADISE

**b** ALTHOUGH the poet enters the ninth canto, he does not yet leave the third sphere <note>The Heaven of Venus, associated with those who were prone to earthly love but redirected that passion toward God.</note>. But having finished his conversation with Charles <note>Charles Martel, King of Hungary, whom Dante met in the previous canto.</note>, he speaks first to Cunizza of Romano, and then with Folco of Marseille. **C** BUT in these first verses, he turns his speech to Clemence <note>The daughter of Charles Martel.</note>, the daughter of Charles, and tells her how, after he had cleared his doubt, he foretold the deceptions that her descendants were to receive. BUT he commanded him <note>Dante</note> to remain silent and let the years move—that is, let time pass, which is nothing other than the revolution of the planets. Nevertheless, he says that the deceptions committed against his people will be justly punished; and having said these words, Charles turned back to God, contemplating Him, because God is that supreme good that fills everything; He is sufficient, or rather more than enough, because He is infinite and creatures are finite. Then the author performs an apostrophe <note>A rhetorical device where the speaker breaks off to address a third party, here humanity at large.</note>, that is, he turns his speech to men and vituperates them because, leaving their supreme good, they turn to vain things, wherefore he rightly calls them "impious creatures," because the creature is pitiless when it leaves its creator, to whom it owes everything.

And behold another of those splendors
drew toward me, and its desire to please me
was signaled by its outward brightening:
The eyes of Beatrice, which were fixed
upon me as before, gave dear assent
and made me certain of my own desire.
"Oh, put a quick remedy to my wish,
blessed spirit," I said, "and give me proof
that I can reflect back to you what I think." <note>Dante asks the spirit to prove that it can read his thoughts by answering his unspoken questions.</note>

from its depths where it was previously singing,

and the springs of Brenta and Piave, <note>This identifies the March of Treviso in northeastern Italy.</note>
There rises a hill, and it does not rise very high,
from where there once descended a firebrand

From one root were both I and he born;

because the light of this star overcame me. <note>She is in the sphere of Venus because she was influenced by the planet of love.</note>

in the cause of my fate, and it does not grieve me,
which might perhaps seem hard to your common folk.

of our heaven which is closest to me,
great fame remained; and before it dies,
This centennial year shall yet be quintupled. <note>original: "sincinqua" — a neologism meaning "to five itself," implying five hundred years.</note>

And this the present crowd does not consider,
which the Tagliamento and Adige shut in; <note>The people of the March of Treviso.</note>

### [Right Column - Commentary]

HE introduces Cunizza of Romano to speak. SHE was the sister of Ezzelino of Romano; a woman of gentle manners, full of humanity and of kind and grateful piety. BUT she was very prone to love, as we demonstrated in the sixth chapter of the *Purgatorio*. Nor should anyone marvel that the poet places among the blessed one whose life had this stain <note>Her reputation for many lovers and marriages.</note>: because he wants to demonstrate that everyone, by amending themselves, can be saved, especially if many virtues are mixed with the vice that weighs them down, as we see in her. Describing then the country where she was born—that is, the March of Treviso—he says "in that part of the Italian land," that is, of Italy, and he calls it "depraved" not to insult Italy, which was so praised by Virgil, BUT he says "depraved" because in his times it was governed by depraved, that is, captive men. BUT I truly believe that if the poet were alive in our times, he would say the same thing or perhaps worse, for our lot is hard. Therefore, in that part of Italy which sits—that is, is placed—between Rialto (the city of Venice where Rialto is) and the springs of Brenta and Piave. These are two rivers that run through the Trevisan territory. A HILL: upon which is a land called Romano, from whence came Ezzelino (otherwise Azzolino), of whom we have narrated sufficiently elsewhere. FROM ONE ROOT: we descended from one father. I SHINE: I resplend because the light of this star overcame me, that is, because the influence of this star <note>Venus</note> had great power over me. BUT I JOYFULLY INDULGE MYSELF: that is, I treat myself with joy. THE CAUSE OF MY FATE: the meaning is, I am supremely content to have had such influence. Because being blessed, she cannot grieve for the sins committed. BUT she supremely rejoices to have performed penance for them. And she also rejoices in the degree where she finds herself; and she does not desire a greater or higher degree. And to ignorant men it might perhaps seem hard to believe that a blessed soul does not grieve for committed sins and does not desire greater beatitude. But this was disputed above.

**P** AFTER Cunizza had spoken what is said above, she turned away and showed Dante the spirit of FOLCO of Marseille, saying: "Great fame has remained in the world of this spirit, who is a precious and shining jewel," that is, full of light and splendor. And this year, which is the hundredth since he left the world, shall yet FIVE ITSELF [SINCINQUA]: that is, this hundredth year will return five times, meaning it will be five hundred years before this fame of his dies. SEE IF MAN SHOULD STRIVE: as if to say, consider by this how much man should strive to make himself excellent before he dies, since the fame of virtue lasts so long after death. SO THAT THE FIRST LIFE LEAVES ANOTHER BEHIND <note>The "first life" is the mortal one; the "other" is the lasting reputation/fame.</note>.

# PARADISE - CANTO IX

<column-break/>

### [Left Column - Poetry]

After your Charles, O beautiful Clemence, <note>Charles Martel, King of Hungary, and his daughter of the same name.</note>
had cleared my mind, he told me of the frauds
that his descendants were destined to endure;

but he added: "Keep silent, and let the years roll by";
so that I can say nothing, except that just mourning
shall follow upon the wrongs done to you.

And already the soul of that holy light
had turned back to the Sun that fills it, <note>Dante uses the Sun as a metaphor for God, the source of all truth.</note>
as to that good which suffices for every thing.

Ah, souls deceived and creatures impious,
who from such a good turn away your hearts,
directing your brows toward vanity!

And behold, another of those splendors
approached me, and by brightening its outward glow <note>The souls in Paradise express joy and the desire to communicate by increasing their radiance.</note>
signified its desire to please me.

The eyes of Beatrice, which were fixed
upon me as before, gave me dear assurance
of her private assent to my desire.

"I pray you, blessed spirit, provide a remedy
for my wish," I said, "and give me proof
that what I think, I can reflect in you." <note>Dante asks the soul to prove it can see his thoughts as they are reflected in the "mirror" of the Divine Mind.</note>

Wherefore the light that was still new to me,
from out its depths, where it had been singing,
continued like one who delights in doing good:

"In that part of the wicked land of Italy
that lies between Rialto and the springs
of the Brenta and the Piave rivers,

a hill rises, and not very high,
from which there once descended a firebrand
that made a great assault upon that region. <note>The "firebrand" refers to the cruel tyrant Ezzelino III da Romano.</note>

Both I and it were born from the same root:
Cunizza was I called, and here I shine
because I was conquered by the light of this star." <note>The Planet Venus, which influences those prone to love.</note>

<column-break/>

### [Right Column - Commentary]

**After your Charles**. Having finished the previous discourse, the author begins the ninth canto, still remaining in the third heaven. He reports the prophecy made by Charles Martel concerning the "frauds" or deceptions that would strike his bloodline, specifically the loss of the throne of Naples to the younger branch of the Angevins. <margin>The House of Anjou.</margin>

**Keep silent**. Charles commands the poet not to reveal the specifics of the future, as the revolution of the spheres—which is how we measure the passage of *time*—will eventually bring about God's vengeance on its own.

**Ah, souls deceived**. *O miseri electi* <note>original: "O miserable chosen ones"</note>. The author performs a brief apostrophe, turning away from the narrative to rebuke those who prefer the "vanity" of earthly things to the infinite good of God. He calls them "impious creatures" because they lack the piety <note>In the Latin sense of *pietas*: duty and devotion.</note> required to honor their Creator.

**Another of those splendors**. This refers to Cunizza da Romano, sister of the tyrant Ezzelino. While her brother was a "firebrand" of destruction and cruelty, she is saved here because her passionate nature, once focused on earthly love, was ultimately transformed into divine love.

**Between Rialto and the springs**. Cunizza identifies her origin by describing the March of Treviso. <gloss>The region in northeastern Italy between Venice and the Alps.</gloss> 

**A firebrand**. This refers to a legend that her mother, while pregnant with Ezzelino, dreamed she was carrying a burning torch. Cunizza notes that they came from the "same root," emphasizing the contrast between her brother's vice and her own salvation through grace.

**Conquered by the light**. She explains her presence in the third sphere by the influence of Venus. *Sub influentia Veneris* <note>original: "Under the influence of Venus"</note>. In the medieval view, the stars incline the soul toward certain dispositions, but free will and grace determine the final destination of the spirit.

<summary>Dante recounts Charles Martel's prophecy regarding the House of Anjou and his return to the contemplation of God. The poet then encounters Cunizza da Romano, who describes the March of Treviso and explains how her history of earthly passion was redeemed in the Heaven of Venus.</summary>
<keywords>Canto IX, Paradiso, Charles Martel, Clemence, Cunizza da Romano, Ezzelino da Romano, March of Treviso, Heaven of Venus, Prophecy, Divine Justice</keywords>

->CANTO NINE 260<-

...who does not repent of the fault. Instead, one rejoices in the power that ordained and provided by God in that star. We gaze upon the art that adorns such an effect; <note>The "art" refers to the divine craftsmanship and the "effect" refers to the influence of the heavens on human nature.</note> that is, we spirits, contemplating the heavens, see the art, namely the power of nature placed there by God with such effect, because from such natural power proceed most wonderful effects. Because that which is below—namely these effects produced down here in the elements and in men—returns to the world above, that is, to the First Cause. That which is below returns, namely the lower world which is by its nature mortal, returns, that is, it becomes like that which is above, namely immortal; just as the upper world, through the influence of Venus which is the cause of generation, allows the human species through succession to become immortal.

"But so that you may carry away all your desires

It was truly fitting to leave her as a palm

their thoughts do not go to Nazareth,

<column-break/>

### [Right Column - Commentary]

<margin>R</margin>
Proceeding in his speech, Folco shows that the most splendid spirit in that star was Rahab. She was the first among the gentile people to believe in the religion of the Old Testament. And in the Book of Joshua, it is written that as he entered the Land of Promise, he fought against Jericho because they had not wanted to receive him. And to better and more quickly capture the city, he sent three spies to understand the layout within and the movements of the men. These men after some days were recognized; and being hunted by the people who wanted to seize them, they fled to the house of Rahab, a woman very much inflamed by the fires of Venus. <note>Rahab was a harlot in Jericho, which explains her placement in the sphere of lovers (Venus).</note> She, moved by love for God and her neighbor, hid them; and because she had a house joined to the city walls, she lowered them out and saved them. And she herself was saved because she arranged with them that when Joshua sacked the land, she would put a scarlet cloth in her windows, which being seen, her house would be preserved. And because [Dante] wants the grades to be distinct in every order of the blessed according to whether their merits are greater or lesser, he therefore imagines that this spirit sparkled, that is, shimmered and shone more than the others because she had more merit.

The history of Rahab continues, and he says that from the triumph that Christ brought back from the devil when he despoiled Limbo, <note>original: "spogliò el limbo"</note> she was assumed from this heaven before any other soul.

PARADISE

**to their hems** <note>original: "uiuagni"</note> <gloss>that is, to their garments</gloss>: the superfluity and pomp of which [the poet] vilifies more extensively elsewhere. **Hem** is the proper term for the edge of cloth. But here he takes the part for the whole. **TO THIS.** To this avarice and the accumulation of **simony** <term>simony: the buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges or offices</term> the Pope attends; and this refers especially to Boniface, whom he mentioned in the *Inferno*: thoughts do not go to **Nazareth**, that is, to the things of God; and he mentions this city because the Mother of the Lord was announced there, and therefore he adds: **There where Gabriel spread his wings** <gloss>that is, his flight</gloss> to bring the announcement to the Virgin, who alone among women remained a virgin after childbirth. But **Vatican**: he predicts that Boniface will soon suffer the penalty for his sins and will be dead. Wherefore the Vatican and the other places of Rome which are sacred—having been the cemetery of the martyrs who, fighting for the faith and following Peter, the first **vicar of Christ** <term>vicar of Christ: a title for the Pope as the earthly representative of Jesus</term>, were killed—will be made free from the **adulterer** through the death of Boniface. He calls him an **adulterer** because the true spouse of the Church and the true Pope was Celestine; or truly an adulterer because, leaving the true spouse, that is, the Church, he gives himself over to simony.

# CANTO X OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

**G**uarding His Son with the Love
that the one and the other eternally
breathe forth,
the first and ineffable Power,
Whatever revolves through mind or through eye,
He created with such order that one cannot
be without a taste of Him who gazes upon it.
Lift then, reader, to the high wheels
your sight with me, directed toward that part
where the one motion and the other strike;
And there begin to gaze with longing at the art
of that Master who within Himself loves it
so much that His eye never departs from it.

[Woodcut illustration: A deity or personification of the Sun sits in a horse-drawn chariot (quadriga) traveling across the starry sky. Below on Earth, figures are depicted in a landscape; one is kneeling in prayer or contemplation, looking upward at the celestial phenomenon.]

The author finds himself already ascended from the third planet to the fourth; and in this tenth chapter he describes the order of the heaven and its motion. Afterward, he narrates how he entered and the excellence of the souls that are in that sphere, and he leads a modern soul to speak. Having ascended, therefore, not without wonder, and considering the uniform motion of the heavens and the erratic motion of the planets, he begins to show that the divine essence, distinct in three persons, made the universe with admirable order and says: The **first Power** <note>original: "ualore"</note>, that is, the Father, to whom is attributed power which is **ineffable** <gloss>that is, unspeakable</gloss>, looking—that is, intending—upon His Son, to whom is attributed **wisdom**, because the Son is the wisdom of the Father. **With the Love**, that is, with the Holy Spirit, which <gloss>that is, which Love</gloss> the one and the other <gloss>that is, the Father and the Son</gloss> eternally breathe forth: because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore the Father, with His power, and with the wisdom of the Son, and with the love of the Holy Spirit, made everything that revolves and is considered and understood; whether by **mind**, as are invisible things, or by **eye**, as are visible things, with such order that whoever gazes upon it cannot be without a **taste of Him**, that is, without knowledge of God. But to avoid error in the things said above, we must hold for certain that God is one and alone in essence; but this one essence, which is one God, is distinct in the three aforementioned persons. He concludes, therefore, that the universe, both visible and invisible, is instituted with such order that no smallest particle of it can decline or depart from such order; nor could there be such order if it did not proceed from a prince and mover who composed and bound together so many things, so diverse and contrary. Nor can anyone have knowledge of these things who does not "taste" what God is. **Lift then**: he invites the reader to consider the motions of the heavens, especially in that part where the one motion strikes against the other. It is known through **astronomy** that the motion of the firmament proceeds from East to West, and the planets make a motion contrary to this, from West to East, always under the **Zodiac**, which divides the **equinoctial circle** <term>equinoctial circle: the celestial equator</term>; and similarly, it is divided by it and enters into equal parts: and one rises to the North, the other declines toward the South, as we demonstrated at length in the second canticle. **The one motion to the other**: because they are contrary. **To gaze with longing** <note>original: "auagegiare"</note> <gloss>that is, to look upon with pleasure and delight</gloss>. **In the art** <gloss>that is, in the admirable mastery which is the nature of things skillfully instituted by God</gloss>. Whence **Petrarch** in the third sonnet: "He who with infinite providence and art / showed his marvelous mastery / and created this and the other hemisphere / and made Jove more gentle than Mars." 
**SEE then how from there** <gloss>that is, from the reader</gloss> **it branches out**.
See how from there it branches out, that is, it departs like a branch from a tree. For it twists from the...

->behold the sphere.<- When it enters Aries, which is the first point of the equator, it creates the spring. When it reaches Cancer, it creates the summer. When it reaches Libra, the autumn. When it reaches Capricorn, the winter. Therefore, because of these four seasons of the year, the poets imagine him in a chariot pulled by four horses. The names of the horses according to Ovid <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, Roman poet; these names appear in his *Metamorphoses*</note> are: Pyroeis, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon. Pyroeis is named from *pyr* <note>original: "pyr"</note> which signifies fire. Eous from *eos* <note>original: "eos"</note> which signifies the dawn. Aethon and Phlegon from *aethin* and *phlegin* <note>original: "ethin & phlegin"</note>, both of which signify to burn. They have, therefore, names derived from the heat of the sun. But Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Latin author and mythographer</note> and many others name the first horse Erythraeus, that is, red, from the red color that the sun has in the morning. The second Actaeon, because toward the third hour <note>approximately 9:00 AM in the medieval system of temporal hours</note> it extends its rays, which the Greeks call *actin* <note>original: "actin"</note>. The third Lampros, that is, splendid, because at midday it shines greatly. The fourth Philogeus, that is, lover of the earth, because toward the evening it descends to the earth. He is called the Sun

**CANTO X 262**

The sense that perceives splendor never saw anything more shining than the sun. Therefore, let us not marvel that our imagination—which can only grasp those things presented to it by the senses—cannot reach such heights. Nevertheless, <note>The commentator distinguishes between sensory imagination and intellectual faith.</note> although man cannot imagine such splendor, he can believe in it and yearn for it, that is, desire to see it.

->**Such was there the fourth family**<-

The author continues by demonstrating that the fourth family—that is, the spirits of this fourth heaven <note>The Heaven of the Sun, where the souls of great theologians and scholars reside.</note>—was such, meaning as shining as was said of Beatrice. He calls Him the "High Father" because He is the true Father who creates, generates, governs, and nourishes. He always "satisfies them" with Himself, just as a father satisfies his family with his own substance. "Showing how He breathes and how He begets": He satisfies them with Himself by demonstrating the single essence within the Divinity and also the Trinity within the Persons. Therefore, he says "how He breathes" <note>original: "come spira"</note> regarding the Eternal Love, that is, the Holy Spirit; and "how He begets" <note>original: "come figlia"</note> regarding how the Father generates the Son from eternity. Thus, God demonstrates to the blessed His unique essence and the Trinity of Persons, because by gazing into Him as if in a mirror, they understand all things. Some do not refer this to God but to the sun, which is read according to its nature shortly before this.

Now if you draw the eye of your mind
from light to light following my praises,
already you remain with thirst for the eighth.
To see every good, within there rejoices
the holy soul who makes the fallacious world
manifest to whoever listens well to him.
The body from which it was hunted lies
down in Cieldauro, and he from martyrdom
and from exile came to this peace.
See further flaming the ardent breath
of Isidore, of Bede, and of Richard,
who in contemplation was more than man.
This one, from whom your gaze returns to me,
is the light of a spirit whose grave thoughts
made death seem to him slow in coming.
It is the eternal light of Siger,
who, lecturing in the Street of Straw,
syllogized truths that brought him envy.
Then, like a clock that calls us
at the hour when the Bride of God rises—

In the eighth light is Boethius: who, because he wrote *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, the poet therefore says that this soul makes the fallacious world manifest: that is, he reveals the deceits and fallacies of this world to whoever hears him. Therefore, O Dante, if you "draw" <note>original: "trani," from the Latin "trano," meaning to pass through or lead across</note> the eye of the mind. For "trano" in Latin signifies "I pass through" and "I lead across." **The body.** Boethius was condemned by Theodoric, King of the Goths, and finally strangled in Pavia. **In Cieldauro.** This is a monastery called *Coelum Aureum* <note>Golden Sky</note>. **Isidore** was Spanish and Bishop of Seville. **Bede** was an English priest; and although he is canonized, he is always called "Venerable" because an angel wrote this name upon his tomb. **Richard** was a monk and was the brother of Hugh of Saint Victor. He was "more than man" in the contemplation of sacred letters, because he surpassed human possibility.

**Siger**, a very great dialectician who possessed in that faculty not a captious and sophistical science, but true knowledge. But he was so excellent that he was not without the emulation and envy of competitors; he lectured in Paris in the Street of Straw <note>Rue du Fouarre, the center of the schools of philosophy</note>. **Then like a clock**: religious orders have clocks and alarms which—

-> PARADISE <-

**B** <note>This letter refers to a specific section of the commentary</note> How foolish are the syllogisms—that is, how imperfect are their arguments and reasonings—because they do not conclude with the truth. A **syllogism** is an argument that provides proof for a doubtful thing, but it must not be defective; the major and minor premises must be true so that the conclusion follows from the things promised. *Who follows after* <note>original: "Chi drieto adiura"</note>: the meaning is this: Since the supreme good consists in the contemplation of divine things, to which I and Beatrice were attentive, the majority of men err because some place the supreme good in riches. Whence they give themselves either to civil law or to **aphorisms** (that is, to medicine), or to the priesthood, or to civil business (that is, to the government of the republic). All of these things, although by their nature they are honest and good, are nothing to those who do them solely for the sake of gain; such a person is neither a good man nor can he be happy. And much less so if he greedily seizes what is not his. Some place happiness in lordships and honors and rule by tyrannical force or by **sophisms** (that is, by fraud). A **sophism** is an argument that appears true but is false, but here he uses it to mean **C** fraud. Some place happiness in leisure and laziness. Some in lust; and all of them err because these cannot be true happiness.

**P** After the lights that formed a crown around Beatrice and Dante, turning themselves, returned to that point from which they had started, they stopped just as a candle stays in a candlestick. He uses this comparison because these Doctors have explained the Holy Scripture inspired by God in the Evangelists and in the other early Doctors. The circle having stopped, Thomas, smiling at Dante's ignorance, began to speak; and the light became more **bright** (that is, more pure). And he said: "Looking into God, from whose rays I shine as in a mirror in which every truth is seen, I learn and understand your thoughts, which is the reason why I speak." Your thoughts are that you **doubt** (that is, you are in uncertainty), and doubting, you have the desire and will that my speech be **re-sifted** (that is, newly distinguished and opened in such plain speech) that your **PERCEPTION** (that is, your intellect) **discerns** (that is, distinguishes and knows) two doubts. The first is where I said of Saint Dominic: *Where one fattens well if one does not stray.* The other doubt is where I said of Solomon: *No second ever rose.* Here, therefore, it is **necessary** (that is, it is required) that a good distinction be made.

**P** Because the difficulty of these verses lies in the ordering of the text, proceed thus: Divine Providence, which governs the visible and invisible world with that counsel in which every **created vision** (that is, every created intellect, both angelic and human) is vanquished before it reaches the bottom. For neither man nor angel, because they have a finite intellect, can reach the depths of the divine counsel. This Providence, therefore, ordained two princes in the Church Militant so that, in favor of said Church, they might be guides and lead her to the port of salvation; **on either side** (that is, with charity and with wisdom). And Providence ordained this **so that she might go** (that is, so that the **bride**, the said Church, might go toward the bridegroom, toward Christ). **FOR** the Church is the bride of **CHRIST**, who on the cross with **loud cries** espoused the bride with His **blessed blood**, which He shed for our redemption; and she goes secure in herself through the guidance of the two said princes, and **more faithful** to Him (that is, with more faith toward Him). And these two were Francis and Dominic. And **one** (that is, Francis) was all **seraphic in ardor** (that is, all burning in charity, because the Seraphim are the first angels to whom charity is attributed). The **other** (that is, Dominic) was, through wisdom, a splendor of **cherubic light**, because wisdom is attributed to the Cherubim. **Of one I shall speak.** It will be sufficient to speak of one of the two, because in praising Francis, one also praises Dominic, because their life and religious purpose were equal in both. Not without the highest artistry does he lead the Dominican <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> to praise Francis and not Dominic; for the said Thomas, being of the Order of Dominic, has more faith in...

CANTO ELEVEN 264

From this slope, where the break in the ridge
most lessens its steepness, a sun was born to the world
as this one sometimes rises from the Ganges. <note>Dante compares the birth of St. Francis to the rising sun. The Ganges refers to the East, where the sun appears most brilliant.</note>

Therefore, let him who speaks of that place
not say "Ascesi" <note>original: "Asceſi" - the old spelling of Assisi, which also means "I have risen."</note>, for that would be saying too little,
but "The Orient," if he wishes to speak properly.

<margin>d Describes the city of Assisi where Saint Francis was born. Topino is a river to the west of Assisi. THE chosen hill: this is to the east. And in this place the blessed Ubaldo of Gubbio performed penance; and from this the river called Chiusi is born. PORTA Sole is the gate of Perugia that leads to Assisi, as is a fact known to many. Fertile slope: Assisi is placed on a slope which is very fertile. Ubaldo: he was first a hermit on this mountain and later was Bishop of Gubbio. FROM this slope: It shows Francis being born in Assisi. Who truly was a sun: because through the sanctity of his life and excellent examples he removed every heretical darkness which in those times greatly occupied human minds. At one time there were Francis, founder of the Order of Minors <note>The Franciscans</note>, and Dominic, born in Caleruega, a place in Spain, who instituted the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>. They flourished after the year one thousand two hundred of our salvation.</margin>

He was not yet very far from his rising
when he began to make the earth feel
some comfort from his great virtue;
For such a lady, as a youth, he ran into war
against his father, to whom, as to death,
no one unlocks the gate of pleasure. <note>The "lady" is Poverty. People avoid Poverty as they avoid death.</note>
And before his spiritual court
and in the presence of his father <note>original: "corā patre" (Latin: before the father)</note> he was united to her;
afterward, from day to day, he loved her more strongly.

<margin>n He was not far from his birth because he was of a young age when the earth and men began to know his virtue and take comfort. FOR: because he ran into war with his father who was Bernardone, a citizen of Assisi and a wool-merchant. For such a lady: that is, for Poverty. To whom: to which Poverty no one unlocks—that is, opens the gate of pleasure—any more than they do for death. And in his spiritual court: because with the counsel of his spiritual father <note>The Bishop of Assisi</note> he made a profession of poverty, and therefore he adds "and before his father." AFTERWARD from day to day he loved her MORE strongly: because his love always grew. This Poverty, deprived of Christ when He returned to heaven (who was her first husband), remained without an invitation—that is, without being sought—for more than eleven hundred years until this man of whom I speak, who is Francis. And he said more than eleven hundred because, as we showed above, twelve hundred years passed from Christ to Francis. Nor did it avail this Poverty that her great boldness of spirit was known everywhere; which was so great that she did not fear Caesar the unconquered emperor when she stood with Amyclas. Lucan writes that while both the armies of Caesar and Pompey were in Epirus, and every man was in great trembling, only Amyclas, a very poor fisherman, having nothing to lose or because death should be desired by him, lived most securely in his little hut where he retired to rest after fishing. Caesar wanted to return to Italy against the force of the winds to bring the rest of his army to Epirus. And finally, driven back by the storm, he retreated to the hut of Amyclas. Nor did it yet avail her to have such constancy with her spouse and such ferocity that she did not abandon him even in death; and not only did she accompany him with Mary even to the cross, but while Mary remained on the ground, she ascended with Christ upon the cross.</margin>

This woman, deprived of her first husband,
eleven hundred years and more, despised and obscure,
remained without an invitation until his time.
Nor did it avail to hear that he found her secure
with Amyclas, at the sound of his voice,
he who made the whole world afraid.
Nor did it avail to be constant or fierce,
so that where Mary remained below,
she with Christ climbed upon the cross.
But so that I do not proceed too obscurely,
take Francis and Poverty for these lovers
henceforth in my diffuse speech.

Men do not consider how much wealth is in voluntary poverty, and how much tranquility of soul. Because truly the infallible Truth said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit" <note>original: "Beati pauperes ſpiritu" (Latin)</note>, that is, humble in heart. Because nothing is lacking to him who desires nothing. And certainly Diogenes the Cynic was rich, living happily and desiring nothing. And Alexander the Great was poor, to whom nothing was sufficient, and the more he acquired, the more he desired. Caesar lived always in anxiety, always in fear. But he found the aforementioned Amyclas very cheerful, of whom Lucan said: "O safe condition of the poor man's life! O humble homes and gifts of the gods not yet understood! To what temples could it happen to tremble at no tumult when Caesar's hand knocks?" <note>original: "O uitae tuta facultas pauperis..." (Latin quote from Lucan's Pharsalia)</note> And Juvenal: "But more are strangled by money amassed with excessive care." Also: "Though you carry but a few small vessels of pure silver, entering on a journey by night, you will fear the sword and the pole in the shadows, and at night you will tremble at the shadow of a reed in the moonlight; the empty traveler sings in the presence of the thief." <note>original: "Cantabat uacuus coram latrone uiator" (Latin)</note>

Their harmony and their joyful countenances,
love and wonder and sweet regard,
caused holy thoughts to be born;
So much so that the venerable Bernard
unshod himself first, and after such peace
he ran, and running, it seemed to him he was slow.

<margin>I Their harmony and their joyful countenances: If every discord is born from nature and from the greed of possessing treasure, voluntary poverty will always create the highest harmony. And if riches are full of care, poverty will be full of joy. Love: that is, the supreme charity with which one ignited the other. Wonder: because one was a mirror of purity and sanctity to the other, they caused holy thoughts to be born. Because harmony and love and being content with one's present state always direct a man to virtuous works. BERNARD:</margin>

**PARADISO**

And they make the people here to be prescient
by the covenant that God made with Noah,

->**Commentary**<-

Here is the fable which we have explained at length elsewhere. **And they make the people here to be prescient**, that is, divining or foretelling, by the covenant that God made with Noah. The meaning is that the celestial arch <note>The rainbow</note> makes man prescient: for in the future the world is not to perish by water as in the times of Noah. And this sentence is in the ninth chapter of Genesis where God says to Noah: *I will establish my covenant with you, and never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood* <note>original Latin: "Statuam pactum meum vobiscum. & nequaquam ultra interficietur omnis caro aquis diluvii"</note>; and a little further down: *This is the sign of the covenant which I give between me and you and every living soul that is with you for everlasting generations. I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and between the earth. And when I cover the sky with clouds, it shall appear.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc est signum federis quod do inter me & vos & ad omnem animam viventem quae est vobiscum in generationes sempiternas. Arcum meum ponam in nubibus celi. & erit signu federis inter me & inter terram. Cumque obduxero coelum nubibus apparebit"</note>

**[Right Column]**
**Q** ...templative. Illuminato was a Friar Minor. Augustine was a Friar Minor. These two were among the first companions of Saint Francis. And although in this circle are placed those who shine like the sun with supreme doctrine and could illuminate others, nevertheless he placed these two here; though they did not shine through doctrine, they illuminated others through the examples of a most holy life. **R** Hugh was from Pavia and a monk of the monastery of Saint Victor. He wrote many things in theology and especially on the Sacraments, on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, on the Hierarchy of Dionysius, and many other works. Some say he was first a canon regular and then a canon at Saint Victor. He was of a most holy life; and they say that when he was coming to death and about to receive the body of Christ, he said: "Go, my soul, with your Redeemer," and then he expired, and the Eucharist was visibly seen to leave the hands of the priest and fly to heaven. **S** Peter the Eater <note>Petrus Comestor, so named because he "devoured" books</note> was a Lombard and wrote the *Scholastic History*. **T** Peter of Spain wrote twelve books on dialectic <note>Logic</note>. **V** Nathan the prophet and prince of priests, who by God's command rebuked David for the adultery committed with the wife of Uriah, as appears in the Book of Kings. **X** John Chrysostom, meaning "Golden Mouth," so named for his supreme eloquence; he calls him "metropolitan" because he was Bishop of Constantinople, to whose care were committed Thrace, Pontus, and Phoenicia. **Y** Anselm was from Normandy, Archbishop of Canterbury. He wrote on the harmony of free will, divine prescience, and predestination; on the fall of the devil; on original sin; and on the incarnation of the Divine Word. **Z** Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus</note> was English <note>The commentator likely confuses him with Alcuin; Rabanus was German</note> and wrote on poetry; he was the brother of Bede. **A** Joachim <note>Joachim of Fiore</note> had the gift of the Holy Spirit in such a way that without much science he opened every obscure passage of Holy Scripture. He wrote on the duration of the world and the things that were to happen in that time. "To envy" means to emulate, not with a vicious envy but with virtuous emulation. "Such a great paladin": there were twelve counts of the palace ordained by Charlemagne to fight for the faith, wherefore Dominic may well be called a paladin, having so ardently fought against the heretics. The meaning is that the inflamed love of Thomas toward Saint Francis moved me to emulate him and do the same toward Saint Dominic.
