A chord <note>original: "Titino"</note>, that is, the sweet sound of many strings when they are stretched in tune. And he adds that although he had not understood the words of the hymn, nevertheless he perceived that such a melody contained the highest praises, because among many words he understood only:
**Arise and Conquer.** <note>original: "Surge & uinci"</note> These two words are spoken in Holy Scripture regarding Christ: Rise from death and conquer the devil. The author feigns that of all the hymn they sang there to Christ, he understood only "Arise and Conquer," to demonstrate that it is easy for everyone to understand that the passion and death of Christ was the victory that freed us from the servitude of the devil; but many other marvelous things contained therein are not understood except by the most learned men. He demonstrates that although he affirms that in all this mental pilgrimage he has found nothing up to this place that binds him with more love, nevertheless he does not contradict what he has already said so many times about Beatrice, nor for this reason does he place her second in his love. **And to see me speak the truth**—that is, you can see that I spoke the truth saying that no other thing had so bound me as this melody, because my pleasure in Beatrice is included in that. And by Beatrice, this is understood. And the pleasure I take in Beatrice becomes more sincere and more pure the higher I ascend, because her eyes showed me all these things.

### Commentary Block 2
**d** He describes how the welcome that Master Cacciaguida gave to Dante was just as piteous <note>In this context, "piteous" means full of natural affection or piety, rather than sorrowful.</note> as that which Anchises gave to Aeneas in the Elysian Fields. **If our greatest Muse**—that is, if Virgil, who writes this and is the greatest Muse (meaning the greatest poet among the Latins)—**deserves credit.** He says this as if to say: do not affirm the fictions created by Virgil, nor that Anchises actually saw Aeneas in the Elysian Fields, as this poet feigns in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*. Rather, it is to demonstrate that Cacciaguida took as much joy in the arrival of Dante as Virgil describes there to have been...

### Cornelia, Mother of the Gracchi

**P** Regarding the rhyme, he mentioned **Cornelia**. She was the daughter of Scipio Africanus and the wife of Tiberio Gracco <note>Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus</note>; a woman of supreme honesty, of a masculine spirit, and of such self-control that when two serpents were found in her house, and the augurs <term>augurs: ancient Roman religious officials who interpreted divine will through signs</term> reported to Tiberius that it was necessary to kill one: and if the female were killed, Cornelia would die; and if the male were killed, he would die. Tiberius, a man of great reputation in the city, judging the death of Cornelia to be more harmful to his family than his own, commanded that the male serpent be killed and the female be saved. She was very eloquent and devoted to studies; and with her teachings, she made her two sons, Gaius and Tiberius, most eloquent orators. She lived for many years...

<summary>This passage recounts the life of Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus, highlighting her education, her husband's sacrifice for her life, and her role in tutoring her famous sons.</summary>

**AND THIS** is the oration that the poet makes to Cacciaguida, in which—because he wishes to ask him about what is to become of him, **WHICH** is a contingent future—he uses an opening in which he gains goodwill. **AND** he demonstrates that it is easy for the spirit, showing that he "uplifts himself," <gloss>that is, he rises up toward God</gloss> in such a way that he sees contingent things before they are: just as we men, without any formal proof, see that a triangle cannot contain within itself two obtuse angles. Every triangle, whether right-angled, acute, or obtuse, cannot have more than one obtuse angle. **O DEAR PLANT**: <note>The Italian "pietra" (stone) in the transcription is likely a typo for "pianta" (plant/root), as the commentary refers to the "living topaz" mentioned previously.</note> this is used metaphorically because above he calls him a "living topaz." **CONTINGENT THINGS** are those that can either be or not be. **BECAUSE** things are either necessary, impossible, or contingent. Necessary things are those that cannot *not* be. **THEREFORE** it was necessary that Dante should die, because all things born must die. **IT WAS** contingent that he should live longer at one time than another.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Dante and his ancestor Cacciaguida in the Heaven of Mars. Cacciaguida has just finished prophesying Dante’s exile and now encourages him to write his poem truthfully, regardless of the offense it may cause to powerful figures.</meta>

->CANTO XVIII 280<-

The light in which my treasure was smiling,
whom I had found there, first became radiant
like a golden mirror in a ray of sun.
Then it responded: "A conscience that is dark
either with its own or with another’s shame
will indeed feel your words to be harsh.
But nonetheless, setting aside every lie,
make your entire vision manifest,
and then let them scratch where the itch is.
For if your voice shall be troublesome
at the first taste, it will leave behind
vital nourishment when it is digested.
This cry of yours shall be like the wind,
which strikes most fiercely the highest towers;
and that is no small argument for your honor.
Therefore, there have been shown to you in these wheels,
upon the mountain, and in the sorrowful valley,
only souls who are known to fame.
For the mind of him who hears will not rest,
nor fix its faith upon an example that has
its roots unknown and hidden,
nor for any other argument that is not apparent."

<note>The "wheels" refer to the spheres of Paradise; the "mountain" is Purgatory; the "sorrowful valley" is Hell.</note>

The poet had proposed his doubt, to which—before he responded—the light in which his treasure was smiling (that is, the spirit of Cacciaguida) became radiant (that is, splendid and shining, just as a golden mirror becomes in a ray of the sun). And the poet imagines this because, by writing the things found in this journey of his, the fame of Cacciaguida remained more luminous. And through this splendor, which was joy within him, he demonstrates that the discourse the poet had made pleased him. And then he responded to the doubt proposed to him in this form: "You, Dante, shall write what you have seen so that the dark (that is, black) conscience (that is, so that men who do not have a pure conscience, but one stained either by their own shame—meaning by sins committed by themselves—or by the shame of others—meaning by the sins of relatives and neighbors whom you shall describe) shall FEEL your harsh word (that is, the infamy that you will give them in your verses). But let what you write be without falsehood or lies; and 'let them scratch where the itch is' <note>original: "lascia pur grattare dove la rogna"</note> (that is, let those who have cause to grieve, grieve; for it is not an unjust thing but most worthy to spread perpetual infamy upon those who have been wicked)."

He most prudently imagines doubting whether it is good to write such a work in which infamy is given to those already dead, which then reflects upon their descendants who are still living; and he rightly concludes that it ought to be written so that these may be an example to those who hear. Through this, everyone might strive to act in a way that they do not fall into such infamy, and their relatives and descendants, through their many virtues, might make themselves unworthy of being struck by such infamy. And therefore he says that "if the voice" (that is, your word) "shall be troublesome at the first taste," like some bitter food given to preserve health, it will provide such a rebuke that it will correct and heal the soul; just as that bitter food, once it is digested and processed, provides such nourishment to the body and restores its health.

->CANTO XVIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE<-

**G**ladly now was that blessed mirror
enjoying only its own word, and I was
tasting mine, tempering the sweet with the bitter.
And that lady who was leading me to God
said: "Change your thought; think that I am
near to Him who lightens every wrong."
I turned myself toward the loving sound
of my comfort; and what love I then saw
in those holy eyes, I leave here unspoken;
Not only because I distrust my own speech,
but because the mind cannot return
so far above itself, unless another guide it.

-># PARADISE<-

<margin>h</margin>

Cacciaguida has already predicted to the poet his exile and refuge. Now, in this eighteenth chapter, he shows him many excellent and beautiful spirits within that Cross of Mars; and afterwards, he ascends to the Heaven of Jupiter. But as for the beginning, he says that already after the words spoken, that blessed mirror—that is, Cacciaguida, in whom divine rays were shining as if in a mirror—was enjoying himself alone. That is to say, he was enjoying himself, of his own word: namely, of that which he had predicted to me and encouraged me in, to endure the hardships and to manifest what I had heard and seen. And I, Dante, was tasting my own: that is, what I was discussing within myself, tempering the bitter with the sweet. For if the exile and the other troubles he had predicted for me were bitter, the honor I was to receive from such a magnanimous lord was sweet to me; and furthermore, my life was destined to endure <note>The commentator refers to Dante's future fame and the longevity of his work</note>. And Beatrice admonished me that I should change my thought: that is, that I should return to the contemplation of heavenly things, and consider that she, already judging me—

# CANTO XVIII. 281

**[Main Poetic Text]**

And at the name of the other Maccabee
I saw another move, spinning in a circle,
and joy was the whip to that top.
So for Charlemagne and for Roland
my attentive gaze followed two more,
as the eye follows its falcon in flight.
Then William and Renouard
and Duke Godfrey drew my sight
along that cross, and Robert Guiscard.
Then, moved and mingled among the other lights,
the soul who had spoken to me showed me
what an artist he was among the singers of heaven.

I turned myself toward my right side
to see in Beatrice my duty,
signaled either by words or by gesture.
And I saw her eyes so pure,
so joyful, that her appearance
surpassed her other and her latest custom.
And as, by feeling greater delight,
a man, by doing well from day to day,
perceives that his virtue advances,
So I perceived that my circling round
together with the heaven had increased its arc.

**[Commentary Text]**

...their cloud: that is, they will cast out a fiery splendor just as we see ignited vapors in a cloud darting about like little torches. And this suits warlike men who are of a choleric nature, similar to Mars and of burning virtue. The poet therefore looked and saw a light move suddenly through the cross, which Cacciaguida named Joshua. Therefore, "as it was done," <note>original: "come l si fe"</note> that is, as soon as the illumination was made. Nor was the speech known to me before the act: that is, at the very same moment that Cacciaguida named Joshua, the flame appeared.

**P** Joshua was the son of Nun: and he was a type, <note>original: "typo"</note> that is, a figure of Christ: not only in name but also in deeds. For succeeding Moses, who was already dead, he crossed the river Jordan; and he destroyed the kingdoms of the enemies and acquired the Promised Land and divided it among the victorious people of Israel. He was called by the Hebrews Joshua ben Nun, <note>original: "Iosue ben nun"</note> that is, Joshua son of Nun. Judas Maccabeus: it would be a prolix and too long a thing to narrate the most brave deeds of the Maccabees, as it is written in the Bible in the Book of Maccabees. In the times of Antiochus the king, there was a wicked transgression among the Hebrew people, and a great part of them, leaving the divine worship, gave themselves to King Antiochus and adored idols; for Antiochus conquered Egypt and afterwards took Jerusalem and despoiled the temple. And in those times Mattathias, with five sons who would not obey the king nor adore idols, did many things in defense of the Law. Afterward he died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year of his life and left as prince of the military Judas Maccabeus, his son. This man, with the help of his brothers, did miraculous things **Q** against the transgressors of the law of God; and he expanded the power of those who observed it; and he was of such strength that on the day he died in battle, he killed a thousand men. This man moved spinning like a top <note>term: "paleo" — a wooden whipping top used as a toy</note> turns when children strike it with the whip, and "joy was the whip to the top." That is, he was moved by joy just as the top is moved by the whip. CHARLEMAGNE: the life and lineage of this man we narrated above in the sixth canto of this canticle. And similarly of Roland we spoke in his place. William was the Count of Orange, <note>note: The text says "doringa," likely referring to William of Orange, a hero of Old French epics</note> son of the Count of Narbonne. Renouard was a most brave fighter against the infidels and a relative of William. **R** GODFREY. In the year of Christian salvation one thousand ninety-six: Peter the **S** Hermit, a man of holy life but previously unknown, raised many Christian princes to undertake the enterprise against the Saracens. Of the army, Duke Godfrey of Bouillon was the leader, most excellent in military discipline. Leaving France, he passed through Germany and Hungary to Constantinople; and through the Hellespont he passed into Asia and captured Nicaea and Antioch and many other cities; and in the third year he took Jerusalem. And when the Christians wished to crown him king of this realm, he refused it, affirming he did not wish to wear a crown of gold in that city where Christ wore one of thorns. He was nonetheless made Duke, and upon his death he was succeeded by Baldwin his brother, who reigned eighteen years and three times defeated the Egyptians and killed the Caliph, their king. Robert **T** Guiscard, Duke of Normandy: of whom we treated in the first canticle. And finally, that blessed soul of Cacciaguida, who had shown him what an artist he was among the singers of heaven.

**h** The poet had already described the Heaven of Mars; and now, wishing to describe that of Jupiter, not departing from Christian theology, he feigns that he turned to Beatrice to see in her his duty. That is, how much it was his debt to describe; and such duty he expected to understand from her either by words or by sign. Therefore, the poet, wishing—as in the other parts of his volume so in this—not to depart from the Christian religion, proceeded according to theology which teaches us the truth: either by words, that is, by open sentences; or by sign, that is, by hidden ones. AND he saw her eyes. In short, her eyes were more lucid and cheerful than other times, and even more lucid than the last time he saw her in the Heaven of Mars, through which it appeared...

# CANTO XVIII. 282

...signs that moved in their wheel, which signifies that they made a circular motion, which is proper to the perfected soul. <note>The "wheel" refers to the souls of the just forming patterns in the sky.</note> Because just as such a motion begins from itself and returns to itself, so the good soul, proceeding from God with its virtues, returns to God. Then, becoming one of these signs—which are D, I, and L—they stopped and were silent, so that there would be a small interval—that is, a small space—between one figure and the other, so it could be understood that each of these letters signified a word. <note>The souls are spelling out "Diligite Iustitiam," meaning "Love Justice."</note>

It is the custom of Greek and Latin poets not only at the beginning of a book to invoke the help of the Muses, but also later when, in writing, they arrive at a great matter, as we see especially in Homer and Virgil. They renew the invocation both to have divine favor and to make the reader attentive, who, hearing the invocation, expects great things.

->**their figures as I have conceived them.**<-
<note>Dante addresses the Muse as "Pegasea" because the Muses' fountain, Hippocrene, was struck open by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus.</note>

PARADISE

And they rule as princes: there is nothing that so maintains love and concord, and preserves human society—to which nature leads us—as much as justice. Therefore, it is no wonder if those who have ruled with supreme justice are now so united in this proud heaven. Understanding this union, the poet did not turn to the eagle as a single entity, but as many spirits; these he calls flowers because they are the ornaments of that heaven where they possess eternal joy. And he says that although they are many flowers, nevertheless not many scents, but only one, issues from them. Then he requests of them that, by breathing the truth into him, they might <term>solve</term> <note>The author uses "solve" in the sense of the Latin *solvere*, meaning to release or break a fast.</note> his state. That is, that they might dissolve and take away the great fast which has long held him in hunger; for he who remains fasting feels hunger. This is a Latinate way of speaking, because <note>original: "solvere ieiunium"</note> to "solve the fast" means to break the fast. This is a metaphor: for you must understand him to express that for a long time he has been fasting—that is, void of that truth for which he has a great hunger—meaning a great desire to know. And the reason why he has been fasting is because on earth he has found no food.

**W**hen he who illumines all the world
descends from our hemisphere

imposed silence on their angelic ringings.

[Woodcut illustration: An eagle formed by spirits in the sky. Below, Dante and Beatrice stand among other figures.]

As in the preceding chapter the eagle demonstrated the incomprehensible justice of God and rebuked kings, so in this one it demonstrates to the author some of the spirits that configured it. This twentieth chapter contains four parts. In the first, it describes what the disposition of the eagle was. In the second, the eagle names five excellent spirits. In the third, it resolves a doubt born from having seen two of those souls <note>A reference to the salvation of Pagans, specifically Trajan and Ripheus.</note>. In the fourth, it describes the depth of predestination. In the verses already written, he places a simile saying that the place where the eagle was appeared as the sky is seen when the sun descends to the other hemisphere: because when the light of the sun is missing, the sky adorns itself with various stars: and so all those spirits kindled with charity appeared like stars in that eagle after the lucid stones—that is, the shining spirits which he calls *lapilli*, meaning precious stones with which Jove, which is the sixth planet, was engemmed—put an end to their songs: and the eagle resumed its speech. And he describes by comparison the discourse of the voice from the neck of the eagle, showing that it rose through the channel of the neck: with that noise that a copious amount of water makes descending from rock to rock: and as the sound of the lute—that is, the *cythera* <note>original: "cythera" — a classical stringed instrument.</note>—takes its form in the neck of said instrument: because in that, the fingers of the one who plays touch the strings. And as through the holes—that is, the openings—of the bagpipe or flute or pipe, the wind—that is, the breath—that the player puts there takes its form of voice by penetrating—that is, passing through—said holes: so through the neck of the eagle rose that murmur: and in the beak the voice became firm, and it spoke those things that my heart desired. And certainly, it is a marvelous fantasy in this poet, who narrates his fiction in such a way that he makes almost the impossible seem credible: and he is much like the genius of the poet Ovid: who in his monstrous transformations makes things almost plausible.

**T**HE eagle speaks to demonstrate to Dante six most excellent spirits which make the form of the eye in the eagle, and it admonishes Dante that he should look fixedly at that part which in a mortal eagle looks at and endures the sun, and this is the eye. And as eagles in this way are able to look...

The part in me that sees and endures the sun
in mortal eagles, he began to me,
now must be looked at fixedly.
Because of the fires of which I form my figure,
those from which the eye in my head sparkles
are the highest of all their ranks.
He who shines in the middle as the pupil
was the singer of the Holy Spirit,
who moved the ark from town to town:
Now he knows the merit of his song...
<note>Referring to King David, who moved the Ark of the Covenant.</note>

...that if one cannot be saved who has not true faith in Christ, in what manner Trajan, not having been a Christian, could
have ascended to heaven. "The kingdom of heaven": the answer in essence is this: that although the divine will does not
allow that one who is not a Christian can ascend to heaven, nevertheless a most ardent charity and undoubting faith
conquers and forces such a will: in a way that it allows the pagan to be saved. Not, however, that the divine will is
conquered as one man conquers another by force. But it is conquered because it wills to be; and thus conquered, it conquers with its benevolence: that is,
with its kindness, as happens when we conquer a friend in a dispute: nevertheless out of humanity,
so that he is not ashamed, we yield and let him win.

# CANTO XXI 281

When Saturn is well-disposed at the birth of a man, it makes him an investigator of ancient and hidden things. It bestows acute reasoning and the discourse of logic; and also, according to Macrobius <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman philosopher whose commentary on the 'Dream of Scipio' was a primary source for medieval cosmology.</note>, that virtue of the mind which the Greeks call *theoretikon* <note>original: "thoriticõ"</note>, that is, the power of contemplating and speculating. This fact led the poet <note>Referring to Dante Alighieri.</note> to represent the contemplative life within this sphere. But to treat <margin><insert>R</insert></margin> the nature of Saturn more closely: this planet is diurnal, masculine, cold, and dry; melancholic, timid, old, lazy, sterile, and malignant. And although it is more remote from the Earth than the others, it is nonetheless more harmful. It is the signifier of the ancients and the predecessor of burials and of the dead; of the earth and of all its cultivation; of buildings, of every metal mine, and of hidden treasures. It signifies large, long beasts, and quartan fevers <note>A fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, traditionally associated with black bile and Saturn.</note> and morphea <note>A skin condition characterized by painless, discolored patches.</note>. It makes a man have foul breath and be a lover of stinking and filthy things. It makes him lazy, slow, pale in color, with a curved body, and thin <unclear>u</unclear>

# CANTO XXI OF PARADISE

In that place <note>The monastery of Santa Croce di Fonte Avellana</note> was I, Peter Damian;

Cephas <note>Saint Peter</note> came, and the great vessel

Now the modern pastors require someone to prop them up
on this side and that, and someone to lead them—
so heavy are they!—and someone to lift their trains from behind.
They cover their palfreys <note>Saddle horses</note> with their mantles,
so that two beasts travel under a single hide.
O Patience, that endures so much!

At this voice I saw many little flames
descend from step to step and whirl,
and every whirl made them more beautiful.
Around this one <note>Peter Damian</note> they came and stopped,
and let out a cry of such high sound
that nothing here could be compared to it;
nor did I understand it, so much did the thunder overcome me.

<margin>In that place: that is, in the hermitage of Catria was I, Peter Damian; and he gives his proper name. And "Peter the Sinner" was I in the house of Our Lady on the Adriatic shore.</margin>

# PARADISE

->**Canto XXII**<-

And I said to him: "The affection that you show
in speaking with me, and the kind countenance
which I perceive and note in all your burning spirits,
has expanded my confidence
just as the sun does to the rose, when it opens
and becomes as wide as its power allows.
Therefore I pray you—and you, Father, assure me—
if I may receive so great a grace that I
might see you with your face uncovered." <note>Dante asks to see the Saint's actual human form, which is currently veiled by the intense light (the "burning spirit") of his beatitude.</note>
Whereupon he: "Brother, your high desire
shall be fulfilled in the final sphere, <note>The Empyrean, the highest heaven beyond space and time.</note>
where all others are fulfilled, and mine as well.
There, every desire is perfect, mature,
and whole; in that sphere alone
is every part exactly where it has always been.
For it is not in space, and it has no poles;
and our stairway reaches all the way up to it,
which is why it steals away from your sight.
Far up as that, the patriarch
Jacob saw it stretching its upper part,
when it appeared to him so laden with angels. <note>A reference to Jacob's Ladder (Genesis 28:12), symbolizing the contemplative path to God.</note>

But to climb it now, no one lifts
their feet from the earth, and my Rule <note>The Rule of Saint Benedict, the foundational document for Western monasticism.</note>
remains below, only to waste the paper it is written on."

<column-break/>

**[Commentary]**

In this section, the author <insert>Dante</insert> addresses the spirit of Saint Benedict with great humility. He explains that the saint's welcoming words have given him the courage to speak openly, comparing his soul to a rose opening under the warmth of the sun. <note>original: "come sol fa la rosa"</note>

Dante’s request is profound: he wishes to see the saint "with uncovered image," meaning he wants to see the human features of the soul rather than the blinding light that surrounds the blessed in Saturn. Benedict responds by explaining the nature of the Empyrean—the "final sphere." Unlike the lower heavens, which move and exist within space, the Empyrean is stationary and eternal. <note>The "poles" mentioned refer to the celestial poles of the rotating physical heavens.</note>

The Saint then laments the state of the world. He cites the ladder of Jacob as a symbol of the contemplative life that leads to the Empyrean, but bitterly remarks that his "Rule"—the set of guidelines for monks—is now ignored. The monks no longer attempt the spiritual climb; thus, the physical books containing his Rule are nothing more than wasted parchment. <note>A sharp critique of the 14th-century monastic orders for their perceived laziness and corruption.</note>

<summary>Dante asks Saint Benedict if he may see his true form, leading to a discourse on the Empyrean and a harsh critique of the decline of monastic discipline.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Benedict, Jacob's Ladder, Empyrean, Monastic Rule, Seventh Heaven, Saturn, Contemplation</keywords>

PARADISE

[Top Left Column]

I saw the daughter of Latona <note>The Moon (Diana)</note> kindled
without that shadow which was the cause
why I once believed her rare and dense.
The aspect of your son, Hyperion, <note>The Sun (Apollo)</note>
I there sustained, and saw how there move
around and near him Maia and Dione: <note>The planets Mercury and Venus</note>
Then appeared to me the tempering of Jove
between his father and his son; and then was clear to me

And all the seven were displayed to me,
how great they are and how swift they are,
and how they are in distant shelter.

[Top Right Column]

**Without that shadow.** Regarding the shadow of the moon and the cause of it, he disputed at length in the sphere of the moon. **The aspect of your son, Hyperion.** Hyperion was, according to the fables, the son of Titan and Vesta and the father of the sun; hence Ovid says: *uidit hanc hyperione natus* <note>original: "Hyperion's son saw her"</note>. Therefore he says, "O Hyperion, I sustained and endured the sight of your son," that is, of the sun your child; because being in heaven, my sight was so strengthened that I could endure the solar rays. **And I saw how Maia and Dione.** That is, Mercury and Venus move around the sun and near to him. Maia was one of the seven daughters of Atlas, and she bore Mercury to Jove; and Mercury in his course never wanders far from the sun. Dione, as we demonstrated above, is the mother of Venus. And he says that these two planets, Venus and Mercury, move around the sun and near the sun. **The tempering of Jove between his father Saturn and his son Mars:** because Jove, being between cold Saturn and hot Mars, becomes temperate; **it was clear to me.** That is, it was manifest to me. **The variation they make.** Because he had already risen so high in contemplation that all these things were known to him.
**The little threshing-floor that makes us so fierce.** He descended with his eyes from sphere to sphere until he reached the earth; and looking at it, it seemed a small thing in comparison to the heavens, of which it is almost the center. And therefore he calls it a "little threshing-floor," that is, a small area. And this is a passage drawn from Boethius. **That makes us so fierce.** He marvels at human folly, which takes such insolence for a thing as small as the earth. **From hills to river-mouths**, that is, from the mountains to the seas. **Then I turned my eyes to the beautiful eyes** of Beatrice; as if to say, I returned to Theology.

[Center Heading]

CANTO XXIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

[Middle Left Column]

As the bird among the beloved
leaves,
having sat on the nest of her sweet
offspring
through the night that hides things from us,
who, to see the longed-for aspects
and to find the food wherewith she feeds them,
in which heavy labors are a joy to her,
anticipates the time upon an open spray,
and with ardent affection awaits the sun,
fixedly watching for the dawn to be born;
so my Lady was standing erect
and attentive, turned toward that region
beneath which the sun shows less haste. <note>The Meridian/Noon</note>

[Middle Right Column]

[Woodcut illustration: Dante and Beatrice stand at the left, witnessing a celestial vision. In the center, a radiant figure of Christ ascends or presides over a gathering of the blessed souls in the Eighth Sphere (the Fixed Stars), set against a backdrop of a church and a starry sky.]

[Bottom Section]

The author had in the preceding chapter described his ascent to the eighth sphere through the sign of Gemini; and at present in this 23rd chapter, he treats of the Triumphant Court <note>The Church Triumphant</note> which appears to him here; and afterward he ascends into the ninth sphere. Therefore, in the first part, he sets down the disposition of Beatrice, who prepared him to see the Church Triumphant. In the second, he describes the leader of this army <note>Christ</note>. In the third, the host that follows him. In the fourth, he describes the ninth sphere. Therefore: **As the bird among the beloved leaves**: because in those she has placed her children, near their nest she waits through the night for the day to come. And to see them and to provide their food with which she feeds them—in which every heavy labor and fatigue is a pleasure—she arrives early and anticipates, waking before the day, and turned toward the east, she awaits the dawn. So Beatrice, to feed Dante with celestial food, stood upright and attentive toward that region where the sun shows less haste: that is, toward the meridian part. For when the sun is in the middle of the sky, it seems to go more slowly than when it is in the east or the west; and he feigns that just as when the sun at midday is over our heads and illuminates everything, so Christ, who led that army, illuminates them all.

He begins to describe the celestial host, and feigns that Beatrice urges him to look at it; she says: "O Dante, why does my face enamor you so much that you do not turn away?" As if to say: "Although I am made so beautiful—because in this place the incomprehensible matter of Christ is treated through me—nevertheless, consider also his family, which truly is a garden that flowers; that is, which produces flowers under the rays of Christ." For just as the rays of the sun illuminate all earthly things and by their power generate them, so Christ, the true sun, illuminates these spirits. "Here is the Rose": Mary the Virgin, who deservedly is equated to the rose, which for its utility in various ailments, for its beauty, and for its scent, holds the principality among flowers. "Lilies": the apostles, teachers, and martyrs, in whom there is the highest whiteness of purity. "I surrendered myself to the battle" denotes that although the eye of the human mind is dazzled in the light of the knowledge of such ineffable things, nevertheless we must contemplate as much as sacred theology commands us, as the text ordains. "I saw many crowds of splendors," that is, of shining spirits, "flashed upon," that is, greatly illuminated by burning rays from above: that is, from the superior part. Just as once my eyes saw a meadow of flowers covered in shadow by the rays of the sun which "just now" <note>original: "pur hor"</note>—that is, recently—"passed through" <note>original: "mei," from the Latin "meare" meaning to pass through</note> through a "broken cloud" <note>original: "fracta nube"</note>. Therefore, thus the spirits shine, struck back by the rays of light that came to them from Christ, just as flowers in a meadow shine when, the meadow being shadowed, they are suddenly struck by the rays of the sun coming through the newly broken clouds. The name of Mary drew me so much to itself with all my soul that I gazed where the "greatest fire" was, that is, the greatest splendor, because I knew that it had to be her. [Middle Commentary Block]
above all the other spheres, which most burns: that is, it heats up more and is more "quickened": that is, it shines more and is more operative and effective than the other volumes: that is, the other heavens. *In the breath of God and in His ways:* because this sphere is closer to God than the others, and therefore receives His power more directly. This is the principle of motion and life; it has a universal formative power over worldly particulars, and from this all others receive, according to the natural order, their conservative and formative power, just as they receive natural being from God. Therefore it was "quickened in the breath of God" because it receives life-giving power from there. *Had above us:* above me and Beatrice. *The inner shore:* the lower part of the circumference. But it was so distant that it could not be seen from the place where I was. And because of this, my eyes could not follow the *crowned flame*: that is, Mary encircled by the angel in the form of a crown. And truly, the human intellect cannot raise itself so high as to see the end of the ascent of Mary, who rose after *her seed*, that is, after Christ. And just as the child sucking the milk takes such pleasure that it cannot contain it within itself, and therefore makes gestures with its hands, stretching them toward the mother to touch her because the affection of the soul is kindled in a way that shows in the exterior parts: so those flames of the blessed spirits stretched toward Mary, demonstrating their affection toward her.

[Right Column - Commentary]
The author feigns that in the eighth [heaven] he saw all the blessed, as if in a place from which, through influence, the grace of God then proceeded, which first precedes all virtuous acts. And he shows that he first meditated on the ascension of Christ, then of Mary. *Queen of Heaven:* The Church sings this antiphon or hymn in the vespers of the Resurrection: <note>original Latin: "Regina coeli letare alleluia. quia quem meruisti portare alleluia. Resurrexit sicut dixit alleluia. Ora pro nobis deum alleluia."</note> "Queen of Heaven, rejoice, alleluia. For He whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia. Has risen, as He said, alleluia. Pray for us to God, alleluia." *Oh, how much is the abundance:* oh, how great is the plenty and the bounty of the beatitude that is *stored up*, placed, and held in those richest coffers: that is, in the minds of the blessed which were very capable of divine grace and which were *good sowers*: that is, excellent plowmen. *Bubulcus* in Latin signifies the plowman, whom we call *bifolco* <term>bifolco: a traditional Italian term for a plowman or ox-driver</term>, whence the Apostle says: <note>original Latin: "qui parce seminat parce et metet & qui seminat in benedictionibus de benedictionibus et metet"</note> "He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings shall reap from blessings." *There they live and enjoy the treasure:* because in the world they acquired through tears and mourning that glory in which

[Bottom Full Width Commentary]
they now rejoice. *There he triumphs:* understand this as Peter the Apostle in his victory: because he conquered the devil, the world, and the flesh. And he triumphs under the Son of God: because if He had not redeemed us, we would have remained in the miserable servitude of the devil. And he says that he *holds the keys to such glory* to agree with the words of Christ saying: <note>original Latin: "et dabo tibi claves regni coelorum. et quodcunque ligaveris super terram ligatum erit et in coelis et quodcunque solveris super terram solutum erit et in coelis."</note> "And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven."

[Large decorative initial Q] O chosen fellowship to the great supper
of the blessed Lamb,
who feeds you in such a way
that your desire is always full;
If by the grace of God this man foretastes
of that which falls from your table,
before death prescribes his time,
Give heed to his immense affection
and bedew him with that which you drink;
you drink ever from the fountain whence comes his thought.
Thus Beatrice; and those joyful souls
made themselves spheres upon fixed poles,
flaming brightly in the manner of comets.
And as wheels in the mechanism of clocks
revolve so that the first, to one who watches,
seems quiet, and the last to fly;

**I**ntroduced in this twenty-fourth canto is Peter the Apostle. Because there are three principal steps that lead us to this celestial kingdom—Faith, Hope, and Charity—the poet imagines that Peter examines him on Faith. Therefore, first is the prayer of Beatrice to the blessed spirits. Then, Peter, through the prayers of Beatrice, examines the author on Faith. In the third part, he treats certain doubts of Faith; in the last, he asks Dante about his belief. Beatrice’s prayer has this beginning: *O chosen fellowship to the great supper*: O company chosen for the beatitude upon which the blessed spirits feed. And the food of this supper is the Lamb, which food ensures that whoever feeds on it is always satisfied. *Sodalitio*: fellowship or company, because in Latin *sodalis* means a companion at the table. *If these*: if this man, that is Dante, *foretastes of that which falls from your table*: that is, before his time he tastes of the celestial glory which the souls already taken into the supreme heaven enjoy, and into which he will later come in due time. *By the grace of God*: without which no good work can be in man. *Before death prescribes his time*: that is, before death occupies and takes away his time of living. *Give heed to his immense affection*: as if to say, it is a just thing that you grant him such grace since he desires it so much. *Bedew him*: that is, bathe him lightly. *Ros* in Latin means "dew," whence they say *Rorare* [to bedew]. Hence: *Rorate celi* <note>Latin: "Drop down dew, ye heavens"</note>. And this is easy for you to do because you drink always from the fountain from which comes every desire of his. Thus Beatrice spoke as is written above. And after these words they *made themselves spheres upon fixed poles*: that is, they made circles that revolved upon their beatitude as wheels revolve upon poles, that is, axles. The meaning is that those souls performed many circular dances. *Flaming*: that is, shining and flaming *in the manner of comets*: which throw out long and fiery rays. We have spoken of the comet before. *And as wheels*: as in a clock there are many wheels where one turns swiftly, another less so, and another even less; and thus they decrease in such a way that the last hardly moves. So those *carols*: that is, the souls that were figuring them. Specifically, *carola* means a round dance. *Differently dancing*: and by this difference he demonstrates more or less beatitude; and therefore he says: *made me judge them swift and slow in their richness.*

From the one I noted of greatest beauty
I saw a fire emerge so happy
that it left none there of greater brightness.
And three times around Beatrice
it revolved with a song so divine
that my imagination does not repeat it to me.
Therefore the pen falters and I do not write it,
for our imagination for such folds <note>Referring to the "folds" or nuances of the vision</note>,
not to mention our speech, is too vivid a color.
"O my holy sister, who so prays us
devoutly by your ardent affection,
you unbind me from that beautiful sphere."

**F**rom that *carol*, that is, the round dance which is more beautiful than the others because it was the one where the Apostles were, there emerged a fire so splendid that none remained there brighter. And this was the soul of Peter, who is among the first happy ones in such a way that none is more happy. And he revolved three times around Beatrice to denote that the doctrine and examples of Peter give true knowledge of the Trinity and of the three theological virtues, and compose our souls in their three principal parts: namely, the rational, the concupiscible <note>desiring</note>, and the irascible <note>spirited</note>. *With a song so divine*: that is, celestial, *that my imagination does not repeat it to me*: as if to say, I do not remember it, nor with my imagination can I recover it. Therefore I do not write it because imagining does not serve me. *Too vivid a color for such folds*: this is a metaphor from painting, where to make the distinction of the folds of a garment it is necessary to apply dark colors; and the meaning is that for such distinctions I find no way. *O holy sister*: and certainly Theology is the sister of Peter. *Who so prays us*: that is, in a way that you pray me through your ardent affection toward Dante that you unbind me and—

# CANTO XXIII <note>The header says XXIII, but the text is actually from Canto XXIV of the Paradiso.</note>

## o iiii

-> After that blessed fire had come to a rest, <-
-> it directed its breath toward my lady, <-
-> speaking in the manner I have described. <-

And she: "O eternal light of the great man
to whom our Lord left the keys
which he brought down of this wondrous joy,

Test this man on points both light and grave,
as it pleases you, concerning the faith
by which you once walked upon the sea.

If he loves well, hopes well, and believes well,
it is not hidden from you, for you have your sight
where everything is seen depicted.

But because that kingdom has made citizens
through the true faith, to glorify it,
it is good that he should happen to speak of it."

Just as the bachelor arms himself and does not speak
until the master proposes the question,
to support it and not to settle it,

So I armed myself with every reason
while she was speaking, to be ready
for such a questioner and such a profession:

"Speak, good Christian, make yourself manifest:
What is faith?" Whereupon I raised my brow
toward that light from which this was breathed.

Then I turned to Beatrice, and she promptly
made a sign to me that I should pour
the water out from my internal fountain.

"May the grace that grants that I confess myself
to the high <term>primipilo</term> <note>A Roman military term for a high-ranking centurion; here used for St. Peter as the leader of the Apostles.</note>,"
I began, "make my conceptions be expressed."

And I followed: "As the truthful pen
wrote of it, father, of your dear brother
who set Rome with you upon the good path:

Faith is the substance of things hoped for
and the evidence of things not seen;
and this appeared to me to be its <term>quidity</term> <note>The essence or "what-ness" of a thing.</note>."

Then I heard: "You feel quite rightly,
if you understand well why he placed it
among the substances and then among the evidences."

<column-break/>

...resolve and make me depart from the sphere and the low place where I was. **After that blessed fire had come to a rest.** The meaning is that after this fire, which is the soul of Peter, had circled three times, he stopped and directed his breath—that is, his speech—toward Beatrice, and Peter spoke the words already mentioned above.

<margin>q</margin> These are the words of Beatrice to the soul of Peter, whom she deservedly calls a **great man**, that is, a man because he was Christ's vicar on earth. And he left him the keys of eternal life which he brought down from heaven to earth. Therefore, Beatrice prays to Peter that he test and examine Dante on faith in every point, both light and easy as well as grave and difficult: **by which faith you walked upon the sea.** For it is written in the Gospel that Peter, being in the boat, said to Christ who was on the shore: *Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you* <note>original: "Si dominus es iube me uenire ad te"</note>, and Christ commanded him to come to Him. Wherefore he descended from the boat into the sea and walked upon the waves without wetting his feet as long as his faith lasted; then, beginning to fail, he started to sink. Wherefore Christ took him and pulled him to Himself, saying to him: *O man of little faith, why did you doubt?* <note>original: "modice fidei quid dubitasti"</note> **IF HE** Dante **loves well**, that is, has true charity, and **hopes well**, that is, has true hope, and **believes well**, that is, has true faith, which are the three theological virtues. It is not hidden from you, Peter, because by looking at God, in whom as in a mirror everything is seen, you can also see this. And because Peter could say in response that there is no need for me to ask since he knows what Dante does, Beatrice adds, saying that you should come to him—that is, to Dante—to speak of faith, because through it he acquired the celestial kingdom.

<margin>u</margin> He turned to Beatrice and she signaled to him that he should respond. This signifies that no one should presume to dispute concerning the faith if Beatrice does not grant it—that is, if one cannot defend it with theology. Then follows the prayer of Dante, in which he prays that that same grace of God which grants that he may confess before Saint Peter may also grant that he can express the concepts of his mind. And he calls Peter **primipilo**: because he was the first who carried the banner of Christ.

<margin>S</margin> **PRIMIPILO**, as Livy shows, was the first rank of soldiers in the Roman army. And Peter was the first in the Church Militant. And then, having invoked the grace of God, he adds the definition of faith, which he sets down as the **truthful pen** of Peter's **dear brother** wrote it—that is, as the Apostle Paul wrote in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11. This Paul, together with Peter, preaching the evangelical doctrine, **set Rome on the good path**, that is,

<margin>T</margin> in the right order and true way, bringing many back to the Christian faith through preachings and miracles. **Faith is the substance of things hoped for.** This is the definition of faith, and the definition is the reason of the thing which demonstrates its being according to its substantial elements. Therefore, faith is the substance of things hoped for—that is, faith is that upon which hope stands and is founded. For if we did not believe that God existed, and was just in a way that prepared a reward for the good and punishment for the evil, we would not believe that by doing good we go to the blessed life. Therefore, hope stands in faith as an accident in its subject; and for this reason, faith is substance. And it is the **evidence of things not seen**—that is, it is proof of things that do not appear and are not seen by us. For with faith, we demonstrate what eternal life is, and so with other things that do not appear. An "evidence" or argument is that which makes one believe doubtful things. **And this appeared to me to be its quidity**: that is, the true definition according to its essential things. For this word

---

**quidity** is the essence or substance of the thing; and it is not an ancient Latin word, but was found by Christian philosophers, derived from this word *quid* [what]. For in asking *quid est homo* [what is man?], we ask concerning his substance, and the answer is "a rational, mortal animal." Just as in asking *qualis est* [of what sort is he?], we ask about the accident, and the answer is "he is good" or "he is bad" and the like.

which was once a vine and now has become a thorn."

<gloss>to sow the plant: that is, to build the holy church which was once a vine, meaning fruitful, and now has become a thorn, meaning sterile.</gloss>

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

**C** Like an excellent dialectician <note>A master of logical debate.</note>, knowing what "substance" implies among the ten categories <note>Refers to Aristotle's Categories, the basic building blocks of reality and logic.</note>, he demonstrates the reason why it is placed in the definition of faith, saying that the things which are manifest to him in heaven are so hidden among men that we cannot know them: but we believe that which we do not see as firmly as if we saw it. And upon this we found our hope, hoping through good works to come to the vision of the things that we believe. Therefore, because hope is founded in faith, we deservedly say that it is "substance." Peter responds: "If that which is acquired down among men through doctrine were as well understood as you, Dante, understand what faith is, the wit of the sophist—that is, of a man who uses sophistical and deceptive arguments—would have no place." Because he who understands the thing well cannot be deceived therein. "Thus breathed": that is, breathing, words issued from that kindled love—that is, from Peter full of charity. And then he added: "You have quite well examined the alloy and the weight of this coin," by comparison: because in money one attends to the substance, that the silver be pure silver, and this is known by the alloy; and as to the substance, then that there be no...

David is the supreme singer: because he is the supreme prophet in the Old Law. LET THEM HOPE in thee: he uses the words of David which are:
*Let all those who know your name hope in you: for you have not forsaken those who seek you* <note>original Latin: "Sperent in te omnes qui noverunt nomen tuum: quoniam non dereliquisti querentes te"</note>. And in your THEODY: that is, deity: because *theos* in Greek signifies God. And then the poet adds, saying: *and who knows not the name of God if he has my faith*, that is, if he has the Christian faith as I have, as if to say every Christian uses it. Therefore, David first instilled it in me, and you, James, afterwards instilled it with his instilling in your canonical epistle. Because what you wrote there you had from him: so that I am so full of this distilling that I "re-rain": that is, I rain back upon others our shower. YOU INSTILLED IN ME: in the canonical epistle of James it says: *Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him* <note>original Latin: "Beatus vir qui suffert temptationem..."</note>; and near the end of the same: *Be patient, confirm your hearts, for the coming of the Lord draws near* <note>original Latin: "Patientes confirmare corda vestra..."</note>.

[Right Column]

temporal [world] in which we serve as soldiers: that is, we fight continually with the world, with the flesh, and with the devil; and if we conquer, we are called to heaven where we triumph over the defeated adversary. Regarding the other two points: out of three questions, Beatrice has answered this one, to which, if the author had answered for himself, it might have seemed like vainglory. Now it follows in the passage and says that the other two points James asked not for the sake of knowing, but so that Dante might report back down in the world how much this virtue pleases [God]: he leaves it to him: because they will not be "hard," i.e., difficult, nor will they be "of boasting," i.e., of vainglory. Therefore he responds, and may the grace of God "allow it," i.e., be pleasing to him.

AS THE STUDENT: that is, he who learns: "follows," responds to the teacher in what he knows: so that his "excellence may be revealed," i.e., manifested. Thus I, responding to the first point, said that hope is nothing other than a "certain expectation," i.e., to wait with certainty for future glory. The definition of the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a famous medieval theologian</note> is: *Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, coming from the grace of God and preceding merits* <note>original Latin: "Spes est certa expectatio future beatitudinis..."</note>. Then, having manifested the primary cause, he manifests the secondary cause, namely the influence of the stars: from which, as written above, the influx of various virtues is born. But although the influx that disposes us to various virtues is born from the stars—and consequently to the hope that through such virtues we shall acquire eternal life—nevertheless it is necessary that such a disposition be aided by doctrine. And therefore he adds that he who is the "supreme singer of the Supreme Leader": that is, David, supreme prophet of the Supreme God, first instilled this hope into his heart.

**WHILE the author was speaking, he saw the light**
**of James always trembling like a lightning flash. Then**
James spoke AND said: "The love of the virtue of hope, which followed me even to the palm and the leaving of the field, wills that I ask you what that hope promises you": that is, what you hope for. AND note that hope followed him even to the palm: that is, even to the victory: which we cannot say we have while we are in this mortal life, because we always fight against the flesh and the devil. BUT when we "leave the field," that is, the place where one fights, which is this world, and we exit victorious because we have conquered every vice: the hope of coming to blessedness accompanies us always even unto that blessedness. BUT it does not enter into it, because a present good is not hoped for, but enjoyed. AND he used the "palm" for victory: because the palm is given to whoever obtains the victory. AND the reason for this we have manifested more extensively elsewhere.

James requesting that the poet manifest to him what hope promises him: he responds that it promises a happy and everlasting life to the soul and the body. And this he proves with the testimony of the scriptures of the New Testament, saying therefore that the new and ancient scriptures set the "mark" of the souls...

--- Page 602 ---
<meta>This page continues the theological critique of the papacy, specifically addressing the legitimacy of a corrupt Pope in the eyes of God versus his legal standing among men.</meta>

...priestly order from the triune and true God. That it is vacant in the presence of the Son of God. He does not say absolutely that it is vacant, because it would follow that he was not a true and legitimate Pope, and consequently nothing he did would be valid. But it is vacant in the sight of the Son of God because he has perverted his office, and consequently Christ reproves him as an apostate. It is not vacant, therefore, among men because his decrees remain valid. But as far as God is concerned, he does not hold such a rank by right, but rather usurps it. *He has made a sewer of my cemetery.* "Sewer" <term>cloaca: a drain or sewer system</term> signifies a trench that receives stenches, filth, and corruptions. "Cemetery," which in Greek signifies a "sleeping place" <note>original: "iaccitorio," from the Greek *koimeterion*</note>, is the place where dead bodies are laid. Therefore, he means that the place which was once the receptacle of holy martyrs full of every virtue and of other good men, now receives simoniacs <note>those who buy or sell sacred church offices</note>, the greedy, plunderers, and the lustful, who are well-likened to blood—that is, to cruelty—and to stench. And just as God was pleased by the virtues of holy men, so his adversary and the adversary of human nature—who, having become a rebel against God, fell from up there in heaven...

<summary>This passage argues that while a corrupt Pope remains legally valid in the eyes of men to maintain church order, he is considered an apostate and a usurper by God, having turned the holy burial grounds of martyrs into a moral sewer.</summary>
<keywords>Papal legitimacy, apostasy, simony, corruption, cemetery, sacred office, divine judgment</keywords>

**PARADISO**

<margin>The Sun is in the fourth heaven, and Dante was in the eighth, preceding it—that is, he was ahead by one sign and more.</margin> Since the poet was in Gemini, the sun was ahead of the entirety of Taurus and part of Aries. **The mind in love:** my mind, enamored with Beatrice. **Who plays the lady with Beatrice:** who follows Beatrice as his lady <note>The original Italian "donnea" implies acting as a courtly lover or serving a lady</note>, burned more than ever to turn his eyes back to her. And certainly, although **Sacred Doctrine** <note>Beatrice is interpreted here as an allegory for Divine Theology</note> is always worthy of being loved, it nevertheless deserves much greater love when it treats of the highest things. **And if nature or art:** Many bodies, whether natural or made by art—such as those sculpted and painted—capture the eyes of others through their beauty and entice them with pleasure, in such a way that this pleasure enters through the eyes into the soul. Whence Petrarch says: *Eyes, weep, accompany the heart, for through your fault I suffer death.* And elsewhere: *Love finds me completely disarmed, and the path open through the eyes to the heart.* And the Latin elegiac poet <note>Likely a reference to Propertius or Ovid</note> says: *If you do not know, the eyes are in...*

# CANTO XXVIII 302

And if the root is in this <note>referring to the Primum Mobile, the outermost moving sphere</note>: its parts extend through the motions of the other heavens. Because this aforementioned First Mover completes its revolution in twenty-four hours. Whence it is the root of days, and the root of months and years, which are distinguished by the sun.

<column-break/>

[Left Column - Main Poem Text]
O greed, who so drowns mortals
beneath you, that no one has the power
to pull their eyes out of your waves!
The will blossoms well in men,
but the continuous rain turns
the true plums into blighted fruit.
Faith and innocence are found
only in little children; then each
flees before the cheeks are covered with hair.
One, still babbling, keeps the fasts,
who later, with his tongue loosened, devours
any food through any phase of the moon;
And another, babbling, loves and listens to
his mother, who, once his speech is full,
then desires to see her buried.
So the white skin turns black
at the first sight of the beautiful daughter
of him who brings morning and leaves evening.

[Right Column - Commentary]
The first exclamation through which Peter damns the insatiable greed for earthly things, which sinks and submerges human minds in the sea of affection for momentary and fleeting goods, so that they cannot lift their eyes to this miraculous region of heaven arranged with such ineffable order. Therefore, with just indignation, he cries: "O greed," that is, O unrestrained desire, "who drowns," that is, submerges in its sea so deeply that no man has the power to pull his eyes out of its waves: that is, out of its perturbations and affections. "The will blossoms well in men." There is born in men a will for the Supreme Good, and it blossoms in them. But afterward, just as constant rain prevents plums from producing true fruit, and they are converted into *bozachioni* <note>blighted, wormy fruit</note> which are full of water and worms: so the rain of greed for earthly things corrupts the sincere will. Similar to that of Ovid: <note>original: "cepisti melius quam desinis ultima primis. Cedunt dissimiles hic vir et ille senex." — You began better than you end; the last parts fall short of the first. This man and that old man turn out differently.</note> and Isaiah: <note>original: "Expectavi ut faceret uvas fecit autem labruscas." — I expected it to bring forth grapes, but it brought forth wild grapes.</note> And that this is so, we see that men in childhood have honest innocence, shame, and purity. Afterward comes a more adult age and changes these virtues into vices, in such a way that before the cheeks—that is, the jaws—are covered with a beard, they have become vicious. And one "babbling," that is, in early childhood when the child cannot yet utter every word (since "to babble" means to be tongue-tied), "fasts"; and then, having become an adult, "devours"—specifically, "to devour" in Latin means to swallow without chewing, which is the act of a glutton and a greedy person—at any time. And another in the same age loves and reveres his mother, who then with "full speech," that is, adult and grown, desires her death. "So the white skin turns black": the meaning is that the white skin which is on the tender face becomes black. "At the first sight": as if in the first age; "of the beautiful daughter": that is, of human nature, which is the daughter of the sun, because the sun is the universal father of all living things. "Who brings morning": that is, produces light when he rises; "and leaves evening": it turns therefore from white to black because from pure it becomes infected with vices. And allegorically we understand the sun to be God himself, of whom the human soul is the daughter.

<column-break/>

[Left Column - Second Poem Stanza]
So that you do not marvel at this,
know that on earth there is no one to govern;
wherefore the human family goes astray.
But before January is entirely un-wintered
by that hundredth part neglected down there,
these supernal circles shall roar so loudly
That the fortune so long awaited
shall turn the sterns to where the prows are,
so that the fleet shall run straight;
And true fruit shall come after the flower.

[Bottom Commentary]
He concludes that no one should marvel if men, who are the family governed by the Shepherd, go astray—that is, leave the right path and the way of reason. Because "there is no one to govern," since the shepherds have become wolves. "But before January is entirely un-wintered": that is, before January (which is currently in winter, beginning with the sun's entry into Capricorn and ending when it leaves Pisces) [is moved to spring by] "the hundredth part" that is "neglected down there" <note>A reference to the error in the Julian calendar where the solar year was slightly miscalculated; Dante predicts this small error will eventually shift the seasons unless corrected.</note>. We showed in the first Cantica that the solar course contains 365 days and a quarter of a day, and beyond the quarter, a hundredth part. But the quarter is accounted for every four years in the leap year...

<summary>Dante laments the corruption of human nature by greed, noting how childhood innocence quickly turns to adult vice. He attributes this societal decay to a lack of proper leadership (governance) on earth, while prophesying a future correction.</summary>

# PARADISE

**P**ost-haste, against the present life
of wretched mortals, she revealed the
truth,
she who "en-paradises" my mind.
As in a mirror a candle's flame
is seen by one whom it lights from behind,
before he has it in sight or thought;
And he turns around to see if the glass
tells him the truth, and sees that it accords
with it, as a note does with its meter.
So my memory recalls
that I did, looking into the beautiful eyes
wherewith Love made the cord to capture me.

**B**ecause in the previous chapter he described the ninth sphere, it is fitting that in this twenty-eighth he describes the orders of the angels who are within it. Beatrice therefore shows him the point of Divinity and the hierarchies of the angels who are around it; then she clarifies certain doubts for him in a way that remains clear. *Post-haste*: after she who "en-paradises"—puts into paradise—my mind, opened and manifested the truth against the present life, full of vices, of wretched mortals. *As in a mirror*: the meaning is that the author, looking into the eyes of Beatrice—from which Love made the cord to capture me—saw the most burning light of the Divinity, which he could not see because his back was turned to it. Just as it happens that having a lit torch behind oneself and not seeing it, if one looks into a mirror in front, one sees the image of the torch and the flame; and turning backward, one sees that the mirror represented the truth to him. And not without reason does the poet relate that he saw the ray of the Deity in the eyes of Beatrice, that is, in the contemplation of Theology. For as Gregory <note>St. Gregory the Great, a Doctor of the Church</note> writes: just as we cannot look at the sun in its own body, but look at it in every other place, so also we cannot discern God in His primary being. But we can look at Him in theological scripture, as if through a certain reflection.

And as I turned, and my own eyes
were touched by what appears in that volume
whenever one gazes intently into its circling,
I saw a point that radiated light
so sharp that the face it inflames
must close because of the intense sharpness;
And whatever star appears smallest from here
would seem a moon placed beside it,
as star is placed with star.

Perhaps as close as a halo appears
to encircle the light that paints it
when the vapor that carries it is most thick;
Distant around the point, a circle of fire
whirled so rapidly it would have surpassed
that motion which most swiftly girds the world;
And this was girt by another,
and that by the third, the third then by the fourth,
the fourth by the fifth, and then the fifth by the sixth.

**H**e describes the true thing whose image he had already seen in the eyes of Beatrice. Therefore, as he was turned backward to where the light was—the image of which he had seen in Beatrice's eyes—and his eyes were touched by that which appears in the volume <note>The "volume" refers to the heavens or the book of the universe</note>, that is, by that which is seen in that Deity which is immense. *Whenever*: that is, every time one "gazes intently," meaning looks diligently. For if one does not look very well, one does not see. Having turned, therefore, he saw a point which radiated: that is, beaming out, it cast a light so sharp and penetrating that it is necessary to close the face, meaning the eyes, which that light inflames and burns. Nor is it a marvel, for if the bodily eye cannot endure the light of the sun, how much more will the eye of the intellect be unable to endure the light of the eternal Sun who made this sensible sun and the moon. He describes God, therefore, under the form and figure of a fixed and immobile point, and further describes the orders of the angels in the form of ignited circles, that is, circles of fire.

**T**he author had already described the First Principle <note>God</note> under the appearance of an immobile and fixed point. Now he describes the orders of the angels under the form of circles of fire. And beginning from the first, he says that it revolves most swiftly, as close to the point as the halo is to the moon—that circle which is generated around the moon by thick and dense vapors. It is certainly an arduous and difficult matter, and established above human possibility, to fully express the angelic nature; but we, from many things written first by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century theologian who wrote on the celestial hierarchy</note> and then by many other theologians, will run through a few things with brevity. And in the fourth order are the **Dominations**, because they possess the power of command, which is most fitting for lordship. The fifth order are the **Virtues**, because they fearlessly and without any hesitation carry out that which God has commanded <gloss>that is, ordered</gloss>. The sixth are the **Powers**, because they resist the powers of the demons; and these second three orders of angels are less quiet and more active than the first three. The seventh are the **Principalities**, acting through a powerful and principal method of teaching by performing supernatural and miraculous things for the instruction of the ignorant. The eighth are the **Archangels**, because they announce the most principal and greatest things, so named because *arche* in Greek signifies "principality"; and this order, being in the middle between the Principalities and the Angels, has taken the name of both the superiors and the inferiors, because being reformed by the Principalities, it reforms and gives life to the Angels in simple unity. "If your fingers are not sufficient

<margin>She solves the doubt in this form, demonstrating that just as the circles of the intelligible world <note>The angelic realms.</note> have more virtue, so the first sphere of the sensible world <note>The physical universe.</note>, because it is near to God, has more virtue. And in this way, the nine orders of angels proportionally correspond to the nine heavens, always the most worthy to the most worthy.</margin>
The physical circles—that is, the heavens that have a body—are wide—that is, broad and great—and narrow—that is, small and tight—according to whether they have more or less virtue. For the ninth sphere is as much greater than that of the moon as it has more virtue. And greater goodness wishes to work greater health—that is, that which has greater virtue produces a more health-giving effect. And a greater effect occupies—that is, a greater body contains within itself greater virtue if it has its parts complete and perfect equally. Therefore, this ninth sphere, which is greater than all the others and sweeps with it all the other spheres—because in turning in twenty-four hours it pulls with it in the same time all the other spheres—corresponds as the most perfect sphere to the first circle of the angels, who are most perfect in love and in knowledge.
BECAUSE she demonstrates that the similarity must be understood according to virtue, and not according to physical quantity. Whence she says: "if you wrap your measure"—that is, place your measure—which you make of the circles of the angels, which are incorporeal, according to their virtue and not to the appearance—that is, to the physical quantity—that is, to the intensive virtue which is spiritual and does not appear, and not to the extensive which is physical and appears. You will see a marvelous consequence and agreement of the greater to the more—that is, of the greater body to more virtue—and of the smaller body to less virtue of each heaven, which are nine, to its Intelligence—that is, to its circle of angels. Therefore:
The ninth sphere corresponds to the **Seraphim**.
The eighth to the **Cherubim**.
Saturn to the **Thrones**.
Jupiter to the **Dominions**.
Mars to the **Virtues**.
The Sun to the **Powers**.
Venus to the **Principalities**.
Mercury to the **Archangels**.
The Moon to the **Angels**.
¶ The comparison is that just as the air remains serene when the north wind blows, so the truth remained clear in me after the response of Beatrice; and it says "when Boreas"—that is, the northern wind...

[Left Column]
And she, who perceived the doubting thoughts
within my mind, said: "The first circles
have shown to you the Seraphim and Cherubim.
Thus swiftly they follow their bonds <note>original: "vimi" (willows/bonds), referring to the divine ties of love</note>
to liken themselves to the Point as much as they can;
and they can in proportion to how sublime they are in vision.
Those other loves who go around them

because they terminated the first triad.
And you must know that they all have delight
insofar as their vision deepens
into the Truth in which every intellect finds peace.
From this it can be seen how the state of being blessed
is founded upon the act that sees,
not on that of love, which follows after;
and of seeing, merit is the measure,
which grace brings forth and good will:
thus from grade to grade the process goes.
The other triad that thus blossoms
in this eternal springtime,
which the nocturnal Ram <note>The constellation Aries; a reference to the season of autumn when Aries is visible at night</note> does not despoil,
perpetually 'Hosanna' sings <note>original: "svernare" (to sing like a bird in spring)</note>

In that hierarchy are the three goddesses: <note>referring to the three ranks</note>
first Dominations, and then Virtues;
the third order is of Powers.
Then in the two penultimate dances <note>original: "tripudi" (joyous dances)</note>
Principalities and Archangels wheel;
the last is entirely of Angelic play.
These orders all gaze upward,
and downward they prevail, so that toward God
all are drawn, and all do draw."

And Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian believed to have written on the celestial hierarchy</note> with such great desire
set himself to contemplate these orders,
that he named and distinguished them as I do.
But Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, who proposed a slightly different order of angels</note> later departed from him;
wherefore, as soon as he opened his eyes
in this heaven, he laughed at his own mistake.
And if a mortal on earth proferred
such a secret truth, I do not wish you to wonder:

with much else of the truth of these circles.

<column-break/>

[Right Column]
<margin>Beatrice shows Dante the orders of the angels to remove the doubts she sees in his mind. So that he understands: that the blessedness of the saints is caused by vision. Because seeing and understanding is the cause of blessedness. Since the mind is nourished by this alone, and this is its nectar and its ambrosia. Seraphim and Cherubim: of whom we have already spoken. And their bonds: their ties and links, which is God: because the desire to know Him makes it so they do not fall away from Him: and they can know Him all the more, the closer they are to Him: and the more they rise to see Him. THRONES of the divine aspect: because as it is said, God through these orders His judgments. It deepens in the Truth, that is, in God: who is the supreme truth. FROM THIS it can be seen. From here it is understood that being blessed consists in seeing, that is, in knowing. And not in loving. Because love proceeds from knowledge: and not knowledge from love. And the creature loves the Creator all the more, the more it knows Him and receives merit and grace according to the measure of knowing. Wherefore from grade to grade, the more it sees, the more it has of grace and good will, that is, of wanting that which God wants. There follows the second triad which is Dominations, Virtues, and Powers: which germinates and puts forth leaves in blessedness: which he calls eternal springtime, which the nocturnal Ram, that is, autumn, does not despoil. Our springtime puts forth leaves, but autumn then makes the leaves fall. But that of heaven stays always green. And he placed the nocturnal Ram for autumn because autumn begins when the sun enters Libra, and then Libra in our hemisphere is only seen by day. Wherefore it follows that Aries (the Ram), the opposite sign, is only seen by night. Here it "sverna," that is, it sings continually Hosanna with three melodies. Since from three choirs proceed three songs. And he places here the three orders of the second hierarchy. Then in the two penultimate dances, in the two penultimate dances which are of the third hierarchy: Principalities and Archangels. And the last which are Angels. These orders all gaze upward. Because the inferior always has the superior in admiration: as a greater thing. Therefore the Seraphim have God in admiration, whom they gaze upon as the supreme good: and by that they are drawn: as by the supreme good: and they draw the Cherubim. And these have God in admiration, and then the Seraphim: and they draw the Thrones: and the Thrones the Dominations, and so the others until the last order. And this draws the other creatures. And always the superior has more power than the inferior: Wherefore it follows that all gaze upward: and all prevail downward, and each draws the inferior toward God: and is drawn by the superior.</margin>

<margin>It shows that the number, the order, the distinctions, and the names of these angels were held by Dionysius, who wrote in the book *On the Divine Names* and *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. Afterward, Gregory disagreed with him, because Dionysius placed the Principalities in the third hierarchy and in the first order: and Gregory placed them in the second order of the second hierarchy, where Dionysius placed the Virtues. But after death, coming to this heaven, he saw his error and laughed at himself. And Beatrice concludes: that the poet should not marvel that a mortal truth, that is, the truth of a mortal man, proferred and manifested such a secret. Because he who had seen it up here in heaven, who was Paul the Apostle when he was caught up to the third heaven, revealed this to him: and many true things of these circles: that is, of these heavens.</margin>
