[Illustration: A woodcut depicting a celestial and infernal scene. At the top, a divine figure is surrounded by angels. In the center, the Archangel Michael, labeled "ST. MICHAEL", wields a sword and shield against a multi-headed dragon. Below, Lucifer, labeled "LUCIFER", is shown as a three-faced monstrous figure falling into a pit of fire where other figures are being tormented.]

Because the poet has already treated the distinction of the nine orders of the angels, it remains in this 29th chapter to treat: where, when, and in what manner the angelic nature was created; and what an angel is; and the number of them. He treats, therefore, first two questions. Afterward, he sets forth the ruin of the wicked angels and touches upon some doubts regarding the intellect, memory, and will of the angels. In the third place, he reproves those who postpone and pervert the Scripture. And finally, he returns to the principal matter of the angels. In the beginning of the chapter, he shows that Beatrice, turned toward God, stood silent until she saw the doubts of the poet; but she stood thus for a brief time. And this brevity and moment he declares by an excellent comparison, saying that it happens as when the sun is in Aries and the moon in Libra (the opposite sign), in such a form that the sun is in the east and the moon in the west: suddenly they change place because one rises to our hemisphere and the other descends. When both the children of Latona—that is, the sun and the moon, as we have already said—covered one by the Ram and the other by the Scales, make a zone (that is, a belt) of the horizon, because both are on the horizon. But one is about to rise and the other to descend. Therefore, when the moon and the sun stand in this form, for that long Beatrice was silent: as long as the moon and the sun stay in the belt of the hemisphere where every *ubi* (that is, every place) and every *quando* (that is, every time) is centered—that is, where it is marked as in a point. Just as in the first cause <note>God</note>, from whence places and times proceed, although in God there is no place because He is immense, nor time because He is eternal. Nevertheless, from Him both the one and the other proceed.

Not to have for Himself a gain of good,
  which cannot be, but so that His splendor
  might, in its resplendence, say *I subsist*.
In His eternity, outside of time,
  outside of every other understanding, as it pleased Him,
  Eternal Love unfolded into new loves.
Nor did He lie before as if sluggish,
  for neither "before" nor "after" preceded
  the moving of God upon these waters.

Looking at Beatrice: in the divinity she recognized three doubts that were in Dante. First, whether time precedes the creation of the universe. Second, where such creation was made. Third, how it was made, whether in an instant or successively. Therefore, she first demonstrates that the cause which moved God to create the universe was not to increase His own blessedness, because nothing can be added to the most perfect. Therefore, it was not to have for Himself a gain of good, because that cannot be. But so that His splendor (that is, His goodness) might show itself in creatures, and could subsist in created nature, and appear in it, and be the substantial form of every creature, because every created thing is good. Whence in Genesis: *And God saw all the things that He had made, and they were very good* <note>original: "Et uidit deus cuncta que fecerat: & erant ualde bona"</note>. And Boethius: *Whom no external causes impelled to fashion the work of flowing matter, but the innate form of the highest good, lacking in envy.* <note>original: "Quem non externe pepulerunt fingere cause materie fluitantis opus Verum insita summi forma boni liuore carens."</note> God wished to communicate His being and goodness with the things created by Him; and to demonstrate His perfection, He distinguished them into three grades: In the first are the purely intellectual creatures, which are the angels placed above the heavens; in the second, purely corporal things placed around the center of the world.

<summary>This page introduces Canto XXIX of Paradiso, where Beatrice explains the creation of the angels and the universe to Dante, emphasizing that God created not for self-gain but to manifest His goodness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and cosmological commentary on Dante's Paradiso, specifically discussing the nature of the celestial spheres and the diversity of human nature.</meta>

->**PARADISE**<-

**Paradise** does not have distinct members, but has all its parts similar in nature and in being. And therefore, everything shines; and it has in every part of it a similar power. And this is the ninth sphere <note>The Primum Mobile, the outermost moving sphere in Ptolemaic cosmology</note>. But the eighth heaven <note>The Starry Heaven or Firmament</note> does not shine entirely and has diverse powers in its parts, because it has diverse stars. Some have a single organ—that is, a star—and in that is its power, as we see in the seven planets. And this is the eighth heaven; through all these motions it is necessary to come to a first immovable mover, which is God, who causes such motions.

But men do not have diversity of degrees <note>in their essential form</note> because they are similar and receive their being from a similar form. But they have degrees according to the steps that proceed from their complexion <term>complexion: the specific balance of bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to determine temperament</term> and according to their will, which proceeds from free will.

Because some are suited to speculation and science, such as those who have soft flesh; but those of hard flesh are suited to sensitive delights and pass into bestiality. Some are in the middle of these two degrees, and those reasonably bring [their potential] into action, and these are suited to civil life. But the more one resists sensuality with reason, the greater is the praise. *To open in new loves the eternal love* <note>original: "Saperse in novi amori l'eterno amore"</note>: God, who is eternal love, opened himself and manifested in new loves—that is, in the—

<margin>The angel understands through forms which he abstracts from things. Neither by composing and dividing, nor by discourse as man does, but he understands through innate forms. Furthermore, that will which is in man is not the same as in the angel, although each is called "will." For man desires the good through the discourse of reason, while the angel does so in an instant. Therefore, just as he understands more excellently than man, so he has a more excellent will. Similarly, memory cannot be said to exist in the angel except equivocally; because memory in us is founded in a bodily organ, and the angel has no body. Also, memory is of past things, and the angel sees all things as present in God.</margin> <note>The commentator is explaining Dante's theology regarding the angelic mind. ->**On Divine Beauty**<-

The deeper one enters into the matter of theology, the more beautiful the things one finds. But when one arrives at the summit of its speculation, where the fountain of power, wisdom, and goodness resides—where the divine essence is described in Trinity and Unity, in divinity and humanity—so great is the beauty of that subject that if all that has been said of it in various places were concluded in one, it would do little to satisfy the mind at this time. And this is because the beauty of God <note>The abbreviation ".b." in the original likely refers to *beatitudine* (blessedness) or *bontà* (goodness), but in this context of the Trinity, it refers to the Divine Beauty of God.</note> in this state is transformed not only beyond us—that is, it not only surpasses the mode and measure of the human intellect—but it is certainly believed that it surpasses the intellect of the highest angels, in such a way that no creature

<column-break/>

can ever fully comprehend it. Therefore, I find myself in the position of those who, wishing to speak of a thing that cannot be expressed, remain silent, or rather, they speak by confessing their own insufficiency.

->**Poetic Reflection**<-

At this stage, I admit I am defeated,
More than ever by any point of my theme; <note>original: "thea-", likely "theama" or "theatrica," referring to the subject or spectacle of the work.</note>
For as the sun does to the most fragile sight,
So does the remembrance of that sweet smile
Deprive my mind of its very self.
From the first day that I saw her face
In this life, until this very sight,
My song has never been cut off from following her;
But now it is necessary that my pursuit desist
From following her beauty further in my verse,
As every artist must do at his limit.

<column-break/>

...to see. Because without illuminating grace, the human sense cannot transcend to these speculations. The high triumph of the Church Triumphant <note>The Church in Heaven</note>; and certainly it is easy to know the Church Militant <note>The Church on Earth</note>: because its works are for the most part placed in active operations and in moral virtues; but to comprehend with the mind the Triumphant—because it is placed in contemplation, which is an incorporeal thing—is very difficult. Of the true kingdom: because this is the true kingdom, and he who serves in this one reigns, while other kingdoms are servitude. Light of the Holy Spirit, which light makes the Creator visible. Just as the material sun, reflecting its rays on earth, makes the things of this world visible to us, so this light makes God visible—not to every creature, but to that one which has its peace (that is, its highest good) placed only in God, and thinks of nothing else: because it has a soul pure from every contagion. This light extends in a circular and spherical figure: and it makes so great a circumference that it would be too wide to encircle the sun. Nor is it anything other than a ray that comes from the highest light, which is God, and reflects at the summit of the First Mover (that is, at the highest part of the ninth heaven, which is the *Primum Mobile*). This ninth heaven receives from that reflection "life" (that is, motion, which is a sign of life) and "power" (that is, the virtue to give its influence to all the heavens).

Just as it would happen if a mountain were in the middle of the waters, it would be seen from top to bottom (that is, from the upper part down to the lower); so the blessed souls, standing above the light all around, mirrored themselves all around in the said light. These souls he imagines to be in more than a thousand seats (that is, in infinite seats). And he says "as many of us as have made return up there" (that is, all those souls who, having come from God through creation, have returned to God through beatitude because of their merits). "My sight in the breadth and in the height": The poet's sight had become so noble that it did not lose its way and did not fail. In the "breadth" (that is, in the altitude) nor in the "height," although each was immense. But he comprehended and discerned the whole, and in it the quantity and the quality. Human sight can discern all these things within a certain space, and once that is passed, the sight becomes confused. But in heaven, neither the "near" nor the "far" adds or subtracts (that is, it does not make the thing grow or diminish); being near does not make one see better, nor far worse, but it appears exactly as it is. "For where God governs without intermediary": someone might say it seems unlikely that one who is far sees as much as one who is close, or one who is high as much as one who is low. To which he responds that in things governed by God, but by means of secondary causes (such as the heavens and the elements and all earthly things), natural law does not allow what is said above. But in the Empyrean heaven, in which God works immediately and without secondary causes, natural law can do nothing. Then it follows that Beatrice drew him like one who, through the desire for knowledge, wants to speak, and through awe remains silent; and she drew him into the "yellow of the rose" (that is, into the center of that sphere, just as in a rose the yellow is in the center). This rose "expands" because the space and the circumference of this heaven is very great, and "rises in tiers" (that is, it is distinguished by its ranks). And it "breathes out an odor" (that is, it casts an odor of praise to the sun, which is the eternal God who illuminates that heaven). This sun "always makes spring" (that is, it always creates springtime there). And she said: "Look how great is the assembly and the number of the blessed souls," who, as John places them in the Apocalypse, are in "white stoles." A *stola* <note>original: "StOla"</note> is a garment long enough to reach the feet.

Beatrice concludes that the celestial seats—which were vacated by the ruin of the rebellious angels and had to be refilled by blessed souls—are almost full. Then she points out an empty seat adorned with a crown; and she says that one is prepared for Henry of Luxembourg, the fourth Emperor <note>Henry VII</note>. And he shall sit in it before Dante sups at those "wedding feasts" (that is, before he comes to that beatitude). This man reigned at the time of the poet while Clement of Gascony <note>Pope Clement V</note> was sitting [on the papal throne]. And she silently denotes that we are in the last...

Therefore, Clement will come to the pit in Hell where he showed that Boniface of Anagni <note>Pope Boniface VIII</note>, his predecessor, was located.

# CANTO XXXI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

In the form, then, of a white rose
the holy militia was shown to me,
which Christ, with His own blood, made His spouse.
But the other <note>The angels</note>, which flying sees and sings
the glory of Him who enamors it,
and the goodness which made it so great,

one moment, and the next return

->[Illustration: A woodcut of the Celestial Rose, a vast stadium-like flower filled with the ranks of the blessed. Below the heavenly vision, the earthly realm is depicted with a church. On the right, a monk kneels in prayer.]<-
->**ST. BERNARD** | **THE MADONNA**<-

Having already treated our poet’s celestial court in general, in this thirty-first chapter he describes it distinctly and in detail. Therefore, in the beginning, he describes the actions and the appearance of the blessed souls and the angels. Then he invokes the Trinity and sets down his most happy contemplation. In the third place, he places Saint Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux, who replaces Beatrice as Dante's guide for the final vision</note> and shows Beatrice returning to her seat. In the final part, Bernard shows him the blessed souls, and especially the Virgin Mary. But in these first verses, summarizing what was said in the preceding chapter, he says that the "holy militia"—that is, the souls of the blessed who, having fought in the world, triumphed in heaven—were in the form of a white rose, which militia Christ redeemed with His death and united to Himself: wherefore she was His spouse. The "other militia"—that is, the angelic one—which sees and understands the glory of God that enamors it and His goodness, which made said angels so great and so noble, and seeing it, sings—that is, praises it. These angels descended into the "great flower"—that is, into the Rose, which is what he calls the seats of the blessed—which flower is adorned with as many leaves as there are seats. And from these leaves, they ascended again to God, in whom their love always dwells: just as bees do, which go out from their hives into the flowers and then return to the hives where their "labor"—that is, their toil—is "savored" because it produces honey. And certainly, it is an excellent comparison between the angels and the bees, because just as bees are prompt and quick in their duty around the king <note>Medieval natural history often referred to the "king bee" rather than the queen</note>, so are the angels in the service of God. The bees delight in the scent...

Walking through the living light,
I moved my eyes along the ranks,
now up, now down, and now circling back.
I saw faces persuasive with charity,
adorned by another's light <note>The light of God</note> and their own smile,
and gestures graced with every dignity.
The general form of Paradise
my gaze had already taken in as a whole,
not yet fixed firmly on any one part.
And I turned with rekindled desire
to ask my Lady about things
concerning which my mind was in suspense.

I intended one thing, and another answered me:
I thought to see Beatrice, and I saw an elder
dressed like the glorious folk.
Spread across his eyes and his cheeks
was a kindly joy, in a pious demeanor
such as befits a tender father.
And "Where is she?" I said suddenly;
wherefore he: "To bring your desire to its goal,
Beatrice moved me from my place.
And if you look up into the third circle
of the highest tier, you will see her again
upon the throne her merits have allotted her."

Without answering, I raised my eyes
and saw her as she made herself a crown,
reflecting from herself the eternal rays.
From that region which thunders highest up,
no mortal eye is so distant,
even if abandoned in the deepest sea,
as was my sight there from Beatrice;
but it made no difference to me, for her image
did not descend to me blurred by any medium.

O Lady, in whom my hope is strong,
and who suffered for my salvation
to leave your footprints in Hell,
of all the many things that I have seen,
from your power and from your goodness
I recognize the grace and the virtue.

PARADISO
As a pilgrim at a temple—whether of Rome, or the Holy Sepulcher, or Saint James <note>Santiago de Compostela</note>—where he has come by a vow, finds refreshment in looking at the form, the ornaments, and the things within, and already hopes for his return so that, having returned, he may tell his people how that temple stands: here the Poet saw the faces of the inhabitants, persuasive with charity. They were so inflamed with charity that they persuaded those who saw them; and they were adorned and decorated with the light of another, that is, the light of the Divine, and with their own smile—that is, their own joy—and with gestures full of all honesty—that is, of all the virtues. And he has already understood the whole form of Paradise in general, but not yet in detail, because he had not fixed his gaze more on one place than another. Then he turned to ask Beatrice about many doubts that held his mind in suspense.

When Dante turned to ask Beatrice about his doubts, she had already returned to her seat. Wherefore he rightly says that he intended one thing—that is, to speak with Beatrice—and another answered him, because Saint Bernard had already come. He <note>the author</note> portrays him as an elder—that is, an old man—kindly, joyful, and pious, as a tender father eager for the salvation of his son ought to be; and he describes him as such as he was in the governing of his monks. Here Dante said, "Where is she?" which signifies that he was seeking to understand through Sacred Theology <note>represented by Beatrice</note> that which he will say shortly after. And Bernard answered him because the doctrine of this elder opened this place for him. Therefore Bernard answered that she had returned to her seat.

**S**ON of grace: And rightly so, because we are not regenerated from the death of sin by our own merits, but by divine grace. Therefore, we are sons of grace. THAT this being joyful, this celestial good, will not be known to you if you keep your eyes on the bottom. As if to say: if you do not detach yourself from the terrestrial slime and fly like an eagle toward the divine sun. I RAISED MY EYES. What this signifies has already been explained above. AND AS FROM MORNING HE DEMONSTRATES by comparison that just as in the morning the eastern part is brighter than the western because the sun begins to illuminate it, so that most supreme part of Paradise was more lucid than the other parts. And as there: that is, in that part of heaven WHERE THE POLE IS AWAITED <note>original: "DOVE SA SPECTA el temo" — 'temo' refers to the pole or shaft of a chariot</note>, that is, the chariot of the sun: putting the pole, which is part of the chariot, for the whole chariot. And the fable of Phaethon <note>The mythological son of Helios who lost control of the sun's chariot</note> was narrated in the 27th Canto of the first canticle. IT BECOMES MORE INFLAMED. That is, it becomes more illuminated: because the brightness always appears greatest where the sun is shortly to appear. THUS THAT peacemaking flame. That is, peaceful flame: because the most ardent charity of Mary was the mediatrix to reconcile man to God. AND IN That midst with spread wings. The spread wings of the angels signify the grace and knowledge that is dilated through all souls. But those were distinct because according to merits they are more or less illuminated. THE faces of radiance. That is, of splendor, which signifies charity. AND OF ART, that is, of exercise: because as I said, they have distinction in their office according to the diversity of grace and glory. A BEAUTY: WHICH was the Virgin Mary. She smiled at the games and songs of the angels, and this created joy in the eyes of all the saints. AND IF I HAD such wealth in speech. A man can imagine much more and better than he can express; and nevertheless the poet demonstrates that even if he had as much wealth—that is, as much faculty in speaking—as he has in imagining, he would not dare to attempt the minimum of her glory. AND WHEN Bernard saw my eyes intent on his warm heat, HE TURNED his own to her. That is, to MARY, with such affection that he made mine more ardent to gaze again. He concludes that the fervor with which Bernard wrote his contemplations of MARY made him more fervent in contemplating her.

[Woodcut illustration: The Celestial Rose is shown as a tiered amphitheater of clouds and stars. Saint Bernard (labeled **S. BERNARDO**) stands as the guide. **H**aving already described Paradise in general, the author wishes in this 32nd chapter to describe it in detail. Therefore, in the first part, he describes the order of the ranks of the blessed of the Old and New Testaments. In the second, he removes a doubt concerning small children. In the third, he narrates the blessedness of our Lady and shows the angel Gabriel. In the last, he shows the principal patricians of this court. Now returning to the first verses, he orders the text thus: That contemplator, that is, Bernard, affectionate, that is, made affectionate or full of affection, assumed and took the free office of teacher: because he was my free teacher to show me all the ranks of Paradise. And he began thus: She who is so beautiful: that is, Eve, the first woman, at the feet of Mary: because in the second seat, after Mary, is she who opened and pierced the wound that Mary closed and anointed. THIS is the wound of human nature caused by the sin of Adam, which made all men unable to have eternal life; of which Eve was the inducing cause, and therefore she pierced and opened this wound; and MARY, through her <insert>son</insert>...

# CANTO XXXII 312

Obedience and purity were the inducing causes that led God the Father to send His Son to take flesh from her <note>The Virgin Mary</note> and redeem humanity from the slavery of sin. Whence it is written: *The woman who harmed is the one who healed* <note>original: "Mulier damnavit quae sanavit"</note>. Eve, through the intervention of the wicked angel in the form of a serpent, wounded the human race. And Mary, through the intervention of the blessed angel, healed it. From the most proud Eve was born the disease; and from the most humble Mary was born the medicine. Whence he said that Mary closed and anointed—that is, mitigated and healed—this wound. In the third row he places Rachel and Beatrice. Rachel was the wife of Jacob and represents the contemplative life, as we have already demonstrated in various places. Sarah was the wife of Abraham, who in her old age gave birth to Isaac. Rebecca was the wife of Isaac, from whom she bore Jacob and Esau. These three are held in great esteem in the Old Testament: Rachel for the love of her husband, Rebecca for her prudence, and Sarah for her fidelity. Judith, a most holy woman, through her greatness of soul freed the Bethulians from Holofernes; we narrated her history above. The great-grandmother of the singer—that is, of David—who, moved by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, sang the Psalms. This man, enamored with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah his knight, had the husband killed in order to have her. Thus he committed adultery, homicide, and treason. Then, repenting of his error, he sang the psalm: *Have mercy on me, O God* <note>original: "Miserere mei deus"</note>. The great-grandmother of David was Ruth, wife of Boaz. And Boaz fathered Obed, and he was the father of Jesse, from whom David was born. These are seven seats: the first of Mary, Queen of Heaven; second of Eve; third of Rachel and Beatrice fourth; fifth of Rebecca; sixth of Judith; seventh of Ruth. Therefore, in the second seat <note>referring to the vertical line of women</note> were those who had lived according to natural law, more in contemplation.

In short, understand that beneath Our Lady, down to the floor of the rose, are souls of the Old Testament, always dividing by seven degrees as they are.

for all these are spirits released
before they had the power of true choice.
You can well perceive this by their faces

Now you doubt, and in doubting you are silent;

Within the vastness of this realm,
a casual point can have no place,
any more than sadness, thirst, or hunger.
For by eternal law it is established,
whatever you see, so that justly
the ring answers to the finger.
And therefore this hurried folk
to the true life is not without cause
entered here more or less excellent.
The King through whom this kingdom rests
in such love and in such delight
that no will dares to desire more.
Creating all minds in His joyful sight,
at His pleasure He endows them with grace
diversely; and here let the effect suffice.
And this is expressly and clearly noted for you
in Holy Scripture regarding those twins
who within their mother had their anger stirred.

We have shown this order and distinction a little
above, and shown who is beneath the throne of the great
Queen, and who is beneath that of Saint John: who was sanctified

of the faith: that is, the faith of those who believed in Christ
to come, and of those who believed in Christ already come.
And know that from the step that sits—that is, it divides the two distinctions,
that is, distinctions and divisions. In all the orders from the middle
downward are the little children saved not by their own merit, but through
baptism and through the faith of their parents. Now you doubt.
Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, Dante's final guide</note> knew Dante doubted whether those seats were given
to the blessed children by chance or not; and therefore he promises to clarify it. And
first he demonstrates that in the vastness—that is, in the greatness of the celestial
kingdom—nothing can be by chance, just as there can be no
sadness, hunger, or thirst. These cannot be there because
sadness is a lack of joy; hunger and thirst are a lack
of food and drink. But Heaven is perfect joy and nothing
is lacking there. Chance cannot exist because whatever is seen
is established by divine law; and justly the ring answers
to the finger—that is, from the place allocated—that is, they are placed in a place
suitable to them as the ring is made suitable to the finger. Therefore this
hurried folk to the true life—that is, these children: they were hurried—that is,
hastened to the true life. It is not without cause that they are more or less excellent
among themselves—that is, among their own kind. The King through whom this kingdom rests:
that is, God the King, through whom the celestial realm rests—that is, it reposes
in such charity and joy that no will of any blessed soul
is "daring"—that is, has the boldness for more; that is, they have as much delight as they
desire. He endows human minds with as much grace as pleases
Him, and endows them diversely, giving more to some and less to others.
And one should not seek why more to this one than to that one, because
 the reason cannot be understood; but let it suffice to know the effect.
This is proven in Holy Scripture by two brothers
born of one birth, Esau and Jacob, of whom God said before
they were born: *I have hated Esau, but I have loved Jacob* <note>original Latin: "Esau odio habui. iacob autem dilexi." quoting Malachi 1:2-3 / Romans 9:13</note>.
These were the sons of Isaac and Rebecca, who as soon
as they were conceived in their mother's womb made
movement and disturbance between them. And God revealed to the father
that from these two were to descend two peoples, and that
the people descended from the elder was to serve the people
descended from the younger. Then at the time of birth, first came out
Esau, red in color, and after him Jacob, small and dark,
who held with his hand the foot of Esau as if to say, "You shall not
go out without me." One cannot therefore give a reason why
God endowed Jacob with more grace than Esau, except because
it so pleased Him. But this is known: that he who has more grace
acts better, and he who acts better merits more, and through this
acquires more glory. Therefore, according to the color of the hair—
that is, as it pleased God that Esau should have the color and red
hair, and Jacob dark—so it pleased Him to give more grace
to Jacob than to Esau. Because Isaac loved Esau more, and
Rebecca loved Jacob more, it was the will of God that Rebecca could
deceive Isaac. THEREFORE the highest light of Paradise
which makes souls blessed, worthily must "put on hair"—
that is, crown itself according to the color of the hair. And finally
he concludes that the blessed children, without reward and merits
of their own behavior—THAT IS, of their VIRTUE—are placed in
different degrees where they have more or less beatitude, and this

**CANTO XXXIII 315**

**V**irgin Mother, daughter of
your son,
humble and exalted more than any
creature,
fixed goal of the eternal counsel:
You are she who human nature
so ennobled that its Maker
did not disdain to become its own making.
Within your womb was rekindled the love

this flower has thus germinated.
Here you are to us a midday torch
of charity, and down among mortals
you are a living fountain of hope.
Lady, you are so great and so powerful
that he who wishes for grace and does not recur to you,
his desire wishes to fly without wings.
Your loving-kindness not only succors

freely precedes the asking.

->[Woodcut illustration: At the top, a figure labeled **SATURN** sits on a throne surrounded by stars. Below, the Virgin Mary is being crowned by angels, with St. Bernard and other figures kneeling in prayer to the left.]<-

¶ This final chapter contains four things: first, through his prayer, Bernard entreats Mary to lead Dante to contemplate the divinity. Then, the poet demonstrates how through the work of Mary he arrived at the ultimate salvation. In the third part, Dante prays to the Supreme God that He might grant him the ability to demonstrate some part of His glory; and so he demonstrates. In the last part, he places how he saw the divinity within the humanity. The prayer of Bernard is composed with the highest artifice. And first, in the preamble, he captures the greatest benevolence, attention, and docility. And certainly, it can excite the highest attention in the listener to attribute such epithets, which in Mary are miraculous, but true, while in others they are impossible: because it does not fall within the nature of any animal that one can be at once mother and virgin, for these are contrary things. Nor daughter of the son; but it fell to Mary by divine grace. Therefore, these things are not said without the wonder of the listener, from which attention results. Nor does he fail to give the highest praise to her of whom they are spoken, which wins benevolence from her. Add the third prerogative: that a mortal woman was made mother of the immortal God. Add the fourth: that she is more humble and more exalted than any other creature. Add the fifth: that she is the fixed goal of eternal counsel. By narrating these things, one can acquire benevolence from Mary and the highest attention from the listener. And let this suffice for the preamble. Furthermore, because this prayer is in the deliberative genre <note>A rhetorical style used to persuade or advise</note>, in which he wishes to persuade the Supreme Queen to entreat grace from God that would make him capable of His light beyond what a man still constituted in the body can do; and such a petition seems impossible. He demonstrates through this prologue that not only is it not impossible for Mary, but it is easy. For if the Most High granted her that, above human nature, she should be mother and virgin, Mother of God, daughter of the son, humble and exalted, He will very easily grant her that she make Dante capable of the divine light. Therefore, he shows his petition to be easy for her. If Mary could do all these things which are above nature, she will therefore be able to show the Supreme God to Dante, though he is still constituted in the flesh, even though it be above human nature. **Virgin Mother**: an unheard-of prerogative and supernatural privilege that the virgin should be mother, and that the woman should be mother of God. If, therefore, she was able to generate the Son of God, she can well guide Dante into His presence. **Daughter of your son**: because she was the daughter of the Almighty Father, who as to divinity is one and the same thing with the Son whom she brought forth. **Humble**: in character and in words, as she said: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord" <note>original Latin: "Ecce ancilla domini"</note>. And in the Psalm: "He has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed" <note>original Latin: "respexit humilitate ancille sue ecce enim ex hoc beatam me dicent omnes generationes"</note>. **Exalted**: because she is the Mother of God, Queen of Heaven, exalted above all saints <note>original Latin: "qa mater dei regina coeli exaltata super omnes sanctos"</note>. **Fixed goal of eternal counsel**: She was not chosen without premeditation, but with counsel—not human and mutable, which can have defects, but divine and eternal, which cannot have deception. **You ennobled human nature** with your infinite virtues, so that its **Maker**—that is, God, the Maker of that same human nature—did not disdain to become **your making** as far as the flesh was concerned. **Within your womb was rekindled the love**: God loved man, His creation, until he was without sin. Then sin extinguished that love. And finally, the incarnation of Christ, performed in the womb of the Virgin, rekindled it. And this advocate of ours was able to join divinity to humanity, and ennoble our vile nature, and recall us from exile, and fill the vacant heaven. From whence **germinated this flower**: that is, the rose...

Here you are among us; here in heaven you are a midday sun <note>original: "meridiana"</note>, that is, such splendor as is in the sun at midday. This Queen produces two wonderful effects: because in pilgrimage—that is, on earth—she turns the souls of sinners toward reaching heaven through the virtue of hope; and in heaven, she preserves the blessed through the virtue of charity. And among mortals, she is a living fountain of hope. These words are very fitting for Bernard, because he says: <note>original Latin: "Securum habes recursum..."</note> You have a secure recourse to God, O man, where the mother stands before the son and the son before the father. The Mother shows the son her breast and paps; the Son shows the father his side and wounds. Therefore, there can be no rejection for you where so many signs of love meet. Your benevolence not only succors. And as Aristotle reports in several places, it is a very great sign of liberality to come forward with a benefit before being asked.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final lines of Dante Alighieri's Paradiso, specifically focusing on the resolution of the poet's vision and the limitations of human understanding when faced with the Divine.</meta>

313                                PARADISO

->The power failed me: Love—that is, the Holy Spirit, which moves the sun and the other stars—that is, all creatures—to love their Creator, turned my will—that is, my volition—to my desire—that is, He caused another will to come to my desire. And since I was unable to fulfill my desire, which was to contemplate the Trinity in perfection, the Holy Spirit turned me toward wanting that which I was capable of wanting. And it is certainly a fitting conclusion to such a great work, because in a single sentence it concludes many things. First, it demonstrates that although the human mind may be bold in its wish to know everything, nevertheless, each person ought to be content with as much light as Divine Grace provides. Furthermore, it admonishes the reader not to judge the excellence of God by the author's words; for he who is finite cannot, even in the smallest part, comprehend the infinite.</note>original: "lō" (longitudo/infinite)</note><-

<summary>This concluding commentary on Dante's Paradiso explains how the Holy Spirit aligns human will with Divine love and warns that human language and intellect are ultimately insufficient to grasp the infinite nature of God.</summary>
<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Paradiso, Holy Spirit, Divine Will, Trinity, human limitation, Divine Grace, theology</keywords>

Which was the thunderbolt that struck me down
Which, having been moved by a sweet smile
Stays far away and then remains dark
Because the spirit does not find reassurance
Thus Love has never dwelled in the midst of the Alps
In the valleys of the river <note>Likely the Arno river, flowing through Florence.</note>
Along which I have always been under your power
Here I live and die as you see me
Thanks to a fierce light
Which, flashing, leads the way to my death.
Alas, no ladies here, no certain groan;
I see no one who grieves for my ill,
If she does not care for me
One can never have help from others.
And these banished ones from your court,
Lord <note>Addressing Love/Cupid as a feudal lord.</note>, she does not care for the blow of your arrow;
Having made of pride a shield for her breast
Such that every arrow there ends its course;
For the armored heart is bitten by nothing.
O my mountain song, you go your way;
Perhaps you will see Florence, my land,
Which strikes me, being out of her mind,
Void of peace and naked of pity;
If you enter within her, go saying: "Now
 
I can no longer make war against my lord;
From where I come, a chain binds him,
Such that your cruelty may bend;
For he has no way to return to freedom."</note>

<summary>The poet laments his exile and the cruelty of a 'stony' lady, personifying his song as a messenger to be sent back to his home city of Florence. He describes his emotional state as a living death, trapped between the harshness of the mountains and the pride of his beloved.</summary>
<keywords>exile, Florence, Love as Lord, mountain song, unrequited love, pride, Arno river</keywords>

# On the Authority and Office of the Notary

In this present public instrument <note>A formal legal document drawn up by a notary</note>, let it be known to all who shall see or read it, that in the year of our Lord's Nativity <unclear>16XX</unclear>, on the <unclear>tenth</unclear> day of the month of October.

<margin>The witness was present</margin>

The illustrious and most excellent Lord <insert>Governor of the Province</insert>, sitting in his tribunal for the administration of justice, has decreed and ordered that the following regulations be observed by all <term>notaries</term> <note>Legal professionals authorized to certify documents and contracts</note> within this jurisdiction.

<column-break/>

Firstly, that no one shall dare to exercise the office of the notary without first having been examined and approved by the College. <gloss>This refers to the professional guild of notaries</gloss>. 

Furthermore, it is commanded that:
*   All records must be kept in a secure place.
*   The <term>protocol</term> <note>The original register of notarial acts</note> must be written clearly.
*   Fees shall not exceed the established <term>tariff</term> <note>A fixed price list for legal services</note>.

<margin>Penalty of ten gold scudi</margin>

Whoever shall act to the contrary shall incur the indignation of the law and the aforementioned fine. This was done and enacted in the presence of the witnesses called for this purpose.

<summary>This document outlines the legal requirements and professional standards for notaries under the authority of a provincial governor, emphasizing the need for official certification and the proper maintenance of records.</summary>
<keywords>notary, legal regulations, professional guild, judicial decree, administrative law, Italy</keywords>
